_description: Operational Workflows corpus - archived from the public site 2026-09-05. 124 canonical journeys whose derived product surface is `operational` (src/canonical/surface.ts). Records are verbatim from production/canonical-dump.json, the validator-generated projection of the hand-authored TypeScript in src/canonical/*.ts, which remains the authoritative source (see sourceMap). See README.md.

records.name: Work created → routing → assignment
records.purpose: Get new work into the smallest responsibility scope that is genuinely valid, and refuse to invent one where the policy is silent.

entity.scope: the individual work item - a case, lead, opportunity, task or request
entity.note: One item, one active routing. A duplicate routing event is not a second assignment, and treating it as one produces two people doing the same work differently.

distinctFrom.because: This decides where the work belongs. OWN-52 decides whether the person it landed on has taken it, which is a different state and frequently a different answer.

requires: a work item created or becoming actionable, of a type that requires someone to be responsible for it
insufficientAlone: a draft not yet submitted
a record created for reference with nothing to be done about it

nodes.asks: Does this item already have an active owner or queue?

branches.label: Already owned
branches.when: an active assignment exists on this item

branches.label: Unowned
branches.when: no active assignment exists

nodes.state: already owned; no second owner created
nodes.reEntry: a genuine ownership change is OWN-54's, not a re-route. A duplicate routing event resolves here rather than producing a rival assignment - unless a multi-owner model is explicitly defined for this work type, which is a policy statement rather than an assumption

nodes.does: Gather the routing inputs the policy actually uses: work type, geography, expertise, existing account relationship, current workload, priority, entitlement, language, business segment

nodes.asks: Does a deterministic valid route exist for this item?

branches.label: Route determined
branches.when: the routing rules resolve to a specific owner, team or queue

branches.label: No route
branches.when: the rules do not resolve, or no rule covers this case

nodes.does: Place the item in the fallback or shared queue the policy names, or raise it for manual routing, recording that no route resolved. No ordering or priority is invented here - where the policy is silent the work waits visibly rather than being sorted by a rule nobody wrote and nobody can review
Route to the resolved owner, team or queue, recording which inputs produced the decision - a routing that cannot explain itself cannot be corrected when it is systematically wrong

nodes.asks: Does this work need a named owner now?

branches.label: Named owner required
branches.when: the work cannot proceed, or its SLA cannot run, without a specific person responsible

branches.label: Queue ownership is enough
branches.when: the queue itself carries responsibility until the work reaches the point where a person picks it up

nodes.on: work needing a named owner
carries: the routing decision and the inputs behind it
any SLA already running, since assignment does not start the clock

nodes.state: queue ownership; no named owner yet
nodes.reEntry: reaching the point where a person is required opens assignment; the queue is an owner, recorded as one rather than as an empty field

guardrails: Where the routing rule is unknown, no priority logic is invented to stand in for it. The item goes to the fallback and says why.
The assignment reason and its inputs are preserved, so a route that is consistently wrong can be found.
One item does not acquire two active owners from duplicate routing events, unless a multi-owner model is explicitly defined for that work type.
records.reusableRule: Work should enter the smallest valid responsibility scope before execution begins.

records.name: Assignment → acceptance → active responsibility
records.purpose: Keep proposed responsibility and accepted responsibility as different states, so work nobody has taken is visible as such.

entity.scope: the work item plus this specific assignment of it
entity.note: Each assignment is its own record. A rejected one and the reassignment that follows are two facts, and the first is routing information worth keeping.

requires: an assignment naming a specific person as proposed owner
insufficientAlone: a notification delivered to that person, which is delivery and not agreement
the item appearing in their queue view

nodes.does: Record the state as ASSIGNED - proposed responsibility. Nothing that requires an active owner may proceed on this state, which is the entire reason it is distinct from the next one

nodes.asks: Does this work type require explicit acceptance?

branches.label: Acceptance required
branches.when: policy or the nature of the work means responsibility has to be taken rather than allocated

branches.label: Assignment is sufficient
branches.when: policy allocates this work type directly, and the owner is responsible on assignment

timeout.after: the acceptance SLA for this work type
timeout.reason: an assignment nobody has answered is not owned, and letting it sit unanswered is how work becomes invisible while appearing allocated

nodes.asks: What did the proposed owner do?

branches.label: Accepted
branches.when: they took responsibility

branches.label: Rejected
branches.when: they declined it

nodes.does: Capture why it was rejected. The reason is routing information - wrong expertise, wrong region, conflict of interest, capacity - and it is what stops the next route repeating the mistake
Invalidate anything the un-accepted assignment queued, so nothing goes out under an ownership that was never taken

nodes.on: an assignment that was not taken
carries: the rejection reason, so routing does not resolve to the same owner again
the SLA already running, which reassignment does not restart

nodes.asks: With the acceptance SLA passed, what does policy do?

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: policy raises unanswered assignments rather than moving them

branches.label: Reassign
branches.when: policy reroutes an assignment that was not answered in time

nodes.on: an assignment unanswered past its SLA
carries: who it was assigned to and when
the work's own SLA, which has been running throughout

nodes.does: Record ACTIVE_OWNERSHIP. From here the owner is answerable for the work, and the distinction from ASSIGNED is what makes that statement true rather than assumed

nodes.on: responsibility becoming active
carries: the assignment and how it was reached
everything the owner will need to actually continue

guardrails: Assigned is not accepted. A report counting assignments as owned work is counting proposals.
A notification delivered to an owner is not responsibility accepted. Delivery is a fact about a message.
Reassignment invalidates the previous owner's pending actions rather than leaving them to fire under an ownership that ended.
records.reusableRule: Assignment creates proposed responsibility; acceptance establishes active responsibility when acceptance is required.

records.name: Owner assignment → context transfer → work start
records.purpose: Give a new owner what they need to continue an existing obligation, rather than an entity with their name on it.

entity.scope: the business entity plus the owner now responsible for it
entity.note: The entity's history belongs to the entity, not to whoever currently holds it. Ownership changes what the record points at, never what it contains.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-52 establishes that someone has taken responsibility. This establishes that they can actually discharge it, which fails independently and more quietly.

requires: a valid ownership assignment taking effect on an entity with existing state

nodes.does: Assemble what the owner needs to continue: the current state, the open obligations, the deadlines running against them, decisions already taken, the history bearing on those decisions, pending dependencies, and anything promised to anyone

nodes.asks: Does that context include sensitive data this owner does not need?

branches.label: More than needed
branches.when: the history contains personal, health, financial or confidential detail beyond what the work requires

branches.label: Proportionate
branches.when: the context is what the work requires and no more

nodes.does: Transfer what the work requires and no more. A handover is not a reason to widen who can see something, and the fact that it moved with the case is not a justification anyone will accept later

nodes.asks: Does policy require the owner to acknowledge critical items?

branches.label: Acknowledgement required
branches.when: there are commitments or deadlines whose transfer has to be confirmed rather than assumed

branches.label: Not required
branches.when: the context transfers without a confirmation step

until: the owner acknowledges the critical items

timeout.reason: unacknowledged critical context is the state in which a deadline is missed by someone who did not know it existed

nodes.on: critical context left unacknowledged
carries: what was not acknowledged and what depends on it
the deadlines still running, which acknowledgement was never going to pause

nodes.does: The owner begins from the current authoritative state. The entity's lifecycle is not restarted, its history is not cleared, and the previous owners remain in the chain - a new owner is a continuation, not a first contact

nodes.state: owner working from current state with inherited context
nodes.reEntry: the next ownership change opens its own transfer

guardrails: A new owner does not restart the lifecycle. The obligation is older than their involvement in it.
Assignment appends to the ownership chain rather than overwriting who held it before.
Context transfer is proportionate. Sensitive detail does not travel simply because it was attached to the case.
records.reusableRule: Ownership becomes operationally useful only when the new owner inherits the context required to continue the existing obligation.

records.name: Ownership change → transfer obligations → continue
records.purpose: Move responsibility for an active entity without losing anything that was already owed, without letting the clock restart, and without rewriting who did what before the change.

entity.scope: the business entity, its previous owner and its next one
entity.note: Three parties in the record. The chain is what makes it possible to say who was responsible at the time something did or did not happen.

requires: a recorded change of owner on an entity with active obligations
insufficientAlone: a request to change ownership that nobody with authority has approved
an owner becoming unavailable, which is OWN-55's escalation and not a transfer

nodes.does: Record the previous owner, the next owner, the reason and the effective time, appended to the ownership chain - and in the same act leave every historical action, decision, payment, document, approval and obligation attributed exactly as it occurred. Preserving authorship is a property of how the change is written rather than a state the entity passes through, and it belongs here because everything after this point is tempted to rewrite it: a new owner appearing as the author of last year's approvals produces a record that is not merely wrong but actively misleading to anyone auditing it

Identify everything still open and everything that depends on who the owner is: tasks, commitments, deadlines, live escalations, follow-ups promised to people, decisions pending, access, responsibilities, pending approvals, notifications, billing and administrative contacts, assigned work, delegations and external representations. Every deadline carries across unchanged - a commitment made to someone outside the organisation does not move because we moved who holds it internally

Invalidate the previous owner's queued actions that they are clearly no longer authorised to take. An action scheduled under an ownership that has ended and delivered afterwards comes from someone who is not responsible any more, and neither the recipient nor the new owner will know that. Actions that may still be valid are not invalidated here - they are held and revalidated once the transfer completes

nodes.asks: Does the incoming owner have to accept the transfer?

branches.label: Acceptance required
branches.when: policy requires the new owner to take it rather than receive it

branches.label: Transfer is effective directly
branches.when: policy moves ownership without a confirmation step, or the cutover has already completed elsewhere

timeout.reason: an unanswered transfer leaves the entity between two owners, which is the one state in which nobody is responsible while the record says somebody is

nodes.asks: Did the incoming owner take it?

branches.label: Accepted
branches.when: they accepted the transfer

branches.label: Declined
branches.when: they declined it

nodes.asks: The transfer did not complete - what does policy provide?

branches.label: A fallback owner
branches.when: policy names a fallback for failed transfers

branches.label: No fallback
branches.when: no fallback is defined

nodes.does: Assign the fallback owner and record that the intended transfer failed, so the fallback is visible as a fallback rather than as the original plan

Take each owner-dependent item from the inventory in turn - access, responsibilities, pending approvals, notifications, billing and administrative contacts, assigned work, delegations, external representations - and establish what it actually attaches to

nodes.asks: Does this dependency belong to the entity or to the person who owned it?

branches.label: To the entity
branches.when: it exists because the entity has an owner rather than because of who that owner was

branches.label: To the previous owner personally
branches.when: it is theirs - a personal commitment, a personal obligation, an individually held right

nodes.does: Move it to the current owner. A billing contact, an administrative notification and an escalation path follow whoever is accountable now, because that is what they were always pointing at

Leave it with the previous owner. Contracts, payments and obligations frequently belong to the entity rather than to its owner, and just as frequently the reverse - each is evaluated rather than moved by default, because moving one wrongly transfers a liability nobody agreed to take on

nodes.asks: Is any pending action authorised only by the previous ownership state?

branches.label: There is
branches.when: an approval, an instruction or a scheduled change rests on the previous owner's authority

branches.label: There is not
branches.when: nothing outstanding depends on who the owner was

nodes.does: Hold it and revalidate before execution. An action approved by somebody who is no longer the owner is an authorisation whose basis has gone, and executing it applies a decision the current owner never made and may not have made

nodes.asks: Does any delegation depend on the previous owner's authority?

branches.label: One or more do
branches.when: delegations were granted by the previous owner out of authority they no longer hold

branches.label: None
branches.when: no live delegation derives from the previous owner

nodes.on: delegations derived from an authority that has changed hands
carries: the delegations, their scope and the authority they were granted from
the explicit fact that a delegation cannot outlive the authority it borrowed, and that only delegation-derived rights are removed

nodes.on: a transfer that failed with no fallback
carries: the entity, its open obligations and their unchanged deadlines
the explicit fact that it currently has no valid owner - which is a state, not an empty field

nodes.on: ownership successfully moved
carries: the full obligation inventory with original deadlines intact
the ownership chain, so the new owner can see what was decided before they arrived
suppresses: every action still queued under the previous ownership

guardrails: A transfer never resets an inherited deadline or commitment. Only an explicit renegotiation of the obligation itself does that, and that is a different event with a different record.
Stale actions from the former owner do not execute after the transfer.
The historical owner chain is preserved in full.
Work is never silently orphaned. A failed transfer escalates rather than leaving a null owner.
An ownership change is not a rewrite of historical attribution: past actions, decisions, payments, documents and approvals stay attributed to whoever performed them.
Pending responsibilities are never transferred blindly; each is evaluated for whether it follows the entity or the person.
Contracts and financial obligations may belong to the entity rather than to its owner and are evaluated separately.
records.reusableRule: Ownership changes who is responsible for an obligation; they do not create a new obligation or reset its history.

records.name: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
records.purpose: Move a blocker up to the level that can clear it, without the original owner putting the work down by raising it.

entity.scope: the work item plus its ownership chain
entity.note: Escalation attaches to the chain rather than replacing it. Who escalated, to whom, and whether ownership moved are three separate facts.

distinctFrom.because: Escalation is usually a request for a decision, not a handover. Where it does move ownership, it hands to OWN-54 to do that properly rather than doing it as a side effect.

requires: a defined escalation condition: an SLA breached or at risk, an authority limit reached, a severity threshold crossed, a blocker the owner cannot clear, repeated failed resolution, or an explicit requirement to escalate
insufficientAlone: an owner finding the work difficult
elapsed time with no defined SLA behind it

nodes.does: Capture why it is escalating and the current context, so the higher authority is deciding rather than re-discovering the case

nodes.asks: Does policy define a valid escalation destination for this?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: an escalation path exists for this work type and condition

branches.label: Undefined
branches.when: no escalation path covers this case

nodes.on: an escalation with no defined destination
carries: the escalation reason and everything gathered
the fact that no path was invented to route it, which is why a person is being asked

nodes.asks: Does escalating transfer ownership, or ask for a decision?

branches.label: Ownership moves
branches.when: policy says the higher authority takes the work rather than advising on it

branches.label: Decision or support only
branches.when: the original owner stays responsible and needs a decision, an authority, or help

nodes.on: an escalation that genuinely moves ownership
carries: the escalation reason as the transfer reason
the open obligations, whose deadlines the transfer does not reset

nodes.does: Record that the original owner remains responsible while the higher authority is asked for a decision or support. Escalating is not putting the work down, and the record has to say so or the case falls between two people who each believe the other has it

timeout.after: the escalation SLA at this level
timeout.reason: an escalation that produces nothing is itself a blocker, and it is the one the original owner cannot escalate around

nodes.asks: What did the higher authority produce?

branches.label: Unblocked, work continues
branches.when: the decision or support clears the blocker and the work goes on

branches.label: Resolved outright
branches.when: the higher authority's decision closes the work itself

nodes.state: blocker cleared; the original owner continues
nodes.reEntry: nothing is handed back, because nothing was handed over - the owner has been responsible throughout and now has what they were missing

nodes.state: resolved at the escalated level
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence is a new escalation, judged with this one in the history

nodes.asks: Is there a further escalation level that has not been used?

branches.label: Level remains
branches.when: the policy's ladder has another rung

branches.label: Ladder exhausted
branches.when: every defined level has been tried

nodes.does: Escalate one level further and record the level. The ladder is walked once - a loop that keeps re-escalating to the same place is how an unresolvable case stays busy without moving

nodes.on: work outliving the whole escalation ladder
carries: every level tried, when, and what came back
the original blocker, still unresolved

guardrails: Escalation is not abandonment. Unless ownership explicitly transfers, the original owner remains responsible throughout.
The escalation path comes from policy. Where none is defined, none is invented.
Repeated escalation is bounded by the ladder rather than by patience.

An exhausted ladder closes as an operational exception with no customer-facing message. The person on the other end of the work is owed an outcome from whoever picks it up, not a notification that our escalation ran out.

Escalation is an internal operational state throughout. Reaching a level creates no customer communication by itself; a message goes out only where a separate communication obligation exists for it, and an internal delay is not news about what the customer wants.
records.reusableRule: Escalation moves unresolved work to the level capable of resolving the specific blocker without losing existing responsibility context.

records.name: Approval request → review → approve, reject or request changes
records.purpose: Bind an approval to the exact version reviewed, and keep approving separate from doing.

entity.scope: the approval request, bound to one specific version of the subject
entity.note: The version binding is the mechanism. An approval attached to an entity rather than a version authorises whatever that entity becomes afterwards. Three identities are kept distinct: the requester (who submitted the version for review), the executor (who acts on the approval once granted, via h.execute), and the approver (who decides). This journey's own purpose - keep approving separate from doing - requires the approver to be a different identity from the requester specifically; it says nothing about the executor, who is routinely the requester acting on their own now-approved request.

distinctFrom.because: This is one decision by one authority. OWN-57 exists because combining several decisions requires an aggregation policy that this journey never has to consult.

requires: a request of a type requiring approval, with an identifiable subject version
insufficientAlone: a draft still being edited, which has no stable version to review

nodes.does: Create the approval request bound to the exact version of the subject under review, recording the requester's own identity alongside it so eligibility can exclude them from acting as approver on this same request, and record the state as PENDING_REVIEW. Requested is not approved, and until this resolves nothing downstream may act as though it were

timeout.reason: nothing is approved by the passage of time, so the deadline produces an escalation or an expiry and never a default yes

nodes.asks: What did the reviewer decide, and is the reviewer eligible to decide it?

branches.label: APPROVED
branches.when: the reviewed version is approved by a reviewer whose identity differs from this request's own requester

branches.label: Self-approval attempted
branches.when: the acting reviewer is the same identity as this request's own requester - not eligible to approve their own request, whatever the decision they recorded

branches.label: REJECTED
branches.when: the reviewed version is rejected

branches.label: CHANGES_REQUESTED
branches.when: the reviewer wants a different version

nodes.does: Record the approval against the exact version reviewed, with who approved it and when. This authorises that version and nothing else

nodes.on: an approved version becoming authorised to proceed
carries: the approved version identifier, which execution must check it is still acting on
the approval record, so an internal yes is not confused with an external acceptance

nodes.on: a rejected approval outcome, including a blocked self-approval attempt
carries: the rejection reason - a content rejection or, for a blocked self-approval attempt, that no eligible review occurred at all
the exact version rejected, which must not later execute

nodes.does: Close this request against this version. A revised subject is a different version and needs its own request - carrying this one forward would approve something nobody read

nodes.state: changes requested; this request closed against this version
nodes.reEntry: a revised version submits a new request. This one does not approve it, whatever the revision turns out to contain

nodes.asks: With the approval SLA passed, what does policy do?

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: policy escalates unreviewed approvals to a higher or alternative authority

branches.label: Expire
branches.when: policy expires the request rather than escalating it

nodes.on: an approval left unreviewed past its SLA
carries: the request and the version awaiting review
how long it has been waiting

nodes.state: expired unreviewed; nothing approved
nodes.reEntry: a new request may be raised against the same or a newer version - the expiry authorises nothing, which is the point of expiring rather than defaulting

guardrails: Requested is not approved. The pending state exists so nothing can quietly proceed on the request itself.
Approval is not execution. It authorises an action that still has to happen and be recorded separately.
The approval names the exact version reviewed. An approval without a version is an authorisation with no boundary.

The requester cannot approve their own request - a decision recorded by the requester against their own request is treated as a blocked self-approval, never as a valid APPROVED or REJECTED outcome, regardless of what the requester themselves recorded.
records.reusableRule: Approval authorizes a specific reviewed state; it should not silently authorize materially different future states.

records.name: Multi-party approval → aggregate required decisions → authorised or blocked
records.purpose: Combine several genuinely independent approval decisions strictly according to the governing policy, and refuse to proceed where no policy defines how.

entity.scope: the approval package, the action and subject version it authorises, and each authority's individual decision
entity.note: Each decision is its own record against its own version. Aggregation reads them; it never replaces them. Several people holding access is not multi-party authorization - the requirement is that distinct authorities approve the same specific thing.

requires: a request that a rule requires more than one independent authority to authorise, with an identifiable action and subject version
insufficientAlone: several people holding administrative access, which means each of them can act alone

nodes.asks: Is the aggregation policy defined for this decision?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: policy states who must decide, in what order if any, what threshold applies, and what constitutes a complete decision set

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: no policy states how these decisions combine

nodes.on: multi-party approval with no governing aggregation policy
carries: the request, the version and the approvers involved

the explicit fact that no majority, quorum, unanimity, threshold or tie-break rule was assumed in order to proceed, and that no assumption was made about which authorities count as independent - without that, one person approving through two roles satisfies a two-person rule and nobody can see that they did
suppresses: any execution that depends on this authorisation

nodes.asks: Are the independence rules between the required authorities defined?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: the policy states what makes two authorities distinct for this decision

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: nothing states what independence means here

nodes.does: Build the approval graph from the policy - parallel, sequential, or whatever structure it defines - together with the threshold the policy sets, and bind the package to the exact action and subject version it authorises. Record which policy defined it, so the aggregation can be explained and audited rather than merely trusted

until: changes are requested by any approver
the action or subject version changes underneath the package

timeout.after: the approval SLA for the package
timeout.reason: a partial decision set is not an authorisation, and waiting longer does not turn it into one

nodes.on: a decision set left incomplete past its SLA
carries: which decisions are outstanding and from whom
how long the package has been open

nodes.asks: What does the policy say about the decisions received?

branches.label: Blocking rejection
branches.when: a rejection that the policy defines as blocking has been recorded

branches.label: Changes requested
branches.when: an approver requires a different version

branches.label: The action or version changed underneath the package
branches.when: what is being authorised is no longer what the collected decisions were given against

branches.label: Required set satisfied
branches.when: the policy's threshold and condition for a complete decision set are met

nodes.does: Re-evaluate the collected decisions against the changed action and version, and discard any that no longer apply. Approvals bind to a version - an approval given for one amount does not carry to a larger one, and carrying it forward is how a threshold gets met for something nobody approved

Verify each counted decision came from a genuinely distinct authority under the policy's independence rules. The same person approving through two roles is one authority counted twice, and it is by far the most common way a two-person rule is satisfied by one person

nodes.asks: Are the counted decisions genuinely independent?

branches.label: Independent
branches.when: each counted decision comes from a distinct authority under the policy's rules

branches.label: Not independent
branches.when: two or more counted decisions resolve to the same authority

nodes.does: Record that the threshold was not genuinely met, naming the duplicate authority, and keep waiting. The count looked satisfied and was not, and saying which decisions collapsed is what lets somebody find a genuinely independent approver rather than re-reading the same one
Record the authorisation as blocked, naming the rejection that blocked it. One approval among several is never read as approval by all required parties

nodes.state: authorisation blocked by a decision the policy treats as blocking
nodes.reEntry: a revised version may be submitted where the policy permits it; the blocking decision stays in the record either way

nodes.does: Identify which decisions already given the revision actually invalidates. Only those are re-opened - an approver whose basis has not changed is not asked to approve the same thing twice, which is how approval fatigue starts

nodes.state: revision required; affected decisions re-opened, unaffected ones retained
nodes.reEntry: the revised version enters as its own package with the retained decisions carried forward

nodes.does: Record AUTHORIZED, naming which decisions satisfied which part of the policy, which authority each came from and the exact action and version they authorised - so that what authorised this can be reconstructed without inferring it, and so a changed action needs the threshold met again

nodes.on: the governing policy's decision set being satisfied
carries: the authorised version and the decision set behind it
the fact that this is internal authorisation, which is not a counterparty's acceptance of anything

guardrails: Aggregation logic comes from the governing policy. Majority, unanimity, quorum, tie-breaks and any n-of-m rule are never inferred, and where none is defined the journey stops rather than choosing one.
One approval is not approval by all required parties.
Sequential dependencies are respected where the policy defines them.
A materially revised subject re-opens the decisions whose basis it changed, and only those.
Multiple administrators are not multi-party authorization.
The same authority is never counted twice where independence is required.
Collected decisions bind to the same action and version; a changed action re-opens the threshold.
records.reusableRule: Multi-party authorization is complete only when the governing decision policy says the required decision set has been satisfied.

records.name: Material change after approval → impact check → re-approval or continue
records.purpose: Work out whether an approval still covers what the subject has become, and re-open only the decisions whose basis stopped being true.

entity.scope: the approved subject, its version history and the approvals bound to those versions
entity.note: Approvals are bound to versions, which is what makes this question answerable at all. Without the binding there is nothing to compare the current state against.

requires: a change to a subject that already carries an approval, before that approval has been fully executed or the work completed
insufficientAlone: a cosmetic change to the subject that touches nothing the approval rested on
a change made after execution, which is a new subject rather than a changed one

nodes.does: Compare the approved version with the current one and establish exactly what changed - value, scope, quantity, discount, destination, risk profile, commercial terms, a critical configuration, or something none of those cover

nodes.asks: Does policy define what counts as material for this subject?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: a materiality rule exists for this kind of subject and change

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: no rule says whether this change matters

nodes.on: a change whose materiality no policy defines
carries: both versions and the difference between them
the existing approvals, held rather than either invalidated or trusted
suppresses: execution of the affected parts while materiality is undetermined

nodes.asks: Is the change material to the basis on which approval was given?

branches.label: Not material
branches.when: the change does not touch anything the approval decision rested on

branches.label: Material
branches.when: the change alters something an approver relied on

nodes.state: existing approval remains valid
nodes.reEntry: a further change is compared against the same approved version - minor edits accumulating into a material difference is exactly what this comparison is for

nodes.does: Identify which approvals rested on the part that changed. An unrelated approval on the same subject is untouched - invalidating everything on every material change teaches approvers that re-approval is routine, which is how it stops being read
Invalidate those approvals, keeping them in the history as approvals that were validly given and then superseded. The original decision is not deleted; it stops applying

nodes.asks: Is execution pending that would now proceed without valid approval?

branches.label: Unsafe execution pending
branches.when: something is scheduled or in flight that the invalidated approval was authorising

branches.label: Nothing in flight
branches.when: no execution depends on the invalidated approvals yet

nodes.does: Hold the affected execution. Only the affected part - holding everything because one term changed is the same error as invalidating every approval
Request re-approval, scoped to the authorities whose basis actually changed rather than to everyone who approved the original

timeout.reason: held execution is not free - it is a commitment sitting still - so an unanswered re-approval escalates rather than waiting indefinitely

nodes.on: re-approval left outstanding past its SLA with execution held
carries: what is held and why
which authorities are outstanding

nodes.asks: Was the changed version approved?

branches.label: Re-approved
branches.when: the required authorities approved the current version

branches.label: Not approved
branches.when: the changed version was rejected

nodes.state: current version approved; held execution may resume
nodes.reEntry: any further change is compared against this newly approved version

nodes.on: a changed version failing re-approval
carries: the rejection reason and the version rejected
the previously approved version, which is still in the history and may be the thing to return to

guardrails: A minor edit does not reset every approval. Only those whose decision basis stopped being true are invalidated.
Materiality is defined by policy, not decided here. Where no rule exists the journey stops and asks.
The approval history is preserved. A superseded approval is recorded as superseded, not removed.
Re-approval is scoped to the affected authority wherever the policy allows it.
records.reusableRule: Material changes should invalidate only the approvals whose original decision assumptions are no longer true.

records.name: Approval rejected → revision eligibility → resubmit or close
records.purpose: Keep rejection from being either a dead end by default or a retry loop, and make sure a rejected version cannot quietly execute later.

entity.scope: the rejected approval request and the exact subject version it rejected
entity.note: The rejection belongs to a version. A later version is a different subject and is judged on its own; this one stays rejected permanently.

requires: a recorded rejection against a specific approval request and subject version

nodes.does: Capture the rejection reason against the exact version rejected, appended. The history of what was rejected and why is what makes an unchanged resubmission recognisable as one

Mark the rejected version as not executable. A rejected version executing later because something downstream read the subject and not the decision is the quietest failure in this category and the hardest to notice afterwards

nodes.asks: Does policy allow this to be revised and resubmitted?

branches.label: Revision permitted
branches.when: policy provides a revision path for this rejection reason

branches.label: Terminal
branches.when: the rejection reason ends it - a structural ineligibility, a prohibition, a decision that is not revisable

nodes.state: rejected, no revision path
nodes.reEntry: none - what would have to change is the rule or the circumstances, and either of those produces a new request rather than a revision of this one

nodes.does: Identify what would actually have to change, taken from the rejection reason rather than left to the requester to guess

timeout.reason: a rejected request left open indefinitely is a commitment nobody is tracking and a queue entry nobody will clear

nodes.state: revision window closed; request expired
nodes.reEntry: a genuinely new request may be raised later, with this rejection in its history

nodes.asks: Does the revision materially address what was rejected?

branches.label: Addressed
branches.when: the revision changes what the rejection was about

branches.label: Unchanged in substance
branches.when: the same version, or a change that does not touch the rejection reason

nodes.state: resubmission refused; nothing material changed
nodes.reEntry: a real revision re-opens this. Sending the same thing back is not a revision, and letting it through is how approval becomes a queue people learn to clear rather than read

nodes.does: Create the new reviewable version, linked to the rejected one and its reason, so the reviewer can see what was asked for and what changed

nodes.on: a genuine revision of a rejected subject
carries: the new version and its link to the rejected one
the original rejection reason, so the review is of the correction rather than of the subject from scratch

guardrails: A rejected version is marked unexecutable and never runs later.
An unchanged resubmission is refused. Repetition is not a revision.
The rejection history is preserved and travels with the revised version.
records.reusableRule: A rejected decision can re-enter approval only through a valid revision path when policy permits it.

records.name: Decision authority change → revalidate pending decisions → transfer or continue
records.purpose: Re-evaluate decisions against who is actually authorised now, without unapproving history or blindly moving what is pending.

entity.scope: the decision process plus the authority holders whose scope changed
entity.note: Pending decisions and completed ones are affected differently by the same event, which is why they are inventoried separately here.

distinctFrom.because: Ownership is who does the work; authority is who may decide. They change independently, and an approver leaving does not move a case any more than a case moving changes who may approve it.

requires: a change to who holds decision authority: an approver leaving, a role change, authority revoked, organisational responsibility moving, an approval limit changing, or a delegation beginning or ending
insufficientAlone: an approver being temporarily unavailable, which is a routing question and not a change of authority
a change to who does the work, which is OWN-54's ownership

nodes.does: Identify what this touches: decisions still pending, decisions already made, deadlines running, and the exact scope of authority that changed. The scope matters - a lowered approval limit affects a different set from a departure
Invalidate anything queued that the former authority is no longer entitled to do, so a decision does not arrive from someone who has stopped being able to make it

nodes.asks: Are pending decisions now sitting with an authority that is no longer valid?

branches.label: Pending decisions stranded
branches.when: at least one open decision is assigned to an authority that can no longer make it

branches.label: Nothing pending affected
branches.when: no open decision depends on the changed authority

nodes.asks: Does a valid alternative authority exist?

branches.label: Valid authority available
branches.when: someone else holds the authority within the required scope

branches.label: None
branches.when: no valid authority currently exists for this decision

nodes.does: Reassign the pending decision, preserving the original request, the exact version under review and the deadline. The clock does not restart because we changed who is reading it - the requester's wait is not reset by our reorganisation

nodes.on: a decision with no currently valid authority
carries: the pending decisions and their unchanged deadlines
the explicit fact that execution requiring this approval remains blocked, rather than proceeding because nobody can say no
suppresses: any execution that depends on the missing authorisation

nodes.asks: Do decisions already made remain valid under the governing policy?

branches.label: Remain valid
branches.when: policy holds that a decision validly made stays made - the ordinary case

branches.label: Revalidation required
branches.when: policy specifies that this kind of authority change invalidates decisions already given

branches.label: Policy unclear
branches.when: no rule states whether these decisions survive the change

nodes.state: completed decisions retained; pending ones reassigned where needed
nodes.reEntry: an approver leaving does not retroactively unapprove what they approved while they held the authority to approve it

nodes.does: Identify which completed decisions this change actually invalidates, and only those. A new authority does not inherit the ability to reopen decisions outside their scope simply by arriving

nodes.on: decisions invalidated by an authority change rather than by a change to the subject
carries: the unchanged subject version, which is what makes this a re-approval rather than a revision
the original request history and its SLA, neither of which the authority change resets

nodes.on: an authority change whose effect on completed decisions no policy defines
carries: the completed decisions in question and who made them
the fact that they have been neither retained nor invalidated pending a ruling

guardrails: An approver's departure does not automatically invalidate every historical approval they gave.
A new authority does not inherit the ability to alter completed decisions outside what policy grants them.
An authority change does not reset the original request history or its SLA unless policy explicitly says so.
Where no valid authority exists, execution requiring approval stays blocked rather than proceeding because nobody is left to refuse it.
records.reusableRule: When decision authority changes, pending and completed decisions must be re-evaluated according to authority validity rather than blindly transferred or discarded.

records.name: Expiry reached → validate current state → expire, extend or replace
records.purpose: Check what the entity actually is at the moment the expiry fires, before applying anything the timer was written to apply.

entity.scope: the time-bound entity and the specific version of it the timer was scheduled against
entity.note: The version binding is the point. A timer scheduled against one version firing against another is the defining failure of scheduled work.

requires: an authoritative expiry moment arriving for a time-bound entity

nodes.does: Re-read the entity's current authoritative version at this moment. The timer holds the expiry that was true when it was written, which is not necessarily the expiry that is true now

nodes.asks: What does the entity's current version say?

branches.label: Already renewed or replaced
branches.when: the entity moved on and this expiry no longer describes it

branches.label: A later extension exists
branches.when: an authoritative extension moved the expiry past this moment

branches.label: Still valid, expiry applies
branches.when: the current version still carries this expiry

nodes.state: stale expiry suppressed; the entity had already moved
nodes.reEntry: the entity's current expiry, whatever it now is, has its own execution

nodes.does: Adopt the new authoritative expiry and invalidate this one. An older timer never overrides a later extension - the extension was a decision and the timer is only a memory of an earlier one

nodes.state: expiry superseded by an extension
nodes.reEntry: the new expiry executes on its own terms when it arrives

nodes.does: Transition the entity to EXPIRED, keeping the record of the period during which it was valid. Expired is a new state on the same entity, not the erasure of the old one. The transition is applied idempotently, so a redelivered job cannot expire it twice

Apply the consequences defined for this entity type - access ending, a reservation released, a benefit becoming unavailable, a credential invalid, renewal no longer possible, requalification required. The consequence belongs to the entity rather than to expiry in general, and expiring is not the same as revoking

nodes.on: an entity having expired
carries: the expired entity and the consequences applied
its validity history, which is what any later re-entry is judged against

guardrails: An old scheduled expiry never overrides a later extension.
The expired state preserves the previous validity history rather than replacing it.
Expiry consequences are entity-specific. Expired is not revoked, and neither is a synonym for the other.
The transition is idempotent; a redelivered job applies it once or not at all.
records.reusableRule: Expiry must be evaluated against the entity's current authoritative version at the moment the transition executes.

records.name: Temporary exception → validity window → revert or formalise
records.purpose: Stop an exception granted for a reason from becoming a permanent state nobody remembers deciding on.

entity.scope: the exception itself - its scope, the authority that granted it and the state it departs from
entity.note: Each grant and each extension is its own record. An exception extended four times is a different fact from one granted once, and only separate records make that countable.

distinctFrom.because: An exception departs from a standing policy and carries an authority who granted it. A temporary state is a lifecycle position; it does not necessarily contradict anything.

requires: an exception granted by someone with authority to grant it, against a standing policy or state
insufficientAlone: a setting that differs from policy with no recorded authority behind it, which is configuration drift rather than an exception

nodes.does: Record the exception type, who authorised it, the reason, its scope, when it starts, and when it expires or is reviewed. An exception with no end date is a policy change that nobody approved as one

until: the condition that justified the exception is resolved
a permanent decision is made about it

timeout.after: the exception's recorded expiry or review date
timeout.reason: the review is the mechanism - an exception that is never revisited is the one that becomes permanent by default

nodes.asks: What resolved it?

branches.label: No longer required
branches.when: the condition that justified the exception has gone

branches.label: Should become permanent
branches.when: the exception turned out to describe how things should work

nodes.on: an exception that should become the rule
carries: the exception, its authority and how long it ran
the fact that formalising it is a permanent change and belongs in an approval rather than in another extension

nodes.asks: At the review point, does an authoritative extension exist?

branches.label: Extended
branches.when: someone with authority extended it, on the record

branches.label: Not extended
branches.when: no extension exists

nodes.does: Adopt the extension as its own record, appended to the extension history, and close this instance. Each extension is counted separately rather than absorbed into one long-running exception - the count is what makes a temporary state that has run for two years visible as one

nodes.state: exception extended; a new window opens as its own instance
nodes.reEntry: the extension is a new instance with a new review date, so the number of extensions is countable rather than hidden inside a single record

nodes.does: Revert to the standard state and mark the exception as no longer usable, so a stale process cannot keep relying on an exception that has ended

nodes.state: exception ended; standard state restored
nodes.reEntry: a new exception is granted on its own authority and its own reason

guardrails: A temporary exception is not indefinite permission. Its end is recorded when it is granted.
Extension history is preserved and countable. An exception extended repeatedly is visible as one.
An expired exception cannot be relied on by a stale process.
Making an exception permanent goes through approval, not through another extension.
records.reusableRule: Temporary exceptions require explicit scope and exit conditions so that exceptional access or policy does not silently become permanent.

records.name: Temporary state → explicit expiry → restore or transition
records.purpose: Give any time-bound state a defined ending, and revalidate before returning anything to what it was.

entity.scope: the entity plus the temporary state placed on it
entity.note: Temporary access, a temporary restriction, a temporary role, a temporary allocation or configuration all share this shape, and each carries its own exit rule.

requires: an entity entering a state that is intended to end

nodes.asks: Does the temporary state carry an explicit expiry or an explicit exit condition?

branches.label: Bounded
branches.when: an expiry time or a condition that ends it is defined

branches.label: Unbounded
branches.when: nothing says how or when it ends

nodes.on: a temporary state created with no ending
carries: the entity and the state placed on it
the fact that a time-bound state with no exit rule is an unmanaged permanent state, which is why this is raised rather than accepted

nodes.does: Record the temporary state, when it took effect, when it expires or what ends it, and the state it would return to

timeout.reason: expiry is the backstop for a condition that may never be met; without it the state has no ending at all

nodes.does: Record that the state ended by its exit condition rather than by expiry. A temporary access revoked early and one that lapsed are different facts about the same entity
Record that the state ended by reaching its expiry with the exit condition unmet

Re-read the entity's current version before returning it anywhere. The state it was going to return to may no longer exist, the entity may no longer be eligible for it, and the authority that granted the original may have ended during the temporary period

nodes.asks: Is the previous state still valid to return to?

branches.label: Still valid
branches.when: the previous state exists and the entity is still eligible for it

branches.label: No longer valid
branches.when: the previous state is gone, or eligibility for it has changed

nodes.does: Restore the previous state and clear the temporary one

nodes.state: temporary state ended; previous state restored
nodes.reEntry: a further temporary state carries its own ending

nodes.on: a temporary state ending with no valid state to return to
carries: the entity, the temporary state that ended and how it ended
the previous state, which is recorded as unavailable rather than silently applied

guardrails: A temporary state without an expiry or an exit condition is raised rather than created. That is the state this journey exists to prevent.
The previous state is not assumed safe to restore. Eligibility and authority can both change during the temporary period.
How the state ended - early or by expiry - is recorded, because the two mean different things about the entity.
records.reusableRule: Temporary states must define how they end; time-bound state without an exit rule is an unmanaged permanent state.

records.name: Reversible state → reversal window → confirm or restore
records.purpose: Undo a transition within its window while restoring only what is independently still valid.

entity.scope: the transition itself - what changed, when, and which of its side effects have already run
entity.note: The side-effect list is what makes a later reversal decidable. Without it, reversing is a guess about what the original transition set in motion.

requires: a transition that policy defines as reversible, with a reversal window
insufficientAlone: a change someone regrets, where no reversal policy exists

nodes.does: Record the previous state, the new state, whether reversal is eligible, its deadline, and which side effects have already executed. That last list is the one that matters - a reversal decided without it either restores too little or promises too much

timeout.reason: the window closing is the ordinary outcome, and after it the new state is simply the state

nodes.state: reversal window closed; the new state is now the normal state
nodes.reEntry: changing it now is a new transition with its own reversal window, not an undo of this one

nodes.asks: Have irreversible side effects already occurred?

branches.label: Something cannot be undone
branches.when: money moved, a message went out, an external system was told, a physical action happened

branches.label: Nothing irreversible
branches.when: everything the transition did can be safely unwound

nodes.on: a reversal request against a transition with irreversible effects
carries: the side effects that already ran and cannot be undone
the state the requester expected to return to, which correction has to reach forward rather than backward

nodes.does: Restore the previous state, and only the previous state. Consent that was withdrawn, credentials that were revoked, tokens that expired, integrations that were cancelled and journeys that were queued and are now obsolete are each judged on their own current validity. Reversing a transition does not rewind the world around it, and restoring an entity wholesale resurrects things that ended for reasons this reversal never addressed
Recalculate the dependent state against what is actually valid now, rather than replaying what was valid before the transition

nodes.asks: Could every dependent state be restored?

branches.label: Fully restored
branches.when: the previous state and everything depending on it are valid again

branches.label: Partially restored
branches.when: the primary state is back and some dependent state could not validly return

nodes.state: transition reversed; previous state fully restored
nodes.reEntry: a further transition on this entity carries its own window

nodes.state: partially restored; some dependent state did not validly return
nodes.reEntry: recorded as partial rather than presented as though nothing had happened - what did not come back is nameable, which is the only way anyone can ask for it

guardrails: Restoring an entity does not automatically restore withdrawn consent, revoked credentials, expired tokens, cancelled integrations or obsolete queued journeys. Each is evaluated on its own current validity.
Where irreversible side effects have run, the route is forward correction or compensation rather than restoration.
A partial restoration is recorded as partial.
records.reusableRule: State reversal restores only what remains valid and reversible; it does not rewind every side effect created by the original transition.

records.name: Expired state → re-entry eligibility → renew, requalify or remain expired
records.purpose: Decide how something expired can become valid again, through the mechanism that actually restores validity rather than by editing the expiry away.

entity.scope: the expired entity, kept distinct from any replacement created for it
entity.note: The expired entity and its replacement are two objects. That a credential was valid until March and that a credential is valid now are different facts, and merging them destroys both.

requires: an action attempted against an expired entity, or an opportunity to restore it arising

nodes.does: Establish what expiry actually did to this entity. Some expiries suspend, some invalidate, some end a relationship outright, and the route back differs for each - reading them all as the same lapse is what produces a renewal flow that cannot renew anything

nodes.asks: Which mechanism restores validity here?

branches.label: Direct renewal
branches.when: the governing system supports renewing this entity in place

branches.label: Requalification
branches.when: validity depends on conditions that must be demonstrated again

branches.label: Replacement
branches.when: the expired entity cannot become valid and a new one has to be issued

branches.label: Prohibited
branches.when: nothing restores validity - the expiry was terminal by design

nodes.on: an expired entity the governing system can renew in place
carries: the entity and its expired validity period
the fact that renewal creates a new validity rather than deleting the gap

nodes.on: validity depending on conditions that have to be demonstrated again
carries: what expired and why it needs requalification
the previous qualification history, which is context rather than a shortcut

nodes.does: Create the replacement entity and keep the expired one as a distinct historical record. The two stay separately addressable, because questions asked later are about one or the other and almost never about both

nodes.state: replacement issued; expired entity retained as history
nodes.reEntry: the replacement carries its own validity and its own expiry

nodes.state: expired, no route back
nodes.reEntry: none - what would have to change is the rule or the entity's circumstances, and either produces a new entity rather than reviving this one

guardrails: An expired entity is not made active by editing its expiry timestamp, unless the governing system explicitly supports extension as a mechanism.
The expired entity and its replacement remain distinguishable.
The expired validity period is preserved. The gap during which nothing was valid is itself a fact.
records.reusableRule: Re-entry after expiry should follow the business mechanism that restores validity rather than silently undoing the expiry.

records.name: Scheduled future transition → validate at execution → apply, cancel or recalculate
records.purpose: Treat a scheduled transition as an intention recorded in the past, and check it against the present before applying it.

entity.scope: the scheduled transition plus the target entity and the version it expected to find
entity.note: The expected version is the mechanism. Without it, execution has no way to tell whether the world moved underneath the schedule.

distinctFrom.because: An expiry is one specific scheduled transition with entity-specific consequences. This is the general mechanism, and every other scheduled change - a plan change at period end, a future cancellation, a scheduled restriction - runs through it.

requires: a state transition scheduled for a future moment against a specific entity

nodes.does: Persist the target entity, the state and version it is expected to be in, the target state, when it takes effect, and why it was scheduled. Recording the expected version is what makes execution-time validation possible at all - without it there is nothing to compare the present against

until: the schedule is replaced by a newer one

timeout.reason: reaching the effective time is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the schedule being withdrawn before it gets there

nodes.does: Invalidate this job. A cancelled or replaced schedule must not still fire - a replacement that leaves the original alive applies both, in whichever order the scheduler happens to run them

nodes.state: schedule cancelled or replaced before its effective moment
nodes.reEntry: the replacing schedule, if there is one, runs as its own instance

nodes.does: Re-read the entity's authoritative current state and version. The schedule is an intention recorded in the past, and this is the only moment at which it can be checked against the present

nodes.asks: Does the entity still match what the schedule expected?

branches.label: Matches
branches.when: the current version is the one the transition was written against

branches.label: Superseded
branches.when: a newer authoritative change has already moved the entity past this

branches.label: Assumptions changed
branches.when: the entity still exists in a comparable state but the reasoning behind the schedule no longer holds

nodes.state: stale transition suppressed; a newer change already applied
nodes.reEntry: an old schedule never overwrites a newer decision, whichever of the two the scheduler happens to reach first

nodes.on: a schedule whose underlying assumptions no longer hold
carries: the original schedule, its reason and the version it expected
the entity's actual current state, so the decision is made again rather than applied blindly

nodes.asks: Has this transition already been applied?

branches.label: Already applied
branches.when: a previous delivery of this same job already made the change

branches.label: Not yet applied
branches.when: the transition has not run

nodes.state: duplicate execution absorbed
nodes.reEntry: schedulers retry by design, so absorbing a redelivery is the normal case rather than an error path

nodes.does: Apply the transition idempotently, keyed so that a redelivery of the same job cannot apply it twice

nodes.state: scheduled transition applied against a validated current state
nodes.reEntry: a further scheduled change is its own intention with its own validation

guardrails: Every scheduled action validates at execution time rather than trusting the state it was written against.
An old scheduled transition never overwrites a newer authoritative change.
Cancelling or replacing a schedule invalidates the original job rather than leaving both alive.
Duplicate execution applies the transition once. Redelivery is expected, not exceptional.
records.reusableRule: Future transitions are intentions, not guaranteed outcomes; their validity must be rechecked when execution time arrives.

records.name: Entitlement grant → provision → verify availability
records.purpose: Hold the distance between a right being granted and the thing behind it actually working.

entity.scope: the entitlement plus the resource or capability being provisioned for it
entity.note: One provisioning run per entitlement, keyed idempotently. Retries and redeliveries are expected, and none of them may provision a second copy.

requires: an entitlement recorded as GRANTED with a scope that implies a resource

nodes.does: Create the provisioning action and record the state as PROVISIONING, keyed so that a redelivered event provisions once. A granted entitlement in PROVISIONING is not yet usable, and nothing downstream may present it as though it were

timeout.reason: a provisioning run that has neither succeeded nor failed within its SLA is a failure that has not reported itself, and treating silence as success is how a customer finds the gap first

nodes.asks: How did provisioning end?

branches.label: Succeeded
branches.when: the provisioning system reports success

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the provisioning system reports failure

nodes.asks: Does actual availability need to be verified?

branches.label: Verification matters
branches.when: the holder's ability to reach the capability is what the entitlement is for, and a reported success is not proof of it

branches.label: The provisioning record is authoritative
branches.when: the provisioning system is itself the source of truth for availability

nodes.does: Check that the capability is genuinely reachable by its holder. A provisioning API returning success is a statement about the API - whether anyone can use the thing is a separate question with its own answer

nodes.asks: Is it actually available?

branches.label: Available
branches.when: the capability is reachable

branches.label: Provisioned but unreachable
branches.when: the resource exists and the holder still cannot use it

nodes.state: ACTIVE; the right is granted, provisioned and usable
nodes.reEntry: a scope change re-opens provisioning for the delta rather than for the whole entitlement

nodes.on: a provisioned resource the holder cannot reach
carries: the entitlement, the provisioning result and what verification actually found
the fact that the grant is valid, so this is an access fault rather than an entitlement question

nodes.asks: What class of failure is this?

branches.label: Transient and retry-safe
branches.when: the failure is expected to clear and the retry budget has room

branches.label: Permanent, or the budget is spent
branches.when: retrying will not help, or has already been tried as often as the budget allows

nodes.does: Retry against a budget fixed at the first failure. The budget does not renew - that is the difference between a retry policy and a loop that provisions forever

nodes.on: provisioning that cannot be completed automatically
carries: the entitlement and what has been attempted
the fact that the customer holds a valid right they currently cannot use

guardrails: A granted entitlement is not a provisioned one. The grant is a business record; provisioning is a distributed operation that can fail on its own.
Provisioning success is not availability. Where the difference matters, availability is checked rather than assumed.
Provisioning is idempotent. Redelivery provisions once.
Retries are bounded by a budget fixed at the first failure.
records.reusableRule: A granted right becomes usable only after the required resource or capability is successfully provisioned and available.

records.name: Entitlement change → recalculate scope → expand, reduce or preserve
records.purpose: Apply only the difference between the old and new rights, rather than re-applying a whole scope over a working one.

entity.scope: the entitlement whose basis changed, and the delta between its previous and new scope
entity.note: The delta is the unit of work. Re-applying the full new scope reprovisions what already worked and revokes what should have survived, and the holder sees both as an outage.

requires: an authoritative change to the basis of an existing entitlement: a plan change, a role change, a contract amendment, a benefit or quantity or coverage change

nodes.does: Compare the previous scope, the new scope and the effective time, and derive the delta. What gets applied is the difference - a capability present in both scopes is not touched at all

nodes.asks: Which way did the scope move?

branches.label: Expanded only
branches.when: capabilities were added and none removed

branches.label: Reduced, or mixed
branches.when: at least one capability is no longer covered, whether or not others were added

nodes.does: Provision the newly granted capabilities, idempotently, and leave everything already working untouched

Apply any expansion, and identify precisely which capabilities are no longer covered. Historical data and resources created under the previous scope are not destroyed by a scope change - a reduction removes a right, not a record

nodes.asks: Do existing commitments or in-flight usage depend on what is being removed?

branches.label: Something depends on it
branches.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, a purchased benefit or an open transaction rests on the capability being removed

branches.label: Nothing depends on it
branches.when: the reduction affects only future use

nodes.on: a scope reduction with live commitments underneath it
carries: the capabilities being removed and their effective time
the commitments that depend on them, which are reconciled separately rather than cancelled by the scope change

nodes.does: Apply the reduction to future access only, idempotently. Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are two different decisions, and this one makes only the first

nodes.state: delta applied; unchanged capabilities untouched
nodes.reEntry: a further basis change is compared against the new scope

guardrails: A reduction in entitlement does not destroy historical data or resources created while the right was held.
Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are separate decisions made by separate journeys.
The delta is applied idempotently, so a redelivered change does not reprovision or re-revoke.
records.reusableRule: Entitlement changes should apply the difference between old and new rights without rewriting the history of what was previously valid.

records.name: Entitlement loss → revoke future capability → reconcile existing obligations
records.purpose: Stop future use of a right that has ended without cancelling what was validly created while it was held.

entity.scope: the entitlement that ended, plus the resources and commitments that depended on it
entity.note: Revocation stays scoped to this entitlement. A right held on another basis is untouched, and the record that this one existed remains.

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts a right that still exists and is designed to come back. This is the right ending, which is why it reconciles obligations rather than holding them.

requires: an authoritative end to a right: a plan downgrade, a contract termination, a role removal, a benefit expiry, an eligibility-linked revocation, or a policy decision

nodes.does: Determine when the loss actually takes effect - immediately, at period end, or on a future date. Assuming immediate is how someone loses what they have already paid for, and everything downstream depends on getting this right
Identify the capabilities affected, scoped to this entitlement alone. A lost role does not revoke rights the same person holds on a different basis

Prevent future use of the affected capabilities from the effective time, idempotently. The record that the entitlement existed and what was done under it is untouched - losing a right does not mean it was never held

nodes.asks: Do valid commitments exist that were created while the right was held?

branches.label: Commitments outstanding
branches.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, an already purchased benefit or an open transaction exists

branches.label: Nothing outstanding
branches.when: the right governed only future use

nodes.on: an entitlement ending with commitments still live under it
carries: each commitment and when it was created relative to the loss
the explicit fact that nothing has been cancelled - the reconciliation decides that on its own terms

nodes.asks: Does a provisioned resource need removing?

branches.label: Resource provisioned
branches.when: something was provisioned for this entitlement and is no longer authorised

branches.label: Nothing provisioned
branches.when: the right had no provisioned resource behind it

nodes.on: a provisioned resource whose entitlement has ended
carries: the resource and the effective loss time
the fact that removal is a capability question and not a data-deletion authorisation

nodes.state: future use revoked; history and commitments intact
nodes.reEntry: the right may be granted again on a new basis, which is a new entitlement rather than a revival of this one

guardrails: Losing an entitlement does not mean the entitlement never existed. The historical record stands.
Existing commitments are reconciled separately and are never cancelled automatically by the loss.
Revocation stays scoped to the affected entitlement.
Stopping future use is idempotent.
records.reusableRule: Losing a right prevents future unauthorized use but does not automatically erase commitments created while the right was valid.

records.name: Access request → authorization check → allow, deny or step up
records.purpose: Decide at the moment of the attempt whether this actor may take this action on this resource.

entity.scope: the individual access request - one actor, one action, one resource
entity.note: The decision belongs to the request. Allowing one action says nothing about the next, and a cached decision is re-checked against critical state that may have moved since.

distinctFrom.because: Approval is a business decision taken in advance about a subject. Authorization is a runtime decision taken at the moment of the attempt, and being approved for something does not authorise every action within it.

requires: an actor attempting a protected action on an identified resource
insufficientAlone: a successful authentication, which establishes who is asking and nothing about what they may do
holding an entitlement to the product the resource belongs to

nodes.does: Evaluate at execution time: the identity, the entitlement, the role and permission, the resource's own scope, the current security state, and the policy requirements for this specific action. A cached decision is re-checked against critical state, because the states that matter most are the ones that change fastest

nodes.asks: What does the current state permit?

branches.label: Fully authorized
branches.when: every required condition is satisfied for this actor, action and resource

branches.label: Authorized subject to stronger verification
branches.when: the conditions are met except for an assurance level this action requires

branches.label: Not authorized
branches.when: at least one required condition fails

nodes.state: ALLOW; this action on this resource, now
nodes.reEntry: the next attempt is decided again. Allowing one action never authorises the following one, however similar it looks

nodes.on: an action requiring an assurance level the current session does not hold
carries: the pending request, so it can resume rather than be retyped
the assurance level required and why this action requires it

nodes.does: Record the denial with its reason category - entitlement missing, permission missing, resource out of scope, security state blocking, or policy prohibition. A bare denial cannot be appealed, debugged, or distinguished from an outage

nodes.state: DENY, with a recorded reason category
nodes.reEntry: a change to any of the evaluated states makes the next attempt a new decision

guardrails: Entitlement to a product is not permission for every action within it.
Authentication success is not authorization. The two answer different questions.
A cached authorization respects current critical state changes rather than the state at the time it was cached.
Every denial carries a reason category.
records.reusableRule: Access should be granted only when the current actor, resource and action satisfy the required authorization conditions at execution time.

records.name: Credential issued → activate → use, expire or revoke
records.purpose: Run an access artifact through its own validity lifecycle, separately from the right it represents.

entity.scope: the individual credential - its id, owner, scope and validity
entity.note: A credential's validity is its own. It can be valid while the entitlement behind it has lapsed, and revoked while that entitlement is perfectly live.

distinctFrom.because: The entitlement is the right. The credential is an artifact that presents it. Treating the artifact as the right means revoking a token looks like removing a benefit.

requires: a credential issued with an owner, a scope and a validity

nodes.does: Store the credential id, owner, scope, issue time, validity, whether activation is required, and its status as ISSUED. Issued is not active, and nothing may present it as usable until it is

nodes.asks: Does this credential require activation before use?

branches.label: Activation required
branches.when: policy requires the holder to activate it

branches.label: Active on issue
branches.when: policy makes it usable as issued

until: the credential is revoked before activation

timeout.reason: an unactivated credential does not become active by waiting, and leaving it ISSUED indefinitely keeps a usable artifact alive that nobody ever claimed

nodes.asks: What happened during the activation window?

branches.label: Activated
branches.when: the holder activated it

branches.label: Revoked first
branches.when: a revocation arrived before activation

nodes.does: Expire the credential unactivated, recording that it was never claimed. An expired-unactivated credential and an expired-active one are different facts about how the artifact was used

nodes.state: EXPIRED, never activated
nodes.reEntry: a replacement credential is issued as a new artifact with its own id and lifecycle

nodes.does: Record the credential as ACTIVE for its scope and validity

timeout.reason: validity ending is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the two things that can end it sooner

nodes.asks: What ended the credential's active life?

branches.label: Revoked
branches.when: an authoritative revocation arrived

branches.label: Replaced
branches.when: a replacement credential was issued for the same purpose

nodes.state: REPLACED; this artifact is no longer usable
nodes.reEntry: the replacement runs its own lifecycle. This one is never reactivated, whatever happens to the replacement
