nodes.on: a credential being revoked
carries: the credential, its scope and its owner
the revocation reason

nodes.does: Re-read the credential's current version before expiring it. An extension or a replacement may have moved its validity since this timer was written, and expiring on the remembered value would undo a later decision

nodes.asks: Does the current version still expire now?

branches.label: Still expiring
branches.when: the current validity ends at this moment

branches.label: Validity moved
branches.when: an extension or replacement changed it

nodes.does: Record the credential as EXPIRED. Expired is not revoked - the artifact reached the end of its validity rather than being withdrawn, and the two mean different things to anyone investigating later

nodes.state: EXPIRED after active use
nodes.reEntry: the entitlement behind it may still be perfectly valid; a new credential is issued for it rather than this one being revived

nodes.state: expiry superseded by an extension or replacement
nodes.reEntry: the current validity governs, and its own end executes when it arrives

guardrails: A credential issued is not a credential active.
Credential validity is not entitlement validity. Either can end while the other holds.
A revoked credential is never restored by a stale activation or refresh event.
Expiry re-reads the current version before applying, so an extension is not undone by an older timer.
records.reusableRule: Credentials are access artifacts with their own validity lifecycle and should not be treated as the entitlement they represent.

records.name: Credential compromise or revocation → disable → replace or re-authenticate
records.purpose: Take a credential out of use immediately, and let any replacement come through its own authorised path.

entity.scope: the specific credentials affected, and their owner
entity.note: Scope is the whole question. One compromised artifact does not implicate unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise reaches them.

requires: a requirement to revoke: suspected or confirmed compromise, a manual revoke, a password or security reset, a device removed, access terminated, or a token invalidation

nodes.does: Determine which credentials are actually affected. One compromised artifact does not revoke unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise implies them - over-revoking on a suspicion locks people out of things that were never at risk, and the lockout becomes the incident

Revoke the affected credentials immediately, ahead of everything else in this journey. Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions - an artifact invalidated at ten o'clock must not still authorise a request queued at one minute to
Invalidate the refresh and activation operations tied to the revoked credentials, so nothing in flight can bring one back after it has been withdrawn

nodes.asks: Is a replacement allowed?

branches.label: Replacement permitted
branches.when: the owner remains entitled and policy allows re-issuing

branches.label: No replacement
branches.when: access is being removed, or the owner is no longer entitled

nodes.state: revoked; no replacement issued
nodes.reEntry: a new credential requires the entitlement and the authorisation to be established again, which is a different journey and not a continuation of this one

nodes.asks: Does issuing a replacement require verification first?

branches.label: Verification required
branches.when: the revocation reason means the requester's identity or control has to be re-established

branches.label: No verification needed
branches.when: the revocation was routine and the owner's identity is not in question

nodes.on: a replacement requiring identity or control to be re-established
carries: the revocation reason, which sets how strong the verification has to be
the fact that the old credential is already revoked and stays revoked whatever the verification concludes

nodes.does: Issue a replacement as a new credential with its own id and its own lifecycle. The revoked artifact is never reactivated - a replacement replaces, and reusing the old identifier would make the revocation unverifiable

nodes.on: a replacement credential being issued
carries: the new credential and the credential it replaces
the revocation reason, which is part of the new artifact's history

guardrails: One credential compromise does not automatically revoke unrelated credentials unless policy requires it.
A replacement never reactivates the revoked credential. It is a new artifact.
Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions, including refresh and activation already in flight.
records.reusableRule: Credential revocation should immediately invalidate the affected access artifact while replacement follows an independently authorized path.

records.name: Deprovision request → dependency check → remove, retain or escalate
records.purpose: Remove a capability that is no longer authorised, after establishing that nothing still depends on the thing being removed.

entity.scope: the provisioned resource or capability, and the entitlement whose end triggered its removal
entity.note: The resource is the entity, not the entitlement. A shared resource outlives any single right to it, which is why dependency is checked before anything is removed.

distinctFrom.because: ACC-74 ends a right and stops future use. This removes the technical resource behind it, which is a separate operation with its own failure modes and its own reasons to wait.

requires: a valid requirement to deprovision: an entitlement ended, an account closed, a role removed, a contract terminated, or a resource explicitly removed
insufficientAlone: a period of non-use, which is not an authorisation to remove anything

nodes.does: Identify the provisioned resources affected, and which of them are shared with anything still entitled

nodes.asks: What still depends on these resources?

branches.label: Shared with a live entitlement
branches.when: another holder is still entitled to the same resource

branches.label: A commitment must complete first
branches.when: an in-progress service or open transaction needs the resource until it finishes

branches.label: Data transfer or a special process applies
branches.when: an export, a handover or a defined termination process has to run before removal

branches.label: Nothing depends on it
branches.when: the resource serves only the entitlement that ended

nodes.state: retained; another entitlement still depends on it
nodes.reEntry: when the last entitlement to the shared resource ends, removal is evaluated again. Removing it now would take it from everyone else who is still entitled

timeout.after: the horizon appropriate to the dependent commitment
timeout.reason: a dependency that never clears leaves an unauthorised capability alive indefinitely, which is the failure deprovisioning exists to prevent

nodes.on: removal requiring an export, handover or defined termination process first
carries: the resource and what has to happen before it can go
the fact that the capability is already unauthorised even though the resource remains

nodes.does: Deprovision idempotently. This removes the capability, not the record of it - historical and audit data is governed by its own retention and deletion lifecycle, and a deprovision that deletes it has performed an irreversible action nobody authorised

timeout.reason: silence is not success, and an unauthorised capability that may still be live is worth escalating rather than assuming away

nodes.asks: How did it end?

branches.label: Succeeded
branches.when: the system reports the resource removed

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the system reports a failure

nodes.asks: Does the access consequence matter enough to verify?

branches.label: Verify it
branches.when: continued access would be a real problem, which is the usual case for anything security-relevant

branches.label: The removal record is sufficient
branches.when: the deprovisioning system is authoritative for whether the capability exists

nodes.does: Confirm the capability is genuinely no longer available. A deprovisioning API returning success is a statement about the API, and the question here is whether anyone can still get in

nodes.state: capability removed; records and audit data untouched
nodes.reEntry: re-provisioning follows a new entitlement rather than an undo. Deleting the retained data is a separate lifecycle with its own authorisation

nodes.asks: Is this failure retry-safe within the budget?

branches.label: Retry
branches.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first attempt has room

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the failure is permanent, or the budget is spent

nodes.does: Retry against the budget fixed at the first failure, idempotently, so a partially completed removal is completed rather than restarted

nodes.on: a capability that could not be removed
carries: the resource, what was attempted, and how long it has been unauthorised
whether the capability is believed to still be reachable, which is what makes this urgent rather than administrative

guardrails: An entitlement ending is not an authorisation for destructive deletion.
Deprovisioning does not delete historical or audit data. That is a separate lifecycle with separate authorisation.
Shared resource dependencies are checked before removal.
Where the access consequence matters, technical success is verified rather than assumed.
Deprovisioning is idempotent, so a retry completes a partial removal rather than restarting it.
records.reusableRule: Deprovisioning removes no-longer-authorized capability only after active dependencies and retention obligations have been reconciled.

records.name: Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process
records.purpose: Hold a verification dependency as its own state, blocking only the process that needs it and releasing it only after everything else is rechecked.

entity.scope: the blocked process plus the verification requirement holding it
entity.note: One instance per requirement per blocked process. The same verification can unblock two processes and is not requested twice for them.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-49 is missing data - a value we do not hold. This is missing confidence - we may hold the value and have not established that it is true. The routes to resolving them share nothing.

requires: a named process that cannot proceed, and the specific verification it requires at a stated scope
insufficientAlone: a general wish for higher identity confidence with no process waiting on it

nodes.does: Record which process is blocked, which verification it needs at what scope and assurance, why, and any deadline. Naming the blocked process is what stops this becoming a standing request for identity documents

nodes.asks: Does an existing valid verification already satisfy this requirement at this scope?

branches.label: Already satisfied
branches.when: a current verification covers the same claim at the required assurance

branches.label: Not satisfied
branches.when: no current verification covers it, or the existing one is at a lower assurance

nodes.does: Reuse the existing verification and record that it was reused rather than re-requested. Asking someone to verify again what they verified last week for the same scope is the fastest way to make verification feel arbitrary rather than protective
Initiate the required verification. The verification itself runs as its own instance; this journey owns only the dependency and the resumption

timeout.after: the deadline of the blocked process, or its SLA
timeout.reason: how long to wait belongs to what is blocked rather than to the verification - a blocked payment and a blocked profile update do not deserve the same patience

nodes.asks: How did the verification end?

branches.label: Succeeded
branches.when: the claim was verified at the required scope

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: verification did not establish the claim

nodes.on: a verification failing while a process waits on it
carries: the failure and the blocked process behind it
the deadline the process is running against, which the failure handling does not reset

nodes.asks: Do the blocked process's other requirements still hold?

branches.label: All still valid
branches.when: nothing else the process needs has lapsed while this ran

branches.label: Something else is now missing
branches.when: another requirement expired or changed during the verification

nodes.state: verification satisfied; the blocked process is free to continue
nodes.reEntry: a further verification requirement is its own dependency with its own instance

nodes.state: verification satisfied, process still blocked on something else
nodes.reEntry: verification succeeding does not guarantee the process will - the other requirement is resolved on its own terms, and pretending this unblocked everything is how a customer is told twice that they are done

nodes.asks: The verification did not complete in time - what does the blocked process do?

branches.label: Expire
branches.when: the process cannot wait and lapses

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the process matters enough that someone should own getting it moving

branches.label: Hold
branches.when: the process waits indefinitely by design, visibly held rather than failed

nodes.state: blocked process expired awaiting verification
nodes.reEntry: a new attempt at the process opens its own dependency

nodes.on: a verification dependency outliving the blocked process's deadline
carries: the blocked process, the requirement and what has been attempted

nodes.state: held, visibly, awaiting verification
nodes.reEntry: the verification arriving later resumes this. Held is recorded as held rather than left looking like an unnoticed stall

guardrails: A verification already valid for the required scope is reused rather than re-requested.
The dependency blocks only the process that requires it.
Verification succeeding does not guarantee the blocked process will succeed. Its other requirements are rechecked.
records.reusableRule: Verification dependencies should block only the process that requires them and release it only after current requirements are revalidated.

records.name: Document submitted → validate → accept, reject or replace
records.purpose: Keep uploading a document and satisfying a requirement as separate facts, and keep an acceptance bound to the requirement it was assessed against.

entity.scope: the submitted document, the requirement it is offered against, and its owner
entity.note: Acceptance is per requirement. The same document may satisfy one requirement and fail another with different acceptance rules, and both results are true at once.

requires: a document submitted against an identified requirement
insufficientAlone: a file uploaded, which is a transfer rather than a submission against anything

nodes.does: Record the document as SUBMITTED against the specific requirement it is offered for. Uploaded is not validated, and nothing may treat the submission as satisfying the requirement while it sits here

Validate the properties this requirement actually cares about: the document type, whether it belongs to the person offering it, readability, completeness, validity dates, the required fields, and integrity or authenticity where the requirement demands them

nodes.asks: What did validation find?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: the document satisfies this requirement's acceptance rules

branches.label: Correctable
branches.when: something specific is wrong that a better submission would fix - unreadable, cropped, an expired copy of a current document

branches.label: Invalid
branches.when: the document cannot satisfy this requirement whatever is resubmitted

nodes.does: Record ACCEPTED for this specific requirement, with what was checked. Accepted here is not universally valid - the same document offered against a different requirement is assessed again on that requirement's rules

nodes.state: ACCEPTED for the stated requirement
nodes.reEntry: the same document offered against another requirement enters as a new submission, because acceptance travels with the requirement rather than with the file

nodes.does: Record REJECTED with the reason. A rejection that does not say what was wrong produces the same submission again

nodes.state: REJECTED for this requirement, with a recorded reason
nodes.reEntry: a different document may be submitted; this one is not reassessed unchanged

nodes.does: Record CORRECTION_REQUIRED, stating specifically what is wrong and what would fix it

timeout.after: the requirement's deadline, or this document's own validity end
timeout.reason: a correction request with no end leaves the requirement permanently half-satisfied, and the process behind it permanently waiting

nodes.state: correction window closed; the requirement remains unsatisfied
nodes.reEntry: a new submission opens its own instance with the full history attached

nodes.does: Link the replacement to the original and keep the original submission and its validation result readable. A replaced document is superseded rather than deleted - what was offered and why it was not accepted is part of the record

nodes.asks: Is another correction round allowed?

branches.label: Round available
branches.when: the number of attempts against this requirement is within the policy limit

branches.label: Limit reached
branches.when: repeated corrections have not produced an acceptable document

nodes.on: repeated corrections failing to satisfy a requirement
carries: every submission and why each was not accepted
the requirement itself, which may be the thing that is wrong rather than the documents

guardrails: Uploaded is not validated.
Accepted for one requirement is not universally valid.
The original submission and its validation history stay auditable after a replacement.
Correction rounds are bounded, and the limit routes to a person rather than to a rejection.
records.reusableRule: A submitted document satisfies a requirement only after validation against that requirement's current acceptance rules.

records.name: Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
records.purpose: Raise identity assurance for a sensitive action, then check the action is still authorised before it runs.

entity.scope: the actor, the specific protected action and the authentication context around it
entity.note: The step-up is scoped to the action that required it. Raising assurance once does not open every sensitive action for the rest of the session.

requires: a protected action whose required assurance exceeds what the current session holds - a sensitive account change, a high-risk transaction, a credential change, a privileged action, or an unusual security context

nodes.does: Preserve the requested action's full context, so it can resume rather than be reconstructed by the person from memory
Initiate the stronger authentication or verification this action requires, scoped to it rather than to the session as a whole

timeout.reason: a step-up that is not completed leaves the action blocked, which is the safe outcome and needs no further decision

nodes.asks: Was the higher assurance established?

branches.label: Established
branches.when: the step-up succeeded

branches.label: Not established
branches.when: the step-up failed

nodes.state: protected action remains blocked; assurance not established
nodes.reEntry: a fresh attempt at the action issues a fresh step-up. Nothing is queued to execute if assurance is established later

nodes.does: Revalidate the requested action against current authorization before anything runs. Passing a challenge raises identity assurance and authorises nothing - the entitlement, the resource or the policy can all have moved while the challenge was in front of the person

nodes.asks: Is the requested action still authorised?

branches.label: Still authorised
branches.when: the action's authorization conditions hold at the raised assurance

branches.label: No longer authorised
branches.when: something the action depended on changed during the challenge

nodes.on: a step-up completed with the action still authorised
carries: the preserved action context and the raised assurance level
the fact that authorization is being decided now rather than inherited from before the challenge

nodes.state: assurance raised; the action is no longer authorised and does not run
nodes.reEntry: the raised assurance stands for its own window; the action is attempted again on its own terms and decided again

guardrails: Step-up success does not automatically execute the stale action.
The requested action is revalidated after the challenge, not before it.
The step-up is scoped to an appropriate assurance window and to the action that required it.
records.reusableRule: Step-up authentication raises identity assurance for a sensitive action without replacing the need to revalidate that action's authorization.

records.name: Parent state change → determine child impact → propagate selectively
records.purpose: Let a parent's state reach only the children that genuinely depend on it, through a rule someone actually wrote.

entity.scope: the parent whose state changed, and each child evaluated individually against the dependency model
entity.note: Children are classified individually. A single verdict for the whole collection is the assumption this journey exists to prevent.

distinctFrom.because: This propagates downward through defined dependencies. REL-96 derives upward through an aggregation policy. They are opposite directions with different rules, and neither is the inverse of the other.

requires: a material state change on a parent entity - an organisation suspended, a master account closed, a contract state changed, a parent resource disabled

nodes.asks: Is a dependency model defined for this parent-child relationship?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: a rule states which child states depend on which parent states, and how

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: nothing states what this parent change should do to its children

nodes.on: a parent state change with no defined dependency model
carries: the parent change and the children that would be affected under a naive inheritance
the explicit fact that nothing was propagated, because inheritance was not assumed
suppresses: any automatic propagation to children while the model is undefined

nodes.does: Classify each child individually against the model: which are directly dependent on the parent's state, which are independently valid, and which carry open obligations. One verdict for the whole collection is the assumption that turns a suspended organisation into eleven deleted subsidiaries

nodes.asks: How does each class resolve?

branches.label: Directly dependent
branches.when: the model says this child's state follows the parent's

branches.label: Independently valid
branches.when: the child stands on its own basis and the model does not make it follow

nodes.state: child state preserved; the parent change does not reach it
nodes.reEntry: a parent change that the model does make this child follow is evaluated when it happens. A parent going inactive does not delete a child that stands on its own

nodes.asks: Do the dependent children carry open obligations?

branches.label: Obligations open
branches.when: a dependent child holds a commitment that would be destroyed by propagation

branches.label: Nothing open
branches.when: the dependent children hold nothing that outlives the propagation

nodes.on: propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation
carries: the obligation and the propagation being held for it
the explicit fact that nothing destructive has been applied to that child yet

nodes.does: Apply the defined consequence to the dependent children only, recording what propagated, to which children, and under which rule. Propagation that cannot say which rule produced it cannot be reviewed, reversed or explained

nodes.state: consequence applied to dependent children, scoped and recorded
nodes.reEntry: a further parent change is classified again against the model

guardrails: A parent going inactive does not delete every child.
A parent restriction does not restrict every child globally unless the model defines it.
Propagation stays scoped and auditable - what went where, under which rule.
Where no dependency model exists, nothing propagates.
records.reusableRule: Parent state changes should propagate only through explicitly defined dependencies rather than through assumed inheritance.

records.name: Child state change → recalculate aggregate parent state
records.purpose: Derive a parent's state from its children through an explicit aggregation policy, recomputed from source rather than nudged by whichever child reported last.

entity.scope: the parent and the full collection of children the policy reads
entity.note: The aggregate is recomputed from the authoritative children, not incremented from the event that arrived. That is what keeps it rebuildable and stops it drifting.

requires: a change to a child state that the parent's aggregation policy reads
insufficientAlone: any child change, where no policy makes the parent depend on it

nodes.asks: Is an aggregation policy defined for this parent state?

branches.label: Defined
branches.when: a policy states how child states combine into the parent's, and what transitions it

branches.label: Not defined
branches.when: no policy states how these children combine

nodes.on: a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it
carries: the parent, the children and the change that arrived
the explicit fact that no ANY, ALL, majority or threshold rule was assumed in order to produce a parent state

nodes.does: Recompute the parent's derived state from the authoritative children using the defined policy, rather than adjusting it from the single child event that arrived. Recomputing from source means the aggregate can be rebuilt at any moment and cannot drift away from what the children actually say

nodes.asks: Does the recomputed aggregate meet the parent's transition criteria?

branches.label: Criteria met
branches.when: the policy's condition for moving the parent's state is satisfied

branches.label: Not met
branches.when: the aggregate moved and the parent's state does not

nodes.does: Update the derived parent state, recording which children and which policy produced it, so the transition can be explained without recomputing it by hand

nodes.state: derived parent state updated from the aggregation policy
nodes.reEntry: the next relevant child change recomputes it again from source

nodes.state: aggregate recomputed; parent state unchanged
nodes.reEntry: this is the ordinary outcome. One child changing is not the parent changing, and most child events correctly end here

guardrails: One child's state does not automatically become the parent's state.
Aggregation semantics come from policy. ANY, ALL, majority and percentage thresholds are never inferred.
The aggregate is recomputable from the authoritative children rather than accumulated from events.
records.reusableRule: Parent state derived from children must follow an explicit aggregation policy rather than simple state copying.

records.name: Duplicate entity detected → assess → keep separate, link or merge
records.purpose: Assess whether two records are the same entity, and route the answer - without consolidating anything.

entity.scope: the candidate set of records suspected of representing one entity
entity.note: The set is the unit. Three records suspected of being one person are assessed together, because a pairwise answer can be internally inconsistent.

distinctFrom.because: Linking is one of the outcomes this assessment can reach. It is a separate journey because a link has its own semantics and its own sharing rules, which the assessment does not decide.

requires: a match between records strong enough to be worth assessing
insufficientAlone: the same name
the same postcode or address
a similar spelling, which is what matching produces most of

nodes.does: Collect the matching evidence and record its strength: verified identifiers, authoritative external IDs, declared ownership, verified contact points, business identifiers and relationship history. A match score is a reason to look and never a conclusion - the same email may be a shared family address, and the same phone number may be a workplace

nodes.asks: What does the evidence actually support?

branches.label: Not the same entity
branches.when: the evidence is explained by something other than identity - a shared household, a shared workplace, a common name

branches.label: Related but distinct
branches.when: the records genuinely represent different entities that have a real relationship

branches.label: Same entity, consolidation looks safe
branches.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, and nothing about the records makes merging risky

branches.label: Ambiguous or high-risk
branches.when: the evidence is suggestive and incomplete, or the records carry state that would be dangerous to consolidate wrongly

nodes.state: KEEP_SEPARATE; the records represent different entities
nodes.reEntry: stronger evidence later re-opens the assessment. Keeping two records apart is reversible; merging them usually is not, which is why this is the default when the evidence does not carry

nodes.on: records that are related and genuinely distinct
carries: both records and the evidence of the relationship between them
the explicit finding that they are not the same entity, so the link does not drift toward being treated as one

nodes.on: a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating
carries: the full evidence set and the confidence it establishes

the explicit fact that this journey has assessed and not authorised - detecting a duplicate is not permission to merge it, and the merge mechanism applies its own evidence requirements before consolidating anything

nodes.on: an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically
carries: the candidate set, the evidence and what specifically is ambiguous about it
what each record currently holds, which is what makes a wrong merge expensive

guardrails: The same name is not the same person.
A shared email or phone number may not prove the same entity - it depends on the model, and households and workplaces share both routinely.
Duplicate detection is not merge authorization. This journey assesses and routes; consolidating records is a separate mechanism with its own evidence requirements.
records.reusableRule: Duplicate detection identifies a reconciliation candidate; merge requires separate evidence that consolidation is safe.

records.name: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
records.purpose: Record that two entities are related and let defined context cross between them, while both remain two entities.

entity.scope: the link itself, plus the two entities it connects
entity.note: Each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. The link is a third record about them, not a step toward becoming one.

requires: a valid relationship or link between two distinct entities
insufficientAlone: a duplicate match, which is a question about whether they are one entity rather than evidence that they are two related ones

nodes.does: Define what this link actually means - the same household, related accounts, linked profiles, a business relationship, a cross-product connection. The semantics decide what may be shared, and a link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing at all

nodes.asks: What context do these link semantics explicitly permit sharing?

branches.label: Defined shared context
branches.when: the link's semantics name specific context that may cross between the entities

branches.label: Nothing shared
branches.when: the link records a relationship and permits no context to cross - which is the common case

nodes.does: Share only the context the semantics explicitly permit. Anything not named is not shared, including things that would obviously be convenient

Confirm each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. Consent does not cross the link, and neither does entitlement or access, unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it - a household link is not permission to email everyone in the household

nodes.asks: Is anything attempting to carry consent, entitlement, credentials or access across the link?

branches.label: Something is propagating
branches.when: a downstream process is treating the link as though the entities were one

branches.label: Nothing is
branches.when: only the permitted context crosses

nodes.does: Block the propagation and record it. This is the specific failure a link becomes when it is quietly treated as a merge, and catching it here is cheaper than discovering it as a consent complaint

nodes.state: linked; two entities, two lifecycles, defined shared context
nodes.reEntry: the link's semantics may be changed, and the link may be ended, but neither turns it into a merge. Consolidating the records is a separate decision with separate evidence

guardrails: Linked is not merged.
Consent does not automatically propagate across linked identities.
Entitlement and access do not propagate unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it.
A link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing.
records.reusableRule: Entity linking enables defined cross-entity context while preserving independent identity and lifecycle state.

records.name: Entity split required → create separate records → allocate history and state safely
records.purpose: Separate what should never have been one record, or what must now be managed apart, without copying the things that do not divide.

entity.scope: the source entity and the entities that result from the split
entity.note: The source entity's history remains the source entity's history. The resulting records inherit allocations, not a rewritten past.

distinctFrom.because: A link connects two records that already exist separately. A split creates that separation where it did not exist, which means deciding what each side gets - and what neither side may simply be given a copy of.

requires: an authoritative requirement to separate state currently held under one entity

nodes.does: Determine the split basis - what actually distinguishes the resulting entities from one another. Without it, allocation becomes a series of individual guesses

Classify every piece of existing information as entity-specific, shared, ambiguous, historical or non-transferable. The last category is the one that gets missed: consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations do not divide by being copied, and duplicating one creates an obligation nobody incurred or a permission nobody gave

nodes.asks: How does each classified item resolve?

branches.label: Clearly one entity's
branches.when: the item belongs unambiguously to one of the resulting entities

branches.label: Genuinely shared
branches.when: the item belongs to the relationship between them rather than to either

branches.label: Non-transferable
branches.when: consent, an entitlement, a credential or a financial obligation, none of which divides

branches.label: Ambiguous
branches.when: the item cannot be attributed on the split basis

nodes.does: Allocate the item to the entity it belongs to
Preserve the item through a relationship or reference model rather than duplicating it into both records. Two copies of one shared history diverge the first time either is edited
Leave it with the entity that holds it and record that it did not divide. A new record existing is not a reason for it to receive a copy of a consent, an entitlement or a debt

nodes.on: state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity
carries: the item, the split basis, and why attribution failed
the fact that it is held unresolved rather than assigned to whichever record was created first

nodes.does: Recalculate each resulting entity's rights, permissions, entitlements, obligations and active journeys from what it now actually holds, rather than from what the source entity held

Record that the split occurred, when, and on what basis. History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate - events that happened to the combined entity happened to the combined entity, and pretending otherwise makes every past event unattributable

nodes.state: entities separated; current state reconstructed, prior history preserved as it happened
nodes.reEntry: each resulting entity now has its own lifecycle. A further split is assessed against whichever of them requires it

guardrails: Consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations are never blindly duplicated across a split.
The audit trail preserves that a split occurred, when, and on what basis.
History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate.
Ambiguous state is held unresolved rather than assigned by default.
records.reusableRule: Entity splitting reconstructs independent current states while preserving the historical fact that the records were previously represented together.

records.name: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
records.purpose: Consolidate records that represent one entity, after every dependent state has been reconciled under its own authority rule.

entity.scope: the source entities, the canonical target, and the merge operation itself as an auditable record
entity.note: The merge operation is its own entity. Its record of conflict decisions and provenance is what makes the consolidated result reviewable, and often what makes it reversible. Authority to authorize a merge is an authorized identity-consolidation role - never inferred from whoever happened to run the duplicate assessment. An irreversible merge (c.evidence's own elevated evidence bar) requires that same authority explicitly exercised at that elevated bar, not merely re-used from the original, lower-stakes authorization that started the operation.

distinctFrom.because: Account consolidation unifies business structure and leaves the people distinct. This consolidates the representations of one entity, which is a decision about identity and carries a far higher evidence bar.

requires: an explicit merge authorization following a duplicate assessment, naming the sources, the target, and the authorized identity-consolidation role that authorised it
or an existing merge_operation_id whose TRM-102 conflict has just been resolved, carrying the resolution and clearance to resume - this is the same operation resuming, not a fresh authorization
insufficientAlone: a duplicate detection, which produces a candidate rather than a decision
a high match score
an assessment concluding the records are probably the same, without an authorisation to act on it

nodes.asks: Is this a fresh merge authorization, or the same operation resuming after TRM-102 resolved a conflict?

branches.label: Fresh authorization
branches.when: no merge_operation_id exists yet for this trigger

branches.label: Resuming after conflict resolution
branches.when: merge_operation_id already exists and TRM-102 has just handed back a resolved (or partially reconciled) conflict, cleared to complete

nodes.does: Create the auditable merge operation: source entity IDs, the canonical target, the basis, the authorized identity-consolidation role that authorised it and its own identity, the time, and every conflict decision as it is made. Provenance is what makes the result reviewable - without it the consolidated record cannot say where any part of itself came from

Inventory the dependent state before anything is touched: identity attributes, consent, preferences, contact points, entitlements, purchases, subscriptions, support cases, opportunities, credentials, active journeys, open obligations and relationships. Each of these answers to a different authority, and a merge that reads them as one list applies one rule to all of them

nodes.asks: Is this merge reversible?

branches.label: Reversible
branches.when: the architecture can separate the records again if the decision turns out to be wrong

branches.label: Irreversible
branches.when: consolidation cannot be undone once applied

nodes.asks: Does the evidence and the authorizing role meet the higher bar an irreversible merge requires?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it at the standard an unrecoverable decision demands, and the identity-consolidation role authorizing it was explicitly exercised at that elevated bar rather than re-used from the operation's original, lower-stakes authorization

branches.label: Not sufficient
branches.when: the evidence would justify a reversible merge and not this one, or the authority behind it was never explicitly raised to the elevated bar this decision requires

nodes.state: not merged; evidence sized for a reversible operation
nodes.reEntry: stronger evidence, or an architecture that makes the merge reversible, re-opens this. Leaving two records separate is recoverable and this is not

nodes.asks: Does conflicting state exist across the sources?

branches.label: Conflicts present
branches.when: two sources hold incompatible values for state that matters

branches.label: No conflicts
branches.when: every state type reconciles without contradiction

nodes.on: conflicting state discovered during merge
carries: the merge operation, the inventory and exactly which state conflicts
the fact that nothing has been consolidated yet, so the conflict is decided before rather than after

nodes.does: Consolidate each state type under its own authority rule. There is no newest-value-wins applied across the board: a newer contact point may supersede an older one, a newer consent does not supersede an older withdrawal, an entitlement is reconciled rather than either kept or duplicated, and a financial obligation is never added to itself
Repoint dependent relationships and active processes onto the canonical entity, so nothing continues to run against a representation that has been superseded

Invalidate the actions still queued against the superseded representations. A downstream synchronisation running on its own schedule will otherwise restore what was just consolidated, which undoes the merge while reporting success

Verify the merge did what it was for and nothing more: no critical obligation lost, no permission more permissive than any source held, no entitlement duplicated, no duplicate active journey still running, and the source history still traceable

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Passed
branches.when: every check holds

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: a check found a lost obligation, a widened permission, a duplicated entitlement or a surviving duplicate journey

nodes.state: merged into the canonical entity, with provenance and source history intact
nodes.reEntry: a further duplicate candidate involving this entity is assessed on its own evidence, with this merge in the record

guardrails: A merge never duplicates a financial obligation.
An opt-out never disappears because another profile was opted in.
Provenance is preserved - the consolidated record can say where each part of it came from.
An irreversible merge requires stronger evidence and authority than a reversible one.

A merge sent to TRM-102 for conflict resolution resumes consolidation on this same merge_operation_id once TRM-102 hands it back resolved - c.origin distinguishes that resumption from a fresh authorization at the same trigger, so a held or partially-reconciled merge does not become a permanent dead end.
records.reusableRule: Entity merge consolidates representations only after dependent state has been reconciled according to the authority rules of each state type.

records.name: Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
records.purpose: Fail safe wherever consolidating would require inventing an authority the system does not have.

entity.scope: the merge operation and the specific state in conflict
entity.note: The conflict attaches to particular state, not to the whole merge. Some conflicts stop everything and most do not, and telling them apart is the journey's main work.

requires: state that two sources hold incompatibly: contradictory identity attributes, a permission conflict, different ownership claims, incompatible account states, duplicate active obligations, or a credential or security conflict

nodes.does: Classify the conflict by domain. The domain decides which authority rule applies, and there is no rule that applies across identity, permission, ownership, obligation and credentials at once

nodes.asks: Does a deterministic authority rule exist for this domain?

branches.label: Rule exists
branches.when: policy states which source wins for this kind of state, and why

branches.label: No rule
branches.when: nothing states how this conflict resolves

nodes.does: Apply the rule and record the basis. A conflict resolved in order to make the merge succeed is not resolved - it has been decided by the only party with an interest in the answer, which is whoever wanted the merge

Record the affected state as MERGE_CONFLICT. The most permissive consent or access value is never selected by default - defaulting that way resolves every ambiguity in the direction that cannot be undone, and it is the direction a merge is already biased toward

nodes.asks: Is this an ambiguous identity conflict?

branches.label: Identity itself is in doubt
branches.when: the conflict suggests these may not be one entity at all

branches.label: Identity is established
branches.when: the conflict is about state held by an entity we are confident is one

nodes.asks: Can the merge safely continue on the portions that carry no conflict?

branches.label: Independent portions exist
branches.when: some state can be consolidated without depending on anything in conflict

branches.label: Everything is entangled
branches.when: the conflicted state is load-bearing for the rest

nodes.does: Hold the entire merge. Where identity itself is in doubt, consolidating anything assumes the thing the merge was supposed to establish
Consolidate only the portions carrying no conflict and no dependency on conflicted state, leaving the rest explicitly unmerged rather than quietly merged with a chosen value

until: an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded

timeout.reason: a merge held in conflict leaves two records in a half-consolidated state, which is worse than either outcome and worth escalating rather than waiting out

nodes.on: a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA
carries: the conflict, its domain and what has been consolidated so far
the fact that the records are currently in a partially reconciled state, which is nobody's intended end state

nodes.asks: How was it settled?

branches.label: Resolved
branches.when: an authority determined the answer and the merge may complete

branches.label: Aborted
branches.when: the merge should not proceed

branches.label: Partially reconciled, remainder unresolvable
branches.when: the independent portions consolidated and the conflicted state stays separate

nodes.on: a merge conflict resolved, with the merge operation cleared to complete
carries: merge_operation_id, the resolution and its basis, and which state was affected
the explicit fact that this conflict is settled - TRM-101 resumes consolidation from its own current point rather than re-authorizing the merge from scratch

nodes.does: Abort the merge, unwinding whatever was partially consolidated where that is possible, and recording precisely what could not be unwound. The sources remain separate and the attempt remains in the record

nodes.state: ABORTED; sources remain separate
nodes.reEntry: a new merge requires new evidence. That an earlier attempt was aborted is part of what the next one is judged against

nodes.state: PARTIALLY_RECONCILED; conflicted state left separate and marked
nodes.reEntry: what remains unmerged is named rather than left as a vague inconsistency, so it can be resolved later on its own evidence

guardrails: A conflict is never resolved merely to make the merge succeed.
The most permissive consent or access state is never chosen by default.
An ambiguous identity conflict stops the entire merge rather than part of it.
What could not be unwound after an abort is recorded rather than assumed away.

A resolved conflict hands back to TRM-101 (h.resume) rather than ending as a record nothing ever acts on - RESOLVED means the merge may complete, and completing it is TRM-101's own job to resume, not this journey's to claim.
records.reusableRule: Merge conflicts should fail safe whenever consolidation would require inventing authority that the system does not possess.

records.name: Account consolidation → dependency reconciliation → unified relationship
records.purpose: Unify business structure across accounts while every person involved stays a separate person.

entity.scope: the accounts being consolidated and the canonical structure that results
entity.note: Accounts consolidate; people do not. The members of the consolidated account remain distinct identities with distinct consent and distinct history.

requires: an authorized consolidation naming the accounts and the canonical target
insufficientAlone: two accounts sharing a domain, a billing address or an administrator

nodes.does: Determine the canonical account structure - which account survives and what the consolidated shape actually is
Inventory across every account being consolidated: members, roles, contracts, subscriptions, resources, entitlements, billing relationships, open cases, ownership and active obligations

nodes.asks: Does any part of this require treating two people as one?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the consolidation only works if two member records are the same person

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: every member remains a distinct identity in the consolidated structure

nodes.state: consolidation stopped; it requires an identity merge
nodes.reEntry: consolidating two people into one identity is a different decision with a far higher evidence bar, assessed and authorised separately. A consolidation that needs it has exceeded what it was authorised to do

nodes.asks: Are the resources transferable to the canonical account?

branches.label: Transferable
branches.when: policy and the resource itself allow it to move

branches.label: Not transferable
branches.when: a contract, a licence or the resource's own nature keeps it where it is

nodes.does: Transfer the resources according to policy, keeping their history with them
Retain the resource under its original relationship, referenced from the canonical account rather than moved into it. A reference keeps it reachable without pretending it changed hands

nodes.asks: Do the accounts carry conflicting obligations?

branches.label: Conflicting
branches.when: two accounts hold obligations that cannot both stand in one structure

branches.label: Compatible
branches.when: the obligations coexist in the consolidated structure

nodes.on: obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure
carries: each obligation, its source account and what makes them incompatible
the explicit fact that nothing has been cancelled by the consolidation

nodes.does: Recalculate account-level roles, access, entitlements, routing and aggregate states from what the consolidated account actually holds. Permissions are recalculated rather than unioned - a union grants everyone the highest access anyone previously had, which turns a structural tidy-up into privilege escalation
Verify that no entitlement was duplicated, no obligation lost, no access became broader than any source account granted, and no resource left orphaned

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Passed
branches.when: every check holds

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: a duplicated entitlement, a lost obligation, widened access or an orphaned resource was found

nodes.state: accounts consolidated; identities untouched
nodes.reEntry: a further consolidation is assessed against the canonical structure this produced

nodes.on: a consolidation whose verification failed
carries: which check failed and on what
the consolidated structure as it currently stands, which is not the intended end state

guardrails: Account consolidation is not person identity merge.
Members of consolidated accounts do not become the same identity.
Account-level permissions are recalculated rather than unioned.
A resource that cannot transfer is referenced rather than moved.
records.reusableRule: Account consolidation unifies business structure while preserving independent identities and reconciling account-level obligations explicitly.

records.name: Primary relationship transfer → validate new primary → transfer dependencies
records.purpose: Move a dependent entity to a new primary, carrying only what the primary relationship actually governs.

entity.scope: the dependent entity, its outgoing primary and its incoming one
entity.note: The dependent's own permissions and consent are not part of the transfer. They belong to the dependent and stay with it.

distinctFrom.because: Changing which primary a dependent hangs from moves a relationship. It consolidates nothing and neither party's identity changes.

requires: an authorized transfer naming the dependent entity, the outgoing primary and the incoming one

nodes.asks: Is the proposed new primary relationship valid?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: the incoming primary can hold this relationship and is entitled to

branches.label: Not valid
branches.when: the incoming primary is ineligible, or the relationship is not permitted between these types

nodes.state: transfer rejected; the existing primary relationship stands
nodes.reEntry: a different incoming primary is validated on its own terms. The dependent is never left between two primaries while the question is open

nodes.does: Identify what the primary relationship actually governs: rights, notifications, responsibilities, billing, access, ownership and open obligations. Anything the dependent holds on its own basis is deliberately not on this list

Transfer only the dependencies the primary relationship governs, preserving the historical primary relationship and the period it covered. Existing obligations move with their deadlines unchanged rather than disappearing in the handover

nodes.asks: Does the dependent hold permission or consent on its own basis?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the dependent gave or withheld something itself, rather than inheriting it

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: everything it held came through the primary relationship

nodes.does: Preserve it independently. It does not transfer, and the incoming primary's state is not inherited over it - a dependent who opted out does not become opted in because their primary is
Verify the dependent now holds exactly one valid required primary relationship - not zero, and not two

nodes.asks: Did verification pass?

branches.label: Exactly one valid primary
branches.when: the transfer landed cleanly

branches.label: None, or more than one
branches.when: the dependent is left without a required primary, or holding two

nodes.state: primary relationship transferred; independent state preserved
nodes.reEntry: a further transfer is validated against the current primary

nodes.on: a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary
carries: the dependent, what was transferred and what it now lacks
its inherited obligations and their unchanged deadlines

guardrails: A primary relationship transfer is not an identity merge.
The historical primary relationship and its period are preserved.
Existing obligations do not disappear during a transfer, and their deadlines do not reset.
The dependent's own permission and consent are never overwritten by the incoming primary's.
records.reusableRule: Changing a primary relationship transfers only the dependencies governed by that relationship, not every state associated with either party.

records.name: Data deletion request → validate scope → hold, delete or retain required data
records.purpose: Decide what a deletion request actually covers, and keep only what an authoritative retention obligation genuinely requires.

entity.scope: the data subject, this deletion request, and the data scope it names
entity.note: The request is bounded by what it asks for and by what governing policy covers. It is not a licence to delete everything we hold, nor a reason to keep everything we would rather not lose.

distinctFrom.because: Closing an account ends a relationship and requests nothing about data. A deletion request concerns data and says nothing about whether the relationship continues. Either can happen without the other.

requires: a deletion request naming a data subject and a scope
insufficientAlone: an account closure, which ends a relationship and requests nothing about data
a subscription cancellation
an unsubscribe, which withdraws permission to contact rather than requesting removal

nodes.asks: Is the requester's identity and authority established for this scope?

branches.label: Established
branches.when: the requester is verified as the data subject or as authorised to act for them

branches.label: Not established
branches.when: identity or authority has not been verified to the level this request requires

nodes.on: a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified
carries: the request and the verification it is blocked on
the request's own deadline, which the verification does not reset

nodes.does: Validate the scope, the jurisdiction and policy context, and which systems and data classes are actually in scope. A deletion request is bounded by what it asks for and by what the governing policy covers - not by everything we happen to hold about the person
Inventory the data in scope and classify each item as DELETABLE, RETAIN_REQUIRED, DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED, ALREADY_DELETED or MANUAL_REVIEW

nodes.asks: Does an authoritative retention obligation cover any of it?

branches.label: Retention required
branches.when: a legal or business obligation names data that must be kept

branches.label: Nothing retained
branches.when: no obligation covers anything in scope

nodes.does: Retain only what an authoritative obligation actually requires, recording which obligation and why. No retention rule is invented - where policy is silent the data is not kept on a guess, because retaining on a guess keeps what should have gone just as surely as deleting on one destroys what had to stay

nodes.asks: What remains, and can it be deleted?

branches.label: Deletable and clear
branches.when: data remains in scope, is eligible, and no dependency blocks it

branches.label: Blocked by a dependency
branches.when: something in scope cannot be removed until a dependency clears

branches.label: Needs manual review
branches.when: the classification could not be settled automatically

branches.label: Nothing left
branches.when: everything in scope is already absent or retained under an obligation

timeout.reason: a deletion request usually carries a legal deadline, and a dependency that has not cleared inside it needs a person rather than more waiting

nodes.on: data approved for deletion or anonymization
carries: the exact scope approved, per system and data class
what is being retained and under which obligation, so execution does not remove it

nodes.on: a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle
carries: the request, its deadline and what specifically is unresolved
the retention obligations already identified

nodes.state: nothing in scope to delete; retained items recorded with their obligations
nodes.reEntry: this is recorded as what it is rather than reported as a deletion. Data arriving later within the same scope is assessed against this request where the policy allows

guardrails: Account closure is not a deletion request.
A deletion request is not immediate physical deletion of every record.
No retention rule is invented. Where the governing policy is silent, data is not retained on a guess.
Audit evidence may need retaining without retaining the operational data alongside it.
records.reusableRule: Data deletion removes data according to defined scope while preserving only information that an authoritative retention obligation requires.

records.name: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
records.purpose: Carry a deletion through every system it has to reach, and keep any part that did not arrive visible.

entity.scope: the deletion job and each affected system's operation individually
entity.note: Each system's operation has its own type and its own terminal state. A single overall status hides the one that failed, which is the only one that matters.

requires: an approved deletion scope, per system and data class, from a validated request

nodes.does: Generate the scoped operation for each affected system - delete, anonymize, detach, restrict or place under retention hold - according to what the governing requirement for that system actually is. One operation type applied everywhere either destroys what had to be kept or keeps what had to go

Execute idempotently, keyed so a redelivered job does not repeat an operation, and so that nothing propagates back through downstream synchronisation to recreate what was just removed. A sync job running on its own schedule will otherwise restore a profile deleted an hour earlier, undoing the work while reporting success

timeout.reason: silence from a system is not confirmation, and a deletion whose SLA passes with systems unheard from is a partial failure that has not reported itself

nodes.asks: How did the operations end?

branches.label: All confirmed
branches.when: every required system reported its operation complete

branches.label: Some failed
branches.when: at least one system reported failure or did not confirm

nodes.asks: Was a further copy of the data discovered while the request was running?

branches.label: In scope
branches.when: a copy was found that the approved scope covers

branches.label: Out of scope
branches.when: a copy was found that the approved scope does not cover

branches.label: Nothing further
branches.when: no new copy surfaced

nodes.does: Generate and execute the operation for the newly discovered copy, within the same job and the same scope

Record the discovered copy as out of scope, naming why. It is not deleted on this request and it is not left unrecorded either - an unrecorded copy is one nobody knows to assess against the next request

Verify that no required target remains unintentionally active or searchable, to whatever guarantee each system actually offers. The deletion audit records what was removed and when, without keeping a copy of the personal data it removed - an audit that preserves the record has recreated the thing the deletion was for

nodes.asks: Did verification confirm every required terminal state?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: every in-scope target reached its required state

branches.label: Something remains
branches.when: a target is still present where it should not be

nodes.state: VERIFIED_COMPLETE; every in-scope obligation reached its terminal state
nodes.reEntry: a later request covering different scope is its own job. Deletion succeeding in the primary store was never the same as deletion everywhere, and this state records that everywhere was checked

nodes.does: Record PARTIAL_DELETION_FAILURE, naming which systems did not reach their required terminal state. This is never represented as complete - a deletion reported as done while a downstream copy survives is the most consequential false report in this library, because it ends the investigation that would have found the copy

nodes.asks: Is a retry available within the policy budget?

branches.label: Retry
branches.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first failure has room

branches.label: Escalate
branches.when: the failure is not clearing, or the budget is spent

nodes.does: Retry the outstanding operations only, idempotently, so a partially completed deletion is completed rather than restarted

nodes.on: a deletion that could not reach its required terminal state everywhere
carries: which systems remain outstanding and what was attempted
the request's deadline, which is often a legal one and does not move because a system did not respond
suppresses: any representation of this deletion as complete while a target remains

guardrails: Deletion succeeding in the primary store is not deletion everywhere.
A failed downstream deletion is never represented as fully complete.
Deletion jobs do not recreate profiles through downstream synchronisation.
The deletion audit does not itself preserve the personal data that was deleted.
records.reusableRule: Distributed deletion is complete only when all in-scope deletion obligations have reached their required terminal state or an explicit retained exception is recorded.

records.name: Integration connection → authenticate → validate → activate
records.purpose: Make an integration active only once it has been proven to do the thing it exists for, rather than once a credential has been saved.

entity.scope: the individual integration connection, with its own credentials, scopes and validated capabilities
entity.note: One connection per configured integration. A second connection to the same provider is a separate one with its own scopes, and neither inherits the other's validation.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes that an integration works at all. INT-113 handles one that worked and has started to stop, which is a question about evidence over a window rather than about setup.

requires: a request to establish an integration connection with an identified provider
insufficientAlone: a credential saved in a settings screen, which stores a secret and connects nothing
a provider selected from a list

nodes.does: Collect and configure the connection parameters this provider requires

nodes.asks: Does authentication succeed?

branches.label: Authenticated
branches.when: the provider accepts the credentials

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the provider rejects them

nodes.state: AUTH_FAILED; not connected
nodes.reEntry: corrected credentials re-enter from the start. Nothing partial is left active, because a half-configured integration is one that fails on its first real operation rather than during setup

nodes.does: Validate the minimum capabilities and scopes this integration actually needs. Authentication proves the provider will talk to us; it says nothing about whether we are permitted to do the things we intend to do

nodes.asks: Is the required access available?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: every capability the integration needs is within the granted scope

branches.label: Insufficient
branches.when: a required capability is outside what was granted

nodes.state: INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE; configuration required
nodes.reEntry: the missing scope is named rather than reported as a generic connection failure - the two produce entirely different remediation and only one of them is actionable

nodes.does: Perform a safe connectivity and capability validation - a read, a dry run, a no-op probe. Validation must not have destructive side effects: proving we can delete something by deleting it is not a test

nodes.asks: Did validation succeed?

branches.label: Validated
branches.when: the probe confirmed the capability works

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the probe did not confirm it

nodes.state: FAILED; authenticated and scoped, not operational
nodes.reEntry: remediation re-enters at validation. This state exists because authenticated and working are different, and reporting the first as the second is the failure this journey is built around

nodes.does: Record the connection as ACTIVE, with the capabilities that were actually validated rather than the ones that were configured

nodes.state: ACTIVE; authenticated, scoped and validated
nodes.reEntry: authorization changes go to INT-112 and health changes to INT-113

guardrails: A saved credential is not a connection.
Authentication success is not sufficient authorization scope.
Connection validation avoids destructive side effects.
A missing scope is named specifically rather than reported as a generic failure.
records.reusableRule: An integration becomes active only after authentication, required scope and minimum operational capability have been validated.

records.name: Integration credential or authorization change → revalidate → continue or degrade
records.purpose: Recheck what an integration can still do whenever its authorization changes, rather than assuming valid credentials mean unchanged access.

entity.scope: the integration connection and the authorization that changed
entity.note: Scope reduction affects the capabilities that depended on the removed scope. Everything else keeps working, and treating the whole connection as broken is its own outage.

requires: a material change to the connection's authorization: a token refreshed, a credential rotated, a scope reduced, an authorization revoked, or a service account changed

nodes.does: Invalidate the cached authorization. A queued retry holding a credential that has since been rotated away must not succeed on it - an old credential coming back through a retry is the specific failure this step exists to prevent

Revalidate the required capabilities against the new authorization. A token refreshing successfully means the provider will talk to us; it says nothing about whether the scope we had is the scope we still have

nodes.asks: What does revalidation show?

branches.label: Fully functional
branches.when: every capability the integration uses is still available

branches.label: Partially functional
branches.when: some capabilities are no longer within the granted scope and others are

branches.label: No longer usable
branches.when: authorization was revoked, or nothing the integration needs remains available

nodes.state: ACTIVE; authorization changed and capability unchanged
nodes.reEntry: the next authorization change revalidates again

nodes.does: Mark the affected capabilities DEGRADED and name exactly which. A reduced scope disables what depended on it, not the integration
Suppress the operations incompatible with the reduced authorization, leaving everything else running

nodes.state: DEGRADED; affected capabilities named, the rest operating
nodes.reEntry: restored scope revalidates and lifts the degradation for the capabilities it covers

nodes.on: authorization leaving the integration unusable
carries: what was revoked and when
any external operations already submitted and still unresolved, which the authorization change does not resolve

guardrails: A successful token refresh does not mean the integration is fully healthy.
A reduced scope affects only the capabilities that depended on it.
Old credentials do not become active again through a stale retry.
records.reusableRule: Integration authorization changes require capability revalidation because valid credentials do not guarantee unchanged operational access.

records.name: Integration health degradation → diagnose → recover, degrade or escalate
records.purpose: Scope a deteriorating integration to what is actually failing, and let recovery be established by evidence rather than by a metric returning to normal.

entity.scope: the integration connection, assessed per capability rather than as a whole
entity.note: Health is measured over a window. A single error is an event; a pattern across a window is evidence, and only the second one means anything.

requires: a meaningful health threshold crossed over a defined window: an elevated error rate, repeated timeouts, a partial endpoint failure, unexpected latency, authentication instability, or a declared provider degradation
insufficientAlone: one transient error
a single timeout
one slow response

nodes.does: Classify the affected scope - which endpoints, which capabilities, which operations. One endpoint failing does not make the integration unhealthy, and disabling everything because of it is a self-inflicted outage larger than the provider's

nodes.asks: What is the nature of the degradation?

branches.label: Transient
branches.when: the pattern is expected to clear and the affected operations are safe to retry

branches.label: Capability-specific
branches.when: particular capabilities are failing while others are unaffected

branches.label: Whole integration unusable
branches.when: the degradation reaches everything the integration does

nodes.does: Retry with backoff, only for operations where retrying is safe. Operations with external side effects are not retried on a health signal - their safety depends on an idempotency key and a known outcome, neither of which a health metric provides
Mark only the affected capabilities DEGRADED, preserving everything unaffected

until: the degradation worsens past the failure threshold

timeout.after: the operational SLA for this integration
timeout.reason: a degradation that neither clears nor worsens within its SLA is a steady state nobody chose, and it is worth escalating rather than watching indefinitely

nodes.asks: Which way did it move?

branches.label: Recovered
branches.when: the health evidence returned to normal across the window

branches.label: Worsened
branches.when: the degradation crossed the failure threshold

nodes.does: Revalidate the degraded capabilities before restoring them. A metric returning to normal is evidence to check rather than a conclusion to act on - the underlying cause may have been a scope change or a provider deprecation that a health graph cannot see

nodes.state: health restored; capabilities revalidated before being re-enabled
nodes.reEntry: a further threshold crossing is assessed against its own window

nodes.on: degradation reaching the failure threshold
carries: the affected scope and the evidence that established it
which capabilities were still working, so the failure stays scoped to what actually failed

nodes.on: a degradation persisting past its operational SLA
carries: the affected capabilities and how long they have been degraded

guardrails: One transient error is not a degraded integration.
Health is judged on evidence across a defined window.
Healthy capabilities are not disabled because an unrelated endpoint failed.
Operations with external side effects are not retried on a health signal alone.
records.reusableRule: Integration degradation should be scoped to the capabilities actually affected while recovery remains evidence-driven.

records.name: External request → pending outcome → confirm, fail or unknown
records.purpose: Keep submitting an external operation and completing one as separate states, and let an unknown outcome stay unknown.

entity.scope: the individual external operation, keyed by its own correlation and idempotency identifiers
entity.note: The identifiers are recorded before submission, because they are what makes any later retry safe or any later outcome attributable - generating them after a failure is too late to help with that failure.

distinctFrom.because: This owns the operation from submission until an outcome exists. INT-115 owns what happens to local state once one does, and most operations pass through both.

requires: an operation submitted to an external provider on behalf of a business action

nodes.does: Persist the operation id, the provider's request id, the action requested, the target entity, the submission time and the idempotency key, and record the state as PENDING_EXTERNAL_OUTCOME. Submitted is not completed, and nothing downstream may report the business action as done on the strength of this

nodes.asks: What did the provider actually return?

branches.label: An authoritative final outcome
branches.when: the response states the business operation's result, not merely that the request arrived

branches.label: Accepted, not completed
branches.when: the response acknowledges receipt - a 200 that means the request is queued is not the operation completing, and treating it as one is the most common error in this journey

until: a callback or webhook delivers the outcome
a poll returns a final result
the provider confirms out of band

timeout.reason: the window ending means we stopped hearing, which is a fact about our visibility rather than about the provider's work

nodes.does: Record the outcome as UNKNOWN, not as failed. A timeout says our side of the conversation ended; it says nothing about whether the provider completed the operation, and the distance between those two statements is a duplicate charge

nodes.on: an operation whose outcome window closed without an authoritative result
carries: the operation and provider request identifiers needed to ask the provider what actually happened
the idempotency key, so that whatever is established can be acted on without re-submitting
the explicit fact that the outcome is unknown rather than failed
suppresses: any retry of this operation until its true state is established

nodes.on: an authoritative outcome existing for this operation
carries: the outcome and the correlation identifiers it arrived with
what local state expected, so the reconciliation can tell agreement from conflict

guardrails: An HTTP 200 may mean the request was accepted, not that the business operation completed.
A timeout is not a failure.
A blind retry may duplicate an external side effect, so nothing is retried while the outcome is unknown.
Correlation and idempotency identifiers are recorded before submission.
records.reusableRule: External submission and external business completion are separate states; ambiguous outcomes require reconciliation before retry.

records.name: External outcome → local state reconciliation → apply or investigate
records.purpose: Apply an external outcome to local state only after establishing that it belongs here, has not already been applied, and still describes what is true.

entity.scope: the external operation the outcome refers to, and the local entity it would change
entity.note: Correlation comes first. An outcome applied to the wrong entity is a worse failure than one that arrives late, and it is much harder to find afterwards.

requires: an authoritative outcome received from or discovered at a provider
insufficientAlone: an acknowledgement of receipt
a status that the provider describes as intermediate

nodes.does: Match the outcome to the operation and entity it belongs to, using the identifiers recorded at submission

nodes.asks: Could the outcome be correlated to a known operation?

branches.label: Correlated
branches.when: it matches a recorded operation and entity

branches.label: Uncorrelated
branches.when: no recorded operation matches it

nodes.on: a provider event that cannot be matched to a known operation
carries: the event as received, unmodified
the explicit fact that it has not been applied to a best-guess entity

nodes.asks: What does local state say about this outcome?

branches.label: Expected
branches.when: local state is waiting for exactly this outcome on this operation

branches.label: Already applied
branches.when: local state already reflects this same outcome

branches.label: Conflicts
