carries: which of the target, the action, a human requester's standing, or an internal referral's own well-formedness failed to hold up
that nobody decided this - it was rejected by the process, and a corrected request (or a corrected referral) is a new request

nodes.asks: Can deterministic policy already decide this?

branches.label: Policy decides it
branches.when: a rule exists that produces the answer without judgment

branches.label: Judgment is genuinely required
branches.when: the outcome turns on authority, discretion or an assessment no rule encodes

nodes.does: Record that no judgment is required and route to the canonical lifecycle that owns the action. A decision case created because the system was uncertain, rather than because judgment is genuinely needed, puts a person in front of a rule that already had an answer - and the queue it builds is exactly where the real decisions then wait

nodes.on: an action a deterministic rule can decide without review
carries: the requested action and the rule that decides it
the explicit fact that no decision case was opened, so nothing is waiting on a reviewer

nodes.asks: Is required information missing before a case can be opened at all?

branches.label: Complete
branches.when: everything needed to put a real question to a reviewer is present

branches.label: Missing, human/customer-originated
branches.when: the request cannot yet be stated as a question anyone could answer, and there is an interactive requester who can be asked to supply it or to withdraw

branches.label: Missing, internally referred
branches.when: an internal referral from a Runtime Mechanism or another Operational Workflow did not carry everything this decision needs - there is no interactive party to wait on, so the gap is the referring party's own handoff contract to fix

nodes.does: Record PENDING_INFORMATION, naming exactly what is missing. This happens before a case exists, so no reviewer has been handed something incomplete to look at and no review time is consumed by a request that was never askable

timeout.after: the window policy allows an unopened request to wait
timeout.reason: a request that can never be stated is not a decision anyone can make, and holding it open indefinitely leaves the requester believing something is in progress

nodes.does: Record that the referral was incomplete and return it to the referring mechanism/workflow, naming exactly what was missing. There is no interactive party to wait on for an internal referral, so this does not open a pending-information wait - the referring party's own next attempt either supplies what was missing or the underlying condition it was escalating has since resolved on its own

nodes.state: returned to the referring mechanism/workflow; no case was opened
nodes.reEntry: the referring party's own re-escalation, once it carries what was missing, is assessed fresh - this exit does not itself remember what was incomplete about the prior attempt

nodes.asks: How did the wait resolve?

branches.label: Information arrived
branches.when: what was missing was supplied

branches.label: Withdrawn
branches.when: the requester withdrew before supplying it

nodes.does: Record the request as lapsed before a case was opened. Nothing was decided, so this is not a rejection and should not be reported to the requester as one

nodes.state: lapsed before a case was opened; nothing was decided
nodes.reEntry: the same request can be made again with the information present, and it is assessed fresh

nodes.does: Create the decision case with its scope stated explicitly - what is being decided, and what is not. A case whose scope is implicit produces a decision whose reach nobody can establish afterwards, and it will be stretched by people acting in good faith to cover things the reviewer never saw
Determine the review route the decision type and the required authority imply, rather than the route that happens to be fastest

nodes.on: a valid decision case needing ownership
carries: request_id, the case, its explicit scope and the authority the decision requires
the referring party - a human requester or the referring mechanism/workflow's own id
the explicit fact that no review has started and no outcome is implied by the case existing

guardrails: A request submitted is not a review started.
No approval case is created merely because the system is uncertain, where deterministic policy can decide.
The decision scope is explicit rather than inferred from the request.
An open case over the same scope suppresses a second one.

A referring party is either a human/customer requester or a named internal referral (a Runtime Mechanism or another Operational Workflow) - never assumed to be the former by default. An internal referral's own authorization to escalate is established under its own canonical rules, not re-litigated here; only the referral's well-formedness is checked.
An internal referral missing required information is returned to the referring party rather than held on an interactive wait nobody on the other end can answer.
records.reusableRule: A decision workflow should exist only when an authorized judgment is genuinely required and the decision scope is clearly defined.

records.name: Decision case → assign reviewer → accept, reassign or escalate
records.purpose: Put the case in front of someone who is actually authorized to decide it, and make that ownership explicit.

entity.scope: the decision case and the reviewer or authority holding it
entity.note: The deadline belongs to the case, not to the assignment. It survives every reassignment the case goes through.

distinctFrom.because: This moves ownership within the same authority level, because someone is unavailable, conflicted or too slow. Escalation moves it to a different or higher authority, because the current level cannot decide the question at all.

OWN-51 routes work to whoever can do it. This routes a decision to whoever is authorized to make it - availability is not eligibility here, and a decision made by an unauthorized reviewer looks valid and is void.

requires: a valid decision case with a stated scope and a required authority level
insufficientAlone: a case whose owner is deliberating within the time allowed
a work task needing an owner, which is OWN-51's routing

nodes.does: Determine the eligible reviewers or queue from the authority rules the decision type requires. Availability is not eligibility - routing to whoever is free produces a decision made by someone who was not authorized to make it, and it will look exactly like a valid one

nodes.asks: Does anyone with the required authority exist and is available?

branches.label: Available
branches.when: an eligible reviewer at the required authority level can take it

branches.label: Nobody at that level
branches.when: the required authority is absent, exhausted or unavailable

nodes.does: Record ASSIGNED with the reviewer, the authority basis for the assignment, and the case's deadline. Assigned is not reviewed - nothing has been looked at, and a status reading otherwise conceals the gap where most SLA breaches actually happen

until: the reviewer declines, is unavailable, is ineligible or is conflicted

timeout.reason: an assignment nobody accepted is a case nobody owns, and it will sit at the top of a queue looking assigned for as long as the SLA is not enforced

nodes.asks: What happened to the assignment?

branches.label: Accepted
branches.when: the reviewer took ownership of the case

branches.label: Declined or ineligible
branches.when: the reviewer cannot or should not hold it

branches.label: The case was withdrawn
branches.when: the decision is no longer required

nodes.does: Record the case as withdrawn before review, and release the assignment. Nothing was decided and no reviewer time was spent

nodes.state: withdrawn before review; no decision exists
nodes.reEntry: a renewed need for the same judgment is a new request rather than a revival of this assignment

nodes.does: Record the assignment SLA as exceeded, with how long it has sat unaccepted. The case's own deadline is untouched by this - what is late is the acceptance, and the decision was always due when it was due

nodes.asks: Is another reviewer with the required authority available?

branches.label: Another eligible reviewer, within the reassignment budget
branches.when: someone else at the required authority level can take it and the case has not exhausted its reassignment rounds

branches.label: None left, or the budget is exhausted
branches.when: no eligible reviewer remains, or the case has been passed around as many times as the model permits

nodes.does: Reassign, preserving the original deadline and everything already recorded on the case. A reassignment that resets the clock rewards the delay, and one that drops the history makes the next reviewer start from nothing while the requester waits through the same work a second time
Record REVIEW_READY with the accepting reviewer. The case has an owner who has agreed to it, which is the first point at which anyone can be said to be responsible for the outcome

nodes.on: a decision case with an accepted owner
carries: the case, its scope, its evidence and the deadline that has travelled with it
the explicit fact that ownership is not review - the state changes again when work actually starts

nodes.on: a case the required authority level cannot take
carries: the case, every assignment attempted and why each failed
the original deadline, which the escalation preserves rather than restarts

guardrails: Assigned is not reviewed.
Routing follows authority requirements rather than convenience.
Reassignment preserves the original deadline and the review history.
Reassignment is bounded rather than repeated until someone happens to accept.
records.reusableRule: Review ownership should be assigned to an actor with the authority and context required to make the requested decision.

records.name: Review started → evaluate evidence → decide or request more information
records.purpose: Turn sufficient evidence into an authorized decision, within the scope the reviewer actually holds.

entity.scope: the decision case and this instance of review against it
entity.note: A case can have several review instances across reassignments and reopenings. Each is recorded; none replaces the last.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-84 recovers from a verification that failed - a mechanical outcome with retry and remediation routes. This is a person exercising judgment against criteria, where the failure mode is deciding outside your authority rather than failing a check.

requires: an authorized reviewer beginning work on an owned decision case
insufficientAlone: a case being assigned, which puts it in front of someone and starts nothing
a case being opened in an interface, where the booking of the state is what matters rather than the page view

nodes.does: Record UNDER_REVIEW with who is reviewing and when it started. Assigned and under review are different states, and the gap between them is where most SLA breaches actually live

Evaluate the available authoritative evidence against the criteria that apply. What is evaluated is evidence - an absent document is absent, and a reviewer's sense of what it probably said is not a substitute for it

nodes.asks: Is this reviewer actually valid for this case?

branches.label: Valid
branches.when: no conflict of interest and no eligibility problem

branches.label: Conflicted or ineligible
branches.when: a conflict or eligibility problem surfaces during the review itself

nodes.does: Record the conflict and step back without deciding. A decision made by a conflicted reviewer is worse than no decision, because it looks like one and will be relied on

nodes.on: a conflict or eligibility problem found mid-review
carries: the case, the evidence gathered so far and the reason this reviewer stepped back
the original deadline, and the explicit fact that no decision was made

nodes.asks: Is this decision within the reviewer's authorized scope?

branches.label: Within scope
branches.when: the reviewer holds the authority the decision requires

branches.label: Beyond it
branches.when: the decision needs an authority level or a discretion this reviewer does not hold

nodes.on: a decision requiring authority the current reviewer does not hold
carries: the evidence and the assessment reached so far, which the escalation preserves
the specific authority the decision requires, so the escalation goes somewhere rather than upward in general

nodes.asks: Does a non-overridable policy constraint bear on this decision?

branches.label: It does, with no exception authority
branches.when: a hard constraint applies and this reviewer cannot set it aside

branches.label: It does, and explicit exception authority exists
branches.when: the reviewer holds a defined authority to grant an exception to it

branches.label: No hard constraint applies
branches.when: the decision is a judgment within ordinary criteria

nodes.does: Record that the decision is constrained by a policy this reviewer cannot override, and decide within it. Manual review that silently overrides a hard constraint produces an approved action the system will later refuse - wasting the review - or will not refuse, which is worse

Record the exception being exercised, the authority for it and the constraint it displaces. An exception exercised without being named is indistinguishable from the constraint not existing, and the next person to look will conclude it never did

nodes.asks: Is the evidence sufficient to decide?

branches.label: Sufficient
branches.when: everything the criteria require is present and assessable

branches.label: Something required is missing
branches.when: a fact the decision turns on is not available

nodes.on: a review blocked by missing evidence
carries: the exact requirement the decision turns on, and why
everything the review has already established, which is preserved rather than discarded

nodes.does: Produce the authorized decision within the case's stated scope - approved, rejected, partially approved, or another explicitly defined outcome. The decision records what it covers, because a decision whose reach is implicit is stretched later by people who were not in the room

nodes.asks: What was decided?

branches.label: Approved
branches.when: the whole requested scope was authorized

branches.label: Partially approved
branches.when: part of the requested scope was authorized and part was not

branches.label: Rejected
branches.when: the requested action was refused

nodes.on: an approved decision
carries: the decision, its maker, its scope, its conditions and its validity where one applies
the explicit fact that approving authorizes an action and performs none of it

nodes.on: a partially approved decision
carries: which scope was approved and which was refused, separately and explicitly
the basis for each, so the partition can be explained rather than reconstructed

nodes.on: a rejected decision
carries: the reason and its category, the maker, the time and the affected scope
the explicit fact that this is an authorized business outcome rather than a failure

guardrails: A review started is not an approval.
Missing evidence is never invented or assumed.
A reviewer decides only within their authorized scope.
Manual review never silently overrides a hard policy constraint without explicit exception authority.
records.reusableRule: Human review converts sufficient evidence into an authorized decision while unresolved evidence remains an explicit information requirement.

records.name: Approval decision → revalidate target → execute, hold or invalidate
records.purpose: Carry an authorization into execution, having checked it still applies to what it was granted against.

entity.scope: the approved decision and the target action it authorizes
entity.note: The approval and the action are two things. The approval is complete the moment it is made; the action has not started.

distinctFrom.because: This carries a whole authorized scope into execution. DEC-187 exists because a partitioned scope raises a separate problem - which parts may proceed, and whether the action can be half-done at all.

requires: an authorized approval decision covering a stated scope

nodes.does: Record the decision, the decision maker, the scope, the time, any conditions attached, and the validity or effective period where one applies. Approved is an authorization - it is not an event that has happened to the target, and the two are recorded as different things

nodes.asks: Is the approved action being executed now?

branches.label: Now
branches.when: execution follows the decision immediately

branches.label: Later
branches.when: the approval will be used at some later point, or carries a validity period

nodes.on: an approval that will be used later than it was granted
carries: the approval, its scope, its conditions and the target version it was granted against
the explicit fact that the gap between decision and use is where a stale approval mutates state nobody authorized

nodes.does: Re-read the target's current state before executing. The approval was granted against the target as it was; executing it against a target that has since changed applies an authorization to something nobody authorized, and the reviewer will be named as having approved it

nodes.asks: Is the target still what was approved?

branches.label: Unchanged in any material way
branches.when: nothing the approval turned on has moved

branches.label: Materially changed
branches.when: something the decision depended on is different

nodes.asks: What do the decision's own semantics require for a changed target?

branches.label: Hold pending re-review
branches.when: the change is material and the semantics send it back rather than voiding it

branches.label: Invalidate
branches.when: the semantics void the approval once its basis moves

branches.label: The change is inside what was approved
branches.when: the approval's scope explicitly contemplated variation of this kind

nodes.does: Hold execution and record what changed. Nothing is executed on an approval whose basis has moved, and nothing is voided either - which of the two applies is a judgment, and it goes back to one

nodes.on: an approval whose target changed materially before execution
carries: the original decision, preserved, and exactly what has changed since
the explicit fact that nothing was executed and the original approval was not edited

nodes.does: Record the approval as invalidated by the change in its basis, preserving the decision itself. It was validly made and its subject no longer exists in the form it was made about

nodes.state: approval invalidated by a changed target; the decision record stands unedited
nodes.reEntry: the action, if still wanted, needs a new decision against the target as it now is. This is not the request having been rejected

nodes.asks: Does the approval carry conditions that must be satisfied before execution?

branches.label: Conditions apply
branches.when: the approval was granted subject to something happening first

branches.label: Unconditional
branches.when: nothing stands between the approval and the action

nodes.asks: Are the conditions satisfied?

branches.label: Satisfied
branches.when: every condition attached to the approval is authoritatively met

branches.label: Not yet
branches.when: at least one condition is outstanding

nodes.does: Record the approval as authorized and not yet executable, naming the outstanding condition. A conditional approval treated as an unconditional one executes an action the reviewer explicitly qualified

timeout.after: the approval's validity period, or the bounded window policy allows a conditional approval to stand
timeout.reason: an approval waiting indefinitely on a condition that never arrives is an authorization with no expiry that nobody decided to grant

nodes.does: Record the approval as expired before its conditions were met. This is not the request having been rejected - it was approved, and the window closed while it waited

nodes.state: APPROVAL_EXPIRED before execution; the approval stands in the record as having been granted
nodes.reEntry: a fresh decision request can be made against the current target. The requester is told the approval lapsed rather than that they were refused

nodes.on: an approval that is valid, in scope and unconditional or satisfied
carries: the exact authorized scope, and the canonical lifecycle that owns the action - the payment, the access grant, the fulfillment, the entitlement change or the account change
the explicit instruction that the approval does not replace that lifecycle's own validation, and that execution is not complete until that lifecycle says it is

guardrails: Approved is not executed.
An approval never bypasses the execution lifecycle's own validation.
An approval applies only to the scope it defined.
A stale approval never mutates newer incompatible state.
records.reusableRule: Approval authorizes a defined action but execution must still confirm that the approved action remains valid against current state.

records.name: Rejection decision → record reason → remediate, close or reapply
records.purpose: Treat a refusal as the business outcome it is, and say what if anything the requester can do next.

entity.scope: the decision case and the rejection issued against it
entity.note: A rejection closes a decision, not a relationship. What follows it comes from policy rather than from how final the word sounds.

distinctFrom.because: This is the first decision's rejection outcome. FBK-47 is the appeal or reconsideration lifecycle, which exists only where policy grants that right - and this journey hands to it rather than performing it.

OWN-59 handles an approval rejected inside a work-ownership flow and asks whether a revision may be resubmitted. This is the decision-case rejection with its full reason taxonomy, and its three separate exits: correctable, reapplicable, and appealable.

requires: an authorized rejection decision on a decision case, within the reviewer's scope
insufficientAlone: a technical failure to process the request, which is an error rather than a decision and belongs in a different queue

nodes.does: Record the reason and its category, the decision maker, the time, the affected scope, and the reapplication or remediation semantics where they are defined. A rejection is an authorized business outcome rather than a technical failure - recording it as an error puts it in the wrong queue, where something will eventually retry it

nodes.asks: Is the reason something the requester can correct?

branches.label: Correctable, with a defined remediation path
branches.when: policy states what would have to change and permits the case to proceed on that basis

branches.label: Not correctable this way
branches.when: the reason is not something a correction addresses, or no remediation path is defined

nodes.does: State exactly what would have to change, drawn from the policy that defines the path. A rejection reason that is not actionable is a refusal, and telling someone their request was declined without saying what would change that is where most escalations come from

nodes.state: rejected, with a defined remediation path stated
nodes.reEntry: the requester satisfying the stated condition opens a new decision request linked to this one, so the reviewer sees what was refused and why

nodes.asks: Does policy permit a new request once the requirements are satisfied?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: policy defines when and on what basis a new request may be made

branches.label: It does not, or says nothing
branches.when: no reapplication right is defined

nodes.does: Record the reapplication conditions policy actually defines - after what period, on what basis, with what evidence. Nothing is invented here: a right to reapply that does not exist becomes one people rely on the moment it is stated, and withdrawing it later is worse than never offering it

nodes.state: rejected, with a defined reapplication right
nodes.reEntry: a new request under those conditions is a new decision case, linked to this one. Nothing resubmits automatically - an automatic resubmission either loops or hides the rejection from whoever needed to see it

nodes.asks: Does policy grant an appeal or reconsideration right?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: a defined appeal or reconsideration mechanism covers this decision

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: no appeal right is defined for this kind of decision

nodes.on: a rejection policy grants an appeal right against
carries: the decision, its reason, its maker and the evidence it was made on
the explicit fact that the appeal reviews the decision and does not re-run it as a fresh request

nodes.does: Record CLOSED_REJECTED with the full reason. The request is not resubmitted automatically and the rejection history stays readable - it is the answer to why this was refused, and it will be asked for

nodes.state: CLOSED_REJECTED; a terminal authorized outcome with no defined path onward
nodes.reEntry: a materially different request is a different case. Repeating the same one changes nothing and is not treated as new

guardrails: Rejected is not a system failure.
Rejected requests are never automatically resubmitted.
Appeal and reapplication rights are never invented.
The rejection history remains auditable.
records.reusableRule: A rejection is an authorized business outcome whose next path depends on whether policy permits correction, reapplication or appeal.

records.name: Partial approval → split scope → execute approved, resolve remaining
records.purpose: Make the authorized and unauthorized halves of one request explicit, so only the first can move.

entity.scope: the decision case and the partitions of its requested scope
entity.note: Every part of the original scope lands in exactly one partition. A part in none of them is a piece of the request nobody answered and nobody will notice.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-185 executes an authorization whose scope is whole. This has to partition a scope first, and then answer a question DEC-185 never faces: whether the action can be half-done at all.

requires: an authorized decision approving part of a requested scope and not the rest

nodes.does: Partition the originally requested scope into what is approved, what is rejected, and what remains pending or needs further review. Every part of the original lands in exactly one - a part in none of them is a piece of the request nobody answered, and the requester finds out by it silently not happening

Persist the decision basis for each partition separately. Approved with exceptions, recorded as a single note, cannot tell anyone six months later which exception applied to what - and that is exactly the question an audit of a partial approval asks

nodes.asks: Is any scope still unresolved rather than decided either way?

branches.label: Some remains open
branches.when: part of the scope needs further review or further evidence

branches.label: Everything is decided
branches.when: each part is either approved or rejected

nodes.does: Keep the unresolved scope active as a live decision case rather than closing it with the rest. Closing a partially approved request as decided leaves the unanswered portion invisible, and the requester assumes it was refused - which is a rejection nobody made and nobody can explain

nodes.asks: Do the governing semantics permit the approved scope to proceed on its own?

branches.label: Separable
branches.when: the action's semantics explicitly allow partial execution

branches.label: Atomic
branches.when: the action's semantics require all of it or none

branches.label: Atomicity is not defined
branches.when: nothing authoritative says whether this action can be half-done

nodes.on: a partial approval against an action with no defined atomicity
carries: the partitions and the action they would apply to
the explicit fact that no atomicity was assumed - whether a thing can be half-done is a property of the thing, and guessing it is how half-provisioned accounts and partly fulfilled contracts appear

nodes.does: Hold the entire action. Executing part of an atomic action produces a half-state the system has no name for, cannot report on, and cannot roll back cleanly

nodes.state: entire action held; the approved scope is authorized and unexecuted because the action cannot be split
nodes.reEntry: when the remaining scope is decided, the whole action is re-evaluated as one rather than assembled from the parts that were approved at different times

nodes.asks: Does the approved scope share side effects with the rejected or pending scope?

branches.label: It shares
branches.when: a charge, a provisioning step or a notification would otherwise run per partition

branches.label: Independent
branches.when: the approved scope's effects touch nothing the other partitions touch

nodes.does: Execute the shared side effect once, for the approved scope only. Splitting a request and running its shared effects per partition charges twice, provisions twice or notifies twice - and the duplicate is found by the recipient rather than by the split that caused it

nodes.on: an approved partition that may proceed independently
carries: only the approved scope, stated explicitly, and the canonical lifecycle that owns the action
the rejected scope, stated explicitly as something that must not be executed - a reviewer refused it, and it travelling in the same request is not authorization
suppresses: any execution touching the rejected or unresolved scope

guardrails: Partial approval is not full approval.
The rejected scope is never executed.
Shared side effects are not duplicated when the scope is split.
Atomicity semantics are never invented.
records.reusableRule: Partial approval should make the authorized and unauthorized portions explicit so only valid scope can proceed.

records.name: Approval validity or expiry → revalidate → use, expire or renew review
records.purpose: Answer, at the moment of use, whether an approval is still one - in time, in context and in count.

entity.scope: the approval decision and the boundaries it was granted within
entity.note: Validity is a question asked at each use rather than a flag set once. An approval valid this morning can be outside its context this afternoon without any clock having run out.

requires: an approval carrying an explicit validity condition, or an approval being used later than it was granted

nodes.does: Evaluate the approval's scope, its valid-from and valid-until where those are defined, the target version or state it was granted against, its conditions, and whether a single-use approval has already been consumed

nodes.asks: Does this approval define an expiry?

branches.label: It defines one
branches.when: a valid-until, a period or a use-by condition was set when it was granted

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the approval was granted without a time limit

nodes.does: Record that this approval carries no expiry, rather than assigning one. Inventing an expiry invalidates authorizations that were granted without limit, and the holder discovers it when the thing they were approved for stops working with no decision behind it

nodes.asks: Is it inside its validity window?

branches.label: Inside
branches.when: the current time falls within valid-from and valid-until

branches.label: Past valid-until
branches.when: the window has closed

nodes.asks: Is this a single-use approval that has already been consumed?

branches.label: Already used
branches.when: the approval permits one use and one has been recorded

branches.label: Not consumed
branches.when: the approval is reusable, or its single use has not happened

nodes.does: Refuse the reuse and record the attempt. A single-use approval used twice authorizes an action once and performs it twice, which is the same failure as a duplicate payment with a signature on it

nodes.state: already consumed; the approval cannot authorize a second execution
nodes.reEntry: a further execution needs a further approval, which is a new decision rather than a re-reading of this one

nodes.asks: Is the target still in the state the approval was granted against?

branches.label: Same, or within what was approved
branches.when: the target's version or state matches what the reviewer was looking at, or the variation is inside the approved scope

branches.label: Changed beyond the approved context
branches.when: the target has moved in a way the approval did not contemplate

nodes.does: Record that valid time was not enough: the approval is inside its window and outside its context. A time-valid approval against a target that has changed is the most convincing kind of wrong authorization, because every visible check passes

nodes.on: an unexpired approval whose target has moved beyond its context
carries: the original approval, preserved, and what has changed in the target since
the explicit fact that nothing was executed and the approval was not edited

nodes.does: Record the approval as usable within its scope, and record this use where the approval is counted. Validity is established at the moment of use rather than carried as a flag someone set earlier

nodes.state: valid and usable within its stated scope
nodes.reEntry: each further use re-evaluates from here, because time, target state and consumption can all have moved since the last one

nodes.does: Record APPROVAL_EXPIRED. This is not the request having been rejected: it was approved, and the authorization lapsed before it was used - and telling the holder the wrong one of those changes whether they think asking again is worth anything

nodes.asks: Does policy allow a renewed review of a lapsed approval?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: policy defines how a lapsed approval may be sought again

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: no renewal path is defined

nodes.on: a lapsed approval policy allows to be sought again
carries: the expired approval and the decision it recorded, as context for the new one
the explicit fact that this is a new decision request against the current target rather than an extension of the old approval

nodes.state: APPROVAL_EXPIRED; the approval stands in the record as having been granted and unused
nodes.reEntry: a new decision request against the current target is assessed fresh, and this lapse is not held against it

guardrails: An approval expiry is never invented where none exists.
Valid time alone is not sufficient where an approval is state-specific or version-specific.
An expired approval is not a rejected request.
A single-use approval cannot authorize a second execution.
records.reusableRule: An approval remains usable only within the time, state and scope boundaries under which it was authorized.

records.name: Decision escalation → higher authority → decide, return or reassign
records.purpose: Move a case to an authority that can actually resolve it, carrying the work already done and predetermining nothing.

entity.scope: the decision case and the escalation acting on it
entity.note: The case is one case throughout. Escalation changes who holds it and changes neither the evidence nor the deadline.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-182 moves ownership at the same authority level because someone cannot take it. This moves the case to a different or higher authority because the current level cannot decide the question at all.
OWN-55 escalates responsibility for work that is stuck. This escalates decision authority specifically - the case is not stuck, it is in front of someone who is not permitted to answer it.

requires: a defined escalation criterion being met - an authority threshold, a policy exception, material risk, a reviewer conflict, complexity, SLA governance, or a disagreement requiring higher authority
insufficientAlone: a case being difficult, which is a reason to think rather than a reason to pass it upward

nodes.does: Record the escalation reason. Escalated is not approved - the case remains undecided and is now in front of someone else, and a status that reads as progress toward approval misleads everyone waiting on it

Preserve the existing evidence, the review history, the original deadline and any non-final assessments already made. An escalation that starts the case from nothing throws away the work that identified why it needed escalating in the first place

nodes.asks: Does an eligible higher or different authority exist?

branches.label: One exists
branches.when: a defined authority level above or beside this one can take the decision

branches.label: None
branches.when: no eligible authority exists, or the escalation levels the model defines are exhausted

nodes.does: Record that no eligible authority exists for this decision, and stop. A case escalated into a level that does not exist becomes permanently owned by nobody, which is the failure mode that makes escalation chains dangerous rather than merely slow

nodes.state: no authority exists to decide this; the case is stopped and named rather than circulating
nodes.reEntry: an authority being defined for this decision type reopens it. Until then it is visibly unresolvable rather than invisibly unassigned

nodes.does: Route to the eligible authority, within the escalation levels the model actually defines. Escalation is bounded - a case that can escalate indefinitely has no owner at any level, and each hop makes the next one easier to justify

until: the escalated authority is able to decide
the escalated authority requires more information
the escalated authority returns the case with direction

timeout.after: the case's original deadline, preserved rather than restarted
timeout.reason: the requester's deadline was never about who happens to be holding the case. An escalation that resets it makes the delay invisible to everyone except the person waiting

nodes.asks: What did the escalated authority do?

branches.label: They can decide
branches.when: the authority holds what the decision requires and is ready to review

branches.label: More information is required
branches.when: the escalated authority identifies evidence the decision turns on

branches.label: Returned with direction
branches.when: the authority gives guidance and sends the case back to be decided at the original level

nodes.on: an escalated case an eligible authority will review
carries: every piece of evidence and every prior assessment, preserved
the specific authority now holding it, which still acts only within what it was granted

nodes.on: an escalated case blocked by missing evidence
carries: the requirement the escalated authority identified
the review history from both levels, so nothing is asked for twice

nodes.does: Record the direction given and return the case to the original level, which decides within it. The higher authority acted only within its own granted authority - guidance is not a decision, and recording it as one attributes an outcome to someone who declined to make it

nodes.on: a case returned with direction rather than decided
carries: the direction given and the authority that gave it
the original deadline, still unchanged, and the explicit fact that no decision was made at the escalated level

nodes.on: an escalated case outliving the deadline it preserved
carries: the case, every level it has passed through and how long each held it
the explicit fact that this is now an ownership problem rather than a decision problem

guardrails: Escalated is not approved.
Escalation never erases previous review work.
Escalation is bounded by defined levels rather than repeated indefinitely.
A higher authority still acts only within the authority it was granted.
records.reusableRule: Escalation changes who is authorized to resolve a decision without changing the underlying evidence or pretending a decision has already been made.

records.name: Decision superseded or reopened → revalidate → continue or new decision
records.purpose: Let a decision be reconsidered without any part of the original being rewritten.

entity.scope: the existing decision and the event challenging it
entity.note: The original decision is immutable. A new decision supersedes it as a later record rather than replacing it in place.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-58 asks whether a material change after approval needs re-approval, inside a work-ownership flow. This owns the decision record's history: what supersedes what, what was already executed, and what a new decision does not undo.

requires: a material event bearing on a prior decision - new evidence, a material target-state change, an authorized reconsideration, an error in the previous decision, or an upstream authoritative correction
insufficientAlone: the requester disagreeing with the outcome, which is an appeal and runs through the appeal mechanism
new information arriving, most of which confirms what was already concluded

nodes.does: Preserve the original decision as a historical fact, exactly as recorded. Nothing about it is edited - a decision record changed in place removes the ability to say what was decided, by whom, and on what basis, which is the only thing anyone ever actually needs from it

Assess whether the event genuinely bears on the decision. New evidence arriving is not the previous decision becoming wrong - most of it confirms what was already concluded, and reopening for each arriving fact produces a case that never closes

nodes.asks: Does the existing decision still hold?

branches.label: It holds
branches.when: the event does not change what the decision turned on

branches.label: Genuinely challenged
branches.when: the event bears directly on the basis the decision was made on

nodes.does: Retain the decision and record that it was reconsidered and held. No duplicate review is opened, and the fact that it was looked at again is itself worth having in the record

nodes.state: original decision retained; reconsidered and unchanged
nodes.reEntry: a further event is assessed on its own merits rather than accumulating into a reopening by weight of attempts

nodes.asks: Is reconsideration authorized, and is it the same decision scope?

branches.label: Authorized, same scope
branches.when: someone with the authority to reconsider is doing so, over the same question

branches.label: Authorized, but a different question
branches.when: what is now being asked is not what the original decision covered

branches.label: Not authorized
branches.when: no reconsideration right or authority applies

nodes.state: reconsideration not authorized; the original decision stands
nodes.reEntry: where policy grants an appeal right, it is exercised through the appeal mechanism rather than by reopening the case here

nodes.does: Create a new decision case, linked to the previous one. A different question decided under an old case's scope produces a decision that reads as covering something it never considered, and it will be relied on that way

nodes.on: a materially different question raised against a decided case
carries: the prior decision and its evidence, as linked context rather than as the scope
the explicit fact that the prior decision stands and is not superseded by this one being opened

nodes.does: Record the case REOPENED, carrying the original decision and all prior evidence forward. Reopened is not the original decision deleted - and the new decision, when it comes, supersedes the old one as a later authoritative record rather than replacing it

nodes.asks: Was the previous decision already executed?

branches.label: Not executed
branches.when: the decision authorized something that never happened

branches.label: Already executed
branches.when: the authorized action was carried out and its consequences are real

nodes.does: Record what was executed and when. The consequences happened - money moved, access was granted, something shipped - and pretending the execution never occurred leaves real effects in place with nothing in the record explaining them

nodes.asks: Do the executed consequences need correcting regardless of what the new decision concludes?

branches.label: They need correcting now
branches.when: the execution was wrong on its own terms - an error, or an upstream correction that invalidates it

branches.label: They stand pending the new decision
branches.when: the execution was validly made and only the reconsidered decision can change what should follow

nodes.on: executed consequences that need correcting independently of the reconsidered decision
carries: what was executed, on whose authority and when
the explicit fact that changing the decision record does not undo any of it - the correction is its own lifecycle with its own outcome

nodes.on: a reopened case ready to be decided again
carries: the original decision, preserved, and everything that has changed since
whether the original was executed, so the new decision is made knowing what already exists in the world

guardrails: Reopened is not the original decision deleted.
New evidence does not automatically invalidate an old decision.
Executed consequences may require a separate correction or reversal lifecycle.
The historical decision record is never mutated in place.
records.reusableRule: Decision reconsideration should preserve prior decisions as history while creating a new authoritative decision state only when current evidence and authority justify it.

records.name: Policy check → evaluate → pass, block or review
records.purpose: Decide whether a specific action is permitted under the rules that actually govern it, at the version that actually applies.

entity.scope: the policy evaluation, the actor or entity it concerns, and the proposed action
entity.note: One evaluation per action per decision point. It is a question about this action rather than a standing judgment about the entity.

distinctFrom.because: This applies rules. DEC-181 opens a workflow for judgment where no rule produces the answer - which is why this journey's third outcome is to hand over rather than to guess.

requires: a proposed action that policy governs, arriving at the point where it is decided
insufficientAlone: a risk score, which estimates likelihood rather than establishing whether a rule permits something

nodes.does: Determine the applicable policy set from the action, the entity, the context, the effective time, the jurisdiction or domain where one is defined, and the current authoritative state. Which rules apply is a fact about this action rather than a global list run against everything

nodes.asks: Is the policy version effective for this action and time determinable?

branches.label: Determinable
branches.when: the applicable version and its effective period are authoritatively known

branches.label: Not determinable
branches.when: which version governs this action cannot be established

nodes.does: Record that the governing policy version could not be established, and evaluate nothing. Picking the current version because it is the one to hand judges an action by a rule that may not have existed when it was taken

Evaluate the requirements of that version against the facts. What is evaluated is a rule against a fact - a risk score is not a policy check, and substituting one produces a block whose reason nobody can state to the person it lands on

nodes.asks: What did the rules determine?

branches.label: Every requirement satisfied
branches.when: the applicable rules permit the action

branches.label: An explicit blocking condition applies
branches.when: a requirement is unmet or a prohibition applies

branches.label: The rules do not determine it
branches.when: no deterministic outcome follows from the applicable policy

nodes.does: Record POLICY_PASS with the version evaluated and what was checked. The record is what makes the pass auditable later - a permitted action with no evaluation behind it cannot be defended

nodes.state: POLICY_PASS for this action under the version evaluated
nodes.reEntry: a later action is evaluated on its own terms. This pass is not a standing clearance and does not carry to anything else

nodes.does: Record POLICY_BLOCK with the rule, its version and the requirement that failed. A block is a rule applying and says nothing about intent - recording it as suspicion attaches a reputation to somebody who hit a threshold

nodes.state: POLICY_BLOCK; this action is not permitted under the applicable rule
nodes.reEntry: the requirement being satisfied, or an authorized exception being granted for it, makes the same action evaluable again. The block concerns this attempt under this version and nothing wider

nodes.does: Record REVIEW_REQUIRED. This is the rules running out rather than a violation being found: nothing has been decided, nothing has been refused, and reporting it to the requester as a rejection is untrue

nodes.on: an action policy cannot determine, or whose governing version cannot be established
carries: the action, the policy set considered and exactly where the rules stopped
the explicit fact that no outcome was invented and nothing has been refused

guardrails: A policy check is not a risk score.
A policy block is not evidence of malicious behaviour.
Policy requirements are never invented.
Evaluation uses the policy version effective for the relevant action and time.
records.reusableRule: Policy evaluation determines whether a specific action is permitted under the rules applicable to that action's current context.

records.name: Risk signal → correlate evidence → clear, monitor, restrict or review
records.purpose: Turn a measurement into a state change no larger than the evidence behind it supports, and no longer-lived than the question stays open.

entity.scope: the risk case and the actor, account, transaction or resource it concerns
entity.note: One case per correlated risk, accumulating signals. A case that opens per signal produces a queue of fragments nobody can assess together. The case is scoped to what the evidence is actually about - a flagged transaction is a flagged transaction, and reading it as a flagged customer is how one anomaly becomes a permanent mark. risk_subject_id is that specific evidence subject (the actor, account, transaction or resource the signal concerns), never the broader actor generally - a.case is the atomic authority for that identity: two signals correlating to the same subject at the same time settle on one case between them, never two.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-90 handles a specific suspicion - that an account is in someone else's hands - and runs a containment and recovery path for it. This is the general evidence lifecycle: most of what it sees clears, and its main job is not over-reacting.

This weighs uncertainty: how reliable the evidence is and what it supports, with no rule needing to have been broken for the question to be worth asking. RSK-194 starts only where an identifiable policy appears to have been breached, and tests that rule against the evidence and the version that governed it. A signal does not become a violation candidate by looking risky - without a governing rule to test, there is nothing for RSK-194 to decide.

requires: a meaningful risk signal - a behaviour or velocity anomaly, an identity inconsistency, a transaction anomaly, a device or context signal, an external risk signal, or repeated unusual activity
a recorded source for it - detection, monitoring, a model, an external party or a dispute outcome - which is context for weighing the signal and never corroboration of it
insufficientAlone: unusual behaviour, which is unusual and not therefore wrong
a single threshold crossing, which is a reading rather than a finding

nodes.does: Correlate the signal with the authoritative context that bears on it - the actor's history, the state of the thing it concerns, other live signals, and what this signal is actually measuring. A model output is an estimate about a person and never a fact about them

nodes.asks: Is the signal clearly benign in context?

branches.label: Benign or a known false positive
branches.when: the context explains it entirely

branches.label: Not explained away
branches.when: the context does not account for it

nodes.does: Record CLEAR with the reason. Clearing is a fact worth keeping - the same signal will fire again on the same behaviour, and a system that never records the clear re-investigates it every time and eventually acts on the repetition

nodes.state: CLEAR; no risk state was created and nothing was restricted
nodes.reEntry: a materially different signal opens its own assessment. The recorded clear is context for it rather than an exemption from it

nodes.asks: What does the combined evidence support?

branches.label: Below any defined threshold
branches.when: the evidence is real and does not reach what policy requires for action

branches.label: A deterministic rule requires blocking
branches.when: a governing rule, rather than an assessment, produces the outcome

branches.label: A material threshold is reached
branches.when: the combined evidence crosses a defined threshold requiring intervention

nodes.does: Record MONITOR and take no restrictive action. Watching is a state in its own right; restricting on one weak signal is a decision the evidence does not support, and the person it lands on did nothing to earn it

until: the evidence accumulating on this case reaches a defined threshold
the accumulated evidence explains the signal as benign

timeout.after: the monitoring horizon defined for this signal type
timeout.reason: a signal that never reaches a threshold is not held open on the actor indefinitely - an unresolved risk state is its own cost to whoever carries it, and nothing was ever established to justify carrying it

nodes.asks: What did the accumulated evidence settle?

branches.label: Benign on the accumulated evidence
branches.when: what arrived explains the signal rather than supporting it

branches.label: A material threshold is now reached
branches.when: the accumulated evidence crosses what policy requires for intervention

nodes.does: Record CLEAR with the reason and release the monitoring state, along with anything held or held back only because the case was open. The case and every signal on it stay readable - clearing a suspicion is not the same as never having had one, and that difference is what tells a first occurrence from a fifth

nodes.state: CLEAR after monitoring; the monitoring state is released and nothing was restricted
nodes.reEntry: a materially different signal opens its own assessment, judged with this case as context rather than as a finding against the actor

nodes.state: monitoring horizon passed without resolution; nothing was restricted
nodes.reEntry: the state does not persist on the actor once the horizon passes. A recurrence is assessed fresh, informed by this case rather than convicted by it

nodes.does: Record the rule that applies and its outcome. This is a rule applying rather than an assessment being made, and the two are recorded differently because only one of them can be argued with

Atomically record the risk case for this risk_subject_id: if no open case already exists for it, create one with its evidence and the provenance of each piece; if a concurrent evaluation already opened one for the same subject between the evidence check and this action, fold this evidence into the existing case rather than creating a second one. A risk state whose basis cannot be shown cannot be appealed, explained or corrected - and this is exactly the state someone will eventually ask us to justify

nodes.asks: What does the evidence call for?

branches.label: A scoped precautionary restriction
branches.when: the risk is material enough that acting now is proportionate to the evidence

branches.label: Judgment before any restriction
branches.when: the evidence is material and the right response is not something a rule determines

nodes.on: risk evidence warranting a scoped restriction
carries: the correlated evidence, its provenance and the specific scope the risk touches
the explicit fact that this is evidence rather than confirmed misconduct, which bounds how wide the restriction may be

nodes.on: material risk evidence needing authorized judgment
carries: the full evidence and its provenance, so the reviewer sees what the model saw
the explicit fact that nothing has been restricted and no conclusion has been drawn about the actor

guardrails: A signal is not confirmed misconduct. The state it opens is a question, and most of them close without an answer against anyone.
An anomaly is not fraud. Unusual and wrong are different findings resting on different evidence.
A risk score is not a factual identity.
A model score is not an authoritative decision unless it has been explicitly governed as one, which is a decision made outside this journey.
One weak signal never triggers maximum restriction. What gets restricted is proportionate to the evidence, and the evidence is what bounds its scope.
Monitoring is not restriction. Watching an open question is a state in its own right, and collapsing the two restricts people the evidence never reached.
This journey restricts nothing itself. Where a restriction is warranted it hands to the journey whose job that is, carrying the fact that nothing has been concluded.
A signal later cleared stays auditable. Erasing it removes the ability to tell a first occurrence from a fifth.
Evidence and its provenance are preserved so the reasoning can be shown.

Concurrent evaluation of the same risk_subject_id yields at most one canonical case - a.case is atomic on that identity, and a losing concurrent evaluator folds its evidence into the existing case rather than opening a second one.
records.reusableRule: Risk signals should change state only in proportion to the combined evidence and the policy-defined consequence of that evidence.

records.name: Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
records.purpose: Stop the smallest thing that manages the risk, and keep a stated route back.

entity.scope: the risk case and the specific capability or action being restricted
entity.note: The restriction is scoped to the risk. Risk owns why and until when; the access lifecycle owns what is actually switched off.

distinctFrom.because: This determines what restriction the risk justifies and holds the release condition. ACC-78 applies and restores the access state. One is the reason, the other is the door.

requires: a defined risk threshold reached, with the correlated evidence behind it

nodes.does: Determine the risk's scope, the specific action or capability implicated, the authority for restricting it, and the duration or review condition where one is defined. A restriction with no stated release condition has no way out and becomes permanent by nobody's decision

nodes.asks: Is there authority to apply this restriction?

branches.label: Authorized
branches.when: a policy or a granted authority permits restricting this scope on this evidence

branches.label: Not established
branches.when: no policy or authority covers restricting this

nodes.does: Choose the smallest restriction sufficient for the identified risk - a hold on the specific transaction, a block on the specific capability, an additional verification, a manual approval requirement, or a bounded access restriction. The restriction's scope matches the risk's scope: an anomaly on one payment method is not a reason to close an account

nodes.asks: Could additional verification resolve this on its own?

branches.label: Verification would resolve it
branches.when: the risk is about who is acting, and proving it would answer the question

branches.label: A restriction is needed regardless
branches.when: the risk is not one a challenge answers

nodes.does: Raise the step-up requirement through the authentication lifecycle, which owns the challenge. This journey keeps the restriction and the release condition, because a passed challenge has to release something and the challenge itself cannot know what

Raise the restriction through the access and capability lifecycle, which owns what is switched off and how. Record it as temporary and reviewable - a temporary restriction is not a final adverse decision, and a system that cannot tell the two apart never releases anything it has stopped

until: the risk clears or the required evidence arrives

timeout.after: the review condition or maximum restriction duration policy defines
timeout.reason: a restriction nobody revisits becomes a termination without a decision, and the person under it has no way to tell the difference

nodes.asks: How did the restriction resolve?

branches.label: Cleared
branches.when: the risk cleared, or the evidence required to release it arrived

branches.label: A terminal decision was taken
branches.when: an authorized decision ends the relationship or the capability permanently

branches.label: Judgment is needed on what happens next
branches.when: the evidence has not cleared and the next step is not one a rule determines

nodes.does: Release the restriction and raise the capability restoration through the access lifecycle, rebuilt from current entitlements rather than from a snapshot taken when the restriction went on. A restriction that outlasted a term or an entitlement does not restore what expired underneath it

nodes.state: restriction released; the risk case closes with what cleared it recorded
nodes.reEntry: new evidence opens a new assessment. The record of what cleared this one is what stops the same evidence being re-litigated

nodes.on: a restriction needing authorized judgment - to apply, to continue or to lift
carries: the evidence, its provenance and the restriction currently in force
the explicit fact that this is a temporary state rather than an adverse finding, and that no conclusion about the actor has been reached

nodes.on: an authorized terminal decision on a risk case
carries: the decision, its authority and the evidence it was made on
the explicit fact that the restriction history and its basis are preserved rather than replaced by the outcome

guardrails: Restriction scope matches risk scope.
Unrelated capabilities are never terminated without a policy basis.
A temporary restriction is not a final adverse decision.
Every restriction states the condition that would release it.
records.reusableRule: Risk controls should constrain only the activity necessary to manage the identified risk while preserving a path to evidence-based resolution.

records.name: Policy violation detected → validate → correct, restrict or escalate
records.purpose: Establish that a rule was actually broken, against the version that governed it, before anything follows from that.

entity.scope: the violation case, the entity or action it concerns, and the policy version it is judged under
entity.note: The version is part of the entity. A case that does not carry which rule it is about cannot be assessed and cannot be defended.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-186 handles what follows an authorized rejection. This determines whether a violation occurred at all and which consequence the policy defines - it may never reach a decision case, and most of its outcomes are corrections rather than refusals.

RSK-192 evaluates risk evidence without requiring any rule to have been broken, and most of what it sees clears. This starts from an identifiable governing rule and asks whether it was actually breached, judged against the version in force at the time. Risk evidence alone never opens a case here; it opens one there.

requires: an action or state that appears to breach an identifiable policy
insufficientAlone: a risk signal, which is evidence about likelihood rather than about a rule having been broken
an unusual pattern, which is not a rule

nodes.does: Identify the policy, the version effective at the time of the suspected action, the action itself, the evidence and the affected scope

nodes.asks: Which policy version governs the suspected action?

branches.label: The version effective when it occurred
branches.when: the action falls under a determinable historical version

branches.label: A later version, where governing rules explicitly say so
branches.when: a rule expressly applies a newer version to past actions

branches.label: Not determinable
branches.when: which version governs cannot be established

nodes.does: Record that a later version is being applied retroactively, and the rule that permits it. Judging a past action by a rule that did not exist then is something a governing rule has to say explicitly - doing it by default makes everybody historically non-compliant on the day a policy changes
Evaluate the evidence against the applicable version's requirements

nodes.asks: Is the violation confirmed under the applicable version?

branches.label: Confirmed
branches.when: the evidence establishes the rule was breached

branches.label: Not confirmed
branches.when: the evidence does not establish a breach of the applicable version

nodes.does: Record no violation, with the version evaluated. Detection is not confirmation, and a cleared case is worth keeping because the same detection will fire on the same behaviour again

nodes.state: no violation under the applicable policy version
nodes.reEntry: a different action, or a policy change with explicit retroactive reach, is assessed on its own terms rather than by re-running this one

nodes.does: Classify the severity and the correctable scope. A violation is not intent - most are configuration, misunderstanding or a rule nobody read, and applying a misconduct consequence to them costs a relationship the evidence never justified losing

nodes.asks: What consequence does the governing policy define?

branches.label: A remediation requirement
branches.when: the policy defines what would bring this back into compliance

branches.label: An immediate scoped restriction
branches.when: the policy requires stopping something while this is resolved

branches.label: A terminal consequence the policy explicitly requires
branches.when: the policy states that this violation ends the relationship or the capability

branches.label: Authorized judgment, or the policy defines no consequence
branches.when: the consequence turns on judgment, or nothing in the policy says what follows

nodes.does: State exactly what would bring the entity back into compliance, and by when. A violation notice that does not say what to do about it is a reprimand, and it produces an escalation rather than a correction

timeout.after: the remediation deadline the policy defines
timeout.reason: an open violation with an expired remediation window is neither resolved nor acted on, and it stays that way until something else surfaces it

nodes.asks: Did the remediation resolve the violation?

branches.label: Resolved
branches.when: the entity is back within the applicable rule

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the remediation did not bring it back into compliance

nodes.does: Record the violation as remediated, preserving what happened and what corrected it. The history stays because a pattern of the same violation is worth seeing, and a record that only shows the current state cannot show one

nodes.state: violation confirmed and remediated; history preserved
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence is a new case linked to this one, which is what makes repetition visible without rewriting the first

nodes.on: a confirmed violation requiring a scoped restriction
carries: the rule, its version, the evidence and the scope actually affected
the explicit fact that this is a rule breached rather than misconduct established, which bounds the restriction

nodes.on: a violation whose consequence, version or remediation outcome needs authorized judgment
carries: the policy, the evidence and exactly where the rules stopped short of a consequence
the explicit fact that no consequence was invented from outside the policy

nodes.on: a violation the policy explicitly attaches a terminal consequence to
carries: the rule, its version, the evidence and the specific provision requiring termination
the full violation history, preserved rather than replaced by the outcome

guardrails: Detection is not a confirmed violation.
A violation is not malicious intent.
The consequence comes from the governing policy rather than from severity felt.
A historical action is evaluated against the policy applicable when it occurred, unless governing rules explicitly say otherwise.
records.reusableRule: A policy violation should be established against the applicable rule and evidence before the system applies the consequence defined for that violation.

records.name: Compliance requirement → collect and verify → satisfied or blocked
records.purpose: Hold one mandatory requirement as its own state, blocking only what genuinely depends on it.

entity.scope: the compliance requirement and the specific process depending on it
entity.note: Satisfied is scoped to the requirement's purpose and validity. The same evidence does not satisfy a different requirement.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-82 orchestrates collecting a verification and resuming what it blocked. This owns the compliance requirement as a business state - which requirement applies, whether existing evidence already satisfies it, and what happens when it cannot be met. It uses that collection mechanism rather than reimplementing one.

requires: an applicable compliance requirement that a specific process cannot proceed without
insufficientAlone: a general onboarding step, which collects what a product needs rather than what a rule mandates

nodes.does: Define the exact requirement and which process depends on it. The requirement is scoped to its purpose - a compliance step that collects everything available is not a requirement but a data grab, and everything extra becomes a retention obligation nobody planned

nodes.asks: Does existing authoritative evidence already satisfy this requirement, within its validity?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: held evidence covers the requirement's scope and is still valid

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: nothing held covers it, or what is held has lapsed or was scoped to something else

nodes.does: Record the requirement SATISFIED from the existing evidence, and do not re-collect. Asking again for what is already held and still valid is the most common reason people abandon a process at the compliance step, and it produces a duplicate of something we already have to retain

Raise the evidence or verification the requirement actually needs through the mechanism that owns it. Compliance does not build its own verification - a parallel identity check will disagree with the canonical one, and there is no principled way to say which of two verified states is real

timeout.after: the deadline the requirement defines, where one exists
timeout.reason: a dependent process blocked on a requirement nobody is completing is stopped without anyone having decided to stop it

nodes.asks: How did the requirement resolve?

branches.label: Satisfied
branches.when: the required evidence was obtained and verified

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the requirement cannot be met with what is available

nodes.asks: What does policy define for an expired requirement deadline?

branches.label: It defines an outcome
branches.when: policy states what happens to the dependent process when the deadline passes

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: no rule states what an expired compliance deadline does

nodes.does: Record the requirement SATISFIED with its scope and its validity. Satisfied is scoped - the same evidence does not satisfy a different requirement, and reusing it beyond its purpose is how one verification silently becomes a general clearance nobody granted

nodes.on: a compliance requirement satisfied, releasing the process that depended on it
carries: the requirement, its scope and its validity period
the explicit instruction that the dependent process revalidates on its own terms - this requirement clearing does not make it otherwise valid

nodes.does: Record the requirement as unsatisfiable, with why. This is a specific requirement failing rather than the entity being non-compliant in general, and the difference decides how much stops

nodes.asks: What do the governing rules say happens to the dependent process?

branches.label: Block it
branches.when: the rules stop the dependent process while the requirement is unmet

branches.label: Close it
branches.when: the rules end the dependent process where the requirement cannot be met

branches.label: The rules do not say
branches.when: nothing authoritative states the consequence for the dependent process

nodes.does: Block only the dependent process, naming the requirement that blocks it and what would satisfy it. Everything not depending on this requirement stays available - one unmet obligation stopping everything an entity can do is a general suspension nobody authorized

nodes.state: dependent process blocked; the requirement is named and unmet
nodes.reEntry: the requirement being satisfied later releases the block, and the dependent process revalidates rather than simply resuming

nodes.does: Close the dependent process under the rule that requires it, recording that it closed for an unmet compliance requirement rather than on its merits

nodes.state: dependent process closed for an unmet compliance requirement
nodes.reEntry: a new attempt with the requirement satisfiable is assessed fresh, and this closure does not stand against it

nodes.on: a compliance requirement whose failure or deadline consequence the rules do not define
carries: the requirement, what was attempted and the process depending on it
the explicit fact that no blocking or closure consequence was invented

guardrails: A compliance requirement never requests unrelated evidence.
A satisfied requirement is scoped to its defined purpose and validity.
A compliance requirement is not generic customer onboarding.
Only the processes depending on the requirement are blocked.
records.reusableRule: Compliance requirements should block only the processes that depend on them and release those processes only when the defined requirement is authoritatively satisfied.

records.name: Compliance or policy hold → preserve state → resolve → resume or terminate
records.purpose: Pause what a policy question makes unsafe, and leave everything else running.

entity.scope: the entity or process on hold, and the hold acting on it
entity.note: The hold pauses future incompatible actions. The entity, its obligations and its deadlines all continue existing underneath it.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-193 restricts because evidence of risk warrants it, and releases on evidence. A hold pauses because a policy or compliance question is open, and releases when that question is answered - the trigger, the authority and the release condition are all different.

requires: an authoritative policy or compliance hold, with an authority behind it

nodes.does: Record the hold reason, its scope, the authority for it, the effective time, which operations it affects, which remain allowed, and what would resolve it. A hold with no stated resolution condition has no way out and becomes a termination nobody decided

Record ON_HOLD and pause only the future actions the hold is incompatible with. Unrelated capabilities stay available where policy permits - a hold on outbound payments is not a reason to stop someone reading their own records

nodes.asks: Do existing commitments require continued handling?

branches.label: They do
branches.when: orders, refunds, reports or obligations created before the hold are still live

branches.label: None outstanding
branches.when: nothing created before the hold is still owed in either direction

nodes.does: Preserve those commitments and route them according to the governing rules. An order already placed, a refund already due and a regulatory report already owed do not stop existing because the entity is on hold - and some of them the hold specifically requires us to keep doing
Leave existing deadlines where they are unless the governing policy explicitly moves them. A hold that silently resets clocks extends obligations nobody agreed to extend, and it shortens none of them

until: the stated resolution requirement is met
a review decision changes the hold
a terminal policy outcome is reached

timeout.after: the maximum hold duration policy defines
timeout.reason: an indefinite hold is a termination without a decision, and the entity under it cannot tell which one it is in

nodes.asks: How did the hold resolve?

branches.label: The requirement was met
branches.when: the stated resolution condition is authoritatively satisfied

branches.label: A terminal policy outcome
branches.when: the policy question resolved against the entity in a way that ends something

branches.label: A review decision is needed
branches.when: resolving it turns on judgment rather than on the stated condition

nodes.does: Re-read the entity's current state before resuming. What resumes is what is valid now - the hold may have outlasted an entitlement, a term or an eligibility, and lifting it does not restore things that expired underneath it
Record the hold lifted and resume the operations that are currently valid, rebuilt from current state rather than from what was paused

nodes.state: hold lifted; operations resumed at what is currently valid
nodes.reEntry: a further policy question is a new hold with its own scope and its own resolution condition. This one stays in the record as something that was applied and answered

nodes.on: a hold whose resolution or continuation needs authorized judgment
carries: the hold, its reason, its age and what has and has not been resolved
the explicit fact that a hold is not a rejection and nothing adverse has been decided

nodes.on: a hold resolving into a terminal policy outcome
carries: the outcome, its authority and the hold record that preceded it
the commitments preserved during the hold, which the termination resolves rather than erases

guardrails: A hold is not a rejection.
A hold never resets deadlines unless governing policy explicitly does so.
Unrelated capabilities remain available where permitted.
Every hold states the condition that would resolve it.
records.reusableRule: A policy or compliance hold temporarily prevents defined actions while preserving the underlying entity and its unresolved obligations.

records.name: Exception request → validate authority → approve, reject or review
records.purpose: Ask for a controlled deviation from a named rule, over a stated scope, from someone entitled to ask.

entity.scope: the exception request and the specific policy, action or entity it concerns
entity.note: An exception names a rule and a scope. One that names neither is a general permission, which is what nobody meant to grant.

distinctFrom.because: This defines what a policy exception is and whether one may even be sought - which rule, what scope, whose authority. Where the answer needs judgment it uses the decision engine rather than being one.

requires: a request to deviate from an identified policy or rule, for an identified scope
insufficientAlone: a policy block having occurred, which is a rule applying rather than a request to set it aside

nodes.does: Capture the policy or rule concerned, the exception requested, its scope, the reason, the requester, any proposed duration or effective window, and the supporting evidence
