nodes.does: Promote it from a target problem to a rollout problem. A failure signature appearing on forty targets is not forty individual problems, and handling them one at a time means nobody ever sees the shape of it

nodes.on: a target failure whose pattern makes it systemic
carries: the shared failure signature and the targets exhibiting it
the explicit fact that this reached rollout scope through evidence of a pattern rather than through a count of failures

nodes.asks: Is a retry safe and likely to help?

branches.label: It is
branches.when: the cause was transient - unreachable, momentarily short of resource, a temporary lock

branches.label: It is not
branches.when: the cause is structural to this target and retrying will reproduce it

nodes.does: Retry against this target only, within a bounded budget and using the same operation identity so a change that actually applied is not applied twice

nodes.asks: Does retry budget remain?

branches.label: Budget remains
branches.when: this target has attempts left

branches.label: Exhausted
branches.when: the attempts this target allows have been used

nodes.state: retrying against this target only; the rollout is unaffected
nodes.reEntry: each attempt reports its own outcome and returns here with the budget one lower. Retrying is bounded rather than continuous

nodes.asks: Can this target safely remain on the previous version?

branches.label: It can
branches.when: the previous version is supported, secure and compatible for this target

branches.label: It cannot
branches.when: staying behind leaves the target unsupported, insecure or incompatible

nodes.does: Record TARGET_EXCEPTION. The exception population stays explicitly visible - a rollout reporting complete while quietly leaving targets behind produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and the forgotten targets are the ones that break in six months with nobody remembering why they are different

nodes.state: TARGET_EXCEPTION; on the previous version, visible and countable
nodes.reEntry: the blocking cause clearing makes the target eligible again, and it is picked up by this change or the next one rather than staying behind permanently

nodes.does: Record that this target cannot stay behind and cannot proceed unattended, with what is blocking it. Leaving it as an exception when it cannot safely be one is how a target ends up unsupported without anybody deciding that it should be

nodes.on: a target that must take the change and cannot
carries: the target, its diagnosis and why remaining on the previous version is not acceptable
the explicit fact that automated attempts are exhausted and the rollout itself is unaffected

guardrails: One target failure is not a rollout failure.
Retries are bounded rather than indefinite.
The exception population remains observable and countable.
Promotion to systemic happens on pattern evidence rather than on failure count.
records.reusableRule: Individual change failures should be recovered at target scope until evidence shows that the problem is systemic.

records.name: Change completed → observe → close, reopen or deprecate previous version
records.purpose: Wait long enough to know the change held, and keep what a recovery would need until it clearly does not.

entity.scope: the completed rollout, the changed population and the exception targets
entity.note: Completion and stability are different claims. The previous version stays available until both the recovery and the audit requirements are satisfied.

requires: the planned target population having reached the intended changed state
insufficientAlone: a rollout dashboard reporting complete, which reports coverage rather than health

nodes.asks: Does this change require post-change observation?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the change touches behaviour, data or paths whose problems surface over time

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the change is fully exercised at application and nothing further can emerge

nodes.does: Record the change as applied and under observation. Deployment completion is not long-term stability - the regressions that matter most surface on a weekly cycle, at month-end, or the first time a rare path runs, all of them after the rollout dashboard turned green

until: a regression appears in the changed population

timeout.reason: the window is the point of the wait - reaching it without a material regression is what makes the change stable rather than merely deployed

nodes.asks: Is the regression material?

branches.label: Material
branches.when: it affects correctness, availability or a business outcome the gate was protecting

branches.label: Not material
branches.when: it is noise, or a known issue already accounted for

nodes.on: a late material regression in a completed change
carries: the regression, when it appeared and across which part of the changed population
the explicit fact that the rollout is complete, so pausing expansion is not the remedy - the question is what to do with a population that already has it

nodes.does: Record CHANGE_STABLE, and record the exception population explicitly alongside it. A change reported stable while its exceptions are invisible produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and every later change inherits that ambiguity

nodes.asks: Can the previous version now be deprecated?

branches.label: It can
branches.when: no target remains on it, and the recovery and audit retention it was held for is satisfied

branches.label: Not yet
branches.when: recovery or audit still depends on it, or exception targets are still running it

nodes.does: Retain the previous version and the state a recovery would need, with the condition that would release it. Deleting it because the rollout completed removes the only thing a late rollback could restore from, and late is exactly when rollbacks are actually needed

nodes.state: CHANGE_STABLE; previous version retained and exception targets named
nodes.reEntry: the retention condition being satisfied allows the previous version to be retired on its own terms. A later regression reopens recovery against a population that still has somewhere to go back to

nodes.on: a previous version nothing depends on any longer
carries: the version, the confirmation that no target runs it and that retention is satisfied
the change lineage, which stays auditable regardless of whether the artifact is retired

guardrails: Deployment completion is not long-term stability.
A previous version or state required for recovery or audit is not deleted immediately.
Exception targets remain explicit in the completion record.
records.reusableRule: Change lifecycle closes only after the applied population demonstrates sufficient stability and remaining version dependencies are resolved.

records.name: Correlated failure detection → incident candidate → confirm or reject
records.purpose: Establish whether several failures actually share a cause, before treating them as one thing.

entity.scope: the incident candidate and every individual failure correlated into it
entity.note: Each affected entity keeps its own case and its own link. The incident is a layer above them rather than a replacement for them.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-192 assesses risk evidence about one actor or transaction. This asks whether failures across many unrelated entities plausibly share an operational cause - a question about the system rather than about anybody using it.

requires: multiple failures or anomalies across entities, exceeding a meaningful correlation threshold
insufficientAlone: a spike in alert volume, which is a count rather than a correlation
several failures happening at once, which is often several failures happening at once

nodes.does: Correlate by time, service or dependency, region, version, provider, resource cohort, failure signature and shared infrastructure. What is being tested is whether these failures plausibly share a cause, rather than whether there are a lot of them

Preserve the link from the candidate to each individual affected entity, and keep each entity's own case open. A correlation that absorbs its members leaves every affected customer without a case of their own, and when the incident closes they have nothing left to point at

nodes.asks: What does the correlating evidence support?

branches.label: A shared cause
branches.when: the failures share a dependency, cohort, signature or infrastructure in a way that explains them together

branches.label: Independent failures
branches.when: the correlation is coincidental and each failure has its own explanation

branches.label: Insufficient evidence
branches.when: a shared cause is plausible and unestablished

nodes.does: Retain the individual cases as independent, and record why they were not merged. Several failures at once is often several failures at once - merging them for operational convenience gives each customer a generic status page instead of an answer to their specific problem

nodes.state: no incident; the individual cases continue independently
nodes.reEntry: further correlated evidence reopens the question. Not merging now does not prevent an incident being confirmed later on better evidence

nodes.does: Record INCIDENT_CANDIDATE and investigate. Candidate is a real state - it starts a look without asserting a shared cause to anybody, and it is what stops a hunch from becoming a status-page announcement

until: evidence rules a shared cause out

timeout.reason: a candidate held open indefinitely is neither an incident anybody is responding to nor a set of cases anybody is working, and both populations wait

nodes.does: Record INCIDENT_CONFIRMED with the correlating evidence that supports it. What is asserted is a shared cause - not that it is known, but that these failures belong together

nodes.on: an incident confirmed on correlating evidence
carries: the correlating evidence and every individual affected entity, still linked and still holding its own case
the explicit fact that a shared cause is asserted and not yet known

guardrails: Multiple failures are not automatically one incident.
Unrelated customer cases are never merged for operational convenience.
Correlation preserves the linkage to each individual affected entity.
records.reusableRule: An incident should be created only when evidence shows multiple failures plausibly share a common operational cause.

records.name: Incident confirmed → determine severity and blast radius → assign command
records.purpose: Establish what is actually affected, how badly, and who is running the response.

entity.scope: the confirmed incident, its blast radius and its operational ownership
entity.note: The incident owner runs the systemic response. The owners of the individual cases keep owing their customers an answer, and neither absorbs the other.

requires: a confirmed incident with its correlating evidence and affected entities
insufficientAlone: an alert that has fired and not been confirmed as an incident
a single failed request with no impact established

nodes.does: Determine the affected systems, capabilities, regions, customers and accounts, dependencies, the start time, the current impact and the business criticality

Set the severity from the actual operational impact. A high event count is not a severity - a retry storm generates a hundred thousand events and affects nobody, and a single failing payment path generates twelve and affects everything downstream of it

Assign incident ownership and command according to the operating model, and record it separately from the owners of the individual cases. The incident owner runs the systemic response; the case owners still owe their customers an answer, and one absorbing the other means whichever survives stops doing the other job
Record ACTIVE_INCIDENT with the scope, the severity and the command as established

nodes.asks: Has the affected scope grown since the incident was confirmed?

branches.label: It has
branches.when: a new cohort, region, dependency or capability is found affected

branches.label: It has not
branches.when: the blast radius as established still holds

nodes.does: Expand the blast radius and re-derive the severity from it. A blast radius fixed at confirmation time understates every incident that spreads, which is most of them - and the response level set against the original scope is then wrong for the whole rest of the incident

nodes.asks: What does the response need first?

branches.label: Immediate containment
branches.when: the impact is ongoing and reducing it does not have to wait for a cause

branches.label: Investigation first
branches.when: the impact is bounded or already stopped, and acting without understanding risks making it worse

branches.label: The impact resolved before the response began
branches.when: the condition passed on its own before anything was done

nodes.on: an active incident needing immediate impact reduction
carries: the blast radius, the severity and the capabilities currently affected
the incident ownership, and the separate case ownerships that continue alongside it

nodes.on: an active incident where understanding comes before acting
carries: the correlating evidence, the timeline and the affected cohort
the explicit fact that no mitigation has been applied, so the system is in its failed state rather than a modified one

nodes.does: Record that the impact ended before the response engaged, preserving the incident and its evidence. A self-resolving incident is still an incident that happened, and it is usually the first occurrence of something that will recur

nodes.state: impact ended before response; the incident and its evidence are preserved
nodes.reEntry: recurrence is assessed against this record. An incident that resolved itself once and returns is a pattern rather than two coincidences

guardrails: Severity reflects actual impact rather than event volume.
A high event count is not a severity.
The incident owner and the individual case owners remain separate.
Blast radius is re-derived as scope grows rather than fixed at confirmation.
records.reusableRule: Incident response begins by establishing the affected scope, severity and accountable operational ownership.

records.name: Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
records.purpose: Reduce the damage now, without pretending the cause has been dealt with.

entity.scope: the incident and the mitigations applied against its impact
entity.note: Each mitigation is recorded as temporary with the condition that would remove it. Nothing here touches the cause.

distinctFrom.because: Mitigation reduces impact while the cause remains. INC-256 acts on the cause and asks whether the service actually came back. A system can be fully mitigated and entirely unfixed, and reporting the first as the second stops the second happening.

requires: an active incident with ongoing impact that could be reduced

nodes.does: Identify the mitigations actually available - disabling a failing feature, shifting traffic, increasing capacity, moving to an alternate provider, rate limiting, a manual fallback, a degraded mode, pausing unsafe operations. Each rejected option is struck from the list, so the search through them terminates

nodes.asks: Is the candidate mitigation safe to apply?

branches.label: Safe
branches.when: its secondary effects are understood and acceptable

branches.label: Unacceptable secondary risk
branches.when: applying it could produce a larger failure than the one it addresses

branches.label: No safe option remains
branches.when: every candidate has been considered and rejected

nodes.does: Reject this option, strike it from the list and consider the next. A workaround that creates a larger failure than the one it addresses is the most expensive kind of response, and it is usually applied under pressure with nobody checking what else it touches

Record that no safe mitigation is available, and say so rather than applying an unsafe one. An incident with no safe containment goes straight to recovery with its full impact visible, which is honest and is what the response should be working from

Apply the mitigation, scoped to what it actually needs to touch, and record it as temporary with the condition that would remove it. A workaround with no stated end becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and is found years later by somebody wondering why a feature is disabled

Record MITIGATED and explicitly not RESOLVED. The impact is smaller and the cause is untouched - reporting mitigation as resolution stops the investigation that would have found the cause, and the incident returns

nodes.asks: Does the mitigation materially change what affected users should do?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: a workaround is now available, or a capability is now degraded rather than absent

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the user-visible position is unchanged

nodes.on: a mitigation that changes user guidance
carries: what is now available, what is still affected, and any safe workaround
the explicit fact that the state is mitigated rather than resolved, so the message does not claim a fix

nodes.asks: Does the mitigation reduce impact enough to stand down the emergency?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the remaining impact is tolerable while the cause is investigated on a normal footing

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: impact remains severe and the cause has to be acted on now

nodes.state: MITIGATED; impact contained, cause untouched, incident still open
nodes.reEntry: the mitigation failing, or the impact growing past it, brings the incident back here. The mitigation stays recorded as temporary and its removal condition stays stated

nodes.on: an incident whose impact cannot be adequately contained
carries: the mitigations attempted, what each achieved and what remains affected
the explicit fact that containment is insufficient, so the corrective action is now the only path to reducing impact

guardrails: Mitigated is not resolved.
A workaround never creates a larger failure than the one it addresses.
A temporary workaround remains explicitly temporary, with the condition that would remove it.
records.reusableRule: Incident mitigation reduces current impact while preserving the distinction between temporary containment and permanent resolution.

records.name: Root cause investigation → hypothesis → confirm or reject → corrective action
records.purpose: Find the thing that actually explains the incident, rather than the thing that was nearest to it.

entity.scope: the incident and the investigation into what caused it
entity.note: Hypotheses are a finite list, tested one at a time. Rejections are recorded so the next investigator does not retest them.

requires: a confirmed incident whose cause is not established
insufficientAlone: the incident having a trigger, which is what set it off rather than what made it possible

nodes.does: Collect the timeline, the logs and evidence, the change history, the dependency state, the affected cohort, the failure signatures and the effects the mitigations had. What a mitigation did or did not fix is itself evidence about the cause

Form hypotheses that would explain the whole incident rather than its first symptom. The change that shipped just before an incident is the most available explanation and is frequently not the cause - often it is what made a latent problem visible, and fixing it leaves the problem in place

Test the current hypothesis against the evidence, including the parts of the evidence it does not explain. A hypothesis that accounts for most of an incident and not its timing, or not its cohort, has not been confirmed

nodes.asks: Does the evidence support this hypothesis?

branches.label: Supported and it explains the incident
branches.when: it accounts for the failure, its timing, its cohort and its behaviour under mitigation

branches.label: Not supported
branches.when: the evidence contradicts it or leaves it unexplained

branches.label: Correlated but unexplained
branches.when: the condition was present and nothing connects it to the failure

nodes.does: Reject the hypothesis and record why, so the next investigator does not retest it. Correlation is not causation, and a condition present during an incident that nothing connects to the failure is a coincidence that will be treated as an answer unless it is rejected explicitly

nodes.asks: Are hypotheses left to test?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: the list has untested candidates

branches.label: None explains it
branches.when: every candidate within the investigation's bounds has been tested and rejected

nodes.does: Record the incident as unexplained rather than attributing it to the most plausible remaining candidate. An unexplained incident is a known gap somebody can work on; a wrongly attributed one is a closed question that will reopen as the same incident with everybody convinced it was fixed

nodes.on: an incident no available hypothesis explains
carries: every hypothesis tested and why each was rejected
the explicit fact that no cause was assigned - the incident is recorded as unexplained rather than closed against a guess

nodes.does: Record ROOT_CAUSE_CONFIRMED with the evidence supporting it and exactly what it explains. Service may already have been restored - restoration and understanding proceed independently, and holding one for the other extends an outage for the sake of tidiness

Define the corrective action the confirmed cause implies, separately from whatever mitigation is currently holding the impact down. The mitigation is a workaround; this is the thing that makes the workaround unnecessary

nodes.on: a confirmed cause with a defined corrective action
carries: the confirmed cause, the evidence for it and the corrective action it implies
the mitigations currently in place, which the corrective action may make removable

guardrails: The first plausible explanation is not the root cause.
Correlation is not causation.
The root cause remains evidence-based rather than assigned by elimination.
Service may be restored before the root cause is known.
records.reusableRule: Root cause is established through evidence that explains the incident, not merely through the first condition correlated with failure.

records.name: Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
records.purpose: Act on the cause and then check the affected population, not the command's return code.

entity.scope: the incident, the recovery action and the capability it is meant to restore
entity.note: The recovery actions available are a finite list defined by the response. Attempts progress through it rather than repeating indefinitely.

requires: an authorized corrective or recovery action against an active incident

nodes.does: Execute the corrective action against the affected scope, through the canonical execution and reliability primitives rather than a bespoke path built during the incident

timeout.reason: an action whose outcome is unknown may or may not have changed the system, and the next decision depends entirely on which

nodes.does: Record the action's outcome as unknown and hold further attempts. Applying a second recovery action on top of one that may have landed is how an incident gets a second cause

nodes.on: a recovery action whose outcome could not be established
carries: the action, the scope it targeted and everything last known about its effect
the explicit instruction that no further recovery action is applied until this one's effect is known
suppresses: any further recovery action while this one's outcome is unknown

nodes.asks: Did the action apply?

branches.label: Applied
branches.when: the corrective action completed against the affected scope

branches.label: Failed
branches.when: the action itself did not complete

nodes.does: Verify from the affected population rather than from the action's own success - service availability, error rates, critical transactions, business functions, dependency health, and the recovery of the cohort that was actually affected. A recovery command succeeding says the command ran, and one successful synthetic check says one path works for one caller

nodes.asks: Is service restored across the affected population?

branches.label: Restored
branches.when: the affected cohort's real traffic succeeds and the critical functions work

branches.label: Partially restored
branches.when: some of the affected population works and some does not

branches.label: Not restored
branches.when: the action applied and the impact continues

nodes.does: Keep the incident active and name the unresolved scope explicitly. A partial restoration reported as recovery leaves the remaining population inside an incident everybody has stopped watching, which is how a long tail of affected customers goes unnoticed for days

nodes.asks: Is another recovery action available?

branches.label: One remains
branches.when: the response defines a further corrective action that has not been attempted

branches.label: None
branches.when: the defined actions are exhausted

nodes.does: Take the next action from the response's defined list. The list is finite, so attempts progress through it and terminate rather than cycling on the same action with different hopes

nodes.on: an incident whose defined recovery actions are exhausted
carries: every action attempted, what each achieved and the scope still affected
the explicit fact that the incident remains active and any partial restoration is named rather than counted as recovery

nodes.does: Record RECOVERY_OBSERVED. What has been established is that the affected population works now - not that it will still be working in an hour, which is the next question and a different one

nodes.on: service observed restored across the affected population
carries: what was verified, across which cohort and against which functions
the explicit fact that this is a first good signal rather than a stable recovery

guardrails: A recovery command succeeding is not service restored.
One successful synthetic check does not prove population recovery.
Partial restoration stays explicit and keeps the incident active.
records.reusableRule: Incident recovery becomes meaningful only when the affected service and user population demonstrate restored operation.

records.name: Service restored → observation window → stable or relapse
records.purpose: Hold the incident open long enough to know the recovery held.

entity.scope: the incident and the recovered service under observation
entity.note: The window is set from the incident's own character rather than from a standard duration.

distinctFrom.because: RET-27 buffers one relationship's recovery signal before concluding the relationship is healthy. This applies the same principle to a shared operational failure - same discipline, different entity, and here a relapse returns a population to an incident rather than a person to a risk state.

requires: verified restoration across the affected population
insufficientAlone: a recovery action completing, which is what produced the signal rather than the signal itself

nodes.does: Record RECOVERY_OBSERVATION. The incident is not resolved - recoveries that hold for ten minutes and fail again are common, and closing on the first good signal means reopening in front of the same customers who were just told it was over

Set the observation window from the incident's own character - how long the failure took to manifest, how often the affected path runs, and whether the fix addressed a cause or a symptom. A fixed window applied to every incident is either too long for a trivial one or far too short for one on a rare path

timeout.after: the observation window set for this incident
timeout.reason: reaching the window without recurrence is what makes the recovery stable. Holding it open longer without need keeps a response engaged on something that has finished

nodes.asks: What appeared during observation?

branches.label: The same failure returned
branches.when: the incident's own signature recurs in the affected population

branches.label: New cases, a different failure
branches.when: something else is failing during the window

nodes.does: Return the incident to ACTIVE. What resumes is this incident rather than a new one - the recurrence is evidence about the recovery, and opening a fresh incident hides that the fix did not hold and makes the pattern invisible

nodes.on: a recovery that did not hold
carries: the recovery that was applied, how long it held and the signature of the relapse
the explicit fact that this is the same incident recurring, which is evidence the confirmed cause was incomplete

nodes.does: Assess it separately rather than absorbing it into this incident. Attaching every failure that occurs during an observation window to the incident makes the incident unfalsifiable - it can never be shown to have ended

nodes.state: an unrelated failure raised separately; this observation continues on its own terms
nodes.reEntry: if the separate assessment shows the two do share a cause, they are correlated on that evidence rather than on having overlapped in time

nodes.does: Record STABLE_RECOVERY with what was observed and for how long. The observation is part of the record, because the next similar incident's window is set against it

nodes.on: a recovery that held through its observation window
carries: what was observed, over what window and across which cohort
the mitigations still in place, which the resolution has to remove or formalize rather than leave running

guardrails: Service restored once is not the incident resolved.
The observation duration and evidence reflect the incident's type rather than a standard.
Observation is not kept artificially long without need.
records.reusableRule: Initial restoration should enter an observation state until sufficient evidence shows the recovery is stable.

records.name: Incident resolution → close operational response → preserve residual cases
records.purpose: Close the shared failure without closing the individual problems it caused.

entity.scope: the incident and the individual cases and obligations linked to it
entity.note: The incident's resolution is a statement about the shared cause. Every linked case reaches its own resolution on its own terms. c.mitigations names all three reachable states explicitly - at least one mitigation applied and now removable, at least one applied and now worth keeping, or none ever applied because resolution came through investigation/root-cause correction alone - because closure is reachable via more than one upstream path and not every path applies a mitigation before resolution criteria are met.

requires: a stable recovery and the incident's own resolution criteria met
insufficientAlone: service being restored, which is one of the criteria rather than all of them

nodes.does: Mark the systemic incident RESOLVED, preserving its timeline, its mitigations and every decision taken during it. The record is what the review works from and what any later recurrence is compared against - an incident that keeps only its outcome teaches nothing
Stop the incident-specific emergency operations - the elevated monitoring, the standing bridge, the suspended changes. These have their own cost and they end with the incident rather than drifting on

nodes.asks: What happens to the temporary mitigations, if any were ever applied?

branches.label: Safe to remove
branches.when: at least one temporary mitigation was applied during the incident, and the corrective action makes it unnecessary

branches.label: They should become permanent
branches.when: at least one temporary mitigation was applied during the incident, and it turned out to be the right long-term behaviour

branches.label: None were ever applied
branches.when: the incident resolved through investigation or root-cause correction alone, reachable when a case never passed through a mitigation-applying stage before the resolution criteria were met - there is nothing to remove or formalize

nodes.does: Remove them and verify the service holds without them. A mitigation left in place because removing it is frightening becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and it joins the set of quietly permanent emergency controls that is the least-understood part of most systems
Formalize it explicitly as a change with an owner and a rationale, rather than leaving a temporary control quietly running forever. Every one of those was meant to last an afternoon

Record explicitly that no temporary mitigation was ever needed for this incident - resolution came from correcting the root cause directly rather than holding the system stable behind an interim control first. This is its own outcome worth recording, not a silent skip, because a reviewer comparing incidents needs to know which recovery pattern this one followed

nodes.asks: Do individual affected cases remain unresolved?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: linked entity-level problems are still outstanding

branches.label: None
branches.when: every linked case has independently reached resolution

nodes.does: Detach them and let each continue on its own recovery. The systemic cause is fixed and the customer whose order failed still has a failed order - closing their case because the incident closed tells them the problem is solved at exactly the moment they discover it is not

nodes.asks: Do financial or remedy obligations remain from the incident?

branches.label: Some remain
branches.when: refunds, credits, compensation or unmet service obligations were created by the incident

branches.label: None
branches.when: nothing is owed as a result of it

nodes.on: obligations surviving an incident's closure
carries: the obligations, their affected scope and what created them
the explicit fact that the incident is resolved and these are not - they run on their own lifecycle at their own pace

nodes.asks: Does this incident qualify for a post-incident review?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: its severity, novelty or recurrence meets the threshold for review

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: it falls below the review threshold and nothing about it was novel

nodes.on: a resolved incident qualifying for review
carries: the timeline, the mitigations, the decisions and the root cause where one was confirmed
the detached cases and surviving obligations, which are part of the incident's real cost

nodes.state: RESOLVED; the shared failure closed and its record preserved
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence is correlated against this record rather than assessed from nothing, which is what makes a pattern visible across incidents

guardrails: An incident resolved is not every individual case resolved.
Temporary mitigations do not silently become permanent.
Incident closure preserves the timeline and the decisions taken.

Every incident reaching resolution has a defined mitigation outcome, including the outcome of never having applied one - closure is never reachable through a mitigation state c.mitigations cannot classify.
records.reusableRule: Incident resolution closes the shared systemic failure while leaving entity-specific obligations open until they independently reach resolution.

records.name: Post-incident review → learn → corrective work → verify
records.purpose: Turn what the incident showed into work somebody owns and somebody checks.

entity.scope: the resolved incident and the corrective work its review produces
entity.note: The review's output is owned work with deadlines. A published document is not a control and is not the deliverable.

requires: a resolved incident meeting the threshold for post-incident review
insufficientAlone: an incident resolved without meeting the review threshold policy defines
a review requested by an individual for an incident the policy does not select

nodes.does: Review the timeline, the detection, the response, the root cause, the blast radius, the mitigations, the communication, the recovery, the control failures and the near misses. What is examined is the system and the response rather than the people - a review that finds a person found the wrong thing, because the person will move on and the condition will not

Identify the corrective and preventive actions the evidence actually supports. An action nobody can trace to something the incident revealed is a good idea rather than a finding, and mixing the two makes the real findings harder to prioritise

nodes.asks: Does the review produce corrective work?

branches.label: It does
branches.when: the evidence supports specific preventive or corrective actions

branches.label: It does not
branches.when: the response worked, the controls held, and nothing the incident revealed needs changing

nodes.does: Record explicitly that the review found no corrective work required, with the reasoning. That is a legitimate outcome and it needs to be a stated one rather than an empty section that reads as an unfinished review

nodes.state: reviewed; no outstanding corrective work
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence reopens the question of whether the conclusion that nothing needed changing was right

nodes.does: Assign owners and deadlines to each corrective action. An action item with no owner is a sentence in a document, and a document is not a control - the whole value of the review is what somebody is now accountable for delivering

until: the required corrective actions are claimed complete
corrective actions are abandoned or superseded

timeout.after: the deadlines assigned to the corrective actions
timeout.reason: prevention work that slips past its deadline unremarked is how the same incident recurs, and by then nobody remembers the action existed

nodes.on: corrective work outliving its assigned deadline
carries: the outstanding actions, their owners and the incident they came from
the explicit fact that the risk the incident revealed is still present

nodes.asks: What happened to the corrective work?

branches.label: Claimed complete
branches.when: the owners report the actions done

branches.label: Abandoned or superseded
branches.when: the actions were dropped or replaced

nodes.does: Record which actions were dropped and on whose authority. Silently abandoned prevention work is the reason the same incident recurs, and without this record nobody can point to the moment it was dropped or ask why

Verify the corrective work where verification is required. An action item created is not a risk reduced, and a document published is not a prevention - what is checked is whether the condition that produced the incident can still produce it

nodes.asks: Did the corrective work actually reduce the risk?

branches.label: Verified
branches.when: the condition the incident exposed can no longer produce it

branches.label: Not effective
branches.when: the work completed and the condition remains reachable

nodes.does: Return the action to its owner with what the verification found. Work completed that did not reduce the risk means the action was aimed at the wrong thing, and repeating it produces the same result
Record the corrective work as complete and verified, with what the verification established

nodes.state: review closed with verified corrective work
nodes.reEntry: a recurrence despite verified prevention is strong evidence the diagnosis was wrong, and is assessed at pattern level rather than as a fresh incident

guardrails: A postmortem is not a blame exercise.
An action item created is not a risk reduced.
Prevention is never marked complete solely because a document was published.
records.reusableRule: Post-incident review converts incident evidence into owned, verifiable improvements rather than treating documentation itself as remediation.

records.name: Incident pattern recurrence → detect systemic weakness → escalate prevention
records.purpose: Notice when the same weakness keeps producing incidents, and stop treating each one as new.

entity.scope: the family of materially similar incidents and the weakness they may share
entity.note: Similarity is established by comparing causes rather than by counting occurrences or matching alert names.

distinctFrom.because: INC-251 correlates failures happening now into one incident. This compares incidents across time to ask whether the same systemic weakness keeps producing them - a question about the prevention strategy rather than about any one response.

requires: multiple incidents across a defined window or context that appear materially similar
insufficientAlone: the same alert firing repeatedly, which is a repeated alert name and nothing more
a raised incident count, which measures how often something was declared rather than why

nodes.does: Compare the root causes, the affected systems, the failure modes, the mitigations, the recovery actions, the corrective actions and any prevention work that was never finished. What is compared is the causes rather than the symptoms - two incidents that both presented as elevated latency can have nothing else in common

nodes.asks: Do these incidents share a systemic weakness?

branches.label: The same weakness recurring
branches.when: the confirmed causes point to one underlying condition that keeps producing failures

branches.label: Superficially similar, different causes
branches.when: they looked alike and their causes are unrelated

branches.label: Not determinable from the evidence
branches.when: the incidents lack confirmed causes, or the comparison is inconclusive

nodes.on: a recurrence pattern the evidence cannot establish
carries: the incidents compared, their causes where confirmed and where they were not
the explicit fact that no shared root cause was inferred from the count - inferring one from repetition is exactly the mistake this journey exists to prevent

nodes.does: Keep them separate and record why the apparent similarity does not hold. Grouping incidents by how they looked produces a pattern that is an artifact of the monitoring rather than of the system, and prevention work aimed at it fixes nothing

nodes.state: incidents kept separate; the apparent pattern was superficial
nodes.reEntry: further incidents with confirmed causes may still establish a genuine pattern. This comparison is recorded so it is not repeated identically

nodes.does: Elevate the prevention priority and create or strengthen the long-term corrective programme. Repeated recovery without prevention is an operational risk, and it should be visible as a risk rather than as a series of incidents that were each handled well

nodes.asks: Was remediation previously attempted for this weakness?

branches.label: It was
branches.when: corrective work from an earlier incident targeted this same condition

branches.label: It was not
branches.when: this weakness has not previously been worked on

nodes.does: Reopen the previous remediation's assumptions. A fix that was applied and did not hold means the diagnosis was wrong rather than the execution, and repeating the same remediation produces the same incident at greater cost and with less credibility

nodes.on: remediation that was applied and did not prevent recurrence
carries: the previous corrective work, what it assumed and what the recurrence shows about that assumption
the explicit fact that increasing customer messaging is not the response to recurrence - the prevention strategy is what has to change

nodes.state: systemic weakness identified; prevention elevated as a standing risk
nodes.reEntry: further recurrence is measured against the elevated programme rather than raising the priority again, so the escalation means something the first time

guardrails: A repeated alert name is not the same root cause.
Customer messaging is not increased simply because incidents recur.
Repeated recovery without prevention stays visible as operational risk.
A shared root cause is never inferred from a count of occurrences.
records.reusableRule: Recurring incidents should change the prevention strategy when evidence shows the same systemic weakness continues to produce failures.

identity.title: Entitlement grant → provision → verify availability
identity.purpose: Hold the distance between a right being granted and the thing behind it actually working.

requires: an entitlement recorded as GRANTED with a scope that implies a resource

nodes.headline: Entitlement granted

Create the provisioning action and record the state as PROVISIONING, keyed so that a redelivered event provisions once. A granted entitlement in PROVISIONING is not yet usable, and nothing downstream may present it as though it were
until provisioning succeeds, or provisioning fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the provisioning SLA

nodes.headline: How did provisioning end?
Does actual availability need to be verified?

Check that the capability is genuinely reachable by its holder. A provisioning API returning success is a statement about the API - whether anyone can use the thing is a separate question with its own answer
Is it actually available?
ACTIVE; the right is granted, provisioned and usable
nodes.detail: a scope change re-opens provisioning for the delta rather than for the whole entitlement

nodes.headline: external:access-recovery
nodes.detail: a provisioned resource the holder cannot reach

nodes.headline: What class of failure is this?
Retry against a budget fixed at the first failure. The budget does not renew - that is the difference between a retry policy and a loop that provisions forever
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: provisioning that cannot be completed automatically

edges.label: on event
edges.when: provisioning succeeds, provisioning fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a provisioning run that has neither succeeded nor failed within its SLA is a failure that has not reported itself, and treating silence as success is how a customer finds the gap first

edges.label: Succeeded
edges.when: the provisioning system reports success

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the provisioning system reports failure

edges.label: Verification matters
edges.when: the holder's ability to reach the capability is what the entitlement is for, and a reported success is not proof of it

edges.label: The provisioning record is authoritative
edges.when: the provisioning system is itself the source of truth for availability

edges.label: Available
edges.when: the capability is reachable

edges.label: Provisioned but unreachable
edges.when: the resource exists and the holder still cannot use it
a provisioned resource the holder cannot reach

edges.label: Transient and retry-safe
edges.when: the failure is expected to clear and the retry budget has room

edges.label: Permanent, or the budget is spent
edges.when: retrying will not help, or has already been tried as often as the budget allows
provisioning that cannot be completed automatically

guardrails: A granted entitlement is not a provisioned one. The grant is a business record; provisioning is a distributed operation that can fail on its own.
Provisioning success is not availability. Where the difference matters, availability is checked rather than assumed.
Provisioning is idempotent. Redelivery provisions once.
Retries are bounded by a budget fixed at the first failure.
governance.reusableRule: A granted right becomes usable only after the required resource or capability is successfully provisioned and available.
governance.entityScope: the entitlement plus the resource or capability being provisioned for it
governance.entityNote: One provisioning run per entitlement, keyed idempotently. Retries and redeliveries are expected, and none of them may provision a second copy.

identity.title: Entitlement change → recalculate scope → expand, reduce or preserve
identity.purpose: Apply only the difference between the old and new rights, rather than re-applying a whole scope over a working one.

requires: an authoritative change to the basis of an existing entitlement: a plan change, a role change, a contract amendment, a benefit or quantity or coverage change

nodes.headline: Entitlement basis changed
Compare the previous scope, the new scope and the effective time, and derive the delta. What gets applied is the difference - a capability present in both scopes is not touched at all
Which way did the scope move?
Provision the newly granted capabilities, idempotently, and leave everything already working untouched

Apply any expansion, and identify precisely which capabilities are no longer covered. Historical data and resources created under the previous scope are not destroyed by a scope change - a reduction removes a right, not a record
Do existing commitments or in-flight usage depend on what is being removed?
Entitlement loss → revoke future capability → reconcile existing obligations
nodes.detail: a scope reduction with live commitments underneath it

nodes.headline: Apply the reduction to future access only, idempotently. Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are two different decisions, and this one makes only the first
delta applied; unchanged capabilities untouched
nodes.detail: a further basis change is compared against the new scope

edges.label: Expanded only
edges.when: capabilities were added and none removed

edges.label: Reduced, or mixed
edges.when: at least one capability is no longer covered, whether or not others were added

edges.label: Something depends on it
edges.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, a purchased benefit or an open transaction rests on the capability being removed

edges.label: Nothing depends on it
edges.when: the reduction affects only future use
a scope reduction with live commitments underneath it

guardrails: A reduction in entitlement does not destroy historical data or resources created while the right was held.
Future access loss and cancelling an existing obligation are separate decisions made by separate journeys.
The delta is applied idempotently, so a redelivered change does not reprovision or re-revoke.
governance.reusableRule: Entitlement changes should apply the difference between old and new rights without rewriting the history of what was previously valid.
governance.entityScope: the entitlement whose basis changed, and the delta between its previous and new scope
governance.entityNote: The delta is the unit of work. Re-applying the full new scope reprovisions what already worked and revokes what should have survived, and the holder sees both as an outage.

identity.title: Entitlement loss → revoke future capability → reconcile existing obligations
identity.purpose: Stop future use of a right that has ended without cancelling what was validly created while it was held.

requires: an authoritative end to a right: a plan downgrade, a contract termination, a role removal, a benefit expiry, an eligibility-linked revocation, or a policy decision

nodes.headline: Entitlement no longer valid

Determine when the loss actually takes effect - immediately, at period end, or on a future date. Assuming immediate is how someone loses what they have already paid for, and everything downstream depends on getting this right
Identify the capabilities affected, scoped to this entitlement alone. A lost role does not revoke rights the same person holds on a different basis

Prevent future use of the affected capabilities from the effective time, idempotently. The record that the entitlement existed and what was done under it is untouched - losing a right does not mean it was never held
Do valid commitments exist that were created while the right was held?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: an entitlement ending with commitments still live under it

nodes.headline: Does a provisioned resource need removing?
Deprovision request → dependency check → remove, retain or escalate
nodes.detail: a provisioned resource whose entitlement has ended

nodes.headline: future use revoked; history and commitments intact
nodes.detail: the right may be granted again on a new basis, which is a new entitlement rather than a revival of this one

edges.label: Commitments outstanding
edges.when: a confirmed reservation, an in-progress service, an already purchased benefit or an open transaction exists

edges.label: Nothing outstanding
edges.when: the right governed only future use
an entitlement ending with commitments still live under it

edges.label: Resource provisioned
edges.when: something was provisioned for this entitlement and is no longer authorised

edges.label: Nothing provisioned
edges.when: the right had no provisioned resource behind it
a provisioned resource whose entitlement has ended

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts a right that still exists and is designed to come back. This is the right ending, which is why it reconciles obligations rather than holding them.

guardrails: Losing an entitlement does not mean the entitlement never existed. The historical record stands.
Existing commitments are reconciled separately and are never cancelled automatically by the loss.
Revocation stays scoped to the affected entitlement.
Stopping future use is idempotent.
governance.reusableRule: Losing a right prevents future unauthorized use but does not automatically erase commitments created while the right was valid.
governance.entityScope: the entitlement that ended, plus the resources and commitments that depended on it
governance.entityNote: Revocation stays scoped to this entitlement. A right held on another basis is untouched, and the record that this one existed remains.

identity.title: Access request → authorization check → allow, deny or step up
identity.purpose: Decide at the moment of the attempt whether this actor may take this action on this resource.

requires: an actor attempting a protected action on an identified resource
insufficientAlone: a successful authentication, which establishes who is asking and nothing about what they may do
holding an entitlement to the product the resource belongs to

nodes.headline: Protected action attempted

Evaluate at execution time: the identity, the entitlement, the role and permission, the resource's own scope, the current security state, and the policy requirements for this specific action. A cached decision is re-checked against critical state, because the states that matter most are the ones that change fastest
What does the current state permit?
ALLOW; this action on this resource, now
nodes.detail: the next attempt is decided again. Allowing one action never authorises the following one, however similar it looks

nodes.headline: Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
nodes.detail: an action requiring an assurance level the current session does not hold

nodes.headline: Record the denial with its reason category - entitlement missing, permission missing, resource out of scope, security state blocking, or policy prohibition. A bare denial cannot be appealed, debugged, or distinguished from an outage
DENY, with a recorded reason category
nodes.detail: a change to any of the evaluated states makes the next attempt a new decision

edges.label: Fully authorized
edges.when: every required condition is satisfied for this actor, action and resource

edges.label: Authorized subject to stronger verification
edges.when: the conditions are met except for an assurance level this action requires

edges.label: Not authorized
edges.when: at least one required condition fails
an action requiring an assurance level the current session does not hold

distinctFrom.because: Approval is a business decision taken in advance about a subject. Authorization is a runtime decision taken at the moment of the attempt, and being approved for something does not authorise every action within it.

guardrails: Entitlement to a product is not permission for every action within it.
Authentication success is not authorization. The two answer different questions.
A cached authorization respects current critical state changes rather than the state at the time it was cached.
Every denial carries a reason category.
governance.reusableRule: Access should be granted only when the current actor, resource and action satisfy the required authorization conditions at execution time.
governance.entityScope: the individual access request - one actor, one action, one resource
governance.entityNote: The decision belongs to the request. Allowing one action says nothing about the next, and a cached decision is re-checked against critical state that may have moved since.

identity.title: Credential issued → activate → use, expire or revoke
identity.purpose: Run an access artifact through its own validity lifecycle, separately from the right it represents.

requires: a credential issued with an owner, a scope and a validity

nodes.headline: Credential issued
Store the credential id, owner, scope, issue time, validity, whether activation is required, and its status as ISSUED. Issued is not active, and nothing may present it as usable until it is
Does this credential require activation before use?
until the credential is activated, or the credential is revoked before activation
nodes.detail: timeout after the activation window

nodes.headline: What happened during the activation window?
Expire the credential unactivated, recording that it was never claimed. An expired-unactivated credential and an expired-active one are different facts about how the artifact was used
EXPIRED, never activated
nodes.detail: a replacement credential is issued as a new artifact with its own id and lifecycle

nodes.headline: Record the credential as ACTIVE for its scope and validity
until a revocation event, or a replacement credential is issued
nodes.detail: timeout after the credential's validity end

nodes.headline: What ended the credential's active life?
REPLACED; this artifact is no longer usable
nodes.detail: the replacement runs its own lifecycle. This one is never reactivated, whatever happens to the replacement

nodes.headline: Credential compromise or revocation → disable → replace or re-authenticate
nodes.detail: a credential being revoked

nodes.headline: Re-read the credential's current version before expiring it. An extension or a replacement may have moved its validity since this timer was written, and expiring on the remembered value would undo a later decision
Does the current version still expire now?
Record the credential as EXPIRED. Expired is not revoked - the artifact reached the end of its validity rather than being withdrawn, and the two mean different things to anyone investigating later
EXPIRED after active use
nodes.detail: the entitlement behind it may still be perfectly valid; a new credential is issued for it rather than this one being revived

nodes.headline: expiry superseded by an extension or replacement
nodes.detail: the current validity governs, and its own end executes when it arrives

edges.label: Activation required
edges.when: policy requires the holder to activate it

edges.label: Active on issue
edges.when: policy makes it usable as issued

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the credential is activated, the credential is revoked before activation

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unactivated credential does not become active by waiting, and leaving it ISSUED indefinitely keeps a usable artifact alive that nobody ever claimed

edges.label: Activated
edges.when: the holder activated it

edges.label: Revoked first
edges.when: a revocation arrived before activation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a revocation event, a replacement credential is issued

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: validity ending is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the two things that can end it sooner

edges.label: Revoked
edges.when: an authoritative revocation arrived

edges.label: Replaced
edges.when: a replacement credential was issued for the same purpose
a credential being revoked

edges.label: Still expiring
edges.when: the current validity ends at this moment

edges.label: Validity moved
edges.when: an extension or replacement changed it

distinctFrom.because: The entitlement is the right. The credential is an artifact that presents it. Treating the artifact as the right means revoking a token looks like removing a benefit.

guardrails: A credential issued is not a credential active.
Credential validity is not entitlement validity. Either can end while the other holds.
A revoked credential is never restored by a stale activation or refresh event.
Expiry re-reads the current version before applying, so an extension is not undone by an older timer.
governance.reusableRule: Credentials are access artifacts with their own validity lifecycle and should not be treated as the entitlement they represent.
governance.entityScope: the individual credential - its id, owner, scope and validity
governance.entityNote: A credential's validity is its own. It can be valid while the entitlement behind it has lapsed, and revoked while that entitlement is perfectly live.

identity.title: Credential compromise or revocation → disable → replace or re-authenticate
identity.purpose: Take a credential out of use immediately, and let any replacement come through its own authorised path.

requires: a requirement to revoke: suspected or confirmed compromise, a manual revoke, a password or security reset, a device removed, access terminated, or a token invalidation

nodes.headline: Authoritative revocation requirement

Determine which credentials are actually affected. One compromised artifact does not revoke unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise implies them - over-revoking on a suspicion locks people out of things that were never at risk, and the lockout becomes the incident

Revoke the affected credentials immediately, ahead of everything else in this journey. Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions - an artifact invalidated at ten o'clock must not still authorise a request queued at one minute to
Invalidate the refresh and activation operations tied to the revoked credentials, so nothing in flight can bring one back after it has been withdrawn
Is a replacement allowed?
revoked; no replacement issued
nodes.detail: a new credential requires the entitlement and the authorisation to be established again, which is a different journey and not a continuation of this one

nodes.headline: Does issuing a replacement require verification first?
Authentication challenge → authenticate, step up or deny
nodes.detail: a replacement requiring identity or control to be re-established

nodes.headline: Issue a replacement as a new credential with its own id and its own lifecycle. The revoked artifact is never reactivated - a replacement replaces, and reusing the old identifier would make the revocation unverifiable
Credential issued → activate → use, expire or revoke
nodes.detail: a replacement credential being issued

edges.label: Replacement permitted
edges.when: the owner remains entitled and policy allows re-issuing

edges.label: No replacement
edges.when: access is being removed, or the owner is no longer entitled

edges.label: Verification required
edges.when: the revocation reason means the requester's identity or control has to be re-established

edges.label: No verification needed
edges.when: the revocation was routine and the owner's identity is not in question
a replacement requiring identity or control to be re-established
a replacement credential being issued

guardrails: One credential compromise does not automatically revoke unrelated credentials unless policy requires it.
A replacement never reactivates the revoked credential. It is a new artifact.
Security revocation takes precedence over queued access actions, including refresh and activation already in flight.
governance.reusableRule: Credential revocation should immediately invalidate the affected access artifact while replacement follows an independently authorized path.
governance.entityScope: the specific credentials affected, and their owner
governance.entityNote: Scope is the whole question. One compromised artifact does not implicate unrelated ones unless policy says the compromise reaches them.

identity.title: Deprovision request → dependency check → remove, retain or escalate
identity.purpose: Remove a capability that is no longer authorised, after establishing that nothing still depends on the thing being removed.

requires: a valid requirement to deprovision: an entitlement ended, an account closed, a role removed, a contract terminated, or a resource explicitly removed
insufficientAlone: a period of non-use, which is not an authorisation to remove anything

nodes.headline: Deprovisioning requirement
Identify the provisioned resources affected, and which of them are shared with anything still entitled
What still depends on these resources?
retained; another entitlement still depends on it
nodes.detail: when the last entitlement to the shared resource ends, removal is evaluated again. Removing it now would take it from everyone else who is still entitled

nodes.headline: until the dependent commitment completes
nodes.detail: timeout after the horizon appropriate to the dependent commitment

nodes.headline: external:data-transfer-or-termination
nodes.detail: removal requiring an export, handover or defined termination process first

nodes.headline: Deprovision idempotently. This removes the capability, not the record of it - historical and audit data is governed by its own retention and deletion lifecycle, and a deprovision that deletes it has performed an irreversible action nobody authorised
until deprovisioning succeeds, or deprovisioning fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the deprovisioning SLA

nodes.headline: How did it end?
Does the access consequence matter enough to verify?
Confirm the capability is genuinely no longer available. A deprovisioning API returning success is a statement about the API, and the question here is whether anyone can still get in
capability removed; records and audit data untouched
nodes.detail: re-provisioning follows a new entitlement rather than an undo. Deleting the retained data is a separate lifecycle with its own authorisation

nodes.headline: Is this failure retry-safe within the budget?
Retry against the budget fixed at the first failure, idempotently, so a partially completed removal is completed rather than restarted
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a capability that could not be removed

edges.label: Shared with a live entitlement
edges.when: another holder is still entitled to the same resource

edges.label: A commitment must complete first
edges.when: an in-progress service or open transaction needs the resource until it finishes

edges.label: Data transfer or a special process applies
edges.when: an export, a handover or a defined termination process has to run before removal

edges.label: Nothing depends on it
edges.when: the resource serves only the entitlement that ended

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the dependent commitment completes

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a dependency that never clears leaves an unauthorised capability alive indefinitely, which is the failure deprovisioning exists to prevent
removal requiring an export, handover or defined termination process first

edges.label: on event
edges.when: deprovisioning succeeds, deprovisioning fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: silence is not success, and an unauthorised capability that may still be live is worth escalating rather than assuming away

edges.label: Succeeded
edges.when: the system reports the resource removed

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the system reports a failure

edges.label: Verify it
edges.when: continued access would be a real problem, which is the usual case for anything security-relevant

edges.label: The removal record is sufficient
edges.when: the deprovisioning system is authoritative for whether the capability exists

edges.label: Retry
edges.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first attempt has room

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: the failure is permanent, or the budget is spent
a capability that could not be removed

distinctFrom.because: ACC-74 ends a right and stops future use. This removes the technical resource behind it, which is a separate operation with its own failure modes and its own reasons to wait.

guardrails: An entitlement ending is not an authorisation for destructive deletion.
Deprovisioning does not delete historical or audit data. That is a separate lifecycle with separate authorisation.
Shared resource dependencies are checked before removal.
Where the access consequence matters, technical success is verified rather than assumed.
Deprovisioning is idempotent, so a retry completes a partial removal rather than restarting it.
governance.reusableRule: Deprovisioning removes no-longer-authorized capability only after active dependencies and retention obligations have been reconciled.
governance.entityScope: the provisioned resource or capability, and the entitlement whose end triggered its removal
governance.entityNote: The resource is the entity, not the entitlement. A shared resource outlives any single right to it, which is why dependency is checked before anything is removed.

identity.title: Ownership assignment → validate authority → assign or reject
identity.purpose: Establish an accountable controller for an entity, by an explicit act rather than by inference.

requires: a request to assign ownership of an identified entity to an identified party
insufficientAlone: somebody holding the highest access role, which is a permission level and not an assignment
somebody having created the entity, which is a fact about history rather than a standing accountability

nodes.headline: Ownership assignment requested

Validate that the entity supports ownership at all, that the assigning party holds the authority to assign it, the proposed owner's identity, their eligibility, the existing ownership state, and whether acceptance is required
Does this entity support an ownership relationship?
Record that this entity has no ownership relationship to assign. Not everything has an owner, and inventing one creates an accountability nobody granted and nobody can be held to
entity does not support ownership; nothing assigned
nodes.detail: the entity's model gaining an ownership concept makes assignment possible. Access and administration continue to be governed on their own terms

nodes.headline: Does the assigning party hold the authority to assign this?

Record the assignment rejected, naming what failed. Access permission is not ownership, and the highest access role is not the owner - an administrator can do everything an owner can do and is still not the party accountable for the entity
assignment rejected; existing ownership state unchanged
nodes.detail: an assignment by an authorized party, or by an eligible proposed owner, is assessed on its own terms

nodes.headline: Is the proposed owner eligible to hold this?
Would this assignment create a prohibited ownership configuration?
Block the assignment and record the configuration it would have produced. A prohibited ownership arrangement created by accident is usually discovered by an audit rather than by the people it affects
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an assignment that would create a prohibited ownership configuration

nodes.headline: Must the proposed owner accept?
Record the assignment as awaiting acceptance. Nobody owns the entity on the strength of an unanswered invitation, and any existing ownership continues unchanged meanwhile
until the proposed owner accepts, or the proposed owner declines
nodes.detail: timeout after the acceptance window the assignment allows

nodes.headline: What did the proposed owner do?
Record the assignment declined. The entity's existing ownership state is untouched, and the decline is a fact worth keeping rather than a failure to retry
assignment declined; existing ownership unchanged
nodes.detail: a different proposed owner is a new assignment. Re-offering the same one changes nothing they have already answered

nodes.headline: Record the assignment as lapsed unanswered. Nothing was assigned, and this is not a decline - the proposed owner said nothing
assignment lapsed unanswered; existing ownership unchanged
nodes.detail: a renewed assignment to the same party is a new offer against the entity as it stands then

nodes.headline: Create the ownership relationship explicitly, recording who assigned it, on what authority, when, and what the owner is accountable for. Ownership is never inferred - it is a record somebody made, and that record is what any later dispute is resolved against
ownership assigned and recorded with its authority
nodes.detail: a change of owner runs through the transfer lifecycle rather than through a second assignment over the top of this one

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the entity type has an accountable controller as part of its model

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the entity has access and administration but no ownership concept

edges.label: They do
edges.when: an existing owner, a governance rule or a defined authority permits it

edges.label: They do not
edges.when: nothing establishes their right to assign ownership of this entity

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: the party meets whatever the entity requires of an owner

edges.label: Not eligible
edges.when: the party cannot hold ownership of this entity

edges.label: It would not
edges.when: the resulting ownership state is one the entity's rules permit

edges.label: It would
edges.when: the result would breach a separation, a limit or a governance constraint
an assignment that would create a prohibited ownership configuration

edges.label: They must
edges.when: ownership carries obligations the party has to take on knowingly

edges.label: They need not
edges.when: the assignment is within what the assigning authority may do unilaterally

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the proposed owner accepts, the proposed owner declines

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unanswered assignment left open indefinitely leaves an entity in a state where two parties each believe the other is accountable for it

edges.label: Accepted
edges.when: they took on the ownership

edges.label: Declined
edges.when: they refused it

distinctFrom.because: ACC-71 qualifies an entitlement - what somebody may do. This establishes who is accountable for the entity itself. An administrator can hold every entitlement the owner holds and still not be the party answerable for it.

guardrails: Access permission is not ownership.
An owner is never inferred from the highest access role.
Ownership assignment is explicit and auditable.
governance.reusableRule: Ownership exists only after an authorized assignment establishes an eligible party as the accountable controller of the entity.
governance.entityScope: the ownable entity and the ownership relationship being created on it
governance.entityNote: Ownership is a relationship somebody created. It is never derived from a role, a permission level or being the first account to touch the entity.

identity.title: Ownership transfer request → validate → pending acceptance or reject
identity.purpose: Propose a future controller without disturbing the one the entity currently has.

requires: a request to move ownership of an identified entity to an identified party

nodes.headline: Ownership transfer requested
Capture the entity, the current owner, the proposed owner, the requester, the request time, the transfer scope and any conditions attached to it

Record explicitly that the current owner remains authoritative. Nothing about their control changes because a request exists - revoking them on the invitation leaves the entity ownerless for the length of an unanswered email, and unanswered is the most common outcome
Does the requester hold the authority to transfer this entity?
Is the proposed owner eligible to hold this entity?
Is the entity transferable, and are the transfer's conditions satisfiable?
Record TRANSFER_REJECTED with what failed - authority, eligibility or transferability. The current owner is unaffected in every case
TRANSFER_REJECTED; the current owner remains the owner
nodes.detail: a transfer becoming possible - a different recipient, a cleared obligation, a proper authority - is a new request

nodes.headline: Is acceptance by the proposed owner required?

Re-read the same facts c.authority/c.eligible/c.transferable checked, immediately before handing off to execution: is the requester's authority still standing, is the proposed owner still eligible, is the entity still transferable. Nothing about this path waits on another party the way the acceptance-required path does, but authorization-for-execution still has to be a fact about the entity now, not a fact about the entity when the request first validated
Does the transfer still hold against current state?

Record PENDING_ACCEPTANCE with the request version. The current owner is still the owner, still accountable, and still able to act - and the request can be withdrawn by them at any point before it completes
PENDING_ACCEPTANCE; ownership unchanged and the request outstanding
nodes.detail: acceptance runs through its own revalidation. A request pending for weeks is a claim about an entity as it was, and is checked against the entity as it is

nodes.headline: Ownership cutover → assign new owner → reconcile old owner
nodes.detail: a transfer authorized to proceed without recipient acceptance, revalidated against current state immediately before this handoff

edges.label: They do
edges.when: the current owner, or a governance rule, permits them to initiate this

edges.label: They do not
edges.when: nothing establishes their right to move this entity

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: they meet what the entity requires of an owner

edges.label: Not eligible
edges.when: they cannot hold ownership of this entity

edges.label: Transferable
edges.when: nothing about the entity's state, obligations or governance prevents a transfer

edges.label: Not transferable
edges.when: an obligation, a hold or a rule prevents ownership moving now

edges.label: It is required
edges.when: ownership carries obligations the recipient must take on knowingly

edges.label: It is not
edges.when: policy permits the transfer to proceed on the requester's authority alone

edges.label: It holds
edges.when: authority, eligibility and transferability all still stand exactly as they did at validation

edges.label: It no longer holds
edges.when: authority, eligibility or transferability changed between validation and this revalidation
a transfer authorized to proceed without recipient acceptance, revalidated against current state immediately before this handoff

distinctFrom.because: This validates that a transfer may be proposed at all. CTL-233 validates that it is still valid when somebody finally accepts it, which is a different question asked against a different state of the world.

guardrails: A transfer requested is not a transfer completed.
The current owner remains authoritative until the transfer is effective.
The current owner is never revoked merely because a request or invitation exists.

Both paths into CTL-234's cutover revalidate immediately beforehand, whether acceptance was required or not - authorization-for-execution is never handed off on a state check that ran only at the original request.
