insufficientAlone: a case being assigned, which puts it in front of someone and starts nothing
a case being opened in an interface, where the booking of the state is what matters rather than the page view

nodes.headline: Authorized review begins
Record UNDER_REVIEW with who is reviewing and when it started. Assigned and under review are different states, and the gap between them is where most SLA breaches actually live

Evaluate the available authoritative evidence against the criteria that apply. What is evaluated is evidence - an absent document is absent, and a reviewer's sense of what it probably said is not a substitute for it
Is this reviewer actually valid for this case?
Record the conflict and step back without deciding. A decision made by a conflicted reviewer is worse than no decision, because it looks like one and will be relied on
Decision case → assign reviewer → accept, reassign or escalate
nodes.detail: a conflict or eligibility problem found mid-review

nodes.headline: Is this decision within the reviewer's authorized scope?
Decision escalation → higher authority → decide, return or reassign
nodes.detail: a decision requiring authority the current reviewer does not hold

nodes.headline: Does a non-overridable policy constraint bear on this decision?

Record that the decision is constrained by a policy this reviewer cannot override, and decide within it. Manual review that silently overrides a hard constraint produces an approved action the system will later refuse - wasting the review - or will not refuse, which is worse

Record the exception being exercised, the authority for it and the constraint it displaces. An exception exercised without being named is indistinguishable from the constraint not existing, and the next person to look will conclude it never did
Is the evidence sufficient to decide?
More information required → collect → revalidate → resume review
nodes.detail: a review blocked by missing evidence

nodes.headline: Produce the authorized decision within the case's stated scope - approved, rejected, partially approved, or another explicitly defined outcome. The decision records what it covers, because a decision whose reach is implicit is stretched later by people who were not in the room
What was decided?
Approval decision → revalidate target → execute, hold or invalidate
nodes.detail: an approved decision

nodes.headline: Partial approval → split scope → execute approved, resolve remaining
nodes.detail: a partially approved decision

nodes.headline: Rejection decision → record reason → remediate, close or reapply
nodes.detail: a rejected decision

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: no conflict of interest and no eligibility problem

edges.label: Conflicted or ineligible
edges.when: a conflict or eligibility problem surfaces during the review itself
a conflict or eligibility problem found mid-review

edges.label: Within scope
edges.when: the reviewer holds the authority the decision requires

edges.label: Beyond it
edges.when: the decision needs an authority level or a discretion this reviewer does not hold
a decision requiring authority the current reviewer does not hold

edges.label: It does, with no exception authority
edges.when: a hard constraint applies and this reviewer cannot set it aside

edges.label: It does, and explicit exception authority exists
edges.when: the reviewer holds a defined authority to grant an exception to it

edges.label: No hard constraint applies
edges.when: the decision is a judgment within ordinary criteria

edges.label: Sufficient
edges.when: everything the criteria require is present and assessable

edges.label: Something required is missing
edges.when: a fact the decision turns on is not available
a review blocked by missing evidence

edges.label: Approved
edges.when: the whole requested scope was authorized

edges.label: Partially approved
edges.when: part of the requested scope was authorized and part was not

edges.label: Rejected
edges.when: the requested action was refused
an approved decision
a partially approved decision
a rejected decision

distinctFrom.because: IDN-84 recovers from a verification that failed - a mechanical outcome with retry and remediation routes. This is a person exercising judgment against criteria, where the failure mode is deciding outside your authority rather than failing a check.

guardrails: A review started is not an approval.
Missing evidence is never invented or assumed.
A reviewer decides only within their authorized scope.
Manual review never silently overrides a hard policy constraint without explicit exception authority.
governance.reusableRule: Human review converts sufficient evidence into an authorized decision while unresolved evidence remains an explicit information requirement.
governance.entityScope: the decision case and this instance of review against it
governance.entityNote: A case can have several review instances across reassignments and reopenings. Each is recorded; none replaces the last.

identity.title: Approval decision → revalidate target → execute, hold or invalidate
identity.purpose: Carry an authorization into execution, having checked it still applies to what it was granted against.

requires: an authorized approval decision covering a stated scope

nodes.headline: Decision approved

Record the decision, the decision maker, the scope, the time, any conditions attached, and the validity or effective period where one applies. Approved is an authorization - it is not an event that has happened to the target, and the two are recorded as different things
Is the approved action being executed now?
Approval validity or expiry → revalidate → use, expire or renew review
nodes.detail: an approval that will be used later than it was granted

nodes.headline: Re-read the target's current state before executing. The approval was granted against the target as it was; executing it against a target that has since changed applies an authorization to something nobody authorized, and the reviewer will be named as having approved it
Is the target still what was approved?
What do the decision's own semantics require for a changed target?
Hold execution and record what changed. Nothing is executed on an approval whose basis has moved, and nothing is voided either - which of the two applies is a judgment, and it goes back to one
Decision superseded or reopened → revalidate → continue or new decision
nodes.detail: an approval whose target changed materially before execution

nodes.headline: Record the approval as invalidated by the change in its basis, preserving the decision itself. It was validly made and its subject no longer exists in the form it was made about
approval invalidated by a changed target; the decision record stands unedited
nodes.detail: the action, if still wanted, needs a new decision against the target as it now is. This is not the request having been rejected

nodes.headline: Does the approval carry conditions that must be satisfied before execution?
Are the conditions satisfied?
Record the approval as authorized and not yet executable, naming the outstanding condition. A conditional approval treated as an unconditional one executes an action the reviewer explicitly qualified
until every attached condition is satisfied
nodes.detail: timeout after the approval's validity period, or the bounded window policy allows a conditional approval to stand

nodes.headline: Record the approval as expired before its conditions were met. This is not the request having been rejected - it was approved, and the window closed while it waited
APPROVAL_EXPIRED before execution; the approval stands in the record as having been granted
nodes.detail: a fresh decision request can be made against the current target. The requester is told the approval lapsed rather than that they were refused

nodes.headline: external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: an approval that is valid, in scope and unconditional or satisfied

edges.label: Now
edges.when: execution follows the decision immediately

edges.label: Later
edges.when: the approval will be used at some later point, or carries a validity period
an approval that will be used later than it was granted

edges.label: Unchanged in any material way
edges.when: nothing the approval turned on has moved

edges.label: Materially changed
edges.when: something the decision depended on is different

edges.label: Hold pending re-review
edges.when: the change is material and the semantics send it back rather than voiding it

edges.label: Invalidate
edges.when: the semantics void the approval once its basis moves

edges.label: The change is inside what was approved
edges.when: the approval's scope explicitly contemplated variation of this kind
an approval whose target changed materially before execution

edges.label: Conditions apply
edges.when: the approval was granted subject to something happening first

edges.label: Unconditional
edges.when: nothing stands between the approval and the action

edges.label: Satisfied
edges.when: every condition attached to the approval is authoritatively met

edges.label: Not yet
edges.when: at least one condition is outstanding

edges.label: on event
edges.when: every attached condition is satisfied

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an approval waiting indefinitely on a condition that never arrives is an authorization with no expiry that nobody decided to grant
an approval that is valid, in scope and unconditional or satisfied

distinctFrom.because: This carries a whole authorized scope into execution. DEC-187 exists because a partitioned scope raises a separate problem - which parts may proceed, and whether the action can be half-done at all.

guardrails: Approved is not executed.
An approval never bypasses the execution lifecycle's own validation.
An approval applies only to the scope it defined.
A stale approval never mutates newer incompatible state.
governance.reusableRule: Approval authorizes a defined action but execution must still confirm that the approved action remains valid against current state.
governance.entityScope: the approved decision and the target action it authorizes
governance.entityNote: The approval and the action are two things. The approval is complete the moment it is made; the action has not started.

identity.title: Rejection decision → record reason → remediate, close or reapply
identity.purpose: Treat a refusal as the business outcome it is, and say what if anything the requester can do next.

requires: an authorized rejection decision on a decision case, within the reviewer's scope
insufficientAlone: a technical failure to process the request, which is an error rather than a decision and belongs in a different queue

nodes.headline: Authorized rejection issued

Record the reason and its category, the decision maker, the time, the affected scope, and the reapplication or remediation semantics where they are defined. A rejection is an authorized business outcome rather than a technical failure - recording it as an error puts it in the wrong queue, where something will eventually retry it
Is the reason something the requester can correct?

State exactly what would have to change, drawn from the policy that defines the path. A rejection reason that is not actionable is a refusal, and telling someone their request was declined without saying what would change that is where most escalations come from
rejected, with a defined remediation path stated
nodes.detail: the requester satisfying the stated condition opens a new decision request linked to this one, so the reviewer sees what was refused and why

nodes.headline: Does policy permit a new request once the requirements are satisfied?

Record the reapplication conditions policy actually defines - after what period, on what basis, with what evidence. Nothing is invented here: a right to reapply that does not exist becomes one people rely on the moment it is stated, and withdrawing it later is worse than never offering it
rejected, with a defined reapplication right
nodes.detail: a new request under those conditions is a new decision case, linked to this one. Nothing resubmits automatically - an automatic resubmission either loops or hides the rejection from whoever needed to see it

nodes.headline: Does policy grant an appeal or reconsideration right?
Appeal or dispute → evidence review → uphold, reverse or modify
nodes.detail: a rejection policy grants an appeal right against

nodes.headline: Record CLOSED_REJECTED with the full reason. The request is not resubmitted automatically and the rejection history stays readable - it is the answer to why this was refused, and it will be asked for
CLOSED_REJECTED; a terminal authorized outcome with no defined path onward
nodes.detail: a materially different request is a different case. Repeating the same one changes nothing and is not treated as new

edges.label: Correctable, with a defined remediation path
edges.when: policy states what would have to change and permits the case to proceed on that basis

edges.label: Not correctable this way
edges.when: the reason is not something a correction addresses, or no remediation path is defined

edges.label: It does
edges.when: policy defines when and on what basis a new request may be made

edges.label: It does not, or says nothing
edges.when: no reapplication right is defined

edges.label: It does
edges.when: a defined appeal or reconsideration mechanism covers this decision

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: no appeal right is defined for this kind of decision
a rejection policy grants an appeal right against

distinctFrom.because: This is the first decision's rejection outcome. FBK-47 is the appeal or reconsideration lifecycle, which exists only where policy grants that right - and this journey hands to it rather than performing it.

OWN-59 handles an approval rejected inside a work-ownership flow and asks whether a revision may be resubmitted. This is the decision-case rejection with its full reason taxonomy, and its three separate exits: correctable, reapplicable, and appealable.

guardrails: Rejected is not a system failure.
Rejected requests are never automatically resubmitted.
Appeal and reapplication rights are never invented.
The rejection history remains auditable.
governance.reusableRule: A rejection is an authorized business outcome whose next path depends on whether policy permits correction, reapplication or appeal.
governance.entityScope: the decision case and the rejection issued against it
governance.entityNote: A rejection closes a decision, not a relationship. What follows it comes from policy rather than from how final the word sounds.

identity.title: Partial approval → split scope → execute approved, resolve remaining
identity.purpose: Make the authorized and unauthorized halves of one request explicit, so only the first can move.

requires: an authorized decision approving part of a requested scope and not the rest

nodes.headline: Decision partially approved

Partition the originally requested scope into what is approved, what is rejected, and what remains pending or needs further review. Every part of the original lands in exactly one - a part in none of them is a piece of the request nobody answered, and the requester finds out by it silently not happening

Persist the decision basis for each partition separately. Approved with exceptions, recorded as a single note, cannot tell anyone six months later which exception applied to what - and that is exactly the question an audit of a partial approval asks
Is any scope still unresolved rather than decided either way?

Keep the unresolved scope active as a live decision case rather than closing it with the rest. Closing a partially approved request as decided leaves the unanswered portion invisible, and the requester assumes it was refused - which is a rejection nobody made and nobody can explain
Do the governing semantics permit the approved scope to proceed on its own?
Decision escalation → higher authority → decide, return or reassign
nodes.detail: a partial approval against an action with no defined atomicity

nodes.headline: Hold the entire action. Executing part of an atomic action produces a half-state the system has no name for, cannot report on, and cannot roll back cleanly
entire action held; the approved scope is authorized and unexecuted because the action cannot be split
nodes.detail: when the remaining scope is decided, the whole action is re-evaluated as one rather than assembled from the parts that were approved at different times

nodes.headline: Does the approved scope share side effects with the rejected or pending scope?

Execute the shared side effect once, for the approved scope only. Splitting a request and running its shared effects per partition charges twice, provisions twice or notifies twice - and the duplicate is found by the recipient rather than by the split that caused it
external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: an approved partition that may proceed independently

edges.label: Some remains open
edges.when: part of the scope needs further review or further evidence

edges.label: Everything is decided
edges.when: each part is either approved or rejected

edges.label: Separable
edges.when: the action's semantics explicitly allow partial execution

edges.label: Atomic
edges.when: the action's semantics require all of it or none

edges.label: Atomicity is not defined
edges.when: nothing authoritative says whether this action can be half-done
a partial approval against an action with no defined atomicity

edges.label: It shares
edges.when: a charge, a provisioning step or a notification would otherwise run per partition

edges.label: Independent
edges.when: the approved scope's effects touch nothing the other partitions touch
an approved partition that may proceed independently

distinctFrom.because: DEC-185 executes an authorization whose scope is whole. This has to partition a scope first, and then answer a question DEC-185 never faces: whether the action can be half-done at all.

guardrails: Partial approval is not full approval.
The rejected scope is never executed.
Shared side effects are not duplicated when the scope is split.
Atomicity semantics are never invented.
governance.reusableRule: Partial approval should make the authorized and unauthorized portions explicit so only valid scope can proceed.
governance.entityScope: the decision case and the partitions of its requested scope
governance.entityNote: Every part of the original scope lands in exactly one partition. A part in none of them is a piece of the request nobody answered and nobody will notice.

identity.title: Approval validity or expiry → revalidate → use, expire or renew review
identity.purpose: Answer, at the moment of use, whether an approval is still one - in time, in context and in count.

requires: an approval carrying an explicit validity condition, or an approval being used later than it was granted

nodes.headline: Approval validity evaluation required

Evaluate the approval's scope, its valid-from and valid-until where those are defined, the target version or state it was granted against, its conditions, and whether a single-use approval has already been consumed
Does this approval define an expiry?

Record that this approval carries no expiry, rather than assigning one. Inventing an expiry invalidates authorizations that were granted without limit, and the holder discovers it when the thing they were approved for stops working with no decision behind it
Is it inside its validity window?
Is this a single-use approval that has already been consumed?
Refuse the reuse and record the attempt. A single-use approval used twice authorizes an action once and performs it twice, which is the same failure as a duplicate payment with a signature on it
already consumed; the approval cannot authorize a second execution
nodes.detail: a further execution needs a further approval, which is a new decision rather than a re-reading of this one

nodes.headline: Is the target still in the state the approval was granted against?

Record that valid time was not enough: the approval is inside its window and outside its context. A time-valid approval against a target that has changed is the most convincing kind of wrong authorization, because every visible check passes
Decision superseded or reopened → revalidate → continue or new decision
nodes.detail: an unexpired approval whose target has moved beyond its context

nodes.headline: Record the approval as usable within its scope, and record this use where the approval is counted. Validity is established at the moment of use rather than carried as a flag someone set earlier
valid and usable within its stated scope
nodes.detail: each further use re-evaluates from here, because time, target state and consumption can all have moved since the last one

nodes.headline: Record APPROVAL_EXPIRED. This is not the request having been rejected: it was approved, and the authorization lapsed before it was used - and telling the holder the wrong one of those changes whether they think asking again is worth anything
Does policy allow a renewed review of a lapsed approval?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a lapsed approval policy allows to be sought again

nodes.headline: APPROVAL_EXPIRED; the approval stands in the record as having been granted and unused
nodes.detail: a new decision request against the current target is assessed fresh, and this lapse is not held against it

edges.label: It defines one
edges.when: a valid-until, a period or a use-by condition was set when it was granted

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the approval was granted without a time limit

edges.label: Inside
edges.when: the current time falls within valid-from and valid-until

edges.label: Past valid-until
edges.when: the window has closed

edges.label: Already used
edges.when: the approval permits one use and one has been recorded

edges.label: Not consumed
edges.when: the approval is reusable, or its single use has not happened

edges.label: Same, or within what was approved
edges.when: the target's version or state matches what the reviewer was looking at, or the variation is inside the approved scope

edges.label: Changed beyond the approved context
edges.when: the target has moved in a way the approval did not contemplate
an unexpired approval whose target has moved beyond its context

edges.label: It does
edges.when: policy defines how a lapsed approval may be sought again

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: no renewal path is defined
a lapsed approval policy allows to be sought again

guardrails: An approval expiry is never invented where none exists.
Valid time alone is not sufficient where an approval is state-specific or version-specific.
An expired approval is not a rejected request.
A single-use approval cannot authorize a second execution.
governance.reusableRule: An approval remains usable only within the time, state and scope boundaries under which it was authorized.
governance.entityScope: the approval decision and the boundaries it was granted within
governance.entityNote: Validity is a question asked at each use rather than a flag set once. An approval valid this morning can be outside its context this afternoon without any clock having run out.

identity.title: Decision escalation → higher authority → decide, return or reassign
identity.purpose: Move a case to an authority that can actually resolve it, carrying the work already done and predetermining nothing.

requires: a defined escalation criterion being met - an authority threshold, a policy exception, material risk, a reviewer conflict, complexity, SLA governance, or a disagreement requiring higher authority
insufficientAlone: a case being difficult, which is a reason to think rather than a reason to pass it upward

nodes.headline: Escalation criterion satisfied

Record the escalation reason. Escalated is not approved - the case remains undecided and is now in front of someone else, and a status that reads as progress toward approval misleads everyone waiting on it

Preserve the existing evidence, the review history, the original deadline and any non-final assessments already made. An escalation that starts the case from nothing throws away the work that identified why it needed escalating in the first place
Does an eligible higher or different authority exist?

Record that no eligible authority exists for this decision, and stop. A case escalated into a level that does not exist becomes permanently owned by nobody, which is the failure mode that makes escalation chains dangerous rather than merely slow
no authority exists to decide this; the case is stopped and named rather than circulating
nodes.detail: an authority being defined for this decision type reopens it. Until then it is visibly unresolvable rather than invisibly unassigned

nodes.headline: Route to the eligible authority, within the escalation levels the model actually defines. Escalation is bounded - a case that can escalate indefinitely has no owner at any level, and each hop makes the next one easier to justify
until the escalated authority is able to decide, or the escalated authority requires more information, or the escalated authority returns the case with direction
nodes.detail: timeout after the case's original deadline, preserved rather than restarted

nodes.headline: What did the escalated authority do?
Review started → evaluate evidence → decide or request more information
nodes.detail: an escalated case an eligible authority will review

nodes.headline: More information required → collect → revalidate → resume review
nodes.detail: an escalated case blocked by missing evidence

nodes.headline: Record the direction given and return the case to the original level, which decides within it. The higher authority acted only within its own granted authority - guidance is not a decision, and recording it as one attributes an outcome to someone who declined to make it
Decision case → assign reviewer → accept, reassign or escalate
nodes.detail: a case returned with direction rather than decided

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: an escalated case outliving the deadline it preserved

edges.label: One exists
edges.when: a defined authority level above or beside this one can take the decision

edges.label: None
edges.when: no eligible authority exists, or the escalation levels the model defines are exhausted

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the escalated authority is able to decide, the escalated authority requires more information, the escalated authority returns the case with direction

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the requester's deadline was never about who happens to be holding the case. An escalation that resets it makes the delay invisible to everyone except the person waiting

edges.label: They can decide
edges.when: the authority holds what the decision requires and is ready to review

edges.label: More information is required
edges.when: the escalated authority identifies evidence the decision turns on

edges.label: Returned with direction
edges.when: the authority gives guidance and sends the case back to be decided at the original level
an escalated case an eligible authority will review
an escalated case blocked by missing evidence
a case returned with direction rather than decided
an escalated case outliving the deadline it preserved

distinctFrom.because: DEC-182 moves ownership at the same authority level because someone cannot take it. This moves the case to a different or higher authority because the current level cannot decide the question at all.
OWN-55 escalates responsibility for work that is stuck. This escalates decision authority specifically - the case is not stuck, it is in front of someone who is not permitted to answer it.

guardrails: Escalated is not approved.
Escalation never erases previous review work.
Escalation is bounded by defined levels rather than repeated indefinitely.
A higher authority still acts only within the authority it was granted.
governance.reusableRule: Escalation changes who is authorized to resolve a decision without changing the underlying evidence or pretending a decision has already been made.
governance.entityScope: the decision case and the escalation acting on it
governance.entityNote: The case is one case throughout. Escalation changes who holds it and changes neither the evidence nor the deadline.

identity.title: Decision superseded or reopened → revalidate → continue or new decision
identity.purpose: Let a decision be reconsidered without any part of the original being rewritten.

requires: a material event bearing on a prior decision - new evidence, a material target-state change, an authorized reconsideration, an error in the previous decision, or an upstream authoritative correction
insufficientAlone: the requester disagreeing with the outcome, which is an appeal and runs through the appeal mechanism
new information arriving, most of which confirms what was already concluded

nodes.headline: Decision challenged or superseded

Preserve the original decision as a historical fact, exactly as recorded. Nothing about it is edited - a decision record changed in place removes the ability to say what was decided, by whom, and on what basis, which is the only thing anyone ever actually needs from it

Assess whether the event genuinely bears on the decision. New evidence arriving is not the previous decision becoming wrong - most of it confirms what was already concluded, and reopening for each arriving fact produces a case that never closes
Does the existing decision still hold?
Retain the decision and record that it was reconsidered and held. No duplicate review is opened, and the fact that it was looked at again is itself worth having in the record
original decision retained; reconsidered and unchanged
nodes.detail: a further event is assessed on its own merits rather than accumulating into a reopening by weight of attempts

nodes.headline: Is reconsideration authorized, and is it the same decision scope?
reconsideration not authorized; the original decision stands
nodes.detail: where policy grants an appeal right, it is exercised through the appeal mechanism rather than by reopening the case here

nodes.headline: Create a new decision case, linked to the previous one. A different question decided under an old case's scope produces a decision that reads as covering something it never considered, and it will be relied on that way
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a materially different question raised against a decided case

nodes.headline: Record the case REOPENED, carrying the original decision and all prior evidence forward. Reopened is not the original decision deleted - and the new decision, when it comes, supersedes the old one as a later authoritative record rather than replacing it
Was the previous decision already executed?

Record what was executed and when. The consequences happened - money moved, access was granted, something shipped - and pretending the execution never occurred leaves real effects in place with nothing in the record explaining them
Do the executed consequences need correcting regardless of what the new decision concludes?
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: executed consequences that need correcting independently of the reconsidered decision

nodes.headline: Review started → evaluate evidence → decide or request more information
nodes.detail: a reopened case ready to be decided again

edges.label: It holds
edges.when: the event does not change what the decision turned on

edges.label: Genuinely challenged
edges.when: the event bears directly on the basis the decision was made on

edges.label: Authorized, same scope
edges.when: someone with the authority to reconsider is doing so, over the same question

edges.label: Authorized, but a different question
edges.when: what is now being asked is not what the original decision covered

edges.label: Not authorized
edges.when: no reconsideration right or authority applies
a materially different question raised against a decided case

edges.label: Not executed
edges.when: the decision authorized something that never happened

edges.label: Already executed
edges.when: the authorized action was carried out and its consequences are real

edges.label: They need correcting now
edges.when: the execution was wrong on its own terms - an error, or an upstream correction that invalidates it

edges.label: They stand pending the new decision
edges.when: the execution was validly made and only the reconsidered decision can change what should follow
executed consequences that need correcting independently of the reconsidered decision
a reopened case ready to be decided again

distinctFrom.because: OWN-58 asks whether a material change after approval needs re-approval, inside a work-ownership flow. This owns the decision record's history: what supersedes what, what was already executed, and what a new decision does not undo.

guardrails: Reopened is not the original decision deleted.
New evidence does not automatically invalidate an old decision.
Executed consequences may require a separate correction or reversal lifecycle.
The historical decision record is never mutated in place.
governance.reusableRule: Decision reconsideration should preserve prior decisions as history while creating a new authoritative decision state only when current evidence and authority justify it.
governance.entityScope: the existing decision and the event challenging it
governance.entityNote: The original decision is immutable. A new decision supersedes it as a later record rather than replacing it in place.

identity.title: Document requirement → determine artifact → create, reuse or waive
identity.purpose: Decide whether a new artifact is genuinely needed, or whether one already exists that answers the requirement.

requires: a business process reaching a point where an artifact is required
insufficientAlone: a process step occurring, which does not by itself mean a new document is needed

nodes.headline: Process reaches document requirement
Determine the required artifact type, its purpose, the required parties, the required data, its validity requirements, and whether an existing artifact could satisfy all of them
Does an existing valid artifact satisfy this requirement?

Reference the existing artifact and its exact version rather than generating another. Regenerating an identical document produces two records claiming the same thing, and a later reader has to work out which one anybody actually acted on
requirement satisfied by an existing valid artifact
nodes.detail: that artifact expiring or being revoked reopens the requirement, which is then assessed fresh rather than assumed still met

nodes.headline: Does an authorized rule waive this requirement?

Record the waiver with the rule and the authority behind it. A requirement quietly skipped is indistinguishable from one nobody noticed, and the difference matters entirely when somebody asks why the document is missing
requirement waived, with the authority recorded
nodes.detail: the waiver's own scope bounds it. A different instance of the same requirement is assessed on its own terms

nodes.headline: Create the document obligation with its type, purpose, parties, required data and validity requirements
Document draft → populate → validate → ready or blocked
nodes.detail: an unmet artifact requirement

edges.label: One does
edges.when: an existing document matches the type, the scope, the parties and is still within its validity

edges.label: None
edges.when: nothing held matches, or what is held has lapsed or was scoped to something else

edges.label: It is waived
edges.when: a rule or an authority explicitly excuses the artifact for this case

edges.label: It stands
edges.when: no waiver applies
an unmet artifact requirement

distinctFrom.because: RSK-195 owns the compliance requirement itself - whether an obligation is met. This owns the artifact lifecycle a requirement may need: which document, generated how, issued when, signed by whom. A compliance requirement can be satisfied without any document, and most documents exist for reasons that are not compliance.

guardrails: A process event does not always require a new document.
An identical artifact is not regenerated unnecessarily.
Reuse respects the existing document's version, scope and validity.
governance.reusableRule: A document should be created only when the process has an unmet artifact requirement that cannot be satisfied by an existing valid record.
governance.entityScope: the business process and the artifact requirement it has reached
governance.entityNote: The requirement names a type, a purpose, parties and validity conditions. Reuse is only possible against all four, not against the type alone.

identity.title: Document draft → populate → validate → ready or blocked
identity.purpose: Build the contents from authoritative sources and prove they are complete before anything is issued.

requires: a document obligation with a defined type and required contents

nodes.headline: Document generation begins

Resolve the required data from its authoritative sources, recording which source and which version each field came from. A document that cannot say where its contents came from cannot be defended when they are questioned, and they will be
Populate the draft from what was resolved, and from nothing else
Validate the required fields, the source versions, the party identities, the document type, the draft's internal consistency, and any required attachments or components
Is the draft complete and valid?

Record BLOCKED or MISSING_REQUIREMENT naming exactly what is absent. Missing data is never filled with a plausible value - a generated file carrying an invented field looks authoritative, reads as authoritative, and is not
until the missing data becomes available, or the document requirement is withdrawn
nodes.detail: timeout after the window the requiring process allows for the artifact

nodes.headline: How did the wait resolve?
Abandon the draft, preserving the record that it was started and why it stopped. Nothing was issued, so nothing about it is authoritative
draft abandoned; nothing was issued
nodes.detail: the requirement arising again starts its own draft. Repopulating this one would use the sources as they were rather than as they are

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a draft blocked past the window the process allows

nodes.headline: Record READY_TO_ISSUE. A generated file is not a valid document - readiness is the validation having passed rather than the rendering having succeeded, and the two are routinely confused because both produce a file
Ready document → issue → immutable issued version
nodes.detail: a validated draft ready for issuance

edges.label: Complete and valid
edges.when: every required element is present, sourced and consistent

edges.label: Something is missing or inconsistent
edges.when: a required field, source, party or component is absent or contradicts another

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the missing data becomes available, the document requirement is withdrawn

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a draft waiting indefinitely on data nobody is supplying blocks the process that needed it, without anyone having decided to block it

edges.label: The data arrived
edges.when: what was missing is now available from an authoritative source

edges.label: Withdrawn
edges.when: the requirement no longer stands
a draft blocked past the window the process allows
a validated draft ready for issuance

guardrails: A generated file is not a valid document.
Missing data is never silently invented.
Source references and their versions remain traceable.
governance.reusableRule: A document becomes issuable only after its required contents have been populated from authoritative sources and validated for completeness.
governance.entityScope: the draft and the source entities its contents came from
governance.entityNote: Each field carries which source and which version it came from. A document that cannot say where its contents originated cannot be defended when they are questioned.

identity.title: Ready document → issue → immutable issued version
identity.purpose: Freeze the artifact at a version that can be identified, referenced and never quietly changed.

requires: a validated draft with the authority to issue it established
insufficientAlone: a draft being ready, which says the contents validate and nothing about whether anyone authorized issuing it

nodes.headline: Document authorized for issuance

Create the issued version, capturing the document id, the version id, the issue time, the issuer, the parties, the content with its hash or reference, the source context it was built from, and the effective semantics where the document defines any

Freeze it. An issued version never changes - a document that can be edited after issue cannot answer what anybody was looking at when they agreed to it, and that is the only question it will ever be asked. Later changes create a successor rather than an edit
Do the document's own semantics make it effective on issue?

Record ISSUED and nothing more. Issuance is the artifact existing in fixed, identifiable form - whether it has any effect is a separate question with its own conditions, and a contract can exist in final form and bind nobody
ISSUED and immutable; effect not established
nodes.detail: any later change creates a new version through the amendment lifecycle. This version is never reopened, edited or reissued under the same identifier

nodes.headline: Record the effective semantics exactly as the document states them, without inventing any. A document type that takes effect at issue says so; assuming it on behalf of one that does not brings terms into force early
Signed document → validate completion → effective or pending condition
nodes.detail: an issued document whose own terms make it effective without signature

edges.label: Not by itself
edges.when: effect depends on signature, a date, a condition or another dependency

edges.label: Effective on issue, by its own terms
edges.when: the document type takes effect at issuance without further conditions
an issued document whose own terms make it effective without signature

guardrails: A draft is not an issued document.
An issued document never silently changes.
Issuance does not automatically make a document effective.
governance.reusableRule: Issuance freezes an auditable version of a document so later changes create new versions rather than rewriting what was previously issued.
governance.entityScope: the document and the specific version being issued
governance.entityNote: This is the boundary between an editable draft and an authoritative record. After it, change means a successor.

identity.title: Signed document → validate completion → effective or pending condition
identity.purpose: Establish when a document actually starts doing something, which is not when it was signed.

requires: all required signatures complete against one version, or an issued document whose own terms make it effective without signature

nodes.headline: Document completion established

Validate that every required signature is present, that each is against the correct version, that each signer held the authority they signed under, which conditions apply, and what the effective date is
Does the completion hold up?

Record the completion as not established, naming exactly what fails. A document that looks signed and is not is the most dangerous state in this category, because everything downstream will treat it as agreement
Document or record conflict → determine authoritative version → reconcile
nodes.detail: signatures that do not bind to the version they are held against

nodes.headline: What governs when this takes effect?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a completed document with no defined effectiveness rules

nodes.headline: Record PENDING_EFFECTIVE_DATE. The document is complete and does nothing yet, which is a real state and not an incomplete one
until the document is superseded or revoked before its date
nodes.detail: timeout after the effective date

nodes.headline: Record PENDING_CONDITION, naming the dependency. A document waiting on an unstated condition is indistinguishable from one that is simply stuck
until the dependency is satisfied, or the dependency becomes unsatisfiable
nodes.detail: timeout after the window the document or its process allows for the condition

nodes.headline: How did the dependency resolve?

Re-read the document's current standing at the effective moment - is this still the authoritative version, has it been superseded or revoked, do the parties still stand. A stale signed version activating a newer business state is exactly the failure the version binding exists to prevent
Does the document still stand at its effective moment?
Record that the document did not take effect, because it was superseded or revoked first. It remains a validly issued and validly signed record of what was agreed - it simply never became operative
Record the condition as unsatisfiable and the document as never effective, naming which dependency failed
complete and never effective; the signed record stands as history
nodes.detail: a successor document runs its own effectiveness. Nothing here is deleted - a signed agreement that never came into force is still evidence of what the parties agreed to

nodes.headline: Record EFFECTIVE with the version, the moment, and what made it so. This is the document's own state - what it then causes elsewhere is a different lifecycle and is not implied by this
Does this document taking effect create or change a business state elsewhere?
external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: an effective document that starts something elsewhere

nodes.headline: EFFECTIVE; the document is in force from the recorded moment
nodes.detail: expiry, revocation or supersession each end future reliance on it through their own lifecycles, and none of them changes that it was effective while it was

edges.label: It holds
edges.when: signatures, versions and authorities all check out

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: a signature is against the wrong version, or a signer lacked the authority
signatures that do not bind to the version they are held against

edges.label: Effective on valid signature
edges.when: the document's terms make completion sufficient

edges.label: A future effective date
edges.when: the document names a date after completion

edges.label: A further dependency
edges.when: effect waits on a condition, an approval or an external event

edges.label: The rules do not define effectiveness
edges.when: nothing states when or whether this document takes effect
a completed document with no defined effectiveness rules

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the document is superseded or revoked before its date

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the effective date is what this wait exists for. It is the normal outcome, and the point at which the document's current standing is checked again

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the dependency is satisfied, the dependency becomes unsatisfiable

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a signed document waiting forever on a condition that will not arrive is an agreement in limbo, and both parties are entitled to know which it is

edges.label: Satisfied
edges.when: the condition governing effect is met

edges.label: Unsatisfiable
edges.when: the condition cannot now be met

edges.label: Still authoritative
edges.when: this version is current, unsuperseded and unrevoked

edges.label: Superseded or revoked
edges.when: something replaced or withdrew it before it took effect

edges.label: It does
edges.when: a relationship, an entitlement, an obligation or an authorization begins from it

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the document's effect is entirely a matter of the record itself
an effective document that starts something elsewhere

distinctFrom.because: SUB-161 makes a continuing relationship active. This makes a document effective, which may be what triggers that - but a document can be effective without creating a relationship, and a relationship can activate without any document.

guardrails: Signed is not automatically effective.
Legal or business effectiveness rules are never invented.
A stale or superseded signed version never activates newer business state.
Effectiveness is revalidated at the effective moment rather than assumed from completion.
governance.reusableRule: Signing establishes documented agreement or authorization; effectiveness begins only when the conditions governing that document's effect are satisfied.
governance.entityScope: the completed document version and the effect it is to have
governance.entityNote: Effectiveness is the document's own state. What it then causes elsewhere is a different lifecycle with its own entity.

identity.title: Document change → new version or amendment → supersede prospectively
identity.purpose: Change an issued artifact by creating a successor, leaving what it replaces exactly as it was.

requires: an authorized need to change an issued document, with the authority established
insufficientAlone: an error being noticed, which identifies a need rather than authorizing a change

nodes.headline: Authorized document change required
Identify the base version, the changed scope, the authority for the change, its effective semantics and the parties it affects
What form does the successor take?
Create the successor as a new draft version, carrying the base forward with the change incorporated. The base version is not touched
Create an amendment that references the base version rather than restating it. What changed stays legible as a change, which a full reissue makes somebody diff two documents to discover

Record the lineage - this successor, its base, the authority and what changed. Lineage is what makes a document history readable; without it a chain of versions is a set of unrelated files with similar names and nobody can say which one anybody signed
until the successor completes its own validation, approval and signature requirements, or the change is abandoned
nodes.detail: timeout after the window the change process allows

nodes.headline: Did the successor become authoritative?
Record the change as abandoned. The base version stands unchanged and unmarked - a superseded flag set in anticipation of a successor that never arrived leaves the current document looking obsolete
change abandoned; the base version remains current and unmarked
nodes.detail: the change can be attempted again as a new successor against whatever version is current then

nodes.headline: Mark the prior version SUPERSEDED for applicable future use. Superseded is not deleted and not historically invalid - the prior version governed everything that happened while it was current, and that stays true regardless of what replaced it
When do the successor's terms apply?

Apply the new terms only from the successor's own effective conditions. Applying them before it is effective enforces terms nobody has agreed to yet, and applying them backwards makes a compliant history retroactively non-compliant
successor authoritative going forward; the prior version preserved and superseded
nodes.detail: a further change creates its own successor against this one, extending the lineage rather than replacing it

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a successor with undefined effective semantics

edges.label: A new version
edges.when: the document is reissued in full with the change incorporated

edges.label: An amendment
edges.when: a separate instrument modifies the base while leaving it standing

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the successor completes its own validation, approval and signature requirements, the change is abandoned

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a successor stuck in progress leaves two versions in play and no clear answer about which governs, which is the exact ambiguity the lineage exists to prevent

edges.label: It did
edges.when: the successor completed validation, approval and any required signatures

edges.label: Abandoned
edges.when: the change was withdrawn or could not complete

edges.label: From its own effective conditions
edges.when: the successor states when it takes effect

edges.label: The effective semantics are not defined
edges.when: nothing states when the new terms begin
a successor with undefined effective semantics

guardrails: A new version does not delete the old version.
Superseded is not historically invalid.
New terms are never applied before the successor's required effective conditions.
Lineage between base and successor is recorded rather than implied.
governance.reusableRule: Document changes create a traceable successor version whose authority begins according to its own approval and effective conditions.
governance.entityScope: the document lineage and the successor version or amendment being created
governance.entityNote: Lineage is the entity. A version without a recorded base and authority is an unrelated file that happens to share a name.

identity.title: Document expiry → revalidate requirement → renew, replace or close
identity.purpose: End future reliance on a time-limited artifact, and stop only what genuinely needs it to be current.

requires: a time-limited document approaching or reaching its defined expiry

nodes.headline: Document validity reaches expiry
Is the expiry defined by the document or its governing rules?

Record that this document carries no expiry, rather than assigning one. Inventing an expiry invalidates something nobody invalidated, and dependent processes then start failing for a reason that does not exist anywhere in the rules
no expiry defined; the document remains valid until something else ends it
nodes.detail: an authority withdrawing it runs through revocation, and a successor replacing it runs through amendment. Neither is expiry

nodes.headline: Determine the active and future processes that depend on this document's current validity. What expires is future reliance - nothing that happened while it was valid changes, and the list is of what needs it now rather than of what ever used it
Record EXPIRED. Expired is not revoked: nobody withdrew it, its time ran out, and everything it authorized while valid remains authorized
Do the governing rules require a replacement or renewal?
Raise a new document requirement, linked to the expired artifact so the successor's purpose is traceable to what it replaces
Document requirement → determine artifact → create, reuse or waive
nodes.detail: an expired document the rules require to be replaced

nodes.headline: May the dependent processes continue after expiry?
Leave the dependent processes running under the rules that permit it, recording that the artifact expired and that they continue by rule rather than by oversight
EXPIRED; dependent processes continue under rules that permit it
nodes.detail: a future action that does require current validity is blocked at its own point rather than by pre-emptively stopping everything

nodes.headline: Block only the future actions that require a currently valid document. Everything not requiring current validity continues - one expired certificate stopping an entire relationship is a suspension nobody decided and nobody can find the authority for
EXPIRED; only the actions requiring current validity are blocked
nodes.detail: a replacement artifact releases the blocked actions. Actions performed while the document was valid remain historical facts

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an expired document whose effect on dependent processes the rules do not define

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: the document or a rule states when its validity ends

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no expiry was ever set for this artifact

edges.label: They require one
edges.when: a current artifact must exist for the process to continue

edges.label: They do not
edges.when: no replacement is mandated by the rules
an expired document the rules require to be replaced

edges.label: They may
edges.when: the governing rules permit them to run on without a current artifact

edges.label: Future actions require current validity
edges.when: specific future actions need a valid document and the rest do not

edges.label: The rules do not say
edges.when: nothing states what the dependent processes do after expiry
an expired document whose effect on dependent processes the rules do not define

distinctFrom.because: Expiry is time running out on terms the document itself set. Revocation is an authority withdrawing it. Nobody decided the first, somebody decided the second, and they carry different consequences for what was relied on meanwhile.

guardrails: Expired is not revoked.
Expiration dates are never invented.
Actions performed while the document was valid remain historical facts.
Only processes requiring current validity are affected.
governance.reusableRule: Document expiry ends future reliance on a time-limited artifact according to its governing rules without rewriting actions completed while it was valid.
governance.entityScope: the time-limited document and the processes depending on its current validity
governance.entityNote: What expires is future reliance. Everything done while it was valid was done while it was valid.

identity.title: Document revocation or withdrawal → stop future reliance → reconcile
identity.purpose: Withdraw an artifact by an authority's decision, exactly as far as that decision reaches.

requires: a revocation or withdrawal by an authority entitled to make it
insufficientAlone: a document expiring, which is time rather than a decision
a successor being issued, which supersedes rather than revokes

nodes.headline: Authoritative revocation occurs
Record the revoked version, the authority, the reason and its category, the revocation time, and the revocation's own effective semantics

Record REVOKED, preserving the document and everything about it. A revoked document's history stays available - it is the evidence for everything done while it stood, and deleting it destroys the explanation for actions that were entirely correct at the time
Identify the pending and future processes relying on this document
What does the revocation's effective scope permit going forward?
Block or revalidate the affected processes, which now have no valid artifact behind them

Apply exactly the scope the revocation names, and nothing wider. A revocation applied more broadly than its own terms withdraws things the authority did not withdraw, and there is no record of who decided that because nobody did
What does the revocation say about actions already completed?
Apply the retroactive consequence the revocation actually states, recording the authority for it. What is applied is what was stated - a revocation that reaches backwards has to say so, and how far

Leave completed actions as they stand. Retroactive invalidity is not inferred - assuming it turns every past action taken under a now-revoked certificate into a problem nobody has decided is a problem, and unwinding them is far harder than not unwinding them
Is a replacement artifact required?
Document requirement → determine artifact → create, reuse or waive
nodes.detail: a revoked document that still needs replacing

nodes.headline: REVOKED; future reliance stopped within the revocation's scope, history preserved
nodes.detail: the revocation being itself withdrawn or narrowed is a further authoritative act, recorded on top rather than by clearing this one

edges.label: No future reliance at all
edges.when: the revocation withdraws the document entirely from here on

edges.label: Limited scope, some reliance continues
edges.when: the revocation names a scope narrower than the whole document

edges.label: It explicitly reaches them
edges.when: the revocation states a retroactive consequence and the authority for it

edges.label: It says nothing about them
edges.when: the revocation addresses future reliance only

edges.label: One is required
edges.when: the processes that relied on this still need a valid artifact

edges.label: None
edges.when: nothing further requires an artifact of this kind
a revoked document that still needs replacing

distinctFrom.because: An amendment replaces a document with a successor that carries the same purpose forward. Revocation withdraws it with nothing behind it - there may be no successor, and the reason is a decision rather than a change of terms.

guardrails: Revoked is not expired.
A revoked document's history remains available and auditable.
Retroactive consequences are never inferred without explicit authority.
The revocation applies exactly its own stated scope.
governance.reusableRule: Revocation stops reliance on a document according to the revocation's effective scope while preserving the historical record of the artifact and prior actions.
governance.entityScope: the revoked document version and the revocation acting on it
governance.entityNote: The revocation has its own effective scope. Applying it more widely withdraws things the authority did not withdraw.

identity.title: Payment initiated → pending → success, failure or unknown
identity.purpose: Keep initiating a payment and knowing what happened to it as separate states, with a third state for not knowing.

requires: an authoritative payment system accepting an attempt against a specific obligation
insufficientAlone: a payment button clicked, which is an intent until an authoritative system has accepted the attempt
an HTTP success from a payment form, which describes the form rather than the money

nodes.headline: Payment attempt initiated

Persist the attempt id, the amount, the currency, the payment method reference, the obligation it targets, the provider reference, the idempotency key and the initiation time, and record PAYMENT_PENDING. The idempotency key exists before submission because it is the only thing that makes a later retry or reconciliation safe
until an authoritative success, or an authoritative failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the payment outcome window

nodes.headline: What did the authoritative system establish?
Financial obligation satisfied → reconcile balance → release dependent state
nodes.detail: a payment succeeding against an obligation

nodes.headline: Payment authorization → capture → settle or release
nodes.detail: an authorization that still requires capture

nodes.headline: Payment failure → classify → recover, alternate or exit
nodes.detail: an authoritative payment failure

nodes.headline: Payment unknown → reconcile → confirm success or failure
nodes.detail: a payment whose outcome window closed without an authoritative result

edges.label: on event
edges.when: an authoritative success, an authoritative failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the window ending means we stopped hearing, which is a fact about our visibility rather than about the money - and in this category the difference between those two is a duplicate charge

edges.label: Funds committed
edges.when: the payment succeeded outright, with no separate capture or settlement step to follow

edges.label: Authorized, capture still required
edges.when: funds are reserved and the movement has not been requested

edges.label: Authoritative failure
edges.when: the payment system states that nothing moved and why
a payment succeeding against an obligation
an authorization that still requires capture
an authoritative payment failure
a payment whose outcome window closed without an authoritative result

distinctFrom.because: INT-114 is the generic shape of an external operation. This carries financial semantics the generic version has no room for: an obligation behind it, an authorization that is not money, and an unknown state whose safe response is to investigate rather than retry.

guardrails: A payment button click is not a payment initiated unless an authoritative system accepted the attempt.

identity.purpose: Model the actual commitment of funds, where reserving, taking and receiving are three different things.

Record AUTHORIZED. Authorized means funds are reserved, not moved - granting an irreversible outcome here grants it against money that has not been taken and may never be

identity.title: Payment unknown → reconcile → confirm success or failure

Preserve the provider reference, the idempotency key, the amount, the target obligation and the last known state, and record PAYMENT_UNKNOWN. Unknown is not failed, and nothing downstream may treat it as such

Suppress any automatic replacement payment. While the original may still have succeeded, initiating another is the single action that converts uncertainty into a duplicate charge - and the customer finds it before we do

until the provider confirms the payment succeeded, or the provider confirms the payment failed, or the customer initiates another payment attempt

Financial obligation satisfied → reconcile balance → release dependent state

nodes.headline: Payment failure → classify → recover, alternate or exit
nodes.detail: a reconciliation establishing that the payment failed

nodes.headline: Duplicate work detected → deduplicate → reuse, suppress or reconcile

edges.when: the provider confirms the payment succeeded, the provider confirms the payment failed, the customer initiates another payment attempt

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: each round is bounded so an unresolved payment escalates to someone rather than being retried into by a process that has lost patience

No replacement payment is initiated automatically while the original may still have succeeded.

identity.purpose: Move the money and confirm it arrived, keeping that separate from having decided it should.

Submit the refund under a stable operation identity and record REFUND_PENDING. The stable identity is what stops a retry or a redelivered response producing a second refund - and a duplicate refund is money that has to be asked for back
until the refund completes, or the refund fails

Record REFUNDED and reconcile against the original transaction and the obligation balance. The original transaction stays historical - a refund is a new financial event and not an edit to the old one, and rewriting the original would remove the evidence that either happened
REFUNDED; funds confirmed returned and balances reconciled
nodes.detail: a further refund against the same transaction is a new request with its own approval

nodes.headline: Record the partial refund and update the remaining refundable amount explicitly, so what is still owed back is carried rather than implied
partially refunded; the remaining refundable amount is explicit
nodes.detail: the remainder is executed as its own operation against the recorded balance

guardrails: Approved is not refunded.
A provider accepting the refund request is not the customer's funds having returned.
A retry never creates a duplicate refund.

governance.entityScope: the approved refund and the original transaction it is issued against
governance.entityNote: A refund is a new financial event rather than an edit to the original transaction, which stays historical throughout.

identity.title: Financial dispute or chargeback → evidence → decision → reconcile
identity.purpose: Run a transaction-level dispute through the authority that decides it, without treating the claim as a finding.

requires: a dispute or chargeback formally opened with the authority or provider that adjudicates it
insufficientAlone: a customer complaining about a charge, which is feedback until it is raised with the body that can reverse it

nodes.headline: Financial dispute opened

Record the dispute id, the transaction, the amount, the reason category, when it opened, the response deadline and the external authority handling it. A dispute being opened is not fraud confirmed and not a loss - it is a claim with a deadline, and most of them are confusion, a forgotten subscription or an unrecognised descriptor
Collect the evidence this dispute category actually requires, which the authority defines rather than we do
Is a response or representation allowed?
Submit before the deadline. A deadline missed is usually decided against us regardless of what the evidence would have shown, which makes the date more important than the argument
until the authority returns a decision
nodes.detail: timeout after the authority's own decision horizon

nodes.headline: UNKNOWN / PENDING; the authority has not decided
nodes.detail: the decision arriving later reconciles normally. Nothing is written off in either direction while the claim is live

nodes.headline: What did the authority decide?

Reconcile the financial balance and the related obligation according to the outcome - won leaves the original transaction standing, lost reverses the funds and reopens what they had discharged, partial does both in proportion, withdrawn leaves everything as it was. In every case the dispute's own history is preserved: the final outcome does not overwrite the record of what was claimed, what was submitted and when
Does the outcome warrant action on the business relationship?
Risk signal → correlate evidence → clear, monitor, restrict or review
nodes.detail: a dispute outcome raising a risk question that has not been answered

nodes.headline: dispute decided and reconciled; history preserved
nodes.detail: a further dispute on the same transaction is its own instance with its own deadline

edges.label: Allowed
edges.when: the process permits us to submit evidence before the deadline

edges.label: Not allowed
edges.when: the category or stage admits no representation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the authority returns a decision

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the decision is not ours to make or to hurry, and an undecided dispute stays an unresolved financial state rather than defaulting either way

edges.label: WON

edges.label: WON
edges.when: the original transaction stands

edges.label: WON

edges.label: WON

edges.when: a pattern or the outcome itself raises a question about the relationship

edges.when: the dispute is settled and says nothing about the relationship
a dispute outcome raising a risk question that has not been answered

distinctFrom.because: FBK-47 reviews a decision we made, under our own process. A chargeback is adjudicated by a card scheme or a regulator with power to move funds regardless of what we conclude, and missing its deadline decides it against us whatever the evidence says.

guardrails: A dispute opened is not fraud confirmed.
A dispute opened is not a dispute lost.
The dispute history is not overwritten by the final outcome.
A generic decision appeal is not a substitute for transaction-level dispute mechanics.
governance.reusableRule: Financial disputes remain unresolved financial states until the governing authority returns an outcome that can be reconciled against the original transaction.
governance.entityScope: the dispute and the specific transaction it contests
governance.entityNote: The dispute is adjudicated by an external authority with its own deadline and its own evidence rules. Our part is representation, not decision.

identity.title: Financial reconciliation → detect mismatch → correct or escalate
identity.purpose: Restore financial consistency by explaining the difference and adjusting it, never by editing the record that is inconvenient.

requires: a material inconsistency across financial records: a payment succeeded with the obligation still open, a refund completed with the balance unchanged, a provider settlement differing from local state, a duplicate charge, a missing transaction, or an incorrect partial balance

nodes.headline: Material financial mismatch detected
Collect the authoritative records from every relevant system rather than reasoning from the one that raised the alarm

Compare transaction identifiers, amounts, currency, statuses, timestamps, obligation allocations, refunds and credits, and settlement state. Amounts in different currencies are not compared or netted - a mismatch across currencies is a context error rather than a discrepancy, and resolving it as one produces a balance that is confidently wrong
What can be established from the records?
until the provider confirms the authoritative state
nodes.detail: timeout after the reconciliation window

nodes.headline: Does an accounting policy cover this correction?

Apply the correction idempotently as an explicit adjustment, preserving the adjustment history. A mismatch is never fixed by deleting the inconvenient transaction - the correction is a new record that explains the difference, and the original stays so the explanation has something to refer to
Verify the final financial state balances according to the defined accounting and business invariants
Does the corrected state balance?
reconciled through an explicit, auditable adjustment
nodes.detail: a further mismatch on the same records is its own reconciliation, with this adjustment in the history

nodes.headline: Record FINANCIAL_RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED, naming exactly which records disagree and by how much. Accounting policy is not invented to close it - an unexplained difference stated plainly is worth more than a resolved one nobody can justify
external:finance-ownership
nodes.detail: a financial difference that cannot be safely resolved

edges.label: A deterministic correction
edges.when: the authoritative records identify what the true state is and what the difference was

edges.label: External confirmation needed
edges.when: the provider holds the answer and has not supplied it

edges.label: Cannot be safely resolved
edges.when: the records disagree in a way the evidence does not settle - and a newer record is not automatically the correct one

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the provider confirms the authoritative state

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unreconciled financial position is a balance nobody can rely on, and waiting past the window turns it into a permanent one

edges.label: Not covered

edges.label: Balanced

guardrails: A financial mismatch is never fixed by deleting inconvenient transaction history.
The newest record is not automatically the correct one.
Corrections are explicit adjustments rather than silent rewrites.
Accounting policy is never invented.
governance.reusableRule: Financial reconciliation restores consistency by explaining and correcting mismatches through authoritative transaction history rather than rewriting financial history.
governance.entityScope: the set of financial records that disagree - transactions, obligations, refunds and settlement state together
governance.entityNote: Several records, several systems. What makes this different from an unknown outcome is that everyone has an answer and the answers do not match.

nodes.headline: Process requires verification

Record which process is blocked, which verification it needs at what scope and assurance, why, and any deadline. Naming the blocked process is what stops this becoming a standing request for identity documents
Does an existing valid verification already satisfy this requirement at this scope?

Reuse the existing verification and record that it was reused rather than re-requested. Asking someone to verify again what they verified last week for the same scope is the fastest way to make verification feel arbitrary rather than protective
Initiate the required verification. The verification itself runs as its own instance; this journey owns only the dependency and the resumption

Record the document as SUBMITTED against the specific requirement it is offered for. Uploaded is not validated, and nothing may treat the submission as satisfying the requirement while it sits here

Validate the properties this requirement actually cares about: the document type, whether it belongs to the person offering it, readability, completeness, validity dates, the required fields, and integrity or authenticity where the requirement demands them

identity.title: Correlated failure detection → incident candidate → confirm or reject
identity.purpose: Establish whether several failures actually share a cause, before treating them as one thing.

requires: multiple failures or anomalies across entities, exceeding a meaningful correlation threshold
insufficientAlone: a spike in alert volume, which is a count rather than a correlation
several failures happening at once, which is often several failures happening at once

nodes.headline: Correlated failures exceed incident threshold

Correlate by time, service or dependency, region, version, provider, resource cohort, failure signature and shared infrastructure. What is being tested is whether these failures plausibly share a cause, rather than whether there are a lot of them

Preserve the link from the candidate to each individual affected entity, and keep each entity's own case open. A correlation that absorbs its members leaves every affected customer without a case of their own, and when the incident closes they have nothing left to point at
What does the correlating evidence support?

Retain the individual cases as independent, and record why they were not merged. Several failures at once is often several failures at once - merging them for operational convenience gives each customer a generic status page instead of an answer to their specific problem
no incident; the individual cases continue independently
nodes.detail: further correlated evidence reopens the question. Not merging now does not prevent an incident being confirmed later on better evidence

until evidence establishes a shared cause, or evidence rules a shared cause out

edges.label: A shared cause

edges.label: Independent failures
edges.when: the correlation is coincidental and each failure has its own explanation

edges.label: Insufficient evidence
edges.when: a shared cause is plausible and unestablished

edges.label: on timeout
