nodes.headline: Authoritative ownership change

Record the previous owner, the next owner, the reason and the effective time, appended to the ownership chain - and in the same act leave every historical action, decision, payment, document, approval and obligation attributed exactly as it occurred. Preserving authorship is a property of how the change is written rather than a state the entity passes through, and it belongs here because everything after this point is tempted to rewrite it: a new owner appearing as the author of last year's approvals produces a record that is not merely wrong but actively misleading to anyone auditing it

Identify everything still open and everything that depends on who the owner is: tasks, commitments, deadlines, live escalations, follow-ups promised to people, decisions pending, access, responsibilities, pending approvals, notifications, billing and administrative contacts, assigned work, delegations and external representations. Every deadline carries across unchanged - a commitment made to someone outside the organisation does not move because we moved who holds it internally

Invalidate the previous owner's queued actions that they are clearly no longer authorised to take. An action scheduled under an ownership that has ended and delivered afterwards comes from someone who is not responsible any more, and neither the recipient nor the new owner will know that. Actions that may still be valid are not invalidated here - they are held and revalidated once the transfer completes
Does the incoming owner have to accept the transfer?
until the incoming owner accepts, or the incoming owner declines

Does this dependency belong to the entity or to the person who owned it?
Move it to the current owner. A billing contact, an administrative notification and an escalation path follow whoever is accountable now, because that is what they were always pointing at

Leave it with the previous owner. Contracts, payments and obligations frequently belong to the entity rather than to its owner, and just as frequently the reverse - each is evaluated rather than moved by default, because moving one wrongly transfers a liability nobody agreed to take on

Hold it and revalidate before execution. An action approved by somebody who is no longer the owner is an authorisation whose basis has gone, and executing it applies a decision the current owner never made and may not have made

guardrails: A transfer never resets an inherited deadline or commitment. Only an explicit renegotiation of the obligation itself does that, and that is a different event with a different record.

How does each class resolve?
child state preserved; the parent change does not reach it
nodes.detail: a parent change that the model does make this child follow is evaluated when it happens. A parent going inactive does not delete a child that stands on its own

nodes.headline: Do the dependent children carry open obligations?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation

nodes.headline: Apply the defined consequence to the dependent children only, recording what propagated, to which children, and under which rule. Propagation that cannot say which rule produced it cannot be reviewed, reversed or explained
consequence applied to dependent children, scoped and recorded
nodes.detail: a further parent change is classified again against the model

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: a rule states which child states depend on which parent states, and how

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: nothing states what this parent change should do to its children
a parent state change with no defined dependency model

edges.label: Directly dependent
edges.when: the model says this child's state follows the parent's

edges.label: Independently valid
edges.when: the child stands on its own basis and the model does not make it follow

edges.label: Obligations open
edges.when: a dependent child holds a commitment that would be destroyed by propagation

edges.label: Nothing open
edges.when: the dependent children hold nothing that outlives the propagation
propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation

distinctFrom.because: This propagates downward through defined dependencies. REL-96 derives upward through an aggregation policy. They are opposite directions with different rules, and neither is the inverse of the other.

guardrails: A parent going inactive does not delete every child.
A parent restriction does not restrict every child globally unless the model defines it.
Propagation stays scoped and auditable - what went where, under which rule.
Where no dependency model exists, nothing propagates.
governance.reusableRule: Parent state changes should propagate only through explicitly defined dependencies rather than through assumed inheritance.
governance.entityScope: the parent whose state changed, and each child evaluated individually against the dependency model
governance.entityNote: Children are classified individually. A single verdict for the whole collection is the assumption this journey exists to prevent.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Child state change → recalculate aggregate parent state
identity.purpose: Derive a parent's state from its children through an explicit aggregation policy, recomputed from source rather than nudged by whichever child reported last.

requires: a change to a child state that the parent's aggregation policy reads
insufficientAlone: any child change, where no policy makes the parent depend on it

nodes.headline: Child state changed
Is an aggregation policy defined for this parent state?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it

nodes.headline: Recompute the parent's derived state from the authoritative children using the defined policy, rather than adjusting it from the single child event that arrived. Recomputing from source means the aggregate can be rebuilt at any moment and cannot drift away from what the children actually say
Does the recomputed aggregate meet the parent's transition criteria?
Update the derived parent state, recording which children and which policy produced it, so the transition can be explained without recomputing it by hand
derived parent state updated from the aggregation policy
nodes.detail: the next relevant child change recomputes it again from source

nodes.headline: aggregate recomputed; parent state unchanged
nodes.detail: this is the ordinary outcome. One child changing is not the parent changing, and most child events correctly end here

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: a policy states how child states combine into the parent's, and what transitions it

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy states how these children combine
a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it

edges.label: Criteria met
edges.when: the policy's condition for moving the parent's state is satisfied

edges.label: Not met
edges.when: the aggregate moved and the parent's state does not

guardrails: One child's state does not automatically become the parent's state.
Aggregation semantics come from policy. ANY, ALL, majority and percentage thresholds are never inferred.
The aggregate is recomputable from the authoritative children rather than accumulated from events.
governance.reusableRule: Parent state derived from children must follow an explicit aggregation policy rather than simple state copying.
governance.entityScope: the parent and the full collection of children the policy reads
governance.entityNote: The aggregate is recomputed from the authoritative children, not incremented from the event that arrived. That is what keeps it rebuildable and stops it drifting.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Duplicate entity detected → assess → keep separate, link or merge
identity.purpose: Assess whether two records are the same entity, and route the answer - without consolidating anything.

requires: a match between records strong enough to be worth assessing
insufficientAlone: the same name
the same postcode or address
a similar spelling, which is what matching produces most of

nodes.headline: Potential duplicate detected

Collect the matching evidence and record its strength: verified identifiers, authoritative external IDs, declared ownership, verified contact points, business identifiers and relationship history. A match score is a reason to look and never a conclusion - the same email may be a shared family address, and the same phone number may be a workplace
What does the evidence actually support?
KEEP_SEPARATE; the records represent different entities
nodes.detail: stronger evidence later re-opens the assessment. Keeping two records apart is reversible; merging them usually is not, which is why this is the default when the evidence does not carry

nodes.headline: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
nodes.detail: records that are related and genuinely distinct

nodes.headline: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
nodes.detail: a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically

edges.label: Not the same entity
edges.when: the evidence is explained by something other than identity - a shared household, a shared workplace, a common name

edges.label: Related but distinct
edges.when: the records genuinely represent different entities that have a real relationship

edges.label: Same entity, consolidation looks safe
edges.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, and nothing about the records makes merging risky

edges.label: Ambiguous or high-risk
edges.when: the evidence is suggestive and incomplete, or the records carry state that would be dangerous to consolidate wrongly
records that are related and genuinely distinct
a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating
an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically

distinctFrom.because: Linking is one of the outcomes this assessment can reach. It is a separate journey because a link has its own semantics and its own sharing rules, which the assessment does not decide.

guardrails: The same name is not the same person.
A shared email or phone number may not prove the same entity - it depends on the model, and households and workplaces share both routinely.
Duplicate detection is not merge authorization. This journey assesses and routes; consolidating records is a separate mechanism with its own evidence requirements.
governance.reusableRule: Duplicate detection identifies a reconciliation candidate; merge requires separate evidence that consolidation is safe.
governance.entityScope: the candidate set of records suspected of representing one entity
governance.entityNote: The set is the unit. Three records suspected of being one person are assessed together, because a pairwise answer can be internally inconsistent.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
identity.purpose: Record that two entities are related and let defined context cross between them, while both remain two entities.

requires: a valid relationship or link between two distinct entities
insufficientAlone: a duplicate match, which is a question about whether they are one entity rather than evidence that they are two related ones

nodes.headline: Cross entity link established

Define what this link actually means - the same household, related accounts, linked profiles, a business relationship, a cross-product connection. The semantics decide what may be shared, and a link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing at all
What context do these link semantics explicitly permit sharing?
Share only the context the semantics explicitly permit. Anything not named is not shared, including things that would obviously be convenient

Confirm each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. Consent does not cross the link, and neither does entitlement or access, unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it - a household link is not permission to email everyone in the household
Is anything attempting to carry consent, entitlement, credentials or access across the link?
Block the propagation and record it. This is the specific failure a link becomes when it is quietly treated as a merge, and catching it here is cheaper than discovering it as a consent complaint
linked; two entities, two lifecycles, defined shared context
nodes.detail: the link's semantics may be changed, and the link may be ended, but neither turns it into a merge. Consolidating the records is a separate decision with separate evidence

edges.label: Defined shared context
edges.when: the link's semantics name specific context that may cross between the entities

edges.label: Nothing shared
edges.when: the link records a relationship and permits no context to cross - which is the common case

edges.label: Something is propagating
edges.when: a downstream process is treating the link as though the entities were one

edges.label: Nothing is
edges.when: only the permitted context crosses

guardrails: Linked is not merged.
Consent does not automatically propagate across linked identities.
Entitlement and access do not propagate unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it.
A link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing.
governance.reusableRule: Entity linking enables defined cross-entity context while preserving independent identity and lifecycle state.
governance.entityScope: the link itself, plus the two entities it connects
governance.entityNote: Each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. The link is a third record about them, not a step toward becoming one.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Entity split required → create separate records → allocate history and state safely
identity.purpose: Separate what should never have been one record, or what must now be managed apart, without copying the things that do not divide.

requires: an authoritative requirement to separate state currently held under one entity

nodes.headline: Entity split required
Determine the split basis - what actually distinguishes the resulting entities from one another. Without it, allocation becomes a series of individual guesses

Classify every piece of existing information as entity-specific, shared, ambiguous, historical or non-transferable. The last category is the one that gets missed: consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations do not divide by being copied, and duplicating one creates an obligation nobody incurred or a permission nobody gave
How does each classified item resolve?
Allocate the item to the entity it belongs to
Preserve the item through a relationship or reference model rather than duplicating it into both records. Two copies of one shared history diverge the first time either is edited
Leave it with the entity that holds it and record that it did not divide. A new record existing is not a reason for it to receive a copy of a consent, an entitlement or a debt
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity

nodes.headline: Recalculate each resulting entity's rights, permissions, entitlements, obligations and active journeys from what it now actually holds, rather than from what the source entity held

Record that the split occurred, when, and on what basis. History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate - events that happened to the combined entity happened to the combined entity, and pretending otherwise makes every past event unattributable
entities separated; current state reconstructed, prior history preserved as it happened
nodes.detail: each resulting entity now has its own lifecycle. A further split is assessed against whichever of them requires it

edges.label: Clearly one entity's
edges.when: the item belongs unambiguously to one of the resulting entities

edges.label: Genuinely shared
edges.when: the item belongs to the relationship between them rather than to either

edges.label: Non-transferable
edges.when: consent, an entitlement, a credential or a financial obligation, none of which divides

edges.label: Ambiguous
edges.when: the item cannot be attributed on the split basis
state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity

distinctFrom.because: A link connects two records that already exist separately. A split creates that separation where it did not exist, which means deciding what each side gets - and what neither side may simply be given a copy of.

guardrails: Consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations are never blindly duplicated across a split.
The audit trail preserves that a split occurred, when, and on what basis.
History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate.
Ambiguous state is held unresolved rather than assigned by default.
governance.reusableRule: Entity splitting reconstructs independent current states while preserving the historical fact that the records were previously represented together.
governance.entityScope: the source entity and the entities that result from the split
governance.entityNote: The source entity's history remains the source entity's history. The resulting records inherit allocations, not a rewritten past.

identity.title: Return authorized → in transit, received, lost or expired
identity.purpose: Track whether an authorised return actually comes back, and hold the states where it might not have.

requires: an active return authorisation with a scope and a validity

nodes.headline: Return authorization active

Define the return method, the destination, the scope and quantity, the authorisation's validity and the tracking reference where one exists. Record AUTHORIZED - permission to return, with nothing yet moved
until the return is dispatched by the requester, or the return is received by us, or a return exception is reported
nodes.detail: timeout after the authorisation's validity

nodes.headline: What happened?

Record IN_RETURN_TRANSIT. A carrier accepting the parcel is not the resource having returned to us - a return-dependent remedy waits for receipt, and issuing one on a tracking number means issuing it for something that may never arrive
until the return is received, or a transit exception is reported
nodes.detail: timeout after the expected transit window plus its tolerance

nodes.headline: Which arrived first?

Record RETURN_UNKNOWN and suppress any return-dependent outcome. A return we cannot locate is neither one that arrived nor one that was never sent, and acting as though it were either produces a remedy issued against nothing or a customer refused for something they did send
Record LOST or EXCEPTION with what the carrier reported, and who bears the risk under the return method that was used
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a return whose whereabouts or outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: Record EXPIRED_UNUSED - the authorisation lapsed and nothing came back. Whether another remedy remains available is a separate question and is asked separately
EXPIRED_UNUSED; nothing returned and the authorisation has lapsed
nodes.detail: a fresh return request is assessed on its own eligibility. The original obligation, if still unresolved, remains so

nodes.headline: Returned item or deliverable → inspect → accept, reject or partial
nodes.detail: a returned resource arriving

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the return is dispatched by the requester, the return is received by us, a return exception is reported

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an authorisation that lapses unused releases whatever was being held against it, and the customer keeps the thing rather than being left in an open process

edges.label: Dispatched
edges.when: the requester handed it to a carrier or return channel

edges.label: Received
edges.when: it arrived with us

edges.label: Exception
edges.when: the carrier or channel reports it lost, damaged in transit or undeliverable

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the return is received, a transit exception is reported

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a return that has neither arrived nor been reported lost is unknown, and treating our silence as its loss writes off something that may be two days away

edges.label: The return
edges.when: the resource reached us

edges.label: An exception
edges.when: the carrier reported a problem
a return whose whereabouts or outcome could not be established
a returned resource arriving

guardrails: Authorized is not returned.
Carrier acceptance is not the resource having returned to the business.
No return-dependent outcome is issued from a tracking number alone unless policy explicitly permits it.
governance.reusableRule: Return authorization establishes permission to return; the return remains operationally unresolved until the resource's return outcome is known.
governance.entityScope: the authorised return and the resource travelling under it
governance.entityNote: A carrier accepting the parcel is a fact about the carrier. The return-dependent remedy waits for receipt by us, not for a tracking number existing.

identity.title: Returned item or deliverable → inspect → accept, reject or partial
identity.purpose: Judge what came back against the conditions it was authorised under, keeping receipt and acceptance apart.

requires: a returned resource physically or logically received against an authorisation

nodes.headline: Returned resource received

Record that the resource was received, with what actually arrived. This fact stands whatever the inspection concludes - a rejected return is still something we are holding, and losing track of it because it failed inspection is how goods disappear into a warehouse nobody reconciles
Are the inspection criteria defined for this kind of return?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a returned resource with no defined acceptance criteria

nodes.headline: Inspect against the criteria that apply - identity, quantity, condition, completeness, included components, the authorised scope, and integrity where it matters
What did the inspection find?
Record RETURN_ACCEPTED for the full authorised scope
Record PARTIALLY_ACCEPTED, naming exactly which scope is accepted and which is not. The two are carried separately because whatever remedy follows applies to one of them and not the other
Record RETURN_REJECTED_AFTER_RECEIPT with the reason. The receipt record stands - we still physically hold the thing, and what happens to it is part of what the remedy decision now has to cover
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a return inspected and its accepted scope established

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: policy states what condition, completeness and scope the return has to meet

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy states what an acceptable return looks like here
a returned resource with no defined acceptance criteria

edges.label: Fully acceptable
edges.when: everything authorised arrived and meets the conditions

edges.label: Partially acceptable
edges.when: some of the returned scope meets the conditions and some does not

edges.label: Not acceptable
edges.when: what arrived does not meet the conditions it was authorised under
a return inspected and its accepted scope established

guardrails: Received is not accepted.
Inspection criteria are policy-defined rather than judged case by case.
A rejected return does not erase the fact that the resource was physically received.
Partial outcomes preserve the exact accepted and rejected scope.
governance.reusableRule: A returned resource satisfies the return requirement only after the received scope has been evaluated against the applicable acceptance rules.
governance.entityScope: the returned resource as received, and the return case it arrived under
governance.entityNote: Physical receipt is recorded regardless of the inspection's outcome. A rejected return is still an object we are holding.

identity.title: Replacement decision → allocate → fulfill → confirm
identity.purpose: Deliver a second time against the same promise, tied to the defect it exists to resolve.

requires: a replacement authorised as the remedy for an identified defect

nodes.headline: Replacement remedy authorized

Record the replacement's relationship to the original fulfillment and the specific defect it exists to resolve. The original's history stays intact - a replacement is a second fulfillment against the same obligation, not a correction of the first one's record
Determine the replacement scope - which part of the original is being replaced, which is not, and whether what is being sent is identical or an accepted equivalent
Is a replacement resource available?
Does policy permit waiting for availability?
until a replacement resource becomes available
nodes.detail: timeout after the tolerable wait for this remedy

nodes.headline: Create the replacement fulfillment without a new commercial charge, unless policy explicitly requires one. A remedy that bills again for what was already paid for is not a remedy, and it converts a recoverable problem into a dispute
until the replacement is fulfilled and delivered, or the replacement fails or is cancelled
nodes.detail: timeout after the remedy deadline

nodes.headline: What happened to the replacement?
Remedy execution → verify outcome → close or continue recovery
nodes.detail: a replacement delivered

nodes.headline: Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a replacement that cannot be delivered

edges.label: Available
edges.when: the replacement scope can be resourced now

edges.label: Not available
edges.when: nothing can currently satisfy the replacement scope

edges.label: Wait permitted
edges.when: the customer and policy both tolerate the replacement arriving later

edges.label: Cannot wait
edges.when: the delay would exceed what policy or the customer accepts

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a replacement resource becomes available

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a replacement that never becomes available is a remedy that is not happening, and saying so is better than an open case that quietly ages

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the replacement is fulfilled and delivered, the replacement fails or is cancelled

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a replacement outliving its deadline has stopped being the remedy in progress and become another unresolved obligation on top of the first

edges.label: Delivered
edges.when: the replacement reached the recipient

edges.label: Failed or cancelled
edges.when: the replacement did not complete
a replacement delivered
a replacement that cannot be delivered

distinctFrom.because: FUL-144 executes an original fulfillment obligation. This creates a second one whose entire purpose is to resolve a specific defect in the first, which changes whether it is charged for and what it has to be verified against.

guardrails: A replacement approved is not a replacement delivered.
A replacement does not create a duplicate commercial charge unless policy explicitly requires one.
The original fulfillment history remains intact.
governance.reusableRule: Replacement creates a new fulfillment obligation whose purpose is to resolve a specific defect in the original fulfillment.
governance.entityScope: the replacement case, linking the original fulfillment to the new one
governance.entityNote: The link is what makes it a remedy rather than a new order. Without it, the replacement is billed for and the original's defect disappears from the record.

identity.title: Remedy execution → verify outcome → close or continue recovery
identity.purpose: Check that the remedy actually satisfied the obligation, rather than that it was carried out.

requires: a selected remedy entering execution against an identified issue
insufficientAlone: a remedy approved, which authorises it and performs none of it

nodes.headline: Remedy execution started

Track the remedy's actual outcome - the replacement delivered, the correction verified, the refund confirmed, the service repeated successfully, the missing component received. What is tracked is the business outcome and never the internal task that was supposed to produce it
until the remedy completes, or the remedy fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the remedy window

nodes.headline: Record the remedy outcome as unknown and suppress any second remedy. In this category the second one is usually money or goods that have already gone out, and it is discovered by whoever receives two of them
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a remedy whose outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: Did the remedy complete?
Does the completed remedy actually resolve the original issue?
Record RESOLVED. The issue closes because the obligation it named is satisfied, not because an internal task is marked done
RESOLVED; the original obligation is fully satisfied
nodes.detail: a later report about the same thing is assessed for recurrence rather than treated as a fresh problem

nodes.headline: Record the remaining obligation explicitly, so what is still owed is a stated scope rather than a vague sense that something is outstanding
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: an obligation still outstanding after a completed remedy

nodes.headline: Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a remedy that failed to complete

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the remedy completes, the remedy fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a remedy whose outcome cannot be established is not a completed one, and issuing a second while the first may have landed produces two replacements or two refunds
a remedy whose outcome could not be established

edges.label: Completed
edges.when: the remedy's own outcome was achieved

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the remedy did not complete

edges.label: Resolved
edges.when: the obligation the issue named is now satisfied

edges.label: Partly resolved
edges.when: part of the obligation is satisfied and part remains

edges.label: Not resolved
edges.when: the remedy completed and the obligation is still outstanding - the replacement arrived and is also wrong
an obligation still outstanding after a completed remedy
a remedy that failed to complete

distinctFrom.because: FBK-46 owns an issue's ownership and closure lifecycle. This verifies that a specific chosen remedy produced its intended business outcome - a narrower question, and one that can fail while the case is being managed perfectly well.

guardrails: A remedy approved is not a remedy executed.
A remedy executed is not necessarily the issue resolved.
An issue is never closed solely because an internal remedy task is marked done.
governance.reusableRule: A remedy closes an issue only when the remedy's intended business outcome has actually satisfied the unresolved obligation.
governance.entityScope: the remedy and the issue it was chosen to resolve
governance.entityNote: Two things, and completing the first does not close the second. A replacement can arrive and still be wrong.

identity.title: Compensation decision → eligibility → grant or reject → deliver
identity.purpose: Decide separately whether impact warrants something beyond fixing the problem, and confirm it actually arrived.

requires: an impact or inconvenience that policy treats as potentially warranting compensation, beyond whatever remedy is fixing the problem
insufficientAlone: an issue existing, which is a problem to solve rather than an impact to compensate
a customer asking for compensation

nodes.headline: Compensation consideration appropriate

Determine the reason, the impact, what remedy already exists or is under way, the policy-defined eligibility and the compensation being considered. Compensation answers impact and inconvenience - it is not the thing that fixes the problem, and a resolved issue does not automatically require one
Has compensation already been granted for this impact?
already compensated for this impact
nodes.detail: a further, distinct impact is assessed on its own. A second grant for the same one is a duplicate rather than a gesture, and it is found by accounting

nodes.headline: Is compensation eligibility and form defined by policy?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: compensation considered with no governing policy

nodes.headline: What does the policy determine?
no compensation; the underlying remedy stands on its own
nodes.detail: a worsening impact, or a remedy that fails, may change the assessment. Resolving a problem well is not an impact requiring compensation

nodes.headline: Authorise the compensation the policy defines, in its defined form and amount
What form does the compensation take?
Refund request → eligibility → approve, reject or review
nodes.detail: compensation taking a financial form

nodes.headline: Entitlement qualification → grant, deny or pending
nodes.detail: compensation taking the form of an entitlement or benefit

nodes.headline: until the compensation is delivered or applied
nodes.detail: timeout after the delivery window

nodes.headline: Verify the compensation actually reached the recipient. A credit that was never applied is a promise the customer discovers was empty, usually while looking for it
compensation delivered and verified; the underlying obligation is a separate matter
nodes.detail: compensation is recorded against this impact and does not settle whether the original obligation was resolved

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: authorised compensation that was not delivered

edges.label: Already compensated
edges.when: a grant covering the same impact exists

edges.label: Nothing granted
edges.when: no compensation covers this impact

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: policy states what impact warrants what compensation, and in what form

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy covers compensation for this kind of impact
compensation considered with no governing policy

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: the impact meets the policy's threshold

edges.label: Not eligible
edges.when: the impact does not meet it - which is the ordinary case for a problem that was fixed promptly

edges.label: Money
edges.when: a refund, a credit or a goodwill payment

edges.label: An entitlement or benefit
edges.when: a service credit, an extension, an upgrade or another right

edges.label: Something delivered operationally
edges.when: goods, a service, or another thing that has to arrive
compensation taking a financial form
compensation taking the form of an entitlement or benefit

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the compensation is delivered or applied

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: authorised is not delivered, and a compensation that was promised and never applied is worse than one that was never offered
authorised compensation that was not delivered

distinctFrom.because: REM-157 chooses what satisfies the obligation. This decides whether the impact of the failure warrants something beyond that. A credit does not deliver the thing that was owed, and treating it as the remedy leaves someone holding money and the same broken outcome.

guardrails: Compensation is not issue resolution.
Resolving an issue does not automatically require compensation.
Compensation amounts and rules are never invented.
Duplicate compensation for the same impact is prevented.
governance.reusableRule: Compensation is an independently authorized response to impact or inconvenience and should not be confused with fixing the underlying problem.
governance.entityScope: the compensation case and the experience or issue that prompted it
governance.entityNote: Independent of the remedy. A resolved problem may warrant compensation and an unresolved one may not, and the two decisions answer different questions.

identity.title: Post-remedy reopen → validate recurrence → continue or new issue
identity.purpose: Tell a recurrence of the same problem apart from a new one, and from a remedy that never actually finished.

requires: a problem reported against a fulfillment whose issue was previously remedied or closed

nodes.headline: Problem reported after remedy

Compare the new report against the original issue - the same fulfillment, the same scope, the same defect, or something adjacent that only sounds alike. A repeated complaint is not automatically the same issue, and a customer describing a second problem in the words they used for the first is common
What is its relationship to the original?
Create a new issue, linked to the prior context where that context is useful. Forcing a distinct problem into an existing case buries it behind a history that does not apply to it
Post-completion issue → validate → remedy route
nodes.detail: a distinct new problem after a previous remedy

nodes.headline: Remedy execution → verify outcome → close or continue recovery
nodes.detail: a remedy recorded as complete whose outcome never arrived

nodes.headline: Reopen the original issue, preserving every previous remedy attempt and its outcome. The reopen count is evidence worth having and does not by itself determine fault or entitle anyone to compensation - it is an input to diagnosis rather than a conclusion
Recalculate the current obligation from what has actually been delivered across every remedy attempt, rather than from the original order
Does the recurrence warrant reassessing the cause?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a remedy that was applied correctly and did not hold

nodes.headline: Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a reopened issue needing a remedy decision

edges.label: The same problem, recurred or never resolved
edges.when: the same defect on the same scope is present again

edges.label: A distinct new problem
edges.when: a different defect, a different scope, or a different fulfillment

edges.label: The previous remedy never actually completed
edges.when: the remedy was recorded as done and its business outcome never arrived
a distinct new problem after a previous remedy
a remedy recorded as complete whose outcome never arrived

edges.label: Reassess
edges.when: a remedy was applied correctly and the problem returned, which usually means the diagnosis was wrong rather than the execution

edges.label: Retry the remedy path
edges.when: the previous attempt failed in execution rather than in diagnosis
a remedy that was applied correctly and did not hold
a reopened issue needing a remedy decision

guardrails: A repeated complaint is not automatically the same issue.
Previous resolutions and remedy attempts are never erased.
The reopen count is useful evidence and does not by itself determine fault or compensation.
A remedy that never completed is resumed rather than duplicated.
governance.reusableRule: Post-remedy recurrence should reopen the original obligation only when the new evidence shows that the same problem remains unresolved or has genuinely recurred.
governance.entityScope: the previously resolved issue and the new report made against it
governance.entityNote: Three possible relationships and they lead to three different places. Assuming any one of them is how a case is duplicated, buried or reopened for the wrong reason.

identity.title: Change candidate → eligibility → ready or blocked
identity.purpose: Decide which targets a change may reach at all, before anyone starts preparing any of them.

requires: a change or version released for controlled application to an identified population
insufficientAlone: a version being published, which makes it available and eligible for nothing

nodes.headline: Change available for controlled application

Evaluate each target's eligibility against what actually governs it - the supported version, device or resource compatibility, the account's configuration, dependencies, required prerequisites, policy eligibility, the environment, capacity, and any required previous state. Eligibility is evaluated per target: inferring it from the entity type assumes a population is uniform, and populations never are
Is this target eligible for the change?

Record EXCLUDED with the specific reason. An excluded target is a known population rather than an absence - a rollout reporting ninety-four percent coverage without naming the other six percent cannot be finished, and nobody can tell an exclusion from an omission
EXCLUDED with a stated reason; the target remains on its current version
nodes.detail: the constraint that excluded it changing makes the target eligible again, and it is re-evaluated rather than assumed still excluded

nodes.headline: Are the required prerequisites present on this target?
Record PENDING_REQUIREMENT naming exactly which prerequisite is missing. Eligible-but-unprepared is a real state, and it is the one that most often gets counted as failed
Record READY_FOR_CHANGE. Eligible is not technically ready, and ready is not applied - what has been established is that this target may take the change, not that it can yet
Change preparation → resolve dependencies → ready or hold
nodes.detail: an eligible target, prepared or with named outstanding prerequisites

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: its current state satisfies everything the change requires of a target

edges.label: Not eligible
edges.when: a compatibility, configuration, environment or policy constraint rules it out

edges.label: All present
edges.when: nothing the change depends on is missing

edges.label: Something missing
edges.when: a dependency, a prior version step or a required condition is absent
an eligible target, prepared or with named outstanding prerequisites

distinctFrom.because: This asks whether a target may take the change. RLT-242 gets it into a state where it can. Ineligible and unprepared are different problems with different owners - one is a decision, the other is work.

guardrails: Available is not eligible.
Eligible is not technically ready.
Compatibility is never inferred from the generic entity type alone.
Excluded targets are named rather than absent from the count.
governance.reusableRule: A change should reach only targets whose current state satisfies the prerequisites required for safe application.
governance.entityScope: the change or version, and each target evaluated against it
governance.entityNote: Eligibility is per target. A population is never uniform, and the targets that differ are the ones the rollout will break on.

identity.title: Change preparation → resolve dependencies → ready or hold
identity.purpose: Get an eligible target into a state where the change can actually be applied to it.

requires: a target established as eligible for an identified change

nodes.headline: Target eligible for planned change

Identify the preparation this change actually requires for this target - a backup, resource capacity, a required configuration, a pre-download, a dependency upgrade, a maintenance window, user or administrator readiness, a required approval. What is required comes from the change and the target rather than from a standard checklist, and forcing unnecessary prerequisites stalls a rollout for reasons nobody can defend
Are all critical dependencies ready?
Hold the target and record the named blockers. A hold with an unnamed blocker is a rollout that has stopped for a reason nobody can look up, and it stays stopped until somebody investigates by hand
until the named blockers clear, or the change becomes obsolete or is superseded
nodes.detail: timeout after the schedule window this change allows for preparation

nodes.headline: How did the wait resolve?

Record the preparation as abandoned because the change it prepared for was superseded. The target returns to eligibility evaluation for whatever the current change is, rather than proceeding with the old one
preparation abandoned; the change it was for no longer applies
nodes.detail: the current change evaluates this target's eligibility on its own terms. Preparation done for the superseded version may or may not still count, and that is the new evaluation's question

nodes.headline: Record the preparation window as expired with the blockers still outstanding. The target is not failed - it was never applied to - and it stays visible as an unprepared member of the population
preparation window expired; target eligible and not ready
nodes.detail: the blockers clearing makes the target preparable again for this change or the next one

nodes.headline: Record CHANGE_READY. Preparation complete is not the change applied - nothing about the target has changed yet, and this readiness will be revalidated before anything does
Change scheduled → wait → revalidate → execute or cancel
nodes.detail: a target prepared for the change

edges.label: All ready
edges.when: everything the change requires is in place on this target

edges.label: Some outstanding
edges.when: at least one critical dependency is missing

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the named blockers clear, the change becomes obsolete or is superseded

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a target held indefinitely against a change that has moved on is neither in the rollout nor excluded from it, and it will be counted as neither

edges.label: Blockers cleared
edges.when: every critical dependency is now in place

edges.label: The change became obsolete
edges.when: a newer version supersedes the one this target was being prepared for
a target prepared for the change

guardrails: Preparation complete is not the change applied.
Unnecessary prerequisites are not forced onto a target.
Current state is revalidated before execution rather than assumed from readiness.
governance.reusableRule: Change preparation resolves the dependencies required for execution without confusing readiness with the change itself.
governance.entityScope: the target and the preparation the change requires of it
governance.entityNote: What is required comes from the change and this target. A standard checklist applied to everything delays a rollout for reasons nobody can defend.

identity.title: Change scheduled → wait → revalidate → execute or cancel
identity.purpose: Check, at the moment of execution, that the change scheduled earlier is still the right one for this target.

requires: a prepared target with a scheduled execution time or window

nodes.headline: Change receives scheduled execution window

Record the target, the change version, the scheduled time or window, the expected current state and the dependency assumptions. What is stored is a set of assumptions, kept so the execution can see what has moved rather than so it can proceed on them
until the change is cancelled for this target, or a newer version supersedes this change, or the target is removed or becomes ineligible
nodes.detail: timeout after the scheduled execution window

nodes.headline: What happened before the window?
Record the schedule cancelled and stand down the job. A cancelled target revived by a stale change job receives a change nobody authorized, and on a device fleet that is discovered by the devices
scheduled change cancelled; the target is untouched
nodes.detail: the target re-entering eligibility for this or a later change is a new evaluation rather than a revival of this schedule

nodes.headline: Stand down this schedule because a newer version exists. Applying the old one after the new one is available installs a regression on purpose, and the job that did it reports success
schedule stood down; a newer change version applies to this target
nodes.detail: the current version evaluates this target's eligibility and schedules on its own terms

nodes.headline: At the execution moment, revalidate the target's eligibility, its version and state, its dependencies, whether the change is still current, any required approval, and whether an incident or change hold is in force. What is checked is now - the stored assumptions are used only to see what moved
Is the change still valid for this target?

Suppress the stale change, naming exactly what changed since it was scheduled. A scheduled change is an intention rather than a guarantee, and executing on assumptions that have expired is how a target under an incident hold receives a deployment
stale scheduled change suppressed; the target is untouched
nodes.detail: the target is re-evaluated for the current change against its current state, which is a fresh eligibility question

nodes.headline: Change execution → apply → verify, fail or unknown
nodes.detail: a scheduled change revalidated at its execution moment

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the change is cancelled for this target, a newer version supersedes this change, the target is removed or becomes ineligible

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the window is what the wait exists for. It is the normal outcome and the point at which every assumption is checked again

edges.label: Cancelled, removed or made ineligible
edges.when: the target should no longer receive this change

edges.label: Superseded
edges.when: a newer version of the change now exists

edges.label: Still valid
edges.when: every assumption the schedule made still holds

edges.label: No longer valid
edges.when: eligibility, state, dependencies, currency or authorization has moved
a scheduled change revalidated at its execution moment

guardrails: Scheduled is not guaranteed execution.
A superseded version invalidates the old schedule.
A cancelled target is never revived by a stale change job.
governance.reusableRule: Scheduled changes are execution intentions whose assumptions must be revalidated at the moment the change is applied.
governance.entityScope: the scheduled change and the target it is scheduled against
governance.entityNote: The schedule stores assumptions. They are kept so the execution can see what has moved, never so it can proceed on them.

identity.title: Change execution → apply → verify, fail or unknown
identity.purpose: Establish that the target actually ended up in the state the change intended, rather than that a command was accepted.

requires: a revalidated target authorized to receive an identified change version

nodes.headline: Authorized change execution begins

Record APPLYING with the change version and a stable operation identity for this target, so a retry re-applies the same change rather than performing a second one. Retries are normal here, and a second application is how a target ends up double-migrated
Execute the change idempotently against the target, through the canonical async and reliability primitives rather than a bespoke retry loop
until the target reports the change applied, or the target reports an authoritative failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the execution timeout for this change and target class

nodes.headline: Record CHANGE_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN and hold any retry. A timeout is not a failure - the change may well have applied, and retrying blindly applies it twice, which for firmware and schema changes is not idempotent in practice however idempotent the command is
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a change whose outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: What did the target report?
Record CHANGE_FAILED with exactly what the target reported. The target is on its previous version and functioning - a failed application is not a broken target
Individual target change failure → retry, isolate or remediate
nodes.detail: a change that failed or left the target in an unintended state

nodes.headline: Record VERIFYING. The command being accepted is not the change being applied, and the change being applied is not the target being in the intended state - three states, and the middle one is where most deployment tooling stops looking

Verify the target actually reached the intended new state - the version it now reports, the configuration it now holds, the behaviour it now exhibits. What is checked is the target's state rather than the command's return code
Is the target in the intended state?
Record that the change applied and the target is not where it should be. This is worse than a clean failure, because the target is now in a state nobody designed and nothing reports it as broken
Record that verification could not run. Unverifiable is not verified, and counting it as success is how a rollout reports a population it has never actually observed

Record CHANGE_APPLIED_VERIFIED with the state the target now reports. Applied and verified is still not healthy - whether the population running this change is well is a rollout-level question observed over time
CHANGE_APPLIED_VERIFIED; the target is in the intended state
nodes.detail: the target's health under the change is observed at rollout scope. A later regression on this target is a health signal rather than an execution failure

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the target reports the change applied, the target reports an authoritative failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a target that reports nothing is unknown rather than failed, and the difference decides whether retrying is safe
a change whose outcome could not be established

edges.label: Applied
edges.when: the target accepted and completed the change

edges.label: Confirmed failure
edges.when: the target authoritatively rejected or failed the change
a change that failed or left the target in an unintended state

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: the target reports the intended version, configuration and behaviour

edges.label: Applied, but not in the intended state
edges.when: the change went through and the target is somewhere else

edges.label: Cannot be verified
edges.when: the verification could not run against this target

distinctFrom.because: RLT-243 decides whether to proceed. This performs the change and establishes what state the target actually reached, which is where the accepted-applied-verified distinction lives.

guardrails: A command accepted is not a change applied.
Applied is not healthy.
A timeout is not a failure.
A retry never applies the same change twice.
governance.reusableRule: A change is complete only after the target's intended new state has been authoritatively verified.
governance.entityScope: the change execution against one target
governance.entityNote: The operation carries a stable identity, so a retry re-applies the same change rather than a second one.

identity.title: Staged rollout → pilot cohort → health gate → expand or hold
identity.purpose: Widen a change only when the targets that already took it show it is safe to widen.

requires: a change approved for progressive application to a defined population

nodes.headline: Change approved for staged rollout
Are the cohort rules explicit?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a staged rollout with implicit cohort or gate rules

nodes.headline: Define the cohorts and the rollout order according to policy, and the health gate each cohort must pass before the next begins. The gate is written before the first cohort deploys, because a gate written afterwards is written knowing the result
Deploy the current cohort. Progression is bounded by the finite cohort list - each pass through this step consumes one, so the rollout terminates rather than cycling
until sufficient health evidence accumulates for this cohort, or a critical regression appears in the changed population
nodes.detail: timeout after the maximum observation window for this cohort

nodes.headline: Was there enough evidence by the end of the window?

Record HOLD. Elapsed time is not evidence - a cohort that produced no traffic produced no information, and expanding because nothing alerted is expanding on the absence of a signal rather than the presence of one
HOLD; the cohort did not produce enough evidence to judge the gate
nodes.detail: evidence accumulating, or the gate being redefined for a low-traffic population, resumes progression. Nothing was reverted and nothing expanded

nodes.headline: Does the health gate pass for this cohort?
Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
nodes.detail: a health gate failing for a deployed cohort

nodes.headline: Are there cohorts left?
Record the planned population as having reached the intended changed state, with the exception population named alongside it
Change completed → observe → close, reopen or deprecate previous version
nodes.detail: a rollout reaching its planned population

edges.label: Explicit
edges.when: the cohorts, their order and the gate each must pass are defined

edges.label: Not explicit
edges.when: who is in which cohort, or what a gate requires, is not written down
a staged rollout with implicit cohort or gate rules

edges.label: on event
edges.when: sufficient health evidence accumulates for this cohort, a critical regression appears in the changed population

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the window bounds how long a cohort may be watched, and reaching it raises the real question - whether enough was actually observed rather than merely enough time

edges.label: Enough
edges.when: the changed cohort produced the volume and variety of activity the gate needs to judge

edges.label: Not enough
edges.when: the cohort was quiet, or the relevant paths never ran

edges.label: It passes
edges.when: failure rate, regressions, performance and business outcome are all within the gate

edges.label: It fails
edges.when: the changed population shows a problem the gate is there to catch
a health gate failing for a deployed cohort

edges.label: More remain
edges.when: the cohort list has entries that have not deployed

edges.label: None
edges.when: every cohort in the list has deployed and passed its gate
a rollout reaching its planned population

distinctFrom.because: This is population progression - whether the next cohort may begin. RLT-249 is one target that could not take the change while the rollout is otherwise fine. Merging them turns every unreachable device into a reason to stop, or every real regression into a target exception.

guardrails: Elapsed time alone is not sufficient rollout evidence.
A rollout never expands merely because no alert fired.
Cohort rules and health gates are explicit and written before deployment.
governance.reusableRule: A staged rollout expands only when previously changed targets provide sufficient evidence that the change is safe to broaden.
governance.entityScope: the rollout, its target population and the cohorts it progresses through
governance.entityNote: The cohort list is finite and explicit. Progression is bounded by it, and each step through it needs its own evidence.

identity.title: Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
identity.purpose: Stop the change spreading while the question of what to do about it is still open.

requires: a pause threshold reached, or an authorized pause of an active rollout

nodes.headline: Rollout pause triggered

Record PAUSED and stop new cohort expansion. Paused is not failed - the targets already changed are still running, most of them fine, and treating a pause as a failure reverts a population that had no problem at all

Preserve the current changed and unchanged populations exactly as they are, and record which is which. A pause that loses track of who has the change can neither resume from where it stopped nor roll back what it applied

Diagnose the issue against the changed population rather than against the change in the abstract. What matters is whether the targets holding this change are safe, which is a different question from whether the change is good
What does the diagnosis support?
Revalidate health against current state before resuming. The population has moved during the pause, and resuming on the health reading that preceded it expands on evidence that is now old
Is the changed population healthy now?
Staged rollout → pilot cohort → health gate → expand or hold
nodes.detail: a pause resolved with the changed population healthy

nodes.headline: Change failure threshold → rollback decision → execute or forward recover
nodes.detail: a paused rollout whose changed population is unsafe

nodes.headline: Terminate future expansion and preserve the already-applied state according to policy. Abandoning a rollout is not reverting it - a population that took the change successfully may well stay on it, and forcing everyone back costs more than the change did
rollout abandoned; the changed population preserved as policy defines
nodes.detail: the population is now split across versions deliberately, and that split is visible. A later change evaluates each target's eligibility from where it actually is

edges.label: Resolved without rollback
edges.when: the cause was external, transient or fixed forward, and the changed targets are fine

edges.label: The already-changed targets are unsafe
edges.when: the population holding the change is at risk where it stands

edges.label: The rollout is abandoned
edges.when: the change will not proceed, whether or not what is applied stays

edges.label: Healthy
edges.when: current evidence clears the gate the pause was raised against

edges.label: Still not healthy
edges.when: the problem persists in the current population
a pause resolved with the changed population healthy
a paused rollout whose changed population is unsafe

guardrails: Paused is not failed.
A pause never automatically reverts healthy targets.
Resumption requires current-state revalidation rather than the reading that preceded the pause.
governance.reusableRule: Rollout pause freezes future expansion while leaving room to determine whether the valid next step is resume, remediation or rollback.
governance.entityScope: the rollout, and the changed and unchanged populations at the moment it paused
governance.entityNote: Both populations are preserved exactly. A pause that loses track of who has the change can neither resume nor roll back.

identity.title: Change failure threshold → rollback decision → execute or forward recover
identity.purpose: Decide whether going back is actually safer than going on, before anyone starts going back.

requires: a defined failure threshold reached across the changed population
insufficientAlone: a single target failing, which is a target-scope problem until the evidence says otherwise

nodes.headline: Change failure threshold reached
Stop further rollout where the threshold requires it, before deciding anything about what is already applied

Determine, under an authorized recovery-decision role, the known-good prior state, the rollback capability, the irreversible side effects, the data and schema compatibility, the forward-recovery option and the affected scope - recording who made this determination, since every branch that follows commits to it and the wrong branch here cannot be undone by choosing differently later
Has the change crossed an irreversible boundary?

Record that rollback is not available, naming the boundary that was crossed. Rolling back across an irreversible boundary produces old code running against new data, which fails differently and worse - and the second failure is harder to diagnose because it looks like the first one returning
Is rollback safe and supported for the affected scope?

Scope the rollback to the affected subset where scoped rollback is supported. Reverting a whole population for a failure confined to one cohort takes a working change away from everybody who had no problem, and each of those reverts can fail on its own
Rollback execution → restore → verify stability
nodes.detail: a rollback chosen as the safer recovery

nodes.headline: external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: a failure where rolling back is unsafe, impossible or worse than going on

edges.label: It has not
edges.when: the previous state is genuinely reachable from where the targets are

edges.label: It has
edges.when: a schema migration, a data transformation or an external commitment has made the previous state unreachable

edges.label: Safe for everything affected
edges.when: the whole affected population can return to the known-good state

edges.label: Safe for a subset only
edges.when: part of the affected scope can revert and part cannot, or the failure is confined

edges.label: Not safe or not possible
edges.when: reverting would break dependencies, data or commitments
a rollback chosen as the safer recovery
a failure where rolling back is unsafe, impossible or worse than going on

distinctFrom.because: This chooses the recovery. RLT-248 performs a rollback and verifies it. Choosing wrong here is irreversible in the other direction - a rollback across a migrated schema cannot be undone by rolling forward again.

guardrails: Failure does not automatically imply rollback.
A rollback is never taken across an irreversible boundary blindly.
Rollback policy accounts for changed data, schema and state.
The rollback-versus-forward-recovery determination is made under a named, authorized recovery-decision role - never inferred silently, given that choosing wrong here is irreversible.
governance.reusableRule: Rollback is one recovery strategy and should be chosen only when returning to the previous state is safer and technically valid.
governance.entityScope: the failing rollout or change and the targets it affects
governance.entityNote: Rollback is one strategy among several. Whether it is available at all depends on what the change has already made irreversible. Choosing wrong here is irreversible in the direction that matters most, so a.determine's own determination - the input every downstream branch commits to - is made under an authorized recovery-decision role, never inferred silently from the technical facts alone.

identity.title: Rollback execution → restore → verify stability
identity.purpose: Return the affected targets to a known-good state and prove that they actually work there.

requires: an authorized rollback with a known-good state and a defined scope

nodes.headline: Rollback authorized
Apply the known-good state or version to the targets in scope, with stable operation identity so a retried rollback reverts once rather than twice
until the targets report the rollback applied, or the rollback reports an authoritative failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the rollback window

nodes.headline: Record the rollback outcome as unknown and hold further action. A population split across two versions with nobody able to say which is where is worse than either version alone
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a rollback whose outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: Did the rollback apply?

Record the rollback as failed, with the population left where it is. A failed rollback is a worse position than the failure that prompted it, and it needs a person rather than another automated attempt

Verify the target state, the service or functionality, dependency compatibility, the critical health metrics, and any artifacts the change left behind that the rollback did not remove. A rollback command succeeding says the old version is installed and nothing about whether the system works - and rollbacks fail on exactly the dependency and data-shape problems that made them necessary
Is the rolled-back population stable?
Record which targets reverted and which did not. A partially rolled-back population is a split fleet, and it needs to be visible as one rather than reported as a rollback that completed

Record that some part of the prior state cannot be restored - data created under the new version, external commitments made, irreversible side effects. Restoring the old version over legitimate new data destroys it, and that is a larger loss than the failure being recovered from
external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: a rollback that cannot fully restore the prior state

nodes.headline: external:human-in-the-loop-lifecycle
nodes.detail: a rollback that failed or completed only in part

nodes.headline: Record ROLLED_BACK_VERIFIED, preserving the failed change in the history. Rollback complete is not the deployment never having happened - the change ran, it affected things, and its record is what explains everything anybody noticed while it was live
ROLLED_BACK_VERIFIED; population restored and the failed change preserved as history
nodes.detail: a corrected change is a new rollout with its own eligibility, and this failure is part of what its gates are set against

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the targets report the rollback applied, the rollback reports an authoritative failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a rollback whose outcome is unknown leaves a population that may be on either version, and every subsequent decision depends on knowing which
a rollback whose outcome could not be established

edges.label: Applied
edges.when: the targets in scope report the known-good state

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the rollback itself did not complete

edges.label: Stable
edges.when: the targets are on the known-good state and functioning

edges.label: Partially rolled back
edges.when: some targets reverted and some did not

edges.label: The previous state is no longer fully recoverable
edges.when: data, commitments or side effects created under the change cannot coexist with the old version
a rollback that cannot fully restore the prior state
a rollback that failed or completed only in part

guardrails: Rollback complete is not the original deployment never having occurred.
The failed change's history is preserved.
Restoring an old version never overwrites legitimate irreversible data created after the change.
A rollback is verified rather than assumed from a successful command.
governance.reusableRule: Rollback restores current operational state while preserving the failed change as historical truth and requiring post-rollback verification.
governance.entityScope: the rollback operation and the targets it is reverting
governance.entityNote: The failed change stays in the record throughout. A rollback restores state and does not erase that the change happened.

identity.title: Individual target change failure → retry, isolate or remediate
identity.purpose: Recover one target that could not take the change, and notice when it stops being one target.

requires: a specific target failing to take the change, or ending in an unintended state

nodes.headline: Individual target change failed

Diagnose the target-specific cause - compatibility, being offline or unreachable, local configuration, a resource shortage, corrupt state, a dependency mismatch. What is being established is whether this target is unusual or whether the change is
Does this failure match a pattern across other targets?

Promote it from a target problem to a rollout problem. A failure signature appearing on forty targets is not forty individual problems, and handling them one at a time means nobody ever sees the shape of it
Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
nodes.detail: a target failure whose pattern makes it systemic

nodes.headline: Is a retry safe and likely to help?
Retry against this target only, within a bounded budget and using the same operation identity so a change that actually applied is not applied twice
Does retry budget remain?
retrying against this target only; the rollout is unaffected
nodes.detail: each attempt reports its own outcome and returns here with the budget one lower. Retrying is bounded rather than continuous

nodes.headline: Can this target safely remain on the previous version?

Record TARGET_EXCEPTION. The exception population stays explicitly visible - a rollout reporting complete while quietly leaving targets behind produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and the forgotten targets are the ones that break in six months with nobody remembering why they are different
TARGET_EXCEPTION; on the previous version, visible and countable
nodes.detail: the blocking cause clearing makes the target eligible again, and it is picked up by this change or the next one rather than staying behind permanently

nodes.headline: Record that this target cannot stay behind and cannot proceed unattended, with what is blocking it. Leaving it as an exception when it cannot safely be one is how a target ends up unsupported without anybody deciding that it should be
external:human-in-the-loop-lifecycle
nodes.detail: a target that must take the change and cannot

edges.label: It matches a pattern
edges.when: the same signature, cause or class appears across targets that should have differed

edges.label: It looks target-specific
edges.when: the cause is local to this target's state or environment
a target failure whose pattern makes it systemic

edges.label: It is
edges.when: the cause was transient - unreachable, momentarily short of resource, a temporary lock

edges.label: It is not
edges.when: the cause is structural to this target and retrying will reproduce it

edges.label: Budget remains
edges.when: this target has attempts left

edges.label: Exhausted
edges.when: the attempts this target allows have been used

edges.label: It can
edges.when: the previous version is supported, secure and compatible for this target

edges.label: It cannot
edges.when: staying behind leaves the target unsupported, insecure or incompatible
a target that must take the change and cannot

distinctFrom.because: RLT-245 governs whether the population progresses. This governs one target that fell out of it. One unreachable device is not a broken release, and treating it as one stops a rollout that was working.

guardrails: One target failure is not a rollout failure.
Retries are bounded rather than indefinite.
The exception population remains observable and countable.
Promotion to systemic happens on pattern evidence rather than on failure count.
governance.reusableRule: Individual change failures should be recovered at target scope until evidence shows that the problem is systemic.
governance.entityScope: the individual target and its failed change attempt
governance.entityNote: Target scope by default. Promotion to rollout scope happens on evidence of a pattern rather than on the count of failures.

identity.title: Change completed → observe → close, reopen or deprecate previous version
identity.purpose: Wait long enough to know the change held, and keep what a recovery would need until it clearly does not.

requires: the planned target population having reached the intended changed state
insufficientAlone: a rollout dashboard reporting complete, which reports coverage rather than health

nodes.headline: Planned population reached changed state
Does this change require post-change observation?

Record the change as applied and under observation. Deployment completion is not long-term stability - the regressions that matter most surface on a weekly cycle, at month-end, or the first time a rare path runs, all of them after the rollout dashboard turned green
until a regression appears in the changed population, or a critical failure appears
nodes.detail: timeout after the post-change observation window

nodes.headline: Is the regression material?
Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
nodes.detail: a late material regression in a completed change

nodes.headline: Record CHANGE_STABLE, and record the exception population explicitly alongside it. A change reported stable while its exceptions are invisible produces a version distribution nobody can account for, and every later change inherits that ambiguity
Can the previous version now be deprecated?

Retain the previous version and the state a recovery would need, with the condition that would release it. Deleting it because the rollout completed removes the only thing a late rollback could restore from, and late is exactly when rollbacks are actually needed
CHANGE_STABLE; previous version retained and exception targets named
nodes.detail: the retention condition being satisfied allows the previous version to be retired on its own terms. A later regression reopens recovery against a population that still has somewhere to go back to

nodes.headline: external:termination-lifecycle
nodes.detail: a previous version nothing depends on any longer

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the change touches behaviour, data or paths whose problems surface over time

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the change is fully exercised at application and nothing further can emerge

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a regression appears in the changed population, a critical failure appears

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the window is the point of the wait - reaching it without a material regression is what makes the change stable rather than merely deployed

edges.label: Material
edges.when: it affects correctness, availability or a business outcome the gate was protecting

edges.label: Not material
edges.when: it is noise, or a known issue already accounted for
a late material regression in a completed change

edges.label: It can
edges.when: no target remains on it, and the recovery and audit retention it was held for is satisfied

edges.label: Not yet
edges.when: recovery or audit still depends on it, or exception targets are still running it
a previous version nothing depends on any longer

guardrails: Deployment completion is not long-term stability.
A previous version or state required for recovery or audit is not deleted immediately.
Exception targets remain explicit in the completion record.
governance.reusableRule: Change lifecycle closes only after the applied population demonstrates sufficient stability and remaining version dependencies are resolved.
governance.entityScope: the completed rollout, the changed population and the exception targets
governance.entityNote: Completion and stability are different claims. The previous version stays available until both the recovery and the audit requirements are satisfied.

identity.title: Policy check → evaluate → pass, block or review
identity.purpose: Decide whether a specific action is permitted under the rules that actually govern it, at the version that actually applies.

entry.trigger: Protected action reaches policy decision point
requires: a proposed action that policy governs, arriving at the point where it is decided
insufficientAlone: a risk score, which estimates likelihood rather than establishing whether a rule permits something

nodes.headline: Protected action reaches policy decision point

Determine the applicable policy set from the action, the entity, the context, the effective time, the jurisdiction or domain where one is defined, and the current authoritative state. Which rules apply is a fact about this action rather than a global list run against everything
Is the policy version effective for this action and time determinable?
