Record that the governing policy version could not be established, and evaluate nothing. Picking the current version because it is the one to hand judges an action by a rule that may not have existed when it was taken

Evaluate the requirements of that version against the facts. What is evaluated is a rule against a fact - a risk score is not a policy check, and substituting one produces a block whose reason nobody can state to the person it lands on
What did the rules determine?
Record POLICY_PASS with the version evaluated and what was checked. The record is what makes the pass auditable later - a permitted action with no evaluation behind it cannot be defended
POLICY_PASS for this action under the version evaluated
nodes.detail: a later action is evaluated on its own terms. This pass is not a standing clearance and does not carry to anything else

nodes.headline: Record POLICY_BLOCK with the rule, its version and the requirement that failed. A block is a rule applying and says nothing about intent - recording it as suspicion attaches a reputation to somebody who hit a threshold
POLICY_BLOCK; this action is not permitted under the applicable rule
nodes.detail: the requirement being satisfied, or an authorized exception being granted for it, makes the same action evaluable again. The block concerns this attempt under this version and nothing wider

nodes.headline: Record REVIEW_REQUIRED. This is the rules running out rather than a violation being found: nothing has been decided, nothing has been refused, and reporting it to the requester as a rejection is untrue
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an action policy cannot determine, or whose governing version cannot be established

edges.label: Determinable
edges.when: the applicable version and its effective period are authoritatively known

edges.label: Not determinable
edges.when: which version governs this action cannot be established

edges.label: Every requirement satisfied
edges.when: the applicable rules permit the action

edges.label: An explicit blocking condition applies
edges.when: a requirement is unmet or a prohibition applies

edges.label: The rules do not determine it
edges.when: no deterministic outcome follows from the applicable policy
an action policy cannot determine, or whose governing version cannot be established

distinctFrom.because: This applies rules. DEC-181 opens a workflow for judgment where no rule produces the answer - which is why this journey's third outcome is to hand over rather than to guess.

guardrails: A policy check is not a risk score.
A policy block is not evidence of malicious behaviour.
Policy requirements are never invented.
Evaluation uses the policy version effective for the relevant action and time.
governance.reusableRule: Policy evaluation determines whether a specific action is permitted under the rules applicable to that action's current context.
governance.entityScope: the policy evaluation, the actor or entity it concerns, and the proposed action
governance.entityNote: One evaluation per action per decision point. It is a question about this action rather than a standing judgment about the entity.

identity.title: Risk signal → correlate evidence → clear, monitor, restrict or review
identity.purpose: Turn a measurement into a state change no larger than the evidence behind it supports, and no longer-lived than the question stays open.

requires: a meaningful risk signal - a behaviour or velocity anomaly, an identity inconsistency, a transaction anomaly, a device or context signal, an external risk signal, or repeated unusual activity
a recorded source for it - detection, monitoring, a model, an external party or a dispute outcome - which is context for weighing the signal and never corroboration of it
insufficientAlone: unusual behaviour, which is unusual and not therefore wrong
a single threshold crossing, which is a reading rather than a finding

nodes.headline: Risk signal received

Correlate the signal with the authoritative context that bears on it - the actor's history, the state of the thing it concerns, other live signals, and what this signal is actually measuring. A model output is an estimate about a person and never a fact about them
Is the signal clearly benign in context?

Record CLEAR with the reason. Clearing is a fact worth keeping - the same signal will fire again on the same behaviour, and a system that never records the clear re-investigates it every time and eventually acts on the repetition
CLEAR; no risk state was created and nothing was restricted
nodes.detail: a materially different signal opens its own assessment. The recorded clear is context for it rather than an exemption from it

nodes.headline: What does the combined evidence support?

Record MONITOR and take no restrictive action. Watching is a state in its own right; restricting on one weak signal is a decision the evidence does not support, and the person it lands on did nothing to earn it
until the evidence accumulating on this case reaches a defined threshold, or the accumulated evidence explains the signal as benign
nodes.detail: timeout after the monitoring horizon defined for this signal type

nodes.headline: What did the accumulated evidence settle?

Record CLEAR with the reason and release the monitoring state, along with anything held or held back only because the case was open. The case and every signal on it stay readable - clearing a suspicion is not the same as never having had one, and that difference is what tells a first occurrence from a fifth
CLEAR after monitoring; the monitoring state is released and nothing was restricted
nodes.detail: a materially different signal opens its own assessment, judged with this case as context rather than as a finding against the actor

nodes.headline: monitoring horizon passed without resolution; nothing was restricted
nodes.detail: the state does not persist on the actor once the horizon passes. A recurrence is assessed fresh, informed by this case rather than convicted by it

nodes.headline: Record the rule that applies and its outcome. This is a rule applying rather than an assessment being made, and the two are recorded differently because only one of them can be argued with

Atomically record the risk case for this risk_subject_id: if no open case already exists for it, create one with its evidence and the provenance of each piece; if a concurrent evaluation already opened one for the same subject between the evidence check and this action, fold this evidence into the existing case rather than creating a second one. A risk state whose basis cannot be shown cannot be appealed, explained or corrected - and this is exactly the state someone will eventually ask us to justify
What does the evidence call for?
Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
nodes.detail: risk evidence warranting a scoped restriction

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: material risk evidence needing authorized judgment

edges.label: Benign or a known false positive
edges.when: the context explains it entirely

edges.label: Not explained away
edges.when: the context does not account for it

edges.label: Below any defined threshold
edges.when: the evidence is real and does not reach what policy requires for action

edges.label: A deterministic rule requires blocking
edges.when: a governing rule, rather than an assessment, produces the outcome

edges.label: A material threshold is reached
edges.when: the combined evidence crosses a defined threshold requiring intervention

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the evidence accumulating on this case reaches a defined threshold, the accumulated evidence explains the signal as benign

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a signal that never reaches a threshold is not held open on the actor indefinitely - an unresolved risk state is its own cost to whoever carries it, and nothing was ever established to justify carrying it

edges.label: Benign on the accumulated evidence
edges.when: what arrived explains the signal rather than supporting it

edges.label: A material threshold is now reached
edges.when: the accumulated evidence crosses what policy requires for intervention

edges.label: A scoped precautionary restriction
edges.when: the risk is material enough that acting now is proportionate to the evidence

edges.label: Judgment before any restriction
edges.when: the evidence is material and the right response is not something a rule determines
risk evidence warranting a scoped restriction
material risk evidence needing authorized judgment

distinctFrom.because: IDN-90 handles a specific suspicion - that an account is in someone else's hands - and runs a containment and recovery path for it. This is the general evidence lifecycle: most of what it sees clears, and its main job is not over-reacting.

This weighs uncertainty: how reliable the evidence is and what it supports, with no rule needing to have been broken for the question to be worth asking. RSK-194 starts only where an identifiable policy appears to have been breached, and tests that rule against the evidence and the version that governed it. A signal does not become a violation candidate by looking risky - without a governing rule to test, there is nothing for RSK-194 to decide.

guardrails: A signal is not confirmed misconduct. The state it opens is a question, and most of them close without an answer against anyone.
An anomaly is not fraud. Unusual and wrong are different findings resting on different evidence.
A risk score is not a factual identity.
A model score is not an authoritative decision unless it has been explicitly governed as one, which is a decision made outside this journey.
One weak signal never triggers maximum restriction. What gets restricted is proportionate to the evidence, and the evidence is what bounds its scope.
Monitoring is not restriction. Watching an open question is a state in its own right, and collapsing the two restricts people the evidence never reached.
This journey restricts nothing itself. Where a restriction is warranted it hands to the journey whose job that is, carrying the fact that nothing has been concluded.
A signal later cleared stays auditable. Erasing it removes the ability to tell a first occurrence from a fifth.
Evidence and its provenance are preserved so the reasoning can be shown.

Concurrent evaluation of the same risk_subject_id yields at most one canonical case - a.case is atomic on that identity, and a losing concurrent evaluator folds its evidence into the existing case rather than opening a second one.
governance.reusableRule: Risk signals should change state only in proportion to the combined evidence and the policy-defined consequence of that evidence.
governance.entityScope: the risk case and the actor, account, transaction or resource it concerns
governance.entityNote: One case per correlated risk, accumulating signals. A case that opens per signal produces a queue of fragments nobody can assess together. The case is scoped to what the evidence is actually about - a flagged transaction is a flagged transaction, and reading it as a flagged customer is how one anomaly becomes a permanent mark. risk_subject_id is that specific evidence subject (the actor, account, transaction or resource the signal concerns), never the broader actor generally - a.case is the atomic authority for that identity: two signals correlating to the same subject at the same time settle on one case between them, never two.

identity.title: Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
identity.purpose: Stop the smallest thing that manages the risk, and keep a stated route back.

requires: a defined risk threshold reached, with the correlated evidence behind it

nodes.headline: Risk threshold requiring intervention reached

Determine the risk's scope, the specific action or capability implicated, the authority for restricting it, and the duration or review condition where one is defined. A restriction with no stated release condition has no way out and becomes permanent by nobody's decision
Is there authority to apply this restriction?

Choose the smallest restriction sufficient for the identified risk - a hold on the specific transaction, a block on the specific capability, an additional verification, a manual approval requirement, or a bounded access restriction. The restriction's scope matches the risk's scope: an anomaly on one payment method is not a reason to close an account
Could additional verification resolve this on its own?

Raise the step-up requirement through the authentication lifecycle, which owns the challenge. This journey keeps the restriction and the release condition, because a passed challenge has to release something and the challenge itself cannot know what

Raise the restriction through the access and capability lifecycle, which owns what is switched off and how. Record it as temporary and reviewable - a temporary restriction is not a final adverse decision, and a system that cannot tell the two apart never releases anything it has stopped
until the risk clears or the required evidence arrives, or a review concludes, or a terminal decision is taken
nodes.detail: timeout after the review condition or maximum restriction duration policy defines

nodes.headline: How did the restriction resolve?

Release the restriction and raise the capability restoration through the access lifecycle, rebuilt from current entitlements rather than from a snapshot taken when the restriction went on. A restriction that outlasted a term or an entitlement does not restore what expired underneath it
restriction released; the risk case closes with what cleared it recorded
nodes.detail: new evidence opens a new assessment. The record of what cleared this one is what stops the same evidence being re-litigated

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a restriction needing authorized judgment - to apply, to continue or to lift

nodes.headline: external:termination-lifecycle
nodes.detail: an authorized terminal decision on a risk case

edges.label: Authorized
edges.when: a policy or a granted authority permits restricting this scope on this evidence

edges.label: Not established
edges.when: no policy or authority covers restricting this

edges.label: Verification would resolve it
edges.when: the risk is about who is acting, and proving it would answer the question

edges.label: A restriction is needed regardless
edges.when: the risk is not one a challenge answers

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the risk clears or the required evidence arrives, a review concludes, a terminal decision is taken

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a restriction nobody revisits becomes a termination without a decision, and the person under it has no way to tell the difference

edges.label: Cleared
edges.when: the risk cleared, or the evidence required to release it arrived

edges.label: A terminal decision was taken
edges.when: an authorized decision ends the relationship or the capability permanently

edges.label: Judgment is needed on what happens next
edges.when: the evidence has not cleared and the next step is not one a rule determines
a restriction needing authorized judgment - to apply, to continue or to lift
an authorized terminal decision on a risk case

distinctFrom.because: This determines what restriction the risk justifies and holds the release condition. ACC-78 applies and restores the access state. One is the reason, the other is the door.

guardrails: Restriction scope matches risk scope.
Unrelated capabilities are never terminated without a policy basis.
A temporary restriction is not a final adverse decision.
Every restriction states the condition that would release it.
governance.reusableRule: Risk controls should constrain only the activity necessary to manage the identified risk while preserving a path to evidence-based resolution.
governance.entityScope: the risk case and the specific capability or action being restricted
governance.entityNote: The restriction is scoped to the risk. Risk owns why and until when; the access lifecycle owns what is actually switched off.

identity.title: Policy violation detected → validate → correct, restrict or escalate
identity.purpose: Establish that a rule was actually broken, against the version that governed it, before anything follows from that.

requires: an action or state that appears to breach an identifiable policy
insufficientAlone: a risk signal, which is evidence about likelihood rather than about a rule having been broken
an unusual pattern, which is not a rule

nodes.headline: Potential policy violation detected
Identify the policy, the version effective at the time of the suspected action, the action itself, the evidence and the affected scope
Which policy version governs the suspected action?

Record that a later version is being applied retroactively, and the rule that permits it. Judging a past action by a rule that did not exist then is something a governing rule has to say explicitly - doing it by default makes everybody historically non-compliant on the day a policy changes
Evaluate the evidence against the applicable version's requirements
Is the violation confirmed under the applicable version?
Record no violation, with the version evaluated. Detection is not confirmation, and a cleared case is worth keeping because the same detection will fire on the same behaviour again
no violation under the applicable policy version
nodes.detail: a different action, or a policy change with explicit retroactive reach, is assessed on its own terms rather than by re-running this one

nodes.headline: Classify the severity and the correctable scope. A violation is not intent - most are configuration, misunderstanding or a rule nobody read, and applying a misconduct consequence to them costs a relationship the evidence never justified losing
What consequence does the governing policy define?

State exactly what would bring the entity back into compliance, and by when. A violation notice that does not say what to do about it is a reprimand, and it produces an escalation rather than a correction
until the remediation is completed, or the remediation authoritatively fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the remediation deadline the policy defines

nodes.headline: Did the remediation resolve the violation?

Record the violation as remediated, preserving what happened and what corrected it. The history stays because a pattern of the same violation is worth seeing, and a record that only shows the current state cannot show one
violation confirmed and remediated; history preserved
nodes.detail: a recurrence is a new case linked to this one, which is what makes repetition visible without rewriting the first

nodes.headline: Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
nodes.detail: a confirmed violation requiring a scoped restriction

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a violation whose consequence, version or remediation outcome needs authorized judgment

nodes.headline: external:termination-lifecycle
nodes.detail: a violation the policy explicitly attaches a terminal consequence to

edges.label: The version effective when it occurred
edges.when: the action falls under a determinable historical version

edges.label: A later version, where governing rules explicitly say so
edges.when: a rule expressly applies a newer version to past actions

edges.label: Not determinable
edges.when: which version governs cannot be established

edges.label: Confirmed
edges.when: the evidence establishes the rule was breached

edges.label: Not confirmed
edges.when: the evidence does not establish a breach of the applicable version

edges.label: A remediation requirement
edges.when: the policy defines what would bring this back into compliance

edges.label: An immediate scoped restriction
edges.when: the policy requires stopping something while this is resolved

edges.label: A terminal consequence the policy explicitly requires
edges.when: the policy states that this violation ends the relationship or the capability

edges.label: Authorized judgment, or the policy defines no consequence
edges.when: the consequence turns on judgment, or nothing in the policy says what follows

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the remediation is completed, the remediation authoritatively fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an open violation with an expired remediation window is neither resolved nor acted on, and it stays that way until something else surfaces it

edges.label: Resolved
edges.when: the entity is back within the applicable rule

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the remediation did not bring it back into compliance
a confirmed violation requiring a scoped restriction
a violation whose consequence, version or remediation outcome needs authorized judgment
a violation the policy explicitly attaches a terminal consequence to

distinctFrom.because: DEC-186 handles what follows an authorized rejection. This determines whether a violation occurred at all and which consequence the policy defines - it may never reach a decision case, and most of its outcomes are corrections rather than refusals.

RSK-192 evaluates risk evidence without requiring any rule to have been broken, and most of what it sees clears. This starts from an identifiable governing rule and asks whether it was actually breached, judged against the version in force at the time. Risk evidence alone never opens a case here; it opens one there.

guardrails: Detection is not a confirmed violation.
A violation is not malicious intent.
The consequence comes from the governing policy rather than from severity felt.
A historical action is evaluated against the policy applicable when it occurred, unless governing rules explicitly say otherwise.
governance.reusableRule: A policy violation should be established against the applicable rule and evidence before the system applies the consequence defined for that violation.
governance.entityScope: the violation case, the entity or action it concerns, and the policy version it is judged under
governance.entityNote: The version is part of the entity. A case that does not carry which rule it is about cannot be assessed and cannot be defended.

identity.title: Compliance requirement → collect and verify → satisfied or blocked
identity.purpose: Hold one mandatory requirement as its own state, blocking only what genuinely depends on it.

requires: an applicable compliance requirement that a specific process cannot proceed without
insufficientAlone: a general onboarding step, which collects what a product needs rather than what a rule mandates

nodes.headline: Compliance requirement becomes necessary

Define the exact requirement and which process depends on it. The requirement is scoped to its purpose - a compliance step that collects everything available is not a requirement but a data grab, and everything extra becomes a retention obligation nobody planned
Does existing authoritative evidence already satisfy this requirement, within its validity?

Record the requirement SATISFIED from the existing evidence, and do not re-collect. Asking again for what is already held and still valid is the most common reason people abandon a process at the compliance step, and it produces a duplicate of something we already have to retain

Raise the evidence or verification the requirement actually needs through the mechanism that owns it. Compliance does not build its own verification - a parallel identity check will disagree with the canonical one, and there is no principled way to say which of two verified states is real
until the requirement is authoritatively satisfied, or the requirement authoritatively fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the deadline the requirement defines, where one exists

nodes.headline: How did the requirement resolve?
What does policy define for an expired requirement deadline?

Record the requirement SATISFIED with its scope and its validity. Satisfied is scoped - the same evidence does not satisfy a different requirement, and reusing it beyond its purpose is how one verification silently becomes a general clearance nobody granted
external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: a compliance requirement satisfied, releasing the process that depended on it

nodes.headline: Record the requirement as unsatisfiable, with why. This is a specific requirement failing rather than the entity being non-compliant in general, and the difference decides how much stops
What do the governing rules say happens to the dependent process?

Block only the dependent process, naming the requirement that blocks it and what would satisfy it. Everything not depending on this requirement stays available - one unmet obligation stopping everything an entity can do is a general suspension nobody authorized
dependent process blocked; the requirement is named and unmet
nodes.detail: the requirement being satisfied later releases the block, and the dependent process revalidates rather than simply resuming

nodes.headline: Close the dependent process under the rule that requires it, recording that it closed for an unmet compliance requirement rather than on its merits
dependent process closed for an unmet compliance requirement
nodes.detail: a new attempt with the requirement satisfiable is assessed fresh, and this closure does not stand against it

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a compliance requirement whose failure or deadline consequence the rules do not define

edges.label: It does
edges.when: held evidence covers the requirement's scope and is still valid

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: nothing held covers it, or what is held has lapsed or was scoped to something else

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the requirement is authoritatively satisfied, the requirement authoritatively fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a dependent process blocked on a requirement nobody is completing is stopped without anyone having decided to stop it

edges.label: Satisfied
edges.when: the required evidence was obtained and verified

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the requirement cannot be met with what is available

edges.label: It defines an outcome
edges.when: policy states what happens to the dependent process when the deadline passes

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: no rule states what an expired compliance deadline does
a compliance requirement satisfied, releasing the process that depended on it

edges.label: Block it
edges.when: the rules stop the dependent process while the requirement is unmet

edges.label: Close it
edges.when: the rules end the dependent process where the requirement cannot be met

edges.label: The rules do not say
edges.when: nothing authoritative states the consequence for the dependent process
a compliance requirement whose failure or deadline consequence the rules do not define

distinctFrom.because: IDN-82 orchestrates collecting a verification and resuming what it blocked. This owns the compliance requirement as a business state - which requirement applies, whether existing evidence already satisfies it, and what happens when it cannot be met. It uses that collection mechanism rather than reimplementing one.

guardrails: A compliance requirement never requests unrelated evidence.
A satisfied requirement is scoped to its defined purpose and validity.
A compliance requirement is not generic customer onboarding.
Only the processes depending on the requirement are blocked.
governance.reusableRule: Compliance requirements should block only the processes that depend on them and release those processes only when the defined requirement is authoritatively satisfied.
governance.entityScope: the compliance requirement and the specific process depending on it
governance.entityNote: Satisfied is scoped to the requirement's purpose and validity. The same evidence does not satisfy a different requirement.

identity.title: Compliance or policy hold → preserve state → resolve → resume or terminate
identity.purpose: Pause what a policy question makes unsafe, and leave everything else running.

requires: an authoritative policy or compliance hold, with an authority behind it

nodes.headline: Policy or compliance hold applied

Record the hold reason, its scope, the authority for it, the effective time, which operations it affects, which remain allowed, and what would resolve it. A hold with no stated resolution condition has no way out and becomes a termination nobody decided

Record ON_HOLD and pause only the future actions the hold is incompatible with. Unrelated capabilities stay available where policy permits - a hold on outbound payments is not a reason to stop someone reading their own records
Do existing commitments require continued handling?

Preserve those commitments and route them according to the governing rules. An order already placed, a refund already due and a regulatory report already owed do not stop existing because the entity is on hold - and some of them the hold specifically requires us to keep doing
Leave existing deadlines where they are unless the governing policy explicitly moves them. A hold that silently resets clocks extends obligations nobody agreed to extend, and it shortens none of them
until the stated resolution requirement is met, or a review decision changes the hold, or a terminal policy outcome is reached
nodes.detail: timeout after the maximum hold duration policy defines

nodes.headline: How did the hold resolve?

Re-read the entity's current state before resuming. What resumes is what is valid now - the hold may have outlasted an entitlement, a term or an eligibility, and lifting it does not restore things that expired underneath it
Record the hold lifted and resume the operations that are currently valid, rebuilt from current state rather than from what was paused
hold lifted; operations resumed at what is currently valid
nodes.detail: a further policy question is a new hold with its own scope and its own resolution condition. This one stays in the record as something that was applied and answered

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a hold whose resolution or continuation needs authorized judgment

nodes.headline: external:termination-lifecycle
nodes.detail: a hold resolving into a terminal policy outcome

edges.label: They do
edges.when: orders, refunds, reports or obligations created before the hold are still live

edges.label: None outstanding
edges.when: nothing created before the hold is still owed in either direction

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the stated resolution requirement is met, a review decision changes the hold, a terminal policy outcome is reached

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an indefinite hold is a termination without a decision, and the entity under it cannot tell which one it is in

edges.label: The requirement was met
edges.when: the stated resolution condition is authoritatively satisfied

edges.label: A terminal policy outcome
edges.when: the policy question resolved against the entity in a way that ends something

edges.label: A review decision is needed
edges.when: resolving it turns on judgment rather than on the stated condition
a hold whose resolution or continuation needs authorized judgment
a hold resolving into a terminal policy outcome

distinctFrom.because: RSK-193 restricts because evidence of risk warrants it, and releases on evidence. A hold pauses because a policy or compliance question is open, and releases when that question is answered - the trigger, the authority and the release condition are all different.

guardrails: A hold is not a rejection.
A hold never resets deadlines unless governing policy explicitly does so.
Unrelated capabilities remain available where permitted.
Every hold states the condition that would resolve it.
governance.reusableRule: A policy or compliance hold temporarily prevents defined actions while preserving the underlying entity and its unresolved obligations.
governance.entityScope: the entity or process on hold, and the hold acting on it
governance.entityNote: The hold pauses future incompatible actions. The entity, its obligations and its deadlines all continue existing underneath it.

identity.title: Exception request → validate authority → approve, reject or review
identity.purpose: Ask for a controlled deviation from a named rule, over a stated scope, from someone entitled to ask.

requires: a request to deviate from an identified policy or rule, for an identified scope
insufficientAlone: a policy block having occurred, which is a rule applying rather than a request to set it aside

nodes.headline: Policy exception requested
Capture the policy or rule concerned, the exception requested, its scope, the reason, the requester, any proposed duration or effective window, and the supporting evidence
Does the policy permit exceptions to this rule?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an exception sought against a rule whose policy says nothing about exceptions

nodes.headline: Record that this rule admits no exceptions, and close the path. A rule that can be excepted by asking is not a rule, and some of them exist precisely because they cannot be set aside by the person they inconvenience
no exception path exists for this rule; the rule stands
nodes.detail: the policy itself changing is a policy change rather than an exception, and it runs through its own lifecycle with its own effective-time semantics

nodes.headline: May this requester ask for an exception to this rule?
Record the request as invalid on standing, naming who may ask. This is not a refusal of the exception on its merits - nobody assessed it - and reporting it as one is untrue
request invalid on standing; the exception itself was not assessed
nodes.detail: the same exception sought by someone the policy admits is assessed on its merits

nodes.headline: Does a deterministic exception rule cover this case?

Record PENDING_REVIEW. The exception needs an authorized judgment and this journey does not make it - it establishes what is being asked for, over what scope, and hands the decision to the mechanism that owns decisions
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an exception requiring authorized judgment

nodes.headline: Evaluate the request against the deterministic exception rule that covers it
What did the exception rule determine?
Record the exception REJECTED, naming the condition that was not met. The underlying policy continues to apply exactly as it did
exception rejected; the policy applies unchanged
nodes.detail: the unmet condition being satisfied makes a fresh request assessable. This rejection concerns the request rather than the requester

nodes.headline: Record the exception APPROVED with exactly which rule it displaces, over what scope, for how long and under what conditions. An exception that names no rule and no scope is a general permission, which is what nobody meant to grant and what will be discovered being used somewhere else
Exception granted → apply scoped override → expire or revoke
nodes.detail: an authorized exception ready to be applied

edges.label: It permits them
edges.when: the policy defines an exception path for this rule

edges.label: It forbids them
edges.when: the policy explicitly admits no exceptions to this rule

edges.label: It is silent
edges.when: nothing states whether this rule can be excepted or by whom
an exception sought against a rule whose policy says nothing about exceptions

edges.label: They may
edges.when: the policy's exception path admits requests from this party

edges.label: They may not
edges.when: the requester is not among those the exception path admits

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the policy defines when this exception is granted without judgment

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: granting it turns on an authorized judgment
an exception requiring authorized judgment

edges.label: Granted
edges.when: the rule's conditions for granting are met

edges.label: Refused
edges.when: the rule's conditions are not met
an authorized exception ready to be applied

distinctFrom.because: This defines what a policy exception is and whether one may even be sought - which rule, what scope, whose authority. Where the answer needs judgment it uses the decision engine rather than being one.

guardrails: An exception requested is not an exception granted.
Exception authority is never invented.
An exception identifies exactly which rule and which scope it affects.
An exception is a controlled deviation rather than removal of the rule.
governance.reusableRule: A policy exception is a controlled authorization to deviate from a defined rule within an explicit scope; it is not removal of the rule itself.
governance.entityScope: the exception request and the specific policy, action or entity it concerns
governance.entityNote: An exception names a rule and a scope. One that names neither is a general permission, which is what nobody meant to grant.

identity.title: Exception granted → apply scoped override → expire or revoke
identity.purpose: Let an authorized deviation apply exactly where it was authorized, and stop applying the moment it should.

requires: an authorized exception naming a rule, a scope and its usage semantics

nodes.headline: Exception becomes authorized
Record the exception id, the policy or rule it displaces, its scope, who authorized it, its valid-from, its valid-until where one applies, its conditions and its usage semantics
Does the exception define an expiry?
Record the boundary as granted, so the exception's own terms decide when it stops rather than any assumption made here

Record that no expiry was set, rather than assigning one. Inventing an expiry revokes an authorization nobody revoked; the absence is itself worth surfacing, because an unbounded exception to a live rule is usually something someone should look at again
until the exception is invoked for an action, or the exception is revoked
nodes.detail: timeout after the exception's valid-until, or the review point set for an unbounded exception

nodes.headline: What happened to the exception?
Is the exception currently valid for this specific action?

Apply normal policy and record the attempt. An exception granted for one action or one entity does not travel to another - leakage here is how a single approved deviation becomes a general practice nobody authorized and nobody can date
Refuse the reuse and record the attempt. A single-use exception used twice authorizes one deviation and performs two

Apply the override for this action only, and record the use. The underlying policy is untouched - an exception overrides a decision rather than disabling a rule, and the next action it does not cover gets the normal answer
Is this a single-use exception?

Atomically mark the exception consumed for this exception_id: the first invocation to reach this action claims the single use and its authority is spent; a concurrent second invocation racing the same single-use exception finds it already consumed rather than being allowed to apply a second override, because exception_id's own one-active-per-key concurrency serializes both invocations' path through c.applicable and this action rather than letting them interleave. Any later invocation is refused rather than quietly honoured
consumed; the exception can authorize nothing further
nodes.detail: a further deviation needs a further exception, which is a new request rather than a re-reading of this grant

nodes.headline: Record the exception EXPIRED and stop all future override, including in work already queued carrying its id. Stale work holding an expired exception is the failure this state exists to prevent - the override arrives long after the authority lapsed and looks identical to a valid one
EXPIRED; the rule applies normally again and the overrides already made stand
nodes.detail: a renewed exception is a new grant with its own scope and validity, assessed on current circumstances rather than extended from this one

nodes.headline: Record the exception REVOKED with its authority and its effective moment, and stop future override immediately. Revocation does not undo the overrides already validly applied - those happened under an authorization that existed at the time, and rewriting them removes the record of a decision that was correct when it was made
REVOKED; future override stopped, prior valid uses preserved
nodes.detail: whether the prior uses need correcting is a separate question with its own lifecycle, and revoking the exception does not answer it

edges.label: It defines one
edges.when: a valid-until, a period or a use limit was set when it was granted

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: no time limit was set

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the exception is invoked for an action, the exception is revoked

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an exception that outlives its authority is a rule quietly disabled, and the disabling is invisible because every use looks like a valid one

edges.label: Invoked
edges.when: an action reached a policy decision point carrying this exception

edges.label: Revoked
edges.when: an authority withdrew it before it expired

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: the same rule, inside the granted scope, inside its validity, and not consumed

edges.label: Out of scope
edges.when: a different rule, a different entity or an action the grant did not name

edges.label: Already consumed
edges.when: a single-use exception that has been used

edges.label: Single-use
edges.when: the grant authorized one deviation

edges.label: Reusable within its validity
edges.when: the grant authorized deviations for a period or a scope rather than a count

distinctFrom.because: RSK-197 establishes that a deviation is authorized. This is the runtime question - is it valid for this action, this entity, right now, and has it already been used up. An exception granted correctly and applied wrongly is still an unauthorized deviation.

guardrails: An exception is not a policy disabled.
An exception for one action or entity never leaks to another.
An expired or revoked exception is never reused by stale work.
An expiration is never invented where none exists.

A single-use exception authorizes exactly one deviation - concurrent invocations against the same exception_id are serialized so at most one can consume it, never two applying the override before either is marked consumed.
governance.reusableRule: Granted exceptions override only the policy decision explicitly authorized for their defined scope and validity.
governance.entityScope: the granted exception and each action it is invoked against
governance.entityNote: The exception is one record; each use is an event on it. Validity is asked at each use rather than set once when it was granted. exception_id's own concurrency is one-active-per-key precisely because validity and consumption are separated across c.applicable, a.override, c.single and a.consume: without serializing invocations against the same exception, two concurrent invocations of a single-use exception could both pass c.applicable's not-consumed check before either reaches a.consume's own mark, applying the override twice against an authorization for one. Serializing per exception_id is what keeps the validity-check-through-consume sequence atomic in effect without collapsing it into one node.

identity.title: Limit or quota reached → block, wait, increase or reset
identity.purpose: Treat a limit being reached as the limit working, and give the constrained action a real path forward.

entry.trigger: Limit threshold reached or would be exceeded
requires: a proposed action measured against a defined limit or quota

nodes.headline: Limit threshold reached or would be exceeded
Determine the limit type, the current usage, the limit amount, the measurement window, the reset semantics, the scope, and the authoritative source of the count
Is the usage figure authoritative?
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a limit decision resting on a usage figure that may be wrong

nodes.headline: Would the proposed action exceed the limit?

Record the usage against the limit atomically with the allowance, so two concurrent actions cannot each see room only one of them has. Checking and then applying separately is how a limit of ten becomes twelve under load, and the overage is discovered afterwards
within the limit; usage recorded atomically
nodes.detail: the next action is measured against the updated usage, which is why the record and the allowance happen together

nodes.headline: Block or hold the affected action only, and record LIMIT_REACHED with the limit, the window and the current usage. Reaching a limit is the limit working - it is not abuse, and a message that implies otherwise is read as an accusation by someone who did exactly what they were permitted to do
What path exists from here?
Is the reset point authoritatively defined?
until the authoritative reset occurs
nodes.detail: timeout after the expected reset point plus its tolerance

nodes.headline: Record the window reset from its authoritative source rather than from an assumed clock. A locally assumed reset grants capacity the authority has not granted, and the two drift apart quietly
window reset; capacity available again under the same limit
nodes.detail: the blocked action is re-attempted and measured against the new window like any other

nodes.headline: LIMIT_REACHED with no route to more capacity in this window
nodes.detail: an authorized change to the limit, or a new window, makes the same action possible. Nothing about this state is a finding against the entity

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a limit increase or override policy permits to be sought

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a limit with no authoritatively defined reset

edges.label: Authoritative
edges.when: the count comes from the source that owns it and is current

edges.label: Derived, stale or possibly incorrect
edges.when: the count is inferred, cached, or disagrees with the owning source
a limit decision resting on a usage figure that may be wrong

edges.label: Within the limit
edges.when: the action fits inside the remaining allowance

edges.label: Exceeds it
edges.when: the action would take usage past the limit

edges.label: The limit resets on its own
edges.when: the measurement window rolls and capacity returns

edges.label: An increase or override is permitted
edges.when: policy provides a route to more capacity

edges.label: Neither
edges.when: the limit is fixed for this entity and this window

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: the window's reset is stated and comes from the source that owns the count

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no authoritative reset point exists for this window

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the authoritative reset occurs

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a reset that does not arrive when it should means the count or the window is wrong, and waiting longer on a broken clock blocks an entity indefinitely
a limit increase or override policy permits to be sought
a limit with no authoritatively defined reset

distinctFrom.because: A limit is a constraint the entity was told about and is entitled to consume. Routing it into risk assessment puts ordinary heavy users in front of a fraud analyst, and produces a risk history for behaviour that was permitted.

guardrails: A limit reached is not abuse.
A reset period is never invented.
A limit is never silently increased.
Concurrent usage updates cannot permit unintended over-consumption.
governance.reusableRule: A limit should constrain only the measured activity governed by that limit until usage, time or authorized policy changes make additional capacity valid.
governance.entityScope: the entity and the specific limit or quota constraining it
governance.entityNote: One limit, one measurement window, one authoritative count. Reaching it is an operational fact about usage and nothing about the user.

identity.title: Policy or risk state changed → re-evaluate affected work → resume, restrict or preserve
identity.purpose: Apply a change where the new authority actually reaches, and leave the past alone.

requires: a material authoritative change - a policy version, a cleared risk case, a moved restriction threshold, a changed compliance requirement, a revoked exception, or a new authoritative classification

nodes.headline: Policy or risk state changed

Identify the active and future work the change actually touches. A policy update that restarts every journey in the system is indistinguishable from an outage, and it buries the handful of cases the change was genuinely about

Preserve completed actions exactly as they are. An action validly completed under the policy that governed it stays valid - a new rule does not make everybody retroactively non-compliant, and rewriting the record on a policy release destroys the evidence that anything ever complied
What are the change's effective-time semantics?

Apply the change to future relevant actions and leave pending work on the version that governed it when it started. Work in flight under an older version is not non-compliant - it is mid-process under the rule it began under
Has a newer evaluation already been applied to this work?

Suppress this evaluation. A queued policy job carrying an older version will otherwise overwrite a decision made under a newer one, and the regression is silent - the record shows a valid evaluation against a rule that has already been superseded
stale policy evaluation suppressed; the newer version's decision stands
nodes.detail: the newest authority governs. A further change is propagated on its own terms rather than by replaying this one

nodes.headline: Re-evaluate the pending work against the governing effective-time semantics, item by item. What is re-evaluated is the pending decision rather than the completed action behind it
What does the re-evaluation require now?

Record that the change was evaluated against this work and required nothing. Recording the non-change is what stops the same evaluation running again on the next release, and it is the evidence that the change was considered rather than missed
evaluated against the change and unchanged by it
nodes.detail: a later change is evaluated on its own terms. This record is what makes it cheap to see this one was already handled

nodes.headline: Capability restoration → revalidate → restore safely
nodes.detail: a restriction the change no longer justifies

nodes.headline: Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
nodes.detail: work the change now requires restricting

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a change with undefined effective-time semantics

edges.label: Prospective only
edges.when: the change governs actions from its effective time onward

edges.label: It reaches work already in flight
edges.when: the change explicitly applies to pending work started under the previous version

edges.label: The semantics are not defined
edges.when: nothing states whether the change reaches work in flight

edges.label: Nothing newer
edges.when: this is the most recent authority applied to it

edges.label: A newer version already governs it
edges.when: the work has already been evaluated under a later policy version than this job carries

edges.label: A current restriction is no longer justified
edges.when: the change removes the basis for something currently restricted

edges.label: A new restriction now applies
edges.when: the change creates a basis for restricting something currently permitted

edges.label: Nothing changes for existing work
edges.when: the change reaches this work and requires nothing different of it
a restriction the change no longer justifies
work the change now requires restricting
a change with undefined effective-time semantics

distinctFrom.because: RSK-191 evaluates one action at its decision point. This propagates a change across work already in flight, where the hard question is not what the rule says but which states the new rule is entitled to reach.

guardrails: A new policy does not mean a historical action was always invalid.
A cleared risk does not automatically restore an unrelated expired entitlement.
A policy update does not indiscriminately restart every existing journey.
A stale policy-evaluation job never overwrites a decision made under a newer version.
governance.reusableRule: Policy and risk changes should alter only the current or future states to which the new authority applies while preserving the historical context under which prior actions occurred.
governance.entityScope: the policy or risk state change and the work it actually touches
governance.entityNote: Completed actions are outside its reach by construction. What it re-evaluates is pending and future work, item by item.

identity.title: Availability query → evaluate capacity → offer valid options
identity.purpose: Produce the options that are genuinely bookable right now, and say plainly that nothing is being held.

requires: a request for bookable times against an identified resource, service or context

nodes.headline: Availability requested
Does an authoritative capacity model exist for this resource and service?

Record that this resource has no authoritative capacity model, and return no options rather than every option. An absent constraint is not an absence of constraint - a resource with nothing configured will otherwise appear infinitely bookable, and the overbooking is discovered by whoever turns up

Evaluate the authoritative constraints together - the resource's capacity, the service's duration, the location and context, eligibility constraints, existing reservations and holds, the operating window, lead-time rules and any defined buffers. Operating hours are not availability: a clinic open until six with every slot taken has nothing at five

Return only the options currently valid for the requested resource and context, labelled as what they are - what appeared bookable at this instant. Nothing here is held, and under contention any of it can be gone before the requester acts
Did any valid option survive the evaluation?
Record NO_AVAILABILITY for the requested window, with the constraint that closed it where that can be said without exposing anything it should not
What does policy offer when the requested window is empty?

Offer the nearest valid window, labelled as a different window rather than presented as the one that was asked for. Someone who wanted Tuesday and is shown Friday should be able to see that at a glance
Record the requester as waitlisted, which reserves nothing. Waitlisted is not reserved, and someone who believes they hold a place they do not hold will plan their day around it
valid options offered; no capacity is held by this query
nodes.detail: any option shown can be taken by someone else before it is requested. The reservation revalidates against current capacity rather than against what was displayed

nodes.headline: waitlisted; nothing is reserved and no time is committed
nodes.detail: capacity being released offers the waitlisted requester a chance to book, which is a new request that has to be confirmed like any other

nodes.headline: NO_AVAILABILITY for the requested resource and window
nodes.detail: availability changes constantly as holds expire and reservations cancel. A later query is answered on its own terms rather than from this result

edges.label: It exists
edges.when: capacity, duration, operating window and any lead-time or buffer rules are defined

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: no authoritative capacity model covers this resource

edges.label: Options exist
edges.when: at least one slot satisfies every constraint

edges.label: None
edges.when: no slot in the requested window satisfies the constraints

edges.label: A different window
edges.when: policy allows offering the nearest valid alternative

edges.label: A waitlist
edges.when: the resource operates a waitlist for released capacity

edges.label: Nothing further
edges.when: policy offers neither

distinctFrom.because: FUL-142 asks whether an accepted obligation can be resourced at all. This asks which specific times a resource can be committed to, for a requester who has not committed to anything yet.

guardrails: A displayed schedule is not guaranteed availability until a reservation or hold succeeds.
Availability is never inferred from generic operating hours.
Availability is evaluated for the requested resource and context rather than for the service in general.
governance.reusableRule: Availability represents capacity that appears bookable at query time; commitment begins only after that capacity is successfully reserved.
governance.entityScope: the availability request and the schedulable resource or service it asks about
governance.entityNote: The request is a question, not a claim on anything. Nothing it returns is protected between being shown and being requested.

identity.title: Renewal execution → financial and dependency check → new term active
identity.purpose: Make the new term exist, once the things it depends on have actually happened.

requires: a renewal decided or scheduled, with the new term's dates and terms
insufficientAlone: a renewal being eligible, which permits the decision rather than being it

nodes.headline: Renewal authorized for execution

Determine what the new term actually requires - payment, contract confirmation, updated eligibility, required verification, resource availability. Which of these apply comes from the relationship's own terms, and assuming payment is the only one renews contracts whose eligibility has lapsed
Does the new term require a financial event?

Raise the renewal's financial obligation through the financial lifecycle, which owns whether it is created, due and satisfied, once per renewal_cycle_id: a redelivered renewal_authorized_for_execution event for the same renewal_cycle_id resolves to the obligation already raised rather than raising a second one. This journey keeps ownership of the new term and waits for that outcome rather than handing the term away - otherwise a failed payment leaves a renewal nobody is holding
until every renewal dependency resolves successfully, or a renewal dependency fails authoritatively
nodes.detail: timeout after the last point at which the new term could still start on time

nodes.headline: How did the dependencies resolve?
Do the governing terms carried from the decision still match what currently governs this relationship?

Re-derive the new term's actual dates, pricing and scope from the relationship's current governing terms rather than the snapshot carried at SUB-163's own decision - the decision to renew is not re-litigated here, only what it renews on. This is the same current-state-over-stale-snapshot discipline CTL-233/CTL-232 and FIN-135 already apply at their own execution points
What is blocking the new term?
Renewal payment failure → grace or recover → renew or lapse
nodes.detail: a renewal blocked by an authoritative payment failure

nodes.headline: Record RENEWAL_PENDING with exactly which dependency is missing. Pending with a named cause can be acted on; pending with no cause becomes a relationship that quietly stops renewing
until the blocking dependency clears
nodes.detail: timeout after the recovery window the governing terms allow

nodes.headline: Create the new term as a new term, with its own dates, price and scope, and leave the previous term intact, once per renewal_cycle_id - if a new term already exists for this renewal_cycle_id (reached again after a redelivered dependency-resolution event), return that existing term rather than creating a second one. Overwriting the old term's dates with the new ones erases that the relationship ran at a different price for a different period, which is the exact record anyone auditing a renewal is looking for
Record the new term ACTIVE from its start date. The relationship now has two terms in its history and one of them is running
Does the new term change the entitlement scope?
Entitlement change → recalculate scope → expand, reduce or preserve
nodes.detail: a new term whose scope differs from the previous one

nodes.headline: NEW_TERM_ACTIVE; the previous term is preserved in full
nodes.detail: the next renewal window opens against this term and is a new cycle with its own decision and its own record

nodes.headline: Record the renewal as failed, with what prevented it. The relationship reaches its term end without a new term, which is a non-renewal reached by failure rather than by decision - and the two are worth distinguishing when someone asks why a customer left
Relationship end → final reconciliation → former or expired state
nodes.detail: a term ending with no new term created

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the renewal carries a charge, a commitment or a financial obligation

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the new term carries no financial requirement, or one already satisfied

edges.label: on event
edges.when: every renewal dependency resolves successfully, a renewal dependency fails authoritatively

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a renewal that has not completed by its own start date has left the relationship between terms, which is a state that has to be named rather than waited through

edges.label: All satisfied
edges.when: every authoritative requirement for the new term is met

edges.label: Something failed
edges.when: a dependency failed authoritatively

edges.label: Unchanged
edges.when: the dates, pricing and terms carried at a.decided's handoff still match the relationship's current governing terms - the ordinary case, since w.dependencies' own window is bounded

edges.label: Materially changed
edges.when: a policy or pricing change landed on the relationship between SUB-163's decision and this point - the decision to renew still stands, but what it renews on does not

edges.label: The renewal payment failed
edges.when: the financial requirement failed authoritatively

edges.label: Recoverable, and not financial
edges.when: a non-financial dependency is missing and could still be supplied

edges.label: Cannot complete
edges.when: the new term cannot be created under any available resolution
a renewal blocked by an authoritative payment failure

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the blocking dependency clears

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the terms define how long a relationship may sit between terms, and exceeding it is a non-renewal whether or not anyone says so

edges.label: It changes
edges.when: the renewing terms grant more, less or different rights than the previous term

edges.label: Unchanged
edges.when: the new term grants exactly what the previous one did
a new term whose scope differs from the previous one
a term ending with no new term created

distinctFrom.because: SUB-163 decides. This executes, and it is where renewals actually fail - on payment, on eligibility that moved, on a resource that is no longer available. A decision is not a term.

guardrails: A renewal scheduled is not a renewal completed.
A payment attempt is not renewal completion.
The previous term is never overwritten with the new term's dates.
A redelivered authorization for the same renewal_cycle_id raises at most one financial obligation and creates at most one new term - never a duplicate of either.

The new term is never created from a stale terms snapshot once w.dependencies' own bounded window has elapsed - c.terms-current re-checks against the relationship's current governing terms immediately before a.new-term, and a.reconcile-terms re-derives dates, pricing and scope from that current state rather than what SUB-163 carried at decision time. The decision to renew itself is never re-litigated here, only what it renews on.
governance.reusableRule: A renewal becomes effective only after the requirements for the new term have actually been satisfied.
governance.entityScope: the renewal operation and the new term it would create
governance.entityNote: The new term is created as a new term. The previous one keeps its dates, its price and its scope, because that is what any later question about the relationship is asked against. renewal_cycle_id identifies this specific renewal cycle - the same relationship renews many times over its life, and each cycle is its own instance; a redelivered renewal_authorized_for_execution event for the same renewal_cycle_id must resolve to the same financial obligation and the same new term, never a second one, while a genuinely later renewal cycle for the same relationship is its own renewal_cycle_id and its own legitimate instance.

identity.title: Expiry reached → validate current state → expire, extend or replace
identity.purpose: Check what the entity actually is at the moment the expiry fires, before applying anything the timer was written to apply.

requires: an authoritative expiry moment arriving for a time-bound entity

nodes.headline: Expiry time reached
Re-read the entity's current authoritative version at this moment. The timer holds the expiry that was true when it was written, which is not necessarily the expiry that is true now
What does the entity's current version say?
stale expiry suppressed; the entity had already moved
nodes.detail: the entity's current expiry, whatever it now is, has its own execution

nodes.headline: Adopt the new authoritative expiry and invalidate this one. An older timer never overrides a later extension - the extension was a decision and the timer is only a memory of an earlier one
expiry superseded by an extension
nodes.detail: the new expiry executes on its own terms when it arrives

nodes.headline: Transition the entity to EXPIRED, keeping the record of the period during which it was valid. Expired is a new state on the same entity, not the erasure of the old one. The transition is applied idempotently, so a redelivered job cannot expire it twice

Apply the consequences defined for this entity type - access ending, a reservation released, a benefit becoming unavailable, a credential invalid, renewal no longer possible, requalification required. The consequence belongs to the entity rather than to expiry in general, and expiring is not the same as revoking
Expired state → re-entry eligibility → renew, requalify or remain expired
nodes.detail: an entity having expired

edges.label: Already renewed or replaced
edges.when: the entity moved on and this expiry no longer describes it

edges.label: A later extension exists
edges.when: an authoritative extension moved the expiry past this moment

edges.label: Still valid, expiry applies
edges.when: the current version still carries this expiry
an entity having expired

guardrails: An old scheduled expiry never overrides a later extension.
The expired state preserves the previous validity history rather than replacing it.
Expiry consequences are entity-specific. Expired is not revoked, and neither is a synonym for the other.
The transition is idempotent; a redelivered job applies it once or not at all.
governance.reusableRule: Expiry must be evaluated against the entity's current authoritative version at the moment the transition executes.
governance.entityScope: the time-bound entity and the specific version of it the timer was scheduled against
governance.entityNote: The version binding is the point. A timer scheduled against one version firing against another is the defining failure of scheduled work.

identity.title: Temporary exception → validity window → revert or formalise
identity.purpose: Stop an exception granted for a reason from becoming a permanent state nobody remembers deciding on.

requires: an exception granted by someone with authority to grant it, against a standing policy or state
insufficientAlone: a setting that differs from policy with no recorded authority behind it, which is configuration drift rather than an exception

nodes.headline: Temporary exception granted
Record the exception type, who authorised it, the reason, its scope, when it starts, and when it expires or is reviewed. An exception with no end date is a policy change that nobody approved as one
until the condition that justified the exception is resolved, or a permanent decision is made about it
nodes.detail: timeout after the exception's recorded expiry or review date

nodes.headline: What resolved it?
Approval request → review → approve, reject or request changes
nodes.detail: an exception that should become the rule

nodes.headline: At the review point, does an authoritative extension exist?

Adopt the extension as its own record, appended to the extension history, and close this instance. Each extension is counted separately rather than absorbed into one long-running exception - the count is what makes a temporary state that has run for two years visible as one
exception extended; a new window opens as its own instance
nodes.detail: the extension is a new instance with a new review date, so the number of extensions is countable rather than hidden inside a single record

nodes.headline: Revert to the standard state and mark the exception as no longer usable, so a stale process cannot keep relying on an exception that has ended
exception ended; standard state restored
nodes.detail: a new exception is granted on its own authority and its own reason

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the condition that justified the exception is resolved, a permanent decision is made about it

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the review is the mechanism - an exception that is never revisited is the one that becomes permanent by default

edges.label: No longer required
edges.when: the condition that justified the exception has gone

edges.label: Should become permanent
edges.when: the exception turned out to describe how things should work
an exception that should become the rule

edges.label: Extended
edges.when: someone with authority extended it, on the record

edges.label: Not extended
edges.when: no extension exists

distinctFrom.because: An exception departs from a standing policy and carries an authority who granted it. A temporary state is a lifecycle position; it does not necessarily contradict anything.

guardrails: A temporary exception is not indefinite permission. Its end is recorded when it is granted.
Extension history is preserved and countable. An exception extended repeatedly is visible as one.
An expired exception cannot be relied on by a stale process.
Making an exception permanent goes through approval, not through another extension.
governance.reusableRule: Temporary exceptions require explicit scope and exit conditions so that exceptional access or policy does not silently become permanent.
governance.entityScope: the exception itself - its scope, the authority that granted it and the state it departs from
governance.entityNote: Each grant and each extension is its own record. An exception extended four times is a different fact from one granted once, and only separate records make that countable.

identity.title: Temporary state → explicit expiry → restore or transition
identity.purpose: Give any time-bound state a defined ending, and revalidate before returning anything to what it was.

requires: an entity entering a state that is intended to end

nodes.headline: Temporary state entered
Does the temporary state carry an explicit expiry or an explicit exit condition?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a temporary state created with no ending

nodes.headline: Record the temporary state, when it took effect, when it expires or what ends it, and the state it would return to
until the exit condition is satisfied
nodes.detail: timeout after the recorded expiry

nodes.headline: Record that the state ended by its exit condition rather than by expiry. A temporary access revoked early and one that lapsed are different facts about the same entity
Record that the state ended by reaching its expiry with the exit condition unmet

Re-read the entity's current version before returning it anywhere. The state it was going to return to may no longer exist, the entity may no longer be eligible for it, and the authority that granted the original may have ended during the temporary period
Is the previous state still valid to return to?
Restore the previous state and clear the temporary one
temporary state ended; previous state restored
nodes.detail: a further temporary state carries its own ending

nodes.headline: Dynamic eligibility → eligible or ineligible → consequence
nodes.detail: a temporary state ending with no valid state to return to

edges.label: Bounded
edges.when: an expiry time or a condition that ends it is defined

edges.label: Unbounded
edges.when: nothing says how or when it ends
a temporary state created with no ending

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the exit condition is satisfied

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: expiry is the backstop for a condition that may never be met; without it the state has no ending at all

edges.label: Still valid
edges.when: the previous state exists and the entity is still eligible for it

edges.label: No longer valid
edges.when: the previous state is gone, or eligibility for it has changed
a temporary state ending with no valid state to return to

guardrails: A temporary state without an expiry or an exit condition is raised rather than created. That is the state this journey exists to prevent.
The previous state is not assumed safe to restore. Eligibility and authority can both change during the temporary period.
How the state ended - early or by expiry - is recorded, because the two mean different things about the entity.
governance.reusableRule: Temporary states must define how they end; time-bound state without an exit rule is an unmanaged permanent state.
governance.entityScope: the entity plus the temporary state placed on it
governance.entityNote: Temporary access, a temporary restriction, a temporary role, a temporary allocation or configuration all share this shape, and each carries its own exit rule.

identity.title: Reversible state → reversal window → confirm or restore
identity.purpose: Undo a transition within its window while restoring only what is independently still valid.

requires: a transition that policy defines as reversible, with a reversal window
insufficientAlone: a change someone regrets, where no reversal policy exists

nodes.headline: Reversible transition occurred

Record the previous state, the new state, whether reversal is eligible, its deadline, and which side effects have already executed. That last list is the one that matters - a reversal decided without it either restores too little or promises too much
until a reversal is requested
nodes.detail: timeout after the reversal deadline

nodes.headline: reversal window closed; the new state is now the normal state
nodes.detail: changing it now is a new transition with its own reversal window, not an undo of this one

nodes.headline: Have irreversible side effects already occurred?
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a reversal request against a transition with irreversible effects

nodes.headline: Restore the previous state, and only the previous state. Consent that was withdrawn, credentials that were revoked, tokens that expired, integrations that were cancelled and journeys that were queued and are now obsolete are each judged on their own current validity. Reversing a transition does not rewind the world around it, and restoring an entity wholesale resurrects things that ended for reasons this reversal never addressed
Recalculate the dependent state against what is actually valid now, rather than replaying what was valid before the transition
Could every dependent state be restored?
transition reversed; previous state fully restored
nodes.detail: a further transition on this entity carries its own window

nodes.headline: partially restored; some dependent state did not validly return
nodes.detail: recorded as partial rather than presented as though nothing had happened - what did not come back is nameable, which is the only way anyone can ask for it

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a reversal is requested

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: the window closing is the ordinary outcome, and after it the new state is simply the state

edges.label: Something cannot be undone
edges.when: money moved, a message went out, an external system was told, a physical action happened

edges.label: Nothing irreversible
edges.when: everything the transition did can be safely unwound
a reversal request against a transition with irreversible effects

edges.label: Fully restored
edges.when: the previous state and everything depending on it are valid again

edges.label: Partially restored
edges.when: the primary state is back and some dependent state could not validly return

guardrails: Restoring an entity does not automatically restore withdrawn consent, revoked credentials, expired tokens, cancelled integrations or obsolete queued journeys. Each is evaluated on its own current validity.
Where irreversible side effects have run, the route is forward correction or compensation rather than restoration.
A partial restoration is recorded as partial.
governance.reusableRule: State reversal restores only what remains valid and reversible; it does not rewind every side effect created by the original transition.
governance.entityScope: the transition itself - what changed, when, and which of its side effects have already run
governance.entityNote: The side-effect list is what makes a later reversal decidable. Without it, reversing is a guess about what the original transition set in motion.

identity.title: Expired state → re-entry eligibility → renew, requalify or remain expired
identity.purpose: Decide how something expired can become valid again, through the mechanism that actually restores validity rather than by editing the expiry away.

requires: an action attempted against an expired entity, or an opportunity to restore it arising

nodes.headline: Re entry attempted or available

Establish what expiry actually did to this entity. Some expiries suspend, some invalidate, some end a relationship outright, and the route back differs for each - reading them all as the same lapse is what produces a renewal flow that cannot renew anything
Which mechanism restores validity here?
external:renewal-lifecycle
nodes.detail: an expired entity the governing system can renew in place

nodes.headline: Qualification state change → route, re-route or exit
nodes.detail: validity depending on conditions that have to be demonstrated again

nodes.headline: Create the replacement entity and keep the expired one as a distinct historical record. The two stay separately addressable, because questions asked later are about one or the other and almost never about both
replacement issued; expired entity retained as history
nodes.detail: the replacement carries its own validity and its own expiry

nodes.headline: expired, no route back
nodes.detail: none - what would have to change is the rule or the entity's circumstances, and either produces a new entity rather than reviving this one

edges.label: Direct renewal
edges.when: the governing system supports renewing this entity in place

edges.label: Requalification
