edges.when: validity depends on conditions that must be demonstrated again

edges.label: Replacement
edges.when: the expired entity cannot become valid and a new one has to be issued

edges.label: Prohibited
edges.when: nothing restores validity - the expiry was terminal by design
an expired entity the governing system can renew in place
validity depending on conditions that have to be demonstrated again

guardrails: An expired entity is not made active by editing its expiry timestamp, unless the governing system explicitly supports extension as a mechanism.
The expired entity and its replacement remain distinguishable.
The expired validity period is preserved. The gap during which nothing was valid is itself a fact.
governance.reusableRule: Re-entry after expiry should follow the business mechanism that restores validity rather than silently undoing the expiry.
governance.entityScope: the expired entity, kept distinct from any replacement created for it
governance.entityNote: The expired entity and its replacement are two objects. That a credential was valid until March and that a credential is valid now are different facts, and merging them destroys both.

identity.title: Scheduled future transition → validate at execution → apply, cancel or recalculate
identity.purpose: Treat a scheduled transition as an intention recorded in the past, and check it against the present before applying it.

requires: a state transition scheduled for a future moment against a specific entity

nodes.headline: Future transition scheduled

Persist the target entity, the state and version it is expected to be in, the target state, when it takes effect, and why it was scheduled. Recording the expected version is what makes execution-time validation possible at all - without it there is nothing to compare the present against
until the schedule is cancelled, or the schedule is replaced by a newer one
nodes.detail: timeout after the effective moment

nodes.headline: Invalidate this job. A cancelled or replaced schedule must not still fire - a replacement that leaves the original alive applies both, in whichever order the scheduler happens to run them
schedule cancelled or replaced before its effective moment
nodes.detail: the replacing schedule, if there is one, runs as its own instance

nodes.headline: Re-read the entity's authoritative current state and version. The schedule is an intention recorded in the past, and this is the only moment at which it can be checked against the present
Does the entity still match what the schedule expected?
stale transition suppressed; a newer change already applied
nodes.detail: an old schedule never overwrites a newer decision, whichever of the two the scheduler happens to reach first

nodes.headline: external:rescheduling-decision
nodes.detail: a schedule whose underlying assumptions no longer hold

nodes.headline: Has this transition already been applied?
duplicate execution absorbed
nodes.detail: schedulers retry by design, so absorbing a redelivery is the normal case rather than an error path

nodes.headline: Apply the transition idempotently, keyed so that a redelivery of the same job cannot apply it twice
scheduled transition applied against a validated current state
nodes.detail: a further scheduled change is its own intention with its own validation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the schedule is cancelled, the schedule is replaced by a newer one

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the effective time is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the schedule being withdrawn before it gets there

edges.label: Matches
edges.when: the current version is the one the transition was written against

edges.label: Superseded
edges.when: a newer authoritative change has already moved the entity past this

edges.label: Assumptions changed
edges.when: the entity still exists in a comparable state but the reasoning behind the schedule no longer holds
a schedule whose underlying assumptions no longer hold

edges.label: Already applied
edges.when: a previous delivery of this same job already made the change

edges.label: Not yet applied
edges.when: the transition has not run

distinctFrom.because: An expiry is one specific scheduled transition with entity-specific consequences. This is the general mechanism, and every other scheduled change - a plan change at period end, a future cancellation, a scheduled restriction - runs through it.

guardrails: Every scheduled action validates at execution time rather than trusting the state it was written against.
An old scheduled transition never overwrites a newer authoritative change.
Cancelling or replacing a schedule invalidates the original job rather than leaving both alive.
Duplicate execution applies the transition once. Redelivery is expected, not exceptional.
governance.reusableRule: Future transitions are intentions, not guaranteed outcomes; their validity must be rechecked when execution time arrives.
governance.entityScope: the scheduled transition plus the target entity and the version it expected to find
governance.entityNote: The expected version is the mechanism. Without it, execution has no way to tell whether the world moved underneath the schedule.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
identity.purpose: Consolidate records that represent one entity, after every dependent state has been reconciled under its own authority rule.

requires: an explicit merge authorization following a duplicate assessment, naming the sources, the target, and the authorized identity-consolidation role that authorised it
or an existing merge_operation_id whose TRM-102 conflict has just been resolved, carrying the resolution and clearance to resume - this is the same operation resuming, not a fresh authorization
insufficientAlone: a duplicate detection, which produces a candidate rather than a decision
a high match score
an assessment concluding the records are probably the same, without an authorisation to act on it

nodes.headline: Merge explicitly authorized
Is this a fresh merge authorization, or the same operation resuming after TRM-102 resolved a conflict?

Create the auditable merge operation: source entity IDs, the canonical target, the basis, the authorized identity-consolidation role that authorised it and its own identity, the time, and every conflict decision as it is made. Provenance is what makes the result reviewable - without it the consolidated record cannot say where any part of itself came from

Inventory the dependent state before anything is touched: identity attributes, consent, preferences, contact points, entitlements, purchases, subscriptions, support cases, opportunities, credentials, active journeys, open obligations and relationships. Each of these answers to a different authority, and a merge that reads them as one list applies one rule to all of them
Is this merge reversible?
Does the evidence and the authorizing role meet the higher bar an irreversible merge requires?
not merged; evidence sized for a reversible operation
nodes.detail: stronger evidence, or an architecture that makes the merge reversible, re-opens this. Leaving two records separate is recoverable and this is not

nodes.headline: Does conflicting state exist across the sources?
Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
nodes.detail: conflicting state discovered during merge

nodes.headline: Consolidate each state type under its own authority rule. There is no newest-value-wins applied across the board: a newer contact point may supersede an older one, a newer consent does not supersede an older withdrawal, an entitlement is reconciled rather than either kept or duplicated, and a financial obligation is never added to itself
Repoint dependent relationships and active processes onto the canonical entity, so nothing continues to run against a representation that has been superseded

Invalidate the actions still queued against the superseded representations. A downstream synchronisation running on its own schedule will otherwise restore what was just consolidated, which undoes the merge while reporting success

Verify the merge did what it was for and nothing more: no critical obligation lost, no permission more permissive than any source held, no entitlement duplicated, no duplicate active journey still running, and the source history still traceable
Did verification pass?
merged into the canonical entity, with provenance and source history intact
nodes.detail: a further duplicate candidate involving this entity is assessed on its own evidence, with this merge in the record

edges.label: Fresh authorization
edges.when: no merge_operation_id exists yet for this trigger

edges.label: Resuming after conflict resolution
edges.when: merge_operation_id already exists and TRM-102 has just handed back a resolved (or partially reconciled) conflict, cleared to complete

edges.label: Reversible
edges.when: the architecture can separate the records again if the decision turns out to be wrong

edges.label: Irreversible
edges.when: consolidation cannot be undone once applied

edges.label: Sufficient
edges.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it at the standard an unrecoverable decision demands, and the identity-consolidation role authorizing it was explicitly exercised at that elevated bar rather than re-used from the operation's original, lower-stakes authorization

edges.label: Not sufficient
edges.when: the evidence would justify a reversible merge and not this one, or the authority behind it was never explicitly raised to the elevated bar this decision requires

edges.label: Conflicts present
edges.when: two sources hold incompatible values for state that matters

edges.label: No conflicts
edges.when: every state type reconciles without contradiction
conflicting state discovered during merge

edges.label: Passed
edges.when: every check holds

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: a check found a lost obligation, a widened permission, a duplicated entitlement or a surviving duplicate journey

distinctFrom.because: Account consolidation unifies business structure and leaves the people distinct. This consolidates the representations of one entity, which is a decision about identity and carries a far higher evidence bar.

guardrails: A merge never duplicates a financial obligation.
An opt-out never disappears because another profile was opted in.
Provenance is preserved - the consolidated record can say where each part of it came from.
An irreversible merge requires stronger evidence and authority than a reversible one.

A merge sent to TRM-102 for conflict resolution resumes consolidation on this same merge_operation_id once TRM-102 hands it back resolved - c.origin distinguishes that resumption from a fresh authorization at the same trigger, so a held or partially-reconciled merge does not become a permanent dead end.
governance.reusableRule: Entity merge consolidates representations only after dependent state has been reconciled according to the authority rules of each state type.
governance.entityScope: the source entities, the canonical target, and the merge operation itself as an auditable record
governance.entityNote: The merge operation is its own entity. Its record of conflict decisions and provenance is what makes the consolidated result reviewable, and often what makes it reversible. Authority to authorize a merge is an authorized identity-consolidation role - never inferred from whoever happened to run the duplicate assessment. An irreversible merge (c.evidence's own elevated evidence bar) requires that same authority explicitly exercised at that elevated bar, not merely re-used from the original, lower-stakes authorization that started the operation.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
identity.purpose: Fail safe wherever consolidating would require inventing an authority the system does not have.

requires: state that two sources hold incompatibly: contradictory identity attributes, a permission conflict, different ownership claims, incompatible account states, duplicate active obligations, or a credential or security conflict

nodes.headline: Critical merge conflict detected
Classify the conflict by domain. The domain decides which authority rule applies, and there is no rule that applies across identity, permission, ownership, obligation and credentials at once
Does a deterministic authority rule exist for this domain?

Apply the rule and record the basis. A conflict resolved in order to make the merge succeed is not resolved - it has been decided by the only party with an interest in the answer, which is whoever wanted the merge

Record the affected state as MERGE_CONFLICT. The most permissive consent or access value is never selected by default - defaulting that way resolves every ambiguity in the direction that cannot be undone, and it is the direction a merge is already biased toward
Is this an ambiguous identity conflict?
Can the merge safely continue on the portions that carry no conflict?
Hold the entire merge. Where identity itself is in doubt, consolidating anything assumes the thing the merge was supposed to establish
Consolidate only the portions carrying no conflict and no dependency on conflicted state, leaving the rest explicitly unmerged rather than quietly merged with a chosen value
until an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded, or the merge is aborted
nodes.detail: timeout after the conflict resolution SLA

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA

nodes.headline: How was it settled?
Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
nodes.detail: a merge conflict resolved, with the merge operation cleared to complete

nodes.headline: Abort the merge, unwinding whatever was partially consolidated where that is possible, and recording precisely what could not be unwound. The sources remain separate and the attempt remains in the record
ABORTED; sources remain separate
nodes.detail: a new merge requires new evidence. That an earlier attempt was aborted is part of what the next one is judged against

nodes.headline: PARTIALLY_RECONCILED; conflicted state left separate and marked
nodes.detail: what remains unmerged is named rather than left as a vague inconsistency, so it can be resolved later on its own evidence

edges.label: Rule exists
edges.when: policy states which source wins for this kind of state, and why

edges.label: No rule
edges.when: nothing states how this conflict resolves

edges.label: Identity itself is in doubt
edges.when: the conflict suggests these may not be one entity at all

edges.label: Identity is established
edges.when: the conflict is about state held by an entity we are confident is one

edges.label: Independent portions exist
edges.when: some state can be consolidated without depending on anything in conflict

edges.label: Everything is entangled
edges.when: the conflicted state is load-bearing for the rest

edges.label: on event
edges.when: an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded, the merge is aborted

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a merge held in conflict leaves two records in a half-consolidated state, which is worse than either outcome and worth escalating rather than waiting out
a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA

edges.label: Resolved
edges.when: an authority determined the answer and the merge may complete

edges.label: Aborted
edges.when: the merge should not proceed

edges.label: Partially reconciled, remainder unresolvable
edges.when: the independent portions consolidated and the conflicted state stays separate
a merge conflict resolved, with the merge operation cleared to complete

guardrails: A conflict is never resolved merely to make the merge succeed.
The most permissive consent or access state is never chosen by default.
An ambiguous identity conflict stops the entire merge rather than part of it.
What could not be unwound after an abort is recorded rather than assumed away.

A resolved conflict hands back to TRM-101 (h.resume) rather than ending as a record nothing ever acts on - RESOLVED means the merge may complete, and completing it is TRM-101's own job to resume, not this journey's to claim.
governance.reusableRule: Merge conflicts should fail safe whenever consolidation would require inventing authority that the system does not possess.
governance.entityScope: the merge operation and the specific state in conflict
governance.entityNote: The conflict attaches to particular state, not to the whole merge. Some conflicts stop everything and most do not, and telling them apart is the journey's main work.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Account consolidation → dependency reconciliation → unified relationship
identity.purpose: Unify business structure across accounts while every person involved stays a separate person.

requires: an authorized consolidation naming the accounts and the canonical target
insufficientAlone: two accounts sharing a domain, a billing address or an administrator

nodes.headline: Account consolidation authorized
Determine the canonical account structure - which account survives and what the consolidated shape actually is
Inventory across every account being consolidated: members, roles, contracts, subscriptions, resources, entitlements, billing relationships, open cases, ownership and active obligations
Does any part of this require treating two people as one?
consolidation stopped; it requires an identity merge
nodes.detail: consolidating two people into one identity is a different decision with a far higher evidence bar, assessed and authorised separately. A consolidation that needs it has exceeded what it was authorised to do

nodes.headline: Are the resources transferable to the canonical account?
Transfer the resources according to policy, keeping their history with them
Retain the resource under its original relationship, referenced from the canonical account rather than moved into it. A reference keeps it reachable without pretending it changed hands
Do the accounts carry conflicting obligations?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure

nodes.headline: Recalculate account-level roles, access, entitlements, routing and aggregate states from what the consolidated account actually holds. Permissions are recalculated rather than unioned - a union grants everyone the highest access anyone previously had, which turns a structural tidy-up into privilege escalation
Verify that no entitlement was duplicated, no obligation lost, no access became broader than any source account granted, and no resource left orphaned
Did verification pass?
accounts consolidated; identities untouched
nodes.detail: a further consolidation is assessed against the canonical structure this produced

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a consolidation whose verification failed

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the consolidation only works if two member records are the same person

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: every member remains a distinct identity in the consolidated structure

edges.label: Transferable
edges.when: policy and the resource itself allow it to move

edges.label: Not transferable
edges.when: a contract, a licence or the resource's own nature keeps it where it is

edges.label: Conflicting
edges.when: two accounts hold obligations that cannot both stand in one structure

edges.label: Compatible
edges.when: the obligations coexist in the consolidated structure
obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure

edges.label: Passed
edges.when: every check holds

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: a duplicated entitlement, a lost obligation, widened access or an orphaned resource was found
a consolidation whose verification failed

guardrails: Account consolidation is not person identity merge.
Members of consolidated accounts do not become the same identity.
Account-level permissions are recalculated rather than unioned.
A resource that cannot transfer is referenced rather than moved.
governance.reusableRule: Account consolidation unifies business structure while preserving independent identities and reconciling account-level obligations explicitly.
governance.entityScope: the accounts being consolidated and the canonical structure that results
governance.entityNote: Accounts consolidate; people do not. The members of the consolidated account remain distinct identities with distinct consent and distinct history.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Primary relationship transfer → validate new primary → transfer dependencies
identity.purpose: Move a dependent entity to a new primary, carrying only what the primary relationship actually governs.

requires: an authorized transfer naming the dependent entity, the outgoing primary and the incoming one

nodes.headline: Primary relationship transfer authorized
Is the proposed new primary relationship valid?
transfer rejected; the existing primary relationship stands
nodes.detail: a different incoming primary is validated on its own terms. The dependent is never left between two primaries while the question is open

nodes.headline: Identify what the primary relationship actually governs: rights, notifications, responsibilities, billing, access, ownership and open obligations. Anything the dependent holds on its own basis is deliberately not on this list

Transfer only the dependencies the primary relationship governs, preserving the historical primary relationship and the period it covered. Existing obligations move with their deadlines unchanged rather than disappearing in the handover
Does the dependent hold permission or consent on its own basis?
Preserve it independently. It does not transfer, and the incoming primary's state is not inherited over it - a dependent who opted out does not become opted in because their primary is
Verify the dependent now holds exactly one valid required primary relationship - not zero, and not two
Did verification pass?
primary relationship transferred; independent state preserved
nodes.detail: a further transfer is validated against the current primary

nodes.headline: Required relationship missing → orphan state → resolve or reassign
nodes.detail: a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: the incoming primary can hold this relationship and is entitled to

edges.label: Not valid
edges.when: the incoming primary is ineligible, or the relationship is not permitted between these types

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the dependent gave or withheld something itself, rather than inheriting it

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: everything it held came through the primary relationship

edges.label: Exactly one valid primary
edges.when: the transfer landed cleanly

edges.label: None, or more than one
edges.when: the dependent is left without a required primary, or holding two
a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary

distinctFrom.because: Changing which primary a dependent hangs from moves a relationship. It consolidates nothing and neither party's identity changes.

guardrails: A primary relationship transfer is not an identity merge.
The historical primary relationship and its period are preserved.
Existing obligations do not disappear during a transfer, and their deadlines do not reset.
The dependent's own permission and consent are never overwritten by the incoming primary's.
governance.reusableRule: Changing a primary relationship transfers only the dependencies governed by that relationship, not every state associated with either party.
governance.entityScope: the dependent entity, its outgoing primary and its incoming one
governance.entityNote: The dependent's own permissions and consent are not part of the transfer. They belong to the dependent and stay with it.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Data deletion request → validate scope → hold, delete or retain required data
identity.purpose: Decide what a deletion request actually covers, and keep only what an authoritative retention obligation genuinely requires.

requires: a deletion request naming a data subject and a scope
insufficientAlone: an account closure, which ends a relationship and requests nothing about data
a subscription cancellation
an unsubscribe, which withdraws permission to contact rather than requesting removal

nodes.headline: Data deletion requested
Is the requester's identity and authority established for this scope?
Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process
nodes.detail: a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified

nodes.headline: Validate the scope, the jurisdiction and policy context, and which systems and data classes are actually in scope. A deletion request is bounded by what it asks for and by what the governing policy covers - not by everything we happen to hold about the person
Inventory the data in scope and classify each item as DELETABLE, RETAIN_REQUIRED, DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED, ALREADY_DELETED or MANUAL_REVIEW
Does an authoritative retention obligation cover any of it?

Retain only what an authoritative obligation actually requires, recording which obligation and why. No retention rule is invented - where policy is silent the data is not kept on a guess, because retaining on a guess keeps what should have gone just as surely as deleting on one destroys what had to stay
What remains, and can it be deleted?
until the blocking dependency clears
nodes.detail: timeout after the request's SLA

nodes.headline: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
nodes.detail: data approved for deletion or anonymization

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle

nodes.headline: nothing in scope to delete; retained items recorded with their obligations
nodes.detail: this is recorded as what it is rather than reported as a deletion. Data arriving later within the same scope is assessed against this request where the policy allows

edges.label: Established
edges.when: the requester is verified as the data subject or as authorised to act for them

edges.label: Not established
edges.when: identity or authority has not been verified to the level this request requires
a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified

edges.label: Retention required
edges.when: a legal or business obligation names data that must be kept

edges.label: Nothing retained
edges.when: no obligation covers anything in scope

edges.label: Deletable and clear
edges.when: data remains in scope, is eligible, and no dependency blocks it

edges.label: Blocked by a dependency
edges.when: something in scope cannot be removed until a dependency clears

edges.label: Needs manual review
edges.when: the classification could not be settled automatically

edges.label: Nothing left
edges.when: everything in scope is already absent or retained under an obligation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the blocking dependency clears

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a deletion request usually carries a legal deadline, and a dependency that has not cleared inside it needs a person rather than more waiting
data approved for deletion or anonymization
a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle

distinctFrom.because: Closing an account ends a relationship and requests nothing about data. A deletion request concerns data and says nothing about whether the relationship continues. Either can happen without the other.

guardrails: Account closure is not a deletion request.
A deletion request is not immediate physical deletion of every record.
No retention rule is invented. Where the governing policy is silent, data is not retained on a guess.
Audit evidence may need retaining without retaining the operational data alongside it.
governance.reusableRule: Data deletion removes data according to defined scope while preserving only information that an authoritative retention obligation requires.
governance.entityScope: the data subject, this deletion request, and the data scope it names
governance.entityNote: The request is bounded by what it asks for and by what governing policy covers. It is not a licence to delete everything we hold, nor a reason to keep everything we would rather not lose.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
identity.purpose: Carry a deletion through every system it has to reach, and keep any part that did not arrive visible.

requires: an approved deletion scope, per system and data class, from a validated request

nodes.headline: Data approved for deletion

Generate the scoped operation for each affected system - delete, anonymize, detach, restrict or place under retention hold - according to what the governing requirement for that system actually is. One operation type applied everywhere either destroys what had to be kept or keeps what had to go

Execute idempotently, keyed so a redelivered job does not repeat an operation, and so that nothing propagates back through downstream synchronisation to recreate what was just removed. A sync job running on its own schedule will otherwise restore a profile deleted an hour earlier, undoing the work while reporting success
until all system confirmations arrive, or a system reports failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the deletion SLA

nodes.headline: How did the operations end?
Was a further copy of the data discovered while the request was running?
Generate and execute the operation for the newly discovered copy, within the same job and the same scope

Record the discovered copy as out of scope, naming why. It is not deleted on this request and it is not left unrecorded either - an unrecorded copy is one nobody knows to assess against the next request

Verify that no required target remains unintentionally active or searchable, to whatever guarantee each system actually offers. The deletion audit records what was removed and when, without keeping a copy of the personal data it removed - an audit that preserves the record has recreated the thing the deletion was for
Did verification confirm every required terminal state?
VERIFIED_COMPLETE; every in-scope obligation reached its terminal state
nodes.detail: a later request covering different scope is its own job. Deletion succeeding in the primary store was never the same as deletion everywhere, and this state records that everywhere was checked

nodes.headline: Record PARTIAL_DELETION_FAILURE, naming which systems did not reach their required terminal state. This is never represented as complete - a deletion reported as done while a downstream copy survives is the most consequential false report in this library, because it ends the investigation that would have found the copy
Is a retry available within the policy budget?
Retry the outstanding operations only, idempotently, so a partially completed deletion is completed rather than restarted
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a deletion that could not reach its required terminal state everywhere

edges.label: on event
edges.when: all system confirmations arrive, a system reports failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: silence from a system is not confirmation, and a deletion whose SLA passes with systems unheard from is a partial failure that has not reported itself

edges.label: All confirmed
edges.when: every required system reported its operation complete

edges.label: Some failed
edges.when: at least one system reported failure or did not confirm

edges.label: In scope
edges.when: a copy was found that the approved scope covers

edges.label: Out of scope
edges.when: a copy was found that the approved scope does not cover

edges.label: Nothing further
edges.when: no new copy surfaced

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: every in-scope target reached its required state

edges.label: Something remains
edges.when: a target is still present where it should not be

edges.label: Retry
edges.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first failure has room

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: the failure is not clearing, or the budget is spent

guardrails: Deletion succeeding in the primary store is not deletion everywhere.
A failed downstream deletion is never represented as fully complete.
Deletion jobs do not recreate profiles through downstream synchronisation.
The deletion audit does not itself preserve the personal data that was deleted.
governance.reusableRule: Distributed deletion is complete only when all in-scope deletion obligations have reached their required terminal state or an explicit retained exception is recorded.
governance.entityScope: the deletion job and each affected system's operation individually
governance.entityNote: Each system's operation has its own type and its own terminal state. A single overall status hides the one that failed, which is the only one that matters.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: From Entitlement Grant to Working Access: Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A journey that holds the gap between granting a right and the thing behind it working, with provisioning steps, waits and an availability check.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: How Entitlement Scope Changes Expand or Reduce Rights
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Model how a scope change applies only the difference between old and new rights, instead of re-applying a whole scope over one that already works.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Entitlement Loss: Revoke Access, Reconcile Commitments
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Examine a journey that stops future use of an ended right while leaving what was validly created intact, and hands off what still depends on it.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Near-identical in subject to ACC-80, which also models ending a capability with dependency and obligation reconciliation.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Authorization Checks at the Moment of Access Attempt
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A decision journey run at the moment of the attempt, weighing whether one actor may take one action on one resource, and where a step-up leads next.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Credential Lifecycle Journey from Issue to Revocation
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Follow an access artifact through its own validity lifecycle, from issue and activation to use, expiry or revocation, apart from the right it stands for.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Credential Revocation and Replacement Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How a compromised credential is taken out of use immediately, while any replacement is issued only through its own separately authorised path.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Deprovisioning Journey: Dependency Check Before Removal
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Model removing a capability that is no longer authorised only after confirming nothing still depends on it, with retain, escalate and handoff branches.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Near-identical in subject to ACC-74, which also models removing capability after an entitlement ends.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Establishing Entity Ownership With an Explicit Act
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How an accountable owner is established by an explicit act rather than inferred. The flow validates the requesting authority, then assigns or rejects it.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Ownership Transfer Request and Validation Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Proposing a future controller without disturbing the one an entity currently has. See how the request is validated, left pending acceptance, or rejected.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Ownership Transfer Acceptance and Revalidation Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: An acceptance made today must still match the transfer proposed. See how the request version is revalidated and then executed or allowed to expire.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Ownership Cutover Without an Uncontrolled Entity
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Moving control between two parties while the entity is never left uncontrolled. Follow the new owner assignment and the reconciliation of the old one.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Granting Scoped Authority on an Owner's Behalf
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Letting somebody act on an owner's behalf inside a boundary, without moving anything. Review how the scope is defined and the grant issued or refused.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Temporary Delegation Expiry and Renewal Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Borrowed authority has to end at its boundary. This flow checks the boundary still belongs to a delegation that exists, then revokes, extends or restores.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Delegation Revocation and Retained Access Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Taking back exactly what was lent and nothing else. The journey removes capabilities that exist because of the delegation, preserving independent access.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Protecting an Entity When Its Owner Is Unavailable
seoMetadata.seoDescription: What holds an entity safely when its owner cannot act? This flow protects the ownership state and works towards recovery rather than the nearest party.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Data Intake, Format Detection and Parsing Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How a submitted dataset is identified, parsed and brought into a stable readable form, or rejected, before anything real is touched. Follow each branch.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Schema and Semantic Data Validation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Checks parsed data against the target's schema and business rules, record by record, then accepts, rejects or quarantines it. Examine every branch here.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Impact Preview and Approval Before a Data Change
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Before a mutation runs, what would it actually do? This flow builds the impact preview so approval attaches to real effects, then confirms or holds it.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Idempotent Import Execution and Record Outcomes
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Applies a frozen, validated change set to production state and keeps every record's outcome. See how complete, partial and failed results are separated.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Partial Import Recovery and Resume Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Only the records that did not land should be touched again. Follow how the failed scope is isolated, corrected and resumed without disturbing the rest.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Migration Readiness and Source-to-Target Mapping
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Proving the target can carry the source's meaning before anything moves. Review the source-to-target mapping and the readiness checks that gate the plan.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Migration Execution and Population Verification
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Moves the population into the target, then proves the result still means what the source meant. Examine the copy, transform and verification steps.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: System Cutover, Observation and Rollback Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Switching which system is authoritative happens once, with a way back defined up front. Follow the observation window and the stabilise or roll back call.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Historical Backfill Without Replaying Stale Actions
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Repairing a gap in the record without re-enacting what those events would have caused. See how the backfill window is scoped and then applied safely.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Data Transformation Error Recovery Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Undoing a wrong data change without undoing the right things that came after. Review the reconciliation and the correct, roll forward or roll back paths.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Decision Request Intake and Routing Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Establishes that authorised judgment is genuinely required and opens a case with a stated scope. Follow the validation and the route, reject or hold exits.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Assigning a Decision Case to an Authorised Reviewer
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Putting a case in front of someone actually authorised to decide it. This flow makes reviewer ownership explicit and covers reassignment and escalation.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Evaluating Evidence to Reach an Authorised Decision
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How sufficient evidence turns into an authorised decision inside the scope the reviewer holds, and when the case goes back for more information instead.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Approved Decision Execution and Revalidation Path
seoMetadata.seoDescription: An authorisation still has to apply to what it was granted against. This flow revalidates the target at execution, then executes, holds or invalidates.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Close neighbour of DEC-188, which also revalidates an approval before use; DEC-185 revalidates the target at execution while DEC-188 tests the approval's own validity boundaries.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Recording a Rejection and the Requester's Options
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Treats a refusal as the business outcome it is. The reason is recorded and the requester is pointed to remediation, to closure or to a route to reapply.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Splitting Scope After a Partial Approval Decision
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Separates the authorised and unauthorised halves of one request so only the approved part can move, and shows how the remaining scope is then resolved.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Approval Validity, Expiry and Revalidation Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: At the moment of use, is the approval still one? This flow revalidates it in time, context and count, then permits use, expires it or reopens the review.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Close neighbour of DEC-185, the approval execution journey; both gate an approval at the point of use, this one on the approval's own validity boundaries.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Decision Escalation to Higher Authority Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Shows how a stalled case moves to an authority that can actually resolve it, carrying the work already done forward without predetermining the outcome.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Reopening a Superseded Decision Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Models how a challenged or superseded decision is revalidated and then continued or replaced, with every part of the original record left as it was.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Near-identical subject to FBK-47 (appeal and dispute review): both model revisiting a decision that has already been made.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Create, Reuse or Waive a Document Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Walks through deciding whether a process needs a new artifact or whether one already exists that answers the requirement, and where each path ends.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Drafting and Validation Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Models how a draft is populated from authoritative sources and checked for completeness, so it reaches a ready or blocked state before anything is issued.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Issuance and Version Freeze Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Shows how an authorized document becomes an issued version that can be identified and referenced later, and that cannot be quietly changed after the fact.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: When a Signed Document Becomes Effective Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Models the gap between signing and taking effect, showing how completion is validated and when a document is effective or held by a pending condition.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Amendment and Versioning Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Shows how an issued artifact is changed by creating a successor that supersedes it going forward, leaving the version it replaces exactly as it was.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Expiry and Renewal Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Covers what happens when a time-limited document reaches expiry, revalidating the requirement and choosing renew, replace or close for dependent work.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Revocation and Withdrawal Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Models withdrawing an artifact on an authority's decision, ending future reliance as far as that decision reaches and reconciling what depended on it.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Payment Attempt and Outcome Routing Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Separates initiating a payment from knowing what happened to it, routing each attempt to success, failure or an explicit unknown-outcome state.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Authorization, Capture and Settlement Journey Flow
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Models the commitment of funds as three states, where reserving, taking and receiving money each hold their own state through to settlement or release.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Unknown Payment Outcome Reconciliation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Establishes what really happened to a payment whose outcome was lost, confirming success or failure before the customer is charged for that attempt again.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Overlaps with FIN-140 (financial reconciliation) on reconciliation search intent; the scopes differ (one payment attempt vs disagreeing record sets) and need separate positioning.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Refund Execution and Confirmation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Moves an approved refund and confirms that it arrived, held deliberately apart from the earlier decision that the refund should be issued at all.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Financial Dispute and Chargeback Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Runs a transaction-level dispute through the authority that decides it, gathering evidence and reconciling it without treating the claim as a finding.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Financial Reconciliation and Mismatch Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Detects a material mismatch across financial records, then explains and corrects the difference or escalates it, never by editing the awkward record.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Overlaps with FIN-135 (unknown payment reconciliation) on reconciliation search intent; the scopes differ (disagreeing record sets vs one payment attempt) and need separate positioning.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Verification Dependency and Process Unblock Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A verification requirement held as its own state, blocking only the process that needs it and releasing that process only once everything is rechecked.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Document Submission and Validation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Uploading a document and satisfying a requirement stay separate facts. Follow validation to accept, reject or replace, bound to the requirement assessed.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Step-Up Authentication Journey Map for Sensitive Actions
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Raising identity assurance before a sensitive action runs, then confirming the action is still authorised. Follow the resume and deny branches in full.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Subject overlaps materially with IDN-85 (authentication challenge); both cover authenticating an actor with a step-up or deny outcome and may compete on the same query.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Incident Correlation and Confirmation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Deciding whether several failures really share one cause before they are treated as a single incident. Follow the candidate to confirmation or rejection.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Incident Severity and Blast Radius Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Once an incident is confirmed, this flow establishes what is affected, how badly it is affected, and who owns and runs the operational response.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Incident Containment and Mitigation Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Reducing damage now without pretending the cause is dealt with. See how containment, mitigation and the protection of critical operations are held apart.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Root Cause Investigation and Corrective Action Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Testing hypotheses until one actually explains the incident rather than the one nearest to it. Follow confirm, reject and corrective action branches.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Incident Recovery and Verification Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Acting on the cause, then checking the affected population instead of a command's return code. Examine the restore, verify and continue paths in the flow.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Recovery Observation Window Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Holding an incident open long enough to know the recovery actually held. This flow models the observation window and the split between stable and relapse.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Incident Resolution and Residual Case Handling Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Closing a shared failure without closing the individual problems it caused. See how linked cases and obligations survive the end of the response.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Post-Incident Review and Corrective Work Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Turning what an incident revealed into corrective work that somebody owns and somebody verifies. Follow the review, assignment and verification sequence.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Recurring Incident Pattern and Prevention Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Noticing when the same weakness keeps producing incidents instead of treating each one as new, then escalating prevention for the whole related family.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Integration Connection and Activation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: An integration becomes active only once it has proven it can do the thing it exists for, not once a credential is saved. Authenticate, validate, activate.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Integration Authorization Change Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Rechecking what an integration can still do whenever its authorization changes, rather than assuming valid credentials mean access stayed the same.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Integration Health Degradation Diagnosis Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Scoping a deteriorating integration to what is actually failing, with recovery established by evidence rather than by a metric returning to normal.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Pending External Operation Outcome Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Submitting an external operation and completing one stay separate states here, and an unknown outcome is allowed to remain unknown. Confirm, fail, unknown.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: External Outcome Reconciliation Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Applying an external outcome to local state only after checking that it belongs here, has not already been applied, and still describes what is true.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Integration Failure Containment and Restore Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Halting work into an integration that cannot function, while keeping enough state to recover without repeating anything the provider may already have done.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Blocked Work Queue and Controlled Resume Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Keeping work that a failed integration blocked, but only where it can later be revalidated and safely resumed. Follow the hold, recover and resume path.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Integration Reconnect and Backfill Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Closing the gap an outage left in what is known, without recreating everything that would have happened had the events arrived on time. Backfill, dedupe.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Synchronization Conflict and Authority Rule Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Settling a cross-system disagreement with an explicit authority rule, and holding the record rather than guessing where no such rule exists for the fields.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: External Dependency Outage and Degradation Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Losing only the capability that genuinely depends on an unavailable provider, while every uncertain outcome is left uncertain. Alternate route or recover.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Subject overlaps materially with INT-113 (integration health degradation) and INT-116 (integration failure); all three model losing and recovering an integration capability.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: New Work Routing to Responsibility Scope Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Routes a new case, lead, task or request into the smallest genuinely valid responsibility scope, and stops where policy is silent. See the routing rules.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Assignment to Accepted Responsibility Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Proposed responsibility and accepted responsibility stay separate states, so work nobody has taken stays visible. Follow the acceptance wait and reminders.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Owner Assignment and Context Transfer Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A new owner receives what they need to continue an existing obligation, not just a record carrying their name. Trace the handover before work starts.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Subject overlaps closely with OWN-54: both cover handing an active entity to a new owner. This page is the context handover after an assignment becomes effective; OWN-54 is the authoritative ownership change and obligation transfer.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Ownership Change and Obligation Transfer Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Responsibility for an active entity moves while open obligations, running clocks and the record of earlier work stay intact. Review each transfer check.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Subject overlaps closely with OWN-53: both cover handing an active entity to a new owner. This page is the authoritative ownership change and obligation transfer; OWN-53 is the context handover after an assignment becomes effective.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Responsibility Escalation to Higher Authority Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Raises a blocker to the level that can clear it, without the original owner putting the work down by escalating. Follow the conditions and return path.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Approval Request, Review and Decision Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Binds an approval to the exact version reviewed and keeps approving separate from doing. Examine the approve, reject and request-changes branches.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Multi-Party Approval Decision Aggregation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Combines several independent approval decisions strictly under the governing policy, and refuses to proceed where none defines how. See each decision held.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Material Change After Approval Impact Check Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: When an approved subject changes before execution, this flow tests whether the approval still covers it and reopens only the decisions that no longer hold.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Rejected Approval and Resubmission Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Rejection is neither a dead end nor an open retry loop. Follow the revision eligibility check, the resubmit route and the block on a rejected version.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Decision Authority Change and Revalidation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Pending decisions are revalidated against who is authorized now, without unapproving history or moving items blindly. See the transfer and continue routes.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Parent State Change Propagation to Child Records Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A parent's state change reaches only the children that genuinely depend on it. Each child is checked against a written dependency rule first.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Parent State Aggregation From Child States Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Recomputes a parent's state from the full set of children the policy reads, rather than following whichever child reported last. See the aggregation logic.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Duplicate Entity Detection and Assessment Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Assesses whether two records represent the same entity and routes the answer to keep separate, link or merge, without consolidating anything here.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Entity Linking With Independent Identity Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Records that two entities are related and lets defined context cross between them while both remain separate entities. Review the self-contained flow.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Entity Split and History Allocation Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Separates what should never have been one record, allocating state and history safely without copying the things that do not divide. See each step.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Authorized Return in Transit Tracking Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Tracks whether an authorized return actually comes back, holding the in-transit, received, lost and expired states. Follow the waits and the handoff.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Returned Item Inspection and Acceptance Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Judges what came back against the conditions it was authorized under, keeping receipt and acceptance apart. See the accept, reject and partial routes.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Replacement Remedy Allocation and Fulfillment Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Delivers a second time against the same promise, tied to the defect it exists to resolve. Walk the allocation, fulfillment and confirmation steps.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Remedy Outcome Verification and Closure Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Checks that a remedy satisfied the obligation rather than that it was carried out. See the verification wait and the close or continue-recovery exits.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Compensation Eligibility, Decision and Delivery Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Decides separately whether impact warrants more than fixing the problem, then confirms it arrived. Follow eligibility, grant or reject, and delivery.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Post-Remedy Issue Recurrence Customer Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A journey for problems reported after a remedy: it separates a true recurrence from a new issue or an unfinished fix, then routes each to its own path.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Change Rollout Eligibility Gate Journey Map Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Before any target is prepared, this journey decides which targets a change may reach at all, evaluating each against it and marking it ready or blocked.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Change Preparation and Dependency Resolution Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How an eligible target is brought into a state where the change can actually be applied, resolving dependencies and holding it when they are unmet.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Scheduled Change Wait and Revalidation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A scheduled change is not always still the right one. The flow waits for the execution window, revalidates against the target, then executes or cancels.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Change Execution and State Verification Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Applying a change to one target and establishing that it ended in the intended state, with verified, failed and unknown outcomes handled separately.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Staged Rollout Cohort and Health Gate Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A staged rollout that widens only when the cohort already carrying the change shows it is safe, with a health gate between each expansion step.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Rollout Pause, Diagnose and Resume Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Freezing an expansion while the decision is open: the flow stops the change spreading, diagnoses it, then resumes, rolls back or ends the rollout.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Rollback or Forward Recovery Decision Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: When a change failure threshold is reached, this router settles whether going back is safer than going forward before any rollback work begins.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Rollback Execution and Stability Verification Flow
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Returning affected targets to a known-good state and proving they actually work there, with the restore steps and the stability check laid out end to end.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Individual Target Change Failure Recovery Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Recovering a single target that could not take the change through retry, isolation or remediation, and noticing when it stops being one isolated target.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Change Completion and Observation Window Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: After the planned population reaches the changed state, the flow observes long enough to know the change held, keeping recovery material until then.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Policy Check Evaluation Journey: Pass, Block or Review
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How a protected action is evaluated against the rules that actually govern it, at the applicable policy version, then routed to pass, block or review.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Risk Signal Evidence Correlation Journey Map Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Turning a risk measurement into a state change no larger than its evidence supports, with clear, monitor, restrict and review paths that expire.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Scoped Risk Restriction and Release Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Restricting the smallest thing that manages the risk while keeping a stated route back, with review and release paths mapped beside the restriction.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Policy Violation Detection and Validation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Establishing that a rule was actually broken, judged against the policy version that governed it, before correction, restriction or escalation.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Compliance Requirement Verification Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: One mandatory requirement held as its own state: the flow collects and verifies what it needs, and blocks only the processes that genuinely depend on it.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Compliance or Policy Hold, Resume or Terminate Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Pausing only what a policy question makes unsafe while everything else keeps running, preserving state until the hold resolves or the work is ended.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Policy Exception Request and Authority Check Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Asking for a controlled deviation from a named rule over a stated scope: the journey validates who may ask, then approves, rejects or sends to review.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Approved Exception Scoped Override Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Letting an authorized deviation apply exactly where it was authorized, invoked action by action, and stopping the moment it expires or is revoked.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Limit or Quota Reached Customer Journey Map Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A limit being reached treated as the limit working: the flow gives the constrained action a real path forward through waiting, an increase or reset.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Policy or Risk State Change Propagation Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Re-evaluating affected work when a policy or risk state changes, applying the new authority only where it reaches and leaving past decisions alone.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Availability Query and Capacity Check Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Answering an availability request with options genuinely bookable right now, while saying plainly that nothing is being held for the person asking.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Subscription Renewal Execution and New Term Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: What has to be true before a new term actually exists: this flow runs the financial and dependency checks that a renewal decision alone cannot settle.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Expiry Execution and Current State Validation Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: At the moment an expiry fires, the entity is rechecked against the version the timer was written for, then expired, extended or replaced accordingly.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Temporary Exception and Validity Window Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Stops an exception granted for a reason from quietly becoming permanent: it runs on a validity window that ends in a revert or in a formalised change.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Temporary State Expiry and Restore Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Gives any time-bound state placed on an entity a defined ending, and revalidates before anything is returned to what it was or moved on to a new state.
seoMetadata.reviewReason: Subject overlaps TIM-66 (temporary-exception): both model a time-bound state ending in revert or transition; TIM-67 is the generic case, TIM-66 the granted-exception case. Confirm the two pages stay distinct.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Reversible Transition and Reversal Window Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: A transition can be undone inside its reversal window, restoring only the side effects that are independently still valid, or confirmed once time runs out.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Post-Expiry Re-Entry and Requalification Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: How something already expired can become valid again through the mechanism that genuinely restores validity, by renewing, requalifying or staying expired.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Scheduled Future Transition Execution Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Treats a scheduled transition as an intention recorded in the past and checks it against the present, then applies, cancels or recalculates it.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Identity and Entity Merge Execution Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Records that represent one entity are consolidated only after every dependent state has been reconciled under its own authority rule, then verified.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Merge Conflict Detection and Resolution Lifecycle Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: What a merge should do when consolidating would mean inventing an authority nobody holds: move to a safe state, resolve the conflict, continue or abort.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Account Consolidation and Dependency Journey Example
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Unifies business structure across several accounts while every person involved stays a separate person, reconciling dependencies into one relationship.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Primary Relationship Transfer and Dependency Journey
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Moves a dependent entity to a new primary after validating it, carrying across only the things the primary relationship actually governs and nothing more.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Data Deletion Request and Retention Scope Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Works out what a deletion request actually covers, then holds, deletes or keeps only the data an authoritative retention obligation genuinely requires.

seoMetadata.seoTitle: Data Deletion Execution and Verification Journey Map
seoMetadata.seoDescription: Carries an approved deletion through every system it must reach, verifying each one and keeping any part that did not arrive visible instead of assumed.
